{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:10:05.810703+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c0e73b9c872f2eb7ccdca92c366c938948c145d73a030154748a3df7fcc56c19","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 21 of arXiv:2608.17509, '2608.17509'] The operators \(W_L(r_a)\) and \(\widetilde{W}_{a,L}\) admit a common
Hilbert--Schmidt factorization: there exists
\(V_{a,L}:L^2(0,L)\to L^2(0,\infty)\) such that
\[
        W_L(r_a)=V_{a,L}^{*}V_{a,L},
        \qquad
        \widetilde{W}_{a,L}=V_{a,L}V_{a,L}^{*}.
\]
Consequently, they are positive trace-class operators with the same nonzero
eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, and for every \(t\in\mathbb C\),
\[
        \det(\operatorname{Id}+t\widetilde{W}_{a,L})
        =
        \det(\operatorname{Id}+tW_L(r_a)).
\]
Moreover, with \(\rho_a:=\sup_{\xi>0}r_a(\xi)\in(0,1)\),
\[
        0\leq W_L(r_a)\leq \rho_a\operatorname{Id},
        \qquad
        0\leq \widetilde{W}_{a,L}\leq \rho_a\operatorname{Id}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.953522+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c0f6569fe40b75e82233252e0aa32767f8b51829c2c878837afe78f36ffb1f4e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 6 (Gaussian-noise bulk and full-trace LSS) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let $f$ satisfy \eqref{eq:Gaussian-f-assumptions-main}, let $\lambda\ge0$ be
fixed, and suppose that the deterministic spike obeys
\begin{equation}
 \norm{x}_2=1,
 \qquad
 \norm{x}_\infty=o(N^{-1/4}),
 \qquad
 \sum_{i=1}^N x_i=O(N^{o(1)}).
\end{equation}
Let $\Gamma$ satisfy (G1)--(G4) with $\theta_{f,\nu}$ replaced by $\theta_f$,
and let $\varphi_1,\ldots,\varphi_k$ be analytic on a neighborhood of
$\overline{D_\Gamma}$ and real-valued on its intersection with $\mathbb R$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \left(
 \mathcal L_{M_{N,\gamma}^f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi_\ell)
 -N\int_{-2}^2\varphi_\ell(t)\rho_{\scal}(t)\,\dd t
 -m_{\varphi_\ell,\Gamma}^{\gamma,f}
 \right)_{\ell=1}^k
 \Longrightarrow
 (G_{\varphi_\ell})_{\ell=1}^k,
\end{equation}
where the limiting vector is centered Gaussian with
\begin{equation}
 \Cov(G_\varphi,G_\psi)
 =\mathcal V_{\kappa_f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi,\psi).
\end{equation}
If $|\theta_f|\le1$, then
$\mathcal L_{M_{N,\gamma}^f}^{\Gamma}(\varphi)
=\Tr\varphi(M_{N,\gamma}^f)$ with probability tending to one, so
\eqref{eq:Gaussian-bulk-CLT-main} is the full-trace CLT.  If
$|\theta_f|>1$ and each $\varphi_\ell$ is also analytic and real-valued on the
real axis near
\begin{equation}
 \rho_f:=\theta_f+\theta_f^{-1},
\end{equation}
then the full-trace CLT is obtained from
\eqref{eq:Gaussian-bulk-CLT-main} by replacing the statistic there with
\begin{equation}
 \left(
 \Tr\varphi_\ell(M_{N,\gamma}^f)
 -N\int_{-2}^2\varphi_\ell(t)\rho_{\scal}(t)\,\dd t
 -m_{\varphi_\ell,\Gamma}^{\gamma,f}
 -\varphi_\ell(\rho_f)
 \right)_{\ell=1}^k
 \Longrightarrow
 (G_{\varphi_\ell})_{\ell=1}^k,
\end{equation}
with the covariance \eqref{eq:Gaussian-covariance-main}.
In particular, all these conclusions hold for every centered and
variance-normalized polynomial-growth transform.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351460+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c0fc8f01bf0470a4e19c40cfcbd48f63ad3e9919d3e37b9d46aff505e0204a9c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 187 (approximate quadratic variation processes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, define $\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ to be the piecewise linear process with increments
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)
	\equiv
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d,B)
	\equiv
	\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a)\Big)
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\tau}(q_d,a)\Big)\,.
	\eeq
For the Ising case, we also define
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}(q_d)
	\equiv \frac{1}{|B||B^{\Ising}|}
	\sum_{a\in B,i\in B^{\Ising}}
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a)\Big)
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i)\Big)
	=
	\Big( \Delta \bar{D}^\sigma(q_d)\Big)
	\Big( \Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)\Big)
	\eeq
for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$; 
as well as
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\Ising}(q_d)
	\equiv
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\Ising}(q_d,B^\Ising)
	\equiv 
	\frac{1}{|B^{\Ising}|}
	\sum_{i\in B^{\Ising}}
	\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i)\Big)^2\,.
	\eeq
Denote also $E^{\sigma,\tau}\equiv Q^{\sigma,\tau}-\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$. We define likewise $\Delta\tilde{Q}^\frozen$ using increments of $X^\frozen$. Then, 
analogously to \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus},
for all $\sigma , \tau \in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have for $B^\frozen \cap [M] = B \neq \emptyset$
	\beq
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\frozen,\sigma,\tau}(q_d,B^\frozen)
	=\frac{|B|}{|B^\frozen|}
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d,B)
	\,.\eeq
A similar relation holds between $\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}$ and $\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\frozen,\sigma,\Ising}$, and likewise between

{"assumptions":["the per-sample relative L2 loss as used by the EMIT/OCO-2 stacking pools; independent errors across rows","the multiplicative-versus-additive question is empirical and is measured by ens_rmt_elast.py (P21 of the RMT program)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T11:47:28.061008+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning / weighted regression","id":"claim_c109e1a78941f0a6a45f877d2453aa489942de8d28e336dd0f0d21122d68470e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fitting a stack (or any linear predictor) under the per-sample relative L2 loss, mean over rows of ||y_i - yhat_i||^2 / ||y_i||^2, is weighted least squares with case weights s_i = 1 / ||y_i||^2. By the two-regimes corollary those are Aitken's variance-stabilising weights exactly when the error scale is proportional to the target norm (multiplicative error, elasticity of log ||e_i|| on log ||y_i|| equal to one); then the relative-metric fit is the efficient one and its optimism is 2m/n relative to its own noise level, regardless of how concentrated 1/||y_i||^2 is. If the error carries an additive floor, the rows with the smallest targets - exactly the rows the relative weights concentrate on - have the largest floor relative to their target, the concentration re-enters, and Kish's n_eff of the relative weights measures how far the fit is from balanced. The discriminating measurement is the elasticity of the out-of-fold residual norm to the target norm and the nonnegative fit ||e_i||^2 = a + b ||y_i||^2 (the floor share a / (a + b median ||y||^2)) on the calibration rows; on a pool whose targets vary by orders of magnitude (the EMIT radiance outputs) the question is live, on one whose targets are homogeneous (the OCO-2 retrievals, n_eff within a few percent of n) the two metrics coincide and it is moot.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["finite simple graphs (loops make P identically 0; parallel edges do not change P)","k a nonnegative integer in the counting definition; the polynomial identity then holds for all k"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479653+00:00","domain":"graph theory","id":"claim_c11359eb703fe597fd324079d34608d788354417c8b886cc4a0e84bab112bea7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a finite graph G and a positive integer k let P(G, k) be the number of proper colourings of the vertices of G with k colours (adjacent vertices receive different colours). (k - n + 1); P(tree on n vertices, k) = k (k - 1)^{n-1}; P(C_n, k) = (k - 1)^n + (-1)^n (k - 1); P is multiplicative over connected components; its coefficients alternate in sign, the leading coefficient is 1, the coefficient of k^{|V| - 1} is -|E|, and the constant term is 0 for a graph with a vertex; the chromatic number is the least positive integer that is not a root; k = 0, 1, ..., chi(G) - 1 are roots; the chromatic polynomial is a specialisation of the Tutte polynomial, P(G, k) = (-1)^{|V| - c(G)} k^{c(G)} T(G; 1 - k, 0). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.594873+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c11c93a31630fef9ceceed0d5860dd7b8408b9f813e6ced1defab956704fd454","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02398, '\\textbf{Convex Order Comparisons for Sub-Gamma Random Variables}'] Recent work has shown that sub-Gaussian random variables are dominated in convex order by a sharp multiple of a Gaussian. We study the analogous question for the sub-Gamma class underlying Bernstein's inequality, with the Laplace law as the majorant. Here the moment generating function is controlled by a Bernstein-type bound over a finite range of frequencies, rather than by a purely quadratic bound. We derive a variational formula for the optimal multiple, show that it is strictly larger than the natural scale $σ\\vee α$, and prove that this value is sharp, being attained by an asymmetric two-point distribution. We then turn to the sub-exponential class, which has a quadratic bound as in the sub-Gaussian case, but only over a bounded range as in the sub-Gamma case. Interestingly, the sub-exponential class displays a different behavior: the optimal multiple is exactly $σ\\vee α$, but is attained only when $α\\leq σ$; when $α> σ$, the constant remains sharp, but equality cannot hold for any non-affine convex function. Both results rely on a sharp finite-range variant of the Kearns-Saul inequality, which is of independent interest. (abstract text taken from the arXiv listing metadata; the TeX carried no abstract environment)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Little: f entire and nonconstant","Great: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a with an isolated essential singularity at a"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.482747+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_c11eee83f3cff31aeab34ce71916569c41ce2b6c167fbad02599fabb55fea697","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Little Picard theorem: if f is entire and nonconstant, then the complement of its image, C minus f(C), contains at most one point; i.e. a nonconstant entire function omits at most one complex value. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:30.016157+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c12bf9d3c3a8abb63308ee247eecf7accaa4b1b45fcd8237561c328d3a969ba9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 5 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] \begin{enumerate}
\item A smooth measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Kato class measure} if it satisfies \( \lim_{\alpha \to \infty}\|U_\alpha \mu\|_{\infty, q} =0.\) Denote by \(\mathcal{K}\) the set of all Kato class measures.
\item  A smooth measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Dynkin class measure} if it satisfies \(\|U_1 \mu\|_{\infty, q} < \infty \). Denote by \(\mathcal{D}\) the set of all Dynkin class measures.
\item A Kato class measure \(\mu\) is {\it a Green-tight measure} for \(R_1\) if, for any \(\varepsilon >0\), there exists a compact set \(K\) such that \(\|R_1(1_{K^c}\mu)\|_\infty \leq \varepsilon\). Denote by \(\mathcal{K}_\infty= \mathcal{K}_\infty(R_1)\) the set of all Green-tight measures.

\item A Radon measure \(\mu\) has {\it finite energy integrals} if there exists \(C>0\) such that, for any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_c\), \(\int |f|d\mu \leq C\sqrt{\mathcal{E}_1(f,f)}\). Denote by \(\mathcal{S}_0\) the set of all Radon measures of finite energy integrals.

\item When $(\form,\dom)$ is transient, a Radon measure \(\mu\) has {\it \(0\)-order finite energy integrals} if there exists \(C>0\) such that, for any \(f \in \mathcal{F}\cap C_c\), \(\int |f|d\mu \leq C\sqrt{\mathcal{E}(f,f)}\). Denote by \(\mathcal{S}_0^{(0)}\) the set of all Radon measures of finite \(0\)-order energy integrals.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega is bounded and open in R^n with C^1 (or piecewise C^1) boundary, so the divergence theorem applies","u is in C^2 up to the closure of Omega","for the Pohozaev form: u = 0 on the boundary, f is continuous, F(t) = integral_0^t f and F(0) = 0","for the nonexistence corollary: n >= 3, Omega star-shaped about the origin, f(u) = |u|^(p-1)u with p >= (n+2)/(n-2), and strict star-shapedness plus Hopf or unique continuation in the critical case"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.396148+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, variational identities and nonexistence","id":"claim_c1db80201085a9bde5ef4703381e7acf672f7231bfba2a288812bae9f615e2b6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a bounded open subset of R^n with boundary of class C^1 and outward unit normal nu. RELLICH IDENTITY: for every u in C^2(closure of Omega) one has integral_Omega (x . grad u) Laplacian(u) dx = ((n-2)/2) integral_Omega |grad u|^2 dx - (1/2) integral_{boundary} (x . nu) |grad u|^2 dS + integral_{boundary} (x . grad u)(du/dnu) dS. POHOZAEV IDENTITY: if in addition u = 0 on the boundary of Omega and -Laplacian(u) = f(u) in Omega with f continuous and F(t) = integral_0^t f(s) ds, then, since on the boundary grad u = (du/dnu) nu, the two boundary terms collapse and one gets ((n-2)/2) integral_Omega |grad u|^2 dx + (1/2) integral_{boundary} (x . nu) |du/dnu|^2 dS = n integral_Omega F(u) dx. CONSEQUENCE (nonexistence): let n >= 3, let Omega be star-shaped with respect to the origin (x . nu >= 0 on the boundary) with C^1 boundary, and let f(u) = |u|^(p-1) u with p >= (n+2)/(n-2). Multiplying the equation by u gives integral |grad u|^2 = integral |u|^(p+1), while Pohozaev gives ((n-2)/2) integral |u|^(p+1) + (1/2) integral_{boundary}(x . nu)|du/dnu|^2 = (n/(p+1)) integral |u|^(p+1). Since p >= (n+2)/(n-2) is exactly n/(p+1) <= (n-2)/2, the boundary term is <= 0 while star-shapedness makes it >= 0; hence it vanishes and integral |u|^(p+1) = 0 for p > (n+2)/(n-2). In the critical case p = (n+2)/(n-2) the two bulk terms cancel identically and one concludes only that (x . nu)|du/dnu|^2 = 0 on the boundary; if Omega is strictly star-shaped (x . nu > 0) this forces du/dnu = 0 on the whole boundary and then u = 0 by the Hopf lemma or unique continuation. WHERE IT FAILS: star-shapedness is essential, not technical - on an annulus {a < |x| < b} in R^n there exist positive radial solutions of -Laplacian(u) = u^p vanishing on both boundary spheres for EVERY p > 1, including supercritical p (Kazdan-Warner). Regularity is also essential: the identity is proved for u in C^2 up to the boundary (it is valid for H^1_0 weak solutions only after elliptic regularity has upgraded them, which requires growth conditions on f), and the boundary must be regular enough for the divergence theorem. The origin matters: star-shapedness is with respect to the point used in the multiplier x . grad u.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726188+00:00","domain":"dispersive partial differential equations","id":"claim_c1ffc6c7824bf7e532852028244a4f3f17e1d97b6a2fce726d3b11f59a0d7c16","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in ‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^q_t L^r_x(R×R^n)} ≤ C‖f‖_{L²} the exponents must satisfy 2/q + n/r = n/2 exactly, and q ≥ 2 (and r ≥ 2). None of these can be relaxed, so an argument that 'interpolates' to a pair off the scaling line, or that uses a short-time-looking pair with q < 2, is wrong. Scaling: for f_λ(x) = f(λx) one has (e^{itΔ}f_λ)(x) = (e^{iλ²tΔ}f)(λx), hence ‖e^{itΔ}f_λ‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} = λ^{−2/q − n/r}‖e^{itΔ}f‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} while ‖f_λ‖_{L²} = λ^{−n/2}‖f‖_{L²}. If 2/q + n/r ≠ n/2 the ratio of the two sides is λ^{n/2 − 2/q − n/r}, which is unbounded as λ → 0 or λ → ∞ for any fixed f ≠ 0. So an estimate off the scaling line fails for every nonzero f. Necessity of q ≥ 2 (the case r > 2; on the scaling line r = 2 forces q = ∞, so there is nothing to prove there): take φ ∈ S(R^n) and f_N = Σ_{k=1}^N e^{−i t_k Δ}φ with t_1 ≪ t_2 ≪ ... ≪ t_N separated enough that Σ_{j≠k}|t_k − t_j|^{−n(1/2−1/r)} is small for every k. Since |⟨e^{isΔ}φ, φ⟩| ≤ (4π|s|)^{−n/2}‖φ‖_{L¹}² → 0, the summands are almost orthogonal in L² and ‖f_N‖_{L²}² ≈ N‖φ‖²_{L²}; and for t within O(1) of t_k the dispersive estimate makes every term but the k-th small in L^r_x, so ‖e^{itΔ}f_N‖_{L^q_t L^r_x} ≳ N^{1/q}‖e^{itΔ}φ‖_{L^q_t([−1,1]) L^r_x}. The ratio is ≳ N^{1/q − 1/2}, unbounded when q < 2. Known excluded endpoints, where the pair is on the scaling line and q = 2 but the estimate is still false: (q,r) = (2,∞) for Schrödinger in n = 2 (Montgomery-Smith), and (q,r) = (2,∞) for the wave equation in n = 3 (Klainerman–Machedon). Also for the wave equation the Lebesgue-space estimate is stated with r < ∞; at r = ∞ one must pass to Besov spaces.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_c26dbe1967eabd9968a58da43f41afdfaebe56d66241b6d5ae45dbc5bb37aa7a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Localized regime of the bounded-density conjecture for quadratic forms (Proposition 4). Let X_1..X_n be independent with densities <=1 and Q(x)=x^T A x with A symmetric. (a) If some 2x2 PRINCIPAL submatrix B of A (two original coordinates i, j) is definite, then ||p_Q||_inf <= pi/sqrt(det B). Proof: condition on the other n-2 ORIGINAL coordinates (independent, so Fubini is genuine); given them Q is a quadratic-plus-linear form in (X_i, X_j); complete the square (B invertible), which shifts (X_i, X_j) and keeps their joint density <=1; for definite B each set {s <= y^T B y <= s+h} is an elliptic annulus of area at most pi h/sqrt(det B), so the conditional density is at most pi/sqrt(det B); average. (b) Hence if A has a 3x3 PRINCIPAL submatrix A_[S] all of whose eigenvalues have modulus >= c>0, and A_[S] is definite or diagonal, then ||p_Q||_inf <= pi/c: for definite A_[S], Cauchy interlacing puts both eigenvalues of every 2x2 principal block of A_[S] at modulus >= c with one sign, so det >= c^2; for diagonal A_[S], two of the three diagonal entries share a sign and form a definite diagonal block with det >= c^2. This contains the separable case. (c) For other well-conditioned blocks the bound K/c is not proved. A block may have no definite 2x2 principal block at all, e.g. [[0,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,0]] (eigenvalues 2, -1, -1), and the rank-3 coarea bound ||p_S||_inf <= K||rho||_inf^{2/3} is false for general bounded densities on R^3: a density rho <= B placed on a thin shell around {S = s} gives p_S of order B s^{1/2}/sqrt(l1 l2 l3) for a definite form, unbounded in s. So the localized regime is settled for forms with a definite 2x2 principal block of determinant >= c^2, in particular when a well-conditioned 3x3 principal block is definite or diagonal; the other localized forms stay open, together with the DELOCALIZED forms (every 3x3 principal block near-singular), which is the CLT regime.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:49.564752+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c27395fdd622af983c5bbb8bf266923ee0bca3378e79f11affe6bc9e95d19078","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 18 (A sufficient condition for proxy-faithfulness) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Let transforms $A,B$ act on the same operand under a common grouping and produce group-RMS profiles with $\sum_g\sigma_g^2=S_A\ge S_B$ and per-group crest factors $M_g=\mathrm{CF}_g\,\sigma_g$ all lying in a band

for a group of size $G$). If that band is tight relative to the proxy gap,
$\bar c^2/\underline c^2 < S_A/S_B$, then the $L^2$ proxy $\sum_g\sigma_g^2$ and the
AbsMax step-size surrogate $\sum_g M_g^2$ rank $A$ and $B$ the \emph{same} way. When
the crest-factor profiles differ enough to break this condition, which a
concentrating transform induces, the ranking can \emph{invert}. Note that the aggregate $\sum_g\sigma_g^2$ is the operand's Frobenius energy divided by $G$, hence unchanged by any orthogonal map: between two rotations $S_A=S_B$ and the sufficient condition is unavailable, so this proposition bites only where the transforms change that energy. {"assumptions":["mu and nu are measures on a common measurable space (X, Sigma); nu may be signed or complex","the epsilon-delta characterisation requires nu finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.251367+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_c2889b5313a76c0af8fa3f49c365322c4a2e27291177d6ab0a182d09f34f8d7d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $\\mu$ and $\\nu$ be measures on the same measurable space $(X, \\Sigma)$, with $\\nu$ possibly signed or complex. $\\nu$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\\mu$, written $\\nu \\ll \\mu$, if $\\nu(A) = 0$ for every $A \\in \\Sigma$ with $\\mu(A) = 0$ (for signed $\\nu$, equivalently $|\\nu|(A) = 0$, where $|\\nu|$ is the total variation). If $\\nu$ is FINITE (or finite signed/complex), this is equivalent to the $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$ condition: for every $\\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\\delta > 0$ with $|\\nu(A)| < \\varepsilon$ whenever $\\mu(A) < \\delta$; for infinite $\\nu$ the $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$ condition is strictly stronger (e.g. $\\nu(A) = \\int_A |x|^{-1}dx$ on $(0,1)$ has $\\nu \\ll$ Lebesgue but fails $\\varepsilon$-$\\delta$). Any measure of the form $\\nu(A) = \\int_A f\\,d\\mu$ with $f \\geq 0$ measurable (or $f \\in L^1(\\mu)$ for signed $\\nu$) satisfies $\\nu \\ll \\mu$; the Radon-Nikodym theorem is the converse under $\\sigma$-finiteness. $\\mu$ and $\\nu$ are mutually singular, $\\mu \\perp \\nu$, if there is $A \\in \\Sigma$ with $\\mu(A) = 0$ and $\\nu(X\\setminus A) = 0$. Lebesgue decomposition: for $\\sigma$-finite $\\mu, \\nu$ there is a unique splitting $\\nu = \\nu_{ac} + \\nu_s$ with $\\nu_{ac} \\ll \\mu$ and $\\nu_s \\perp \\mu$. Related but different: a FUNCTION $F: [a,b]\\to\\mathbb{R}$ is absolutely continuous iff its Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure is absolutely continuous w.r.t. Lebesgue measure iff $F(x) = F(a) + \\int_a^x F'$ with $F' \\in L^1$; the Cantor function is continuous, increasing, but not absolutely continuous (its measure is singular). Sharp edge: $\\nu \\ll \\mu$ is not symmetric, and $\\nu \\ll \\mu$ with $\\mu \\ll \\nu$ (equivalence) does not make the density bounded or bounded below.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356302+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c28ac3ae4d8e7ea64f8166fb4e0c699b29ccee4086b9570d919c226f9391a1e9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 232 (truncated Lipschitz algorithm) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Consider an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ with input $(\bG, \bg^\aux)$. Denote its output $\bx\equiv\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. For $a\in [M]$, define the random variable
	\[\fm_a\equiv
		\fm_a(\bG,\bg^\aux;\cA_N)
		\equiv
		\frac{(\bg^a,\bx)}{N^{1/2}}\,,
	\]
where we recall that $\bg^a$ is the $a$-th row of $\bG$.
	For $K > 0$, define
	\[
		S_K(\cA_N) = \bigg\{
			a \in [M] : 
			\Big|\E\fm_a(\bG,\bg^\aux;\cA_N)\Big|
			\ge K
		\bigg\}\,.
	\]
Let $\hbG \in \R^{M\times N}$ be a matrix of i.i.d. gaussians independent of $(\bG, \bg^\aux)$.
	Then define the \textbf{truncated algorithm} $\cA_{N[K]}$ as the function
	\[\cA_{N[K]}\Big(\bG, 
	\bg^{\aux+}
	\equiv(\bg^\aux, \hbG)\Big)
	\equiv
	\cA_N\Big(\tbG(\bG,\hbG;S_K(\cA_N)), \bg^\aux\Big)\,,
	\]
where $\tbG$ is the row-splicing operation from Definition~\ref{d:row.splice}. In words, if $|\E\fm_a| \ge K$, then $\cA_{N[K]}$ ignores the $a$-th row $\bg^a$ of $\bG$ and replaces this input with the independent gaussian vector $\hat\bg$. 	Clearly $\cA_{N[K]}$ is also an $L$-Lipschitz function, with output
	\[\tilde{\bx} \equiv 
		\cA_{N[K]}(\bG, (\bg^\aux, \hbG)) \stackrel{\textit{d}}{=}
		\bx
		= \cA_N(\bG, \bg^\aux)\,.
	\]
It follows that $\cA_{N[K]}$ is also an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:Lip}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the transversal obstruction is for the cyclic square (Cayley table of Z_n) with n even; it does not transfer to arbitrary Latin squares of even order","Tarry's result is specific to order 6; orthogonal mates exist for every order other than 2 and 6","a transversal is a set of n cells, one per row, column and symbol"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.048970+00:00","domain":"combinatorial designs (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_c2a935feb9d5a1be9d3032095348234a9a1e5cc7691477012e8f97b64cdb76ec","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Tarry (1900) showed by exhaustion that no Latin square of order 6 has an orthogonal mate, so Euler's thirty-six officers problem has no solution; a pair of orthogonal Latin squares exists for every order n except n = 2 and n = 6 (Bose, Shrikhande, Parker 1960, refuting Euler's conjecture for all n congruent to 2 mod 4 beyond 6). A Latin square has an orthogonal mate if and only if it can be decomposed into n disjoint transversals. For the cyclic Latin square of order n (the Cayley table of the integers mod n): when n is odd the diagonals give n disjoint transversals, so it has an orthogonal mate; when n is even it has no transversal at all, because a transversal would be a complete mapping of Z_n and the sum of all elements of Z_n, n/2, is not zero (a parity obstruction), so in particular it has no orthogonal mate. The even-order cyclic result is a statement about the cyclic square only; other Latin squares of the same even order (n = 4, 8, 10, ...) can have transversals and mates.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.487730+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c2a9c143acf14884e7e7bf65ba91862dada2d77b3e9a7c21ab741649264bddd8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor lq-to-lr of arXiv:2601.19145, 'Stochastic Persistence in Infinite Dimensions'] Fix $T > 0,p > 1$, $q \in (2,\infty]$ and suppose that $u_t,y_t^+,y_t^- \in L^p(\Omega;C([0,T];C(\overline D)_+))$ and there is $0 < \eta^* \leq 1/2$ such that, for all $r \in [2,q)$, $Z_t \in L^p(\Omega \times [0,T]; \gamma(\mathcal{U},\mathcal{B}_{\eta^*-1/2,r}))$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:15:36.154577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c2eb21a5cc39c0c3fffe3fb5b1b7a2350df0572a37ca7f08d6204162f254e734","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 10 (Product-shell bookkeeping) of arXiv:2609.01570, 'A Proof of Fraenkel's Conjecture'] For distinct \(a,b\in A\), write
\[
 d_{ab}=\normQ{ab^{-1}},\qquad P_{ab}=bd_{ab}.
\]
Then
\[
 P_{ab}\in\{a,Q-a,Q+a,2Q-a,2Q+a,\ldots\},
 \qquad \frac1{d_{ab}}=\frac b{P_{ab}}.
\]
For every \(a\in A\), every subset \(B\subseteq A\setminus\{a\}\),
and all real numbers \(L\ge0\) and \(T>0\), if
\[
 \sum_{b\in B}b\le L
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
 P_{ab}\ge T\quad(b\in B),
\]
then
\[
 \sum_{b\in B}\frac1{d_{ab}}\le\frac LT.
\]
Also, \(P_{ab}=a\) implies \(b\mid a\).

In the special case \(s=1\), call \(b\) good when
\(b\mid Q-1\) or \(b\mid Q+1\).  If such a good \(b\) satisfies
\(P_{ab}\in\{Q-a,Q+a\}\), then \(b\mid a-1\) or \(b\mid a+1\).
If moreover \(a>1\) and \(b>a\), this forces \(b=a+1\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:52:47.241752+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3092bf5adfd353dc1b6027a3f20a6ae44e2f31050c739a2a2102928d191e63b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 (weak pullback calculus) of arXiv:2609.01093, 'Ideal MHD below the classical well-posedness threshold'] Let $X$ be an orientation-preserving global bi-Lipschitz map as above.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $E_i$ is skew-adjoint on $L^2(\mu)$. In particular
  \[
   \int_{\Real_y^n}(E_if)\phi d\mu=-\int_{\Real_y^n}f(E_i\phi)d\mu
  \]
  whenever $f,\phi,E_if,E_i\phi\in L^2(\mu)$.
\item[(ii)] Let $F=F^i\eframe_i$ be a vector field along $X$ whose Cartesian components belong to $L^1_{\rm loc}(\Real^n_y;\Rn)$. If
  $q,c^{ij}\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mu)$, then
  \[
   \Div_{\gmetric}F=q,
   \qquad
   (\curl_{\gmetric}F)^{ij}=c^{ij}
  \]
  in the conjugated distributional sense if and only if
  \[
   \partial_a(J\Kmat_i^aF^i)=Jq,
   \qquad
   \partial_a\!\left(J\Kmat_i^aF^j-J\Kmat_j^aF^i\right)=Jc^{ij}
   \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real^n_y).
  \]
  Equivalently, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Real^n_y)$,
  \begin{equation}
   \int q\varphi d\mu=-\int F^i\Kmat_i^a\partial_a\varphi d\mu,\qquad
   \int c^{ij}\varphi d\mu=-\int\bigl(F^j\Kmat_i^a-F^i\Kmat_j^a\bigr)
          \partial_a\varphi d\mu.
  \end{equation}
  With the convention in \eqref{eq:metric-tensor-divergence}, the same
  calculation gives, whenever
  $H:=\Div_{\gmetric}T\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mu)$,
  \begin{equation}
   JH^j
   =\partial_a(J\Kmat_i^aT^{ji})
   \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Real_y^n)
  \end{equation}
  for every locally integrable tensor $T$.
\item[(iii)] If $\mathcal C_X^{-1}F\in W^{1,p}_{\rm loc}$ for some
  $1\le p\le\infty$, then 
  \begin{equation}
      \partial_aF^i=A_a^jE_jF^i,
  \end{equation}
  and the conjugated divergence and curl in
  (ii) agree almost everywhere with the pointwise formulas $\Kmat^a_i\partial_aF^i$ and
  $\Kmat^a_i\partial_aF^j-\Kmat^a_j\partial_aF^i$.
\item[(iv)] The conjugated derivatives commute on their common
distributional domain:
  \[
   E_iE_j=E_jE_i.
  \]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space","A is dissipative","the range condition Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or dense) is the hypothesis at issue"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772454+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups, boundary value problems","id":"claim_c354d651b0d3d4c7e46b9aa4b5480a1f39abee205e5d85399db455e11dffea4d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: A is densely defined, dissipative, AND Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or at least dense) for some λ_0 > 0. What fails without the range condition: a dissipative operator can be closed and densely defined and still generate nothing. Counterexample: X = L²(0, 1), A f = f' with D(A) = {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(0) = f(1) = 0}. Then A is densely defined and closed, and Re⟨f', f⟩ = (|f(1)|² − |f(0)|²)/2 = 0, so A is dissipative (indeed both A and −A are). But solving λf − f' = g with f(0) = 0 gives f(x) = −∫_0^x e^{λ(x−s)}g(s) ds, and the second boundary condition f(1) = 0 forces the constraint ∫_0^1 e^{−λs} g(s) ds = 0: Ran(λ − A) is a closed subspace of codimension 1, not dense, for every λ > 0. Hence A is not a generator, although dropping one boundary condition (D = {f ∈ H¹ : f(1) = 0}) gives exactly the generator of the left shift semigroup. The range condition is what encodes 'the right number of boundary conditions'. What fails without density: X = C[0,1] with the sup norm, A f = f' on D(A) = {f ∈ C¹[0,1] : f(1) = 0}. Solving λ f − f' = g with f(1) = 0 gives f(x) = ∫_x^1 e^{λ(x−s)}g(s)ds, so ‖f‖ ≤ ‖g‖/λ: A is dissipative and Ran(λ − A) = X for every λ > 0. Yet the closure of D(A) is {f ∈ C[0,1] : f(1) = 0}, a proper closed subspace, so A generates no C_0-semigroup on C[0,1] (generators are densely defined); it generates one on the smaller space. Density is automatic only when X is reflexive, which C[0,1] is not. Related trap: for the norm inequality version, dissipativity means ‖(λ − A)x‖ ≥ λ‖x‖ for all λ > 0 - checking it for a single λ, or checking Re⟨Ax, x⟩ ≤ 0 only on a core without knowing the operator is closed or closable there, proves nothing about the closure being a generator unless the range condition is verified on that same core.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:06:42.683852+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c3b7e779e62c432a68ec0191123230a19ac04e5aa7494f32c23cf10738870265","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thmq of arXiv:2411.03942, 'Asymptotic expansions relating to the distribution of the product of correlated normal ran'] Let $\mu_X,\mu_Y\in\mathbb{R}$, $\sigma_X,\sigma_Y>0$, $-1<\rho<1$ and $n\geq1$. 

Let $q=1-p$. 

\vspace{2mm}

\noindent 1. Suppose that $r_X+r_Y\not=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow1$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=s(1+\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/q)+\frac{|r_X+r_Y|\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{1+\rho}}\sqrt{\ln(1/q)}+\frac{n-3}{4}\ln(\ln(1/q))\nonumber\\
&\quad+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1+\rho)^{(n+1)/4}}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{|r_X+r_Y|\sqrt{n}}\bigg)^{(n-1)/2}\bigg)+\frac{n}{8}\bigg(\frac{1+\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)(r_X-r_Y)^2\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{n}{4}\frac{(r_X+r_Y)^2}{1+\rho}-\frac{n}{2(1-\rho^2)}\big(r_X^2+r_Y^2-2\rho r_X r_Y\big)\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{(n-3)\sqrt{n}}{8}\frac{|r_X+r_Y|}{\sqrt{1+\rho}}\frac{\ln(\ln(1/q))}{\sqrt{\ln(1/q)}}\bigg\}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln(1/q)}}\bigg). 
\end{align}
\noindent 2. Suppose that $r_X+r_Y=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow1$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=s(1+\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/q)+\frac{1}{2}(n-2)\ln(\ln(1/q))+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1+\rho)^{n/2}}{2^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)}\bigg)-\frac{nr_X^2}{2}\bigg\}\nonumber\\
&\quad+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\ln(1/q)}\bigg). 
\end{align}
\noindent 3. Suppose that $r_X-r_Y\not=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow0$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=-s(1-\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/p)+\frac{|r_X-r_Y|\sqrt{n}}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\sqrt{\ln(1/p)}+\frac{n-3}{4}\ln(\ln(1/p))\nonumber\\
&\quad+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1-\rho)^{(n+1)/4}}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}\bigg(\frac{1-\rho}{|r_X-r_Y|\sqrt{n}}\bigg)^{(n-1)/2}\bigg)+\frac{n}{8}\bigg(\frac{1-\rho}{1-\rho}\bigg)(r_X+r_Y)^2\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{n}{4}\frac{(r_X-r_Y)^2}{1-\rho}-\frac{n}{2(1-\rho^2)}\big(r_X^2+r_Y^2-2\rho r_X r_Y\big)\nonumber\\
&\quad+\frac{(n-3)\sqrt{n}}{8}\frac{|r_X-r_Y|}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\frac{\ln(\ln(1/p))}{\sqrt{\ln(1/p)}}\bigg\}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\ln(1/p)}}\bigg). 
\end{align}
\noindent 4. Suppose that $r_X-r_Y=0$. Then, as $p\rightarrow0$,
\begin{align}Q(p)&=-s(1-\rho)\bigg\{\ln(1/p)+\frac{1}{2}(n-2)\ln(\ln(1/p))+\ln\bigg(\frac{(1-\rho)^{n/2}}{2^{n/2}\Gamma(n/2)}\bigg)-\frac{nr_X^2}{2}\bigg\}\nonumber\\
&\quad+O\bigg(\frac{1}{\ln(1/p)}\bigg). 
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is measure-preserving on a standard Borel (Lebesgue) probability space","mu is T-invariant; entropies are Kolmogorov-Sinai entropies with values in [0, +infinity]","the ergodic decomposition is taken over the sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets","convex combinations are of T-INVARIANT measures only","no finiteness of entropy and no continuity of the entropy map is assumed or asserted"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732492+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy","id":"claim_c423ff08a284a7ccfc7dc1d8f089019abb153806f7c00355fd50d003464125fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a STANDARD Borel (Lebesgue) probability space, and let I be the sub-sigma-algebra of T-invariant sets.

ERGODIC DECOMPOSITION. There is a measurable family x -> mu_x of T-invariant Borel probability measures on X such that (i) mu_x is a version of the conditional measure of mu given I, so mu(A) = integral of mu_x(A) d mu(x) for every A in B and integral of f d mu = integral over x of (integral of f d mu_x) d mu(x) for f in L^1(mu); (ii) mu_x is ERGODIC for mu-a.e. x; (iii) the family is essentially unique. Writing P for the law of the random measure x -> mu_x, one gets mu = integral of nu dP(nu) supported on the ergodic T-invariant measures -- the Choquet representation of mu in the simplex of invariant measures.

AFFINITY OF ENTROPY. Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy is affine in the measure, with values in [0, +infinity]:
  for every finite measurable partition Q,   h_mu(T, Q) = integral of h_{mu_x}(T, Q) d mu(x);
  and                                        h_mu(T)    = integral of h_{mu_x}(T) d mu(x).
In particular, for T-invariant mu and nu and t in [0,1],  h_{t mu + (1-t) nu}(T) = t h_mu(T) + (1-t) h_nu(T).

SHARP EDGES. (1) AFFINE IS NOT CONTINUOUS: nu -> h_nu(T) is affine on the simplex of invariant measures but is in general NOT weak-* continuous; for expansive homeomorphisms it is upper semicontinuous, and in general it can fail even that. Do not use affinity to pass to weak-* limits. (2) The decomposition genuinely needs a standard/Lebesgue space; on a pathological measure space conditional measures need not exist and the statement can fail. (3) The convex combination must be of INVARIANT measures -- entropy is undefined for a non-invariant measure, so there is no affinity statement along an arbitrary path in the space of measures. (4) The identity holds in [0, +infinity]; if h_mu(T) = +infinity the integral is +infinity, and no finiteness is assumed anywhere. (5) The affinity is a property of measure-theoretic entropy, not of topological entropy: the variational principle gives h_top(T) = sup over invariant nu of h_nu(T), which is a supremum over the simplex, so it is attained (if at all) at ergodic measures precisely BECAUSE h is affine -- but h_top itself is not an average.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.388242+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c48365866ce534c77114704d0db89b51cd9ee0418e1cdad2bbed722719835d1f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem homo multilinear recursion of arXiv:2412.07936, 'Simple Norm Bounds for Polynomial Random Matrices via Decoupling'] [Homogeneous Multilinear Recursion]

Let ${\bf x} = \{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ be a sequences of i.i.d random variables with ${\mathbb E} x_i= 0$,  ${\mathbb E} x_i^2= 1$ and $|x_i| \leq L$ for all $1\leq i \leq n$. Let $\{{\bf A}_{{\bf i}}\}_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n}$ be a multi-indexed sequence of deterministic matrices of the same dimension. Define a permutation symmetric, homogeneous multilinear polynomial random matrix of degree $d$ as
$$
{\bf F}({\bf x}) =  \sum_{{\bf i} \in {\mathcal T}^d_n} \left( {\bf A}_{{\bf i}} \cdot \prod_{j \in \{i_1,\dots, i_d \}} x_j\right).
$$
Let $a,b,c\in {\mathbb Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $d = a+b+c$. Then for $2 \leq t \leq \infty,$
$$
{\mathbb E} \norm{{\bf F}({\bf x}) - {\mathbb E} {\bf F}({\bf x})}_{4t}^{4t} ~\leq~ \sum_{\substack{a,b,c: \\ a+b+c=d}} (48dt)^{4dt} \cdot L^{4ct} \norm{{\bf F}_{a,b,c}}_{4t}^{4t}.
$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.350409+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c49ed582047c4cb6f5e89c53325b0de3d7f6b9478d7f83ec9740f9f1a7410e51","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 179 (annealed second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ 
be defined by \eqref{e:barD} and \eqref{e:barD.plus} (see also \eqref{e:drift.error.II}). We have 
the second moment bound 
	\[\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}
		{p(q_d)}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS \delta}{N}\,,
	\]
for all $0\le d\le \dmax-1$. The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ in place of $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$.
\begin{proof}
Recalling the notation from
\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.g} and \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y},
we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.II} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)}
		{[\delta_d p(q_d)]^{1/2}}
	= 
	\frac1{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\sum_{a\in B}
	\frac{\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)}{|B|^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1})\bigg)
	\equiv
	\frac1{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)\,.
	\]
Note that $\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)$ is measurable with respect to $\cG(q_d)$. 
It follows by applying Lemma~\ref{l:y.subgaus} that 
	\[
	\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{\delta_d p(q_d)}
	=\frac{1}{M}\E\bigg[\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)} 
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)^2
		\bigg]
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}}{M}
	\E\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)} 
	\frac{\|\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)\|^2}{N}\,.
	\]
We then note that if $\ind_B\in\R^M$ is the indicator of the coordinates in $B$, then
	\[
	\|\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)\|
	=\bigg\| \bar{\bG}(q_d) \frac{\ind_B}{|B|^{1/2}}\bigg\|
	\le \|\bar{\bG}(q_d)\|\,,
	\]
from which it follows that
	\[\frac{\E[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{\delta_d p(q_d)}
	\le
	\frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS 
		\E[\|\bar{\bG}(q_d)\|^2]}{MN}
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\BUCKETS}{N}\,,
	\]
where the last bound follows from Lemma~\ref{l:wishart}.
This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.507698+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4a29a9821f86641b73c9a2bd61db74a52d87562589038f7e6c1d25cbde5925f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 16 (From scalar wavelets to vector-valued wavelets) of arXiv:2608.30589, 'Vector-Valued Wavelet Bases as Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$-Module Bases: A Construc'] Let $(\phi,\psi)$ be an orthonormal wavelet basis of $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ associated with an MRA.
Fix $m\ge 2$ and set $D=2^m$. Define $\Phi,\Psi$ by \eqref{eq:Phi-def}--\eqref{eq:Psi-def}.
For $k\in\mathbb Z$ and $j\ge 0$ set
\[
\widetilde\Phi_k=\Phi(\cdot-k),
\qquad
\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}=D^{j/2}\Psi(D^j\cdot-k).
\]

Then the family
\[
\{\widetilde\Phi_k\}_{k\in\mathbb Z}\ \cup\ \{\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\}_{j\ge 0,\ k\in\mathbb Z}
\]

\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] is an orthogonal wavelet basis of the Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m)$ (for the usual scalar $L^2$ inner product); moreover $\|\widetilde\Phi_k\|_{L^2}^2=\|\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\|_{L^2}^2=m$,
\item[(b)] is an $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--orthonormal system in the Hilbert $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--module
$\big(L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m),\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\big)$, i.e.
\[
\big\langle \widetilde U_\alpha,\widetilde U_\beta\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}
=\delta_{\alpha,\beta}\,I_m
\quad(\alpha,\beta\in\{(0,k)\}\cup\{(j,k):j\ge 0\}),
\]
and it is a Parseval $\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$--module frame with the canonical reconstruction
\[
f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\big\langle f,\widetilde\Phi_k\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,\widetilde\Phi_k
+\sum_{j\ge 0}\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\big\langle f,\widetilde\Psi_{j,k}\big\rangle_{\mathbb{M}_m(\mathbb{R})}\,\widetilde\Psi_{j,k},
\qquad f\in L^2(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}^m),
\]
with convergence in the module norm.
Moreover, each component inherits compact support, regularity and vanishing moments from $\phi$ and $\psi$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:50:30.562017+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4a7efd4ffd532c6e9f1d326b2cbedbb130db89d3f3815a1d60f3704ee973b3b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 13 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] A weak solution of \eqreftag{eq:cond-Fokker-planck-a} is a measurable map
\[
    \tilde \P:\R_+\times\Xc\longrightarrow \Pc(\R^d),
    \qquad
    (t,x)\longmapsto \tilde\P_{t,x},
\]
together with a Borel vector field
$
    \hat A:\R_+\times\R^d\longrightarrow\R^d,
$
such that the following conditions hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item 
    For \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\in\Xc\), the map
    \(t\mapsto \tilde \P_{t,x}\) is weak continuous.

    \item 
    There exists \(p>1\) such that, for every \(T>0\),
    \[
    \int_0^T
    \int_\Xc
    \int_{\R^d}
    \left|
    \hat A(t,y)
    -
    a\bigl(t,x,y,\tilde\P_{t,x}\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(y)
    \right|^p
    \tilde\P_{t,x}(dy)\,\mu(dx)\,dt
    <\infty.
    \]

    \item

    for \(\mu\)-a.e. \(x\in\Xc\),
    \[
    \E^{\tilde\P_{t,x}}[h]
    =
    \E^{\tilde\P_{0,x}}[h]
    +
    \int_0^t
    \E^{\tilde\P_{s,x}}\!\left[
    \nabla h(Y)\cdot
    \left(
    \hat A(s,Y)
    -
    a\bigl(s,x,Y,\tilde\P_{s,x}\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(Y)
    \right)
    +
    \Delta h(Y)
    \right]ds .
    \]

    \item 
    If
    $
    \P_t(dx,dy)
    :=
    \mu(dx)\,\tilde\P_{t,x}(dy),
$
    then, for a.e. \(t\ge0\),
    \[
    \hat A(t,y)
    =
    \E^{\P_t}\!\left[
        a\bigl(t,X,y,(\P_t)_X\bigr)
        \mid Y=y
    \right],
    \qquad
    \P_t\text{-a.s.}
    \]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.336865+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4b0b3c78d60a8233c772b75e1763993f89eda62c0d6d97c1f53fbebf289d552","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 26 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] We collect the adjoint and interval-size differentiability statements in one proposition.

\textup{(i)} The formal adjoint is
\[
\cA_L^*v=d\int_{-L}^{L}J(x-y)v(y)\,dy-(qv)'(x)+b(x)v(x).
\]
It possesses a positive principal eigenfunction $\phi_L^*$ satisfying
\[
\cA_L^*\phi_L^*+\lambda_p(L)\phi_L^*=0\ \hbox{in }(-L,L),\quad \phi_L^*(-L)=0,
\]
and this eigenfunction is unique up to multiplication. For all $u,v\in C^1([-L,L])$ satisfying $u(L)=0$ and $v(-L)=0$,
\[
\int_{-L}^{L}v\cA_Lu\,dx=\int_{-L}^{L}u\cA_L^*v\,dx.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\phi_L'(L)<0,\quad \phi_L^*(L)>0,\quad \phi_L(-L)>0.
\]

\textup{(ii)} Let $\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}=(\alpha,\beta)$ and let $\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=\Lp(\cA_{\Omega_{\alpha,\beta}})$. Assume the coefficients are $C^2$ and normalize the direct and adjoint eigenfunctions by
\[
\int_\alpha^\beta\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(x)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(x)\,dx=1.
\]
Then $\lambda$ is $C^1$ in $(\alpha,\beta)$ and
\[
\partial_\beta\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=q(\beta)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}'(\beta)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(\beta)<0,
\]
while
\[
\partial_\alpha\lambda(\alpha,\beta)=d\phi_{\alpha,\beta}(\alpha)\int_\alpha^\beta J(x-\alpha)\phi_{\alpha,\beta}^*(x)\,dx>0.
\]
Thus moving the outflow endpoint to the right and moving the inflow endpoint to the left both strictly decrease the principal eigenvalue, but the two shape derivatives have different structures.

\textup{(iii)} The maps $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ and, after pull-back to $(-1,1)$ and the above normalization, $L\mapsto\phi_L$, $L\mapsto\phi_L^*$ are continuous. On every compact interval $[L_0,L_1]\Subset(0,\infty)$ the convergence is uniform in $C^1$ for the eigenfunctions.

\textup{(iv)} The map $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ is of class $C^1$ on $(0,\infty)$. With the normalization above,
\[
\partial_L\lambda_p(L)=q(L)\phi_L'(L)\phi_L^*(L)-d\phi_L(-L)\int_{-L}^{L}J(x+L)\phi_L^*(x)\,dx.
\]
In particular, $\partial_L\lambda_p(L)<0\quad L>0$.
Thus $L\mapsto\lambda_p(L)$ is strictly decreasing.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. real summands","Lambda finite in a neighbourhood of 0, which makes Lambda^* a good rate function","the rate is exponential in n; polynomial prefactors are NOT captured"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.782174+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4dfaffbd4e619148e1df048b6bc2f3b8bb7627b05d4a288d55a3707d2b749ea","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. real random variables with cumulant generating function Lambda(lambda) = log E[ exp(lambda X_1) ] and Legendre transform Lambda^*(x) = sup_{lambda in R} ( lambda x - Lambda(lambda) ). Assume Lambda(lambda) < infinity for every lambda in a neighbourhood of 0. Then the empirical means S_n/n satisfy the LARGE DEVIATION PRINCIPLE with speed n and good convex rate function Lambda^*: for every closed set C, limsup_n (1/n) log P( S_n/n in C ) <= - inf_{x in C} Lambda^*(x), and for every open set G, liminf_n (1/n) log P( S_n/n in G ) >= - inf_{x in G} Lambda^*(x). In particular, for x > E[X_1], (1/n) log P( S_n/n >= x ) -> - Lambda^*(x), so the Chernoff upper bound is exact at the level of the exponential rate although it can be off by polynomial factors: the sharper Bahadur-Rao asymptotic supplies a factor of order n^{-1/2}. The exponential moment hypothesis is what makes Lambda^* a GOOD rate function, meaning its sublevel sets are compact; on the real line the large deviation principle itself continues to hold without it, but the rate function may fail to be good and the statement must then be handled with care. Heavy-tailed laws with no exponential moments have Lambda^* identically 0 above the mean, and their large deviations are governed by a single big jump rather than by a rate function of this shape. [Cramer (1938); see Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.2.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:41:11.642553+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4e252b7a033cd99fd34781147ec03c758d618ba59d61bf0c7ad4e09060628ff","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:saddle of arXiv:2411.13875, 'Large deviations at the origin of random walk in random environment'] Fix $\kappa > 0$ and let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_j \in \mathcal P_\mathbb V^{(\kappa)}$ be all distinct. (or stationary ergodic with care) elliptic environment on Z^d","The statement concerns the UNION of the two directional events","Directional 0-1 law is open for d >= 3"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.990370+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c4f0b35296bb24abc03e25c08c3620d73cbcb1dad336577101e148e2359e4818","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Kalikow's zero-one law (1981; Zerner-Merkl 2001 for the sharp form): for random walk in an i.i.d. elliptic random environment on Z^d and a direction l, let A_l = {X_n . l -> +infinity}. Then P_0(A_l union A_{-l}) is 0 or 1. It does NOT say that P_0(A_l) itself is 0 or 1: the directional zero-one law P_0(A_l) in {0,1} is a theorem in d = 1 (Solomon) and d = 2 (Zerner-Merkl, using planarity: two walks in the same environment must intersect), and is an OPEN PROBLEM for d >= 3 (Drewitz-Ramirez Open Question 3.2; Kalikow's law is often misquoted as the directional one). Kalikow's proof: the event A_l union A_{-l} is invariant under a coupling of walks started at different points that follow the same environment after they meet in a slab, and its probability is a function of the environment's tail sigma-field, hence 0 or 1 by Kolmogorov. Consequences: under transience in some direction the regeneration structure of Sznitman-Zerner applies to the union event; Zerner's law of large numbers then gives X_n/n -> v or -c v. Typical failure: Treating Kalikow's zero-one law as if it determines transience, mistaking the statement that the probability is 0 or 1 for a claim that it equals 1; the theorem only rules out intermediate probabilities and leaves open, often genuinely unresolved, which side of the dichotomy holds for a specific environment law, which is precisely the content of the still largely open general ballisticity conjecture for random walk in random environment in dimension d>=2. Canonical reference: Kalikow, 1981, Annals of Probability; Zeitouni, 2004, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499560+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_c53552d7811e343a9c322a0f0f633c47f09d36f9fce8bd51339ed0e1ea11dbf9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"(1) One omitted value is not enough. The family {exp(nz) : n ≥ 1} on the unit disk omits the value 0 everywhere, but it is not normal, not even in the extended sense: on the left half of the disk exp(nz) → 0 while on the right half |exp(nz)| → ∞, and a locally uniform limit on the connected set D would have to be holomorphic throughout or identically ∞. Montel's fundamental normality test needs two distinct omitted values, and that is sharp. (2) When two values are omitted, the conclusion is normality in the extended sense: the constant functions f_n = n omit 0 and 1 and converge to ∞, so a proof that assumes the limit is a finite holomorphic function must first exclude the ∞ branch (typically by a bound at one point or by the maximum principle). (3) Pointwise bounds are not local bounds. Montel's first theorem needs a bound uniform on each compact set; pointwise boundedness of the family is genuinely weaker (Runge's theorem produces sequences of polynomials converging pointwise on C to a discontinuous function, so such a sequence is pointwise bounded and not normal). (4) Normality is not convergence: it only yields subsequences, and the limit may leave the class one is working in — the injective maps z/n converge to a constant, and the limit of a normal family of functions in some prescribed family need not satisfy the same constraint unless Hurwitz-type arguments are added.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c574fba2347e734a070686822f78efb69bc3f308b61775e623e7cd7013108c3f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a real parameter delta >= 0 the SQUARED BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta started at y >= 0, written BESQ^delta, is the unique strong solution of dY_t = 2 sqrt( |Y_t| ) dW_t + delta dt with Y_0 = y; the solution is nonnegative, and pathwise uniqueness holds despite the non-Lipschitz diffusion coefficient by the Yamada-Watanabe criterion, which requires only Holder continuity of exponent 1/2. The BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta, BES^delta, is X_t = sqrt(Y_t); for X > 0 it solves dX_t = dW_t + ((delta - 1)/(2 X_t)) dt. When delta = d is a positive INTEGER, BES^d started at |x| has the law of the radial part |B_t| of a d-dimensional Brownian motion started at x - a fact that makes the family the natural interpolation of radial Brownian motion to non-integer dimension. ADDITIVITY: BESQ^delta started at y and an independent BESQ^{delta'} started at y' add to a BESQ^{delta + delta'} started at y + y'; this holds for the SQUARED process and is false for the Bessel process itself. The index nu = delta/2 - 1 is the other common parameterisation and is the one that appears in the modified Bessel functions of the transition density; delta and nu must not be confused. For 0 <= delta < 2 the point 0 is reached from y > 0, and the BESQ^delta equation itself fixes what happens there: 0 is absorbing for delta = 0 and instantaneously reflecting for 0 < delta < 2, so the squared process needs no extra boundary convention (the equation for X = sqrt(Y) holds only while X_t > 0). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:01:22.604561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c58051e42f1cdb52d00da99d8a39d79eba60a06c0b7bae6dd919be3b622b9291","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def:rplfbm of arXiv:2606.21049, '\textsc{Locality of rough path lifts}'] Let $H \in (0, \frac 12]$ and $0 < \eta <H$ with $1/\eta < \lfloor 1/H \rfloor + 1$.
A \emph{local $\eta$-H\"older rough path lift} (\emph{local $\eta$-RPL} for short) of $X$ is a random variable $\boldsymbol{X} \colon \Omega \to C^{\eta\text{-}\mathrm{H\ddot ol}}([0,1], \mathcal G^{\lfloor 1/H \rfloor}(\mathbb R^d))$ such that $\boldsymbol{X}^{(1)} = X$ and
for any $(s,t) \in \triangle$ and $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n \in [d]$ with $n \leq \lfloor 1/H \rfloor$, denoting $\boldsymbol{X}_{s,t} \coloneqq \boldsymbol{X}^{-1}_s\boldsymbol{X}_t$, it holds that $\boldsymbol{X}_{s,t}^{\alpha_1 \ldots \alpha_n}$ is $\mathscr r_{s,t}^{-1}(\mathcal F^{\alpha_1\ldots \alpha_n}_{s,t})$-measurable. 
We furthermore say that $\boldsymbol{X}$ is square-integrable if $\boldsymbol{X}_{s,t}^{\alpha_1 \ldots \alpha_n} \in L^2\Omega$ for all $(s,t) \in \triangle$ and $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n \in [d]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:48:30.919238+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c58d7bd3c00ae14afbf9fb38c6a5e7c51170ee1dda6fc27ba01135c99252a6aa","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 10 (Derivations and $p$-Powers) of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$. Let $x\in K$. Let $D,E$ be derivations on $K$.

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The $p$-times composition 
        $D^{\circ p}=D^p$
        is a derivation on $K$.
        \item Derivations kill $p$-powers: 
        $$D(x^p)=0.$$
        In particular, all derivations are derivations over $k$.
        \item (Jacobson's formula) There exists a universal Lie polynomial $s$ such that 
        $$\left(D+E\right)^p=D^p+E^p+s(D,E).$$
        \item (Hochschild's formula) We have 
        $$\left(xD\right)^p=x^pD^p+\left(xD\right)^{\circ (p-1)}(x)D.$$
        \item We have
        \[
        [D,xE]=D(x)E+x[D,E].
        \]
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.026141+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5b407679b1fe1959a73a0566bb925060e9ec554806f1451d75afae06ecacbd7","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $(\mathcal{L}_t)_{t=0}^{T}$ be a nonnegative process adapted to a filtration $(\mathscr F_t)_{t=0}^{T}$. Let $\mathcal G\subseteq \mathscr F_0$ be an initial sigma-field, and let $B$ be a nonnegative $\mathcal G$-measurable random variable such that $\mathcal{L}_0\leq B$. Fix $\kappa\in(0,1]$, and let $G_0,\ldots,G_{T-1}$ be events with $G_t\in\mathscr F_t$.

Assume that, for every $t=0,\ldots,T-1$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (\textbf{Deterministic non-expansion}) $\mathcal{L}_{t+1}\leq \mathcal{L}_t$ almost surely.
\item (\textbf{Good-step contraction}) On $G_t$,
\[
\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{t+1}\mid \mathscr F_t]\leq (1-\kappa)\mathcal{L}_t.
\]
\item (\textbf{Conditional bad-event control}) For deterministic numbers $\delta_t\geq0$,
\[
\mathbb{P}(G_t^c\mid \mathcal G)\leq \delta_t.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then
\be
\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_T\mid\mathcal G]
\leq \left((1-\kappa)^T+\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\delta_t\right)B.
\ee","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236391+00:00","domain":"numerical analysis","id":"claim_c5e1eefee3a99acd765d978e051f62579879b0225ba57349cf7cbd16a9d39226","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"An algorithm computing an approximation y_hat to y = f(x), for an input x in floating-point arithmetic with unit roundoff u, is backward stable if for every admissible input x the computed output equals the exact result of the same problem applied to a slightly perturbed input: y_hat = f(x_hat) for some x_hat with ||x_hat - x|| = O(u) * ||x||. Informally, a backward stable algorithm gives an exactly correct answer to a slightly wrong question. Backward stability of the algorithm, combined with a bound on the conditioning of the problem f at x (its sensitivity to perturbations of the input), yields a bound on the forward error ||y_hat - y|| / ||y||, since the forward error is controlled, to first order, by the backward error multiplied by the condition number of the problem.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:11:57.316418+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5e2294fec4f1778f0a7807ae65946d06987fa620d71eb33df8aac6607482cb0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2607.23401, 'Limit Theorems for the Pitman-Yor Frequency Spectrum'] Let $J,k,n, (m_i)_{1\le i\le n}$ be integers
  with $0\le J< n$, $1\le k\le n$, and 
  $0\le m_i\le n$, $1\le i\le n$.
Let $m_{+}^{(J)}= \sum_{j=1}^Jm_j$ and
$m_{++}^{(J)}= \sum_{j=1}^Jjm_j$, with
$m_{+}^{(0)}=m_{++}^{(0)}=0$, 
$m_{+}=m_{+}^{(n)}=k$, $m_{++}=m_{++}^{(n)}=n$,
$k^{(J)}=k-m_{+}^{(J)}$ and 
$n^{(J)}=n-m_{++}^{(J)}$.
Let  $\mu_j$, $J+1\le j\le n$,  be positive constants with
$\mu_+^{(J)}=\sum_{j=J+1}^n \mu_j$.
Let $\bfm^{(J)}= (m_{J+1},\ldots,m_n)$ and 
  \ben
  A_{kn}^{(J)}=\Big\{m_j\ge 0, J+1\le j\le n: \,
 \sum_{j=J+1}^nm_j= k^{(J)},\, 
\sum_{j=J+1}^n jm_j=n- m_{++}^{(J)}\Big\},
\een
and let 
 $\big(X_{in}^{(J)}\big)_{1\le i\le  k^{(J)}}$ be i.i.d. with
\be
\PP\big(X_{1n}^{(J)}=j\big) =
\frac{\mu_j}{\mu_+^{(J)}},\ J+1\le j\le n.
\ee
Then 
\be
\sum_{\bfm^{(J)}\in A_{kn}^{(J)}}
\prod_{j=J+1}^n \frac{ \mu_j^{m_j}}{m_j!}
=
\frac{\big(\mu_+^{(J)} \big)^{ k^{(J)}}}
{k^{(J)}!}
 \PP\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{ k^{(J)}} X_{in}^{(J)}= n^{(J)}\Big).
\ee (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:59:58.429950+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c5f63169a5f0b5277765e55b52aea5c68d0689f3dcdb3e5458df04f981e1bb46","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:decomp of arXiv:2604.22453, 'Adapted Wasserstein Barycenters of Gaussian Processes'] For $L, M \in \mathscr{L}(T, d)$, we have 
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{ABW}}^2(L, M) = \sum_{t=1}^T \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L,\, A_t^M\bigr).
\end{equation}

\begin{proof}
Fix $L,M\in\mathscr{L}(T,d)$. Applying (equation eqn:d.BW of the paper) to the column covariances $A_t^L=L_{\cdot,t}L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal}$ and $A_t^M=M_{\cdot,t}M_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal}$ yields
\[
\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L, A_t^M\bigr) = \|L_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 + \|M_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 - 2 \bigl\| L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t} \bigr\|_*.
\]
Summing over $t \in [T]$ gives
\begin{equation} 
\sum_{t=1}^T \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L, A_t^M\bigr) = \sum_{t=1}^T \|L_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 + \sum_{t=1}^T \|M_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 - 2 \sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t} \bigr\|_*.
\end{equation}
It remains to identify the three sums on the right-hand side of (equation eq:decomp.sum of the paper) with the corresponding terms in (equation eq:ABW of the paper). Since the block-columns $L_{\cdot,1}, \ldots, L_{\cdot,T}$ collect all the blocks of $L$, we have
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \|L_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 = \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{s=1}^T \|L_{t,s}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 = \|L\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2,
\]
and likewise
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \|M_{\cdot,t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 = \|M\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2.
\]
For the last sum, the $d\times d$ diagonal block of $L^{\intercal}M$ indexed by $t$ is
\[
(L^{\intercal} M)_{t,t}
=L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t}
=\sum_{s=1}^T L_{s,t}^{\intercal} M_{s,t}.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| L_{\cdot,t}^{\intercal} M_{\cdot,t} \bigr\|_* = \sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| (L^{\intercal} M)_{t,t} \bigr\|_*.
\]
Substituting these three identities into (equation eq:decomp.sum of the paper) gives
\[
\sum_{t=1}^T \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{BW}}^2\bigl(A_t^L, A_t^M\bigr) = \|L\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 + \|M\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2 - 2 \sum_{t=1}^T \bigl\| (L^{\intercal} M)_{t,t} \bigr\|_* = \mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{ABW}}^2(L, M),
\]
where the last equality is the definition (equation eq:ABW of the paper) of $\mathrm{dist}_{\mathrm{ABW}}$. This proves (equation eq:decomp of the paper).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. summands with zero mean, finite positive variance and finite third absolute moment","C absolute; no numerical value is asserted by this node"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781708+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c61887eb90f5f5439cc5008180f95323c8799e4deb9e67787c8bcc7cf73a75be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be i.i.d. with E[X_1] = 0, E[X_1^2] = sigma^2 in (0, infinity), and rho = E|X_1|^3 < infinity. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T17:07:35.313136+00:00","domain":"set theory","id":"claim_c619e145faa54d71a70d2a407f2b55f1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The axiom of choice (AC) states: for every family (A_i)_{i in I} of nonempty sets, indexed by a set I, there exists a function c on I with c(i) in A_i for every i. Equivalently, every family of nonempty sets admits a choice function selecting one member of each set; every Cartesian product of nonempty sets is nonempty; every surjection has a right inverse; and every set of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets has a transversal selecting exactly one element from each. Over Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory ZF, AC is equivalent to Zorn's lemma, the well-ordering theorem, and Tychonoff's theorem for arbitrary compact spaces. AC asserts existence, not a specified construction; Zermelo formulated it in 1904 in order to prove the well-ordering theorem. AC is independent of ZF, assuming ZF is consistent: Godel (1938) established relative consistency of ZF+AC using the constructible universe, and Cohen (1963) established relative consistency of ZF+not-AC by forcing. Choice for every finite index set is a theorem of ZF. Choice for arbitrary countable families of nonempty sets is not provable in ZF in general.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:48:24.296313+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c663f0050fa00804b63b2073413d20b8a9c40d3970d812ab2b12faa032d9f2c2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm optimali of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] {\bf (P-2)}
Consider the secretary problem
with the  Mallows distribution with $q=q_n\in(0,1)$ in the case that the largest number is  of highest rank..

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1-\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=1$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1-\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
n-M_n^*\sim\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
\noindent iii. Let $q\in(0,1)$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*=n-L, \ \text{where}\ L \ \text{satisfies}\ \frac q{1-q}\le L<\frac 1{1-q}.
$$
The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=(1-q)q^{L-1}L>\frac1e.
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.284240+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c66ceef19aa9d88a35c37ed0c3b56b4596efc977ac22d9acc6e886344d586d94","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def:smc of arXiv:2604.20629, 'Rates of forgetting for the sequentially Markov coalescent'] Let $(Y_{\ell})_{\ell\ge0}$ be a Markov
jump process on $(0,\infty)$ with the following dynamics. When $Y_{\ell}=y$,
the process waits an exponential time $r(y)=y$ before jumping,
at which time the process takes on
the new value $Y'=Uy+Z$, where $U\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$ is the
recombination time on the current tree expressed as a fraction of
the tree height, and $Z\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ is the additional coalescence
time after the recombination event. 

Equivalently, one may construct $(Y_{\ell})$ from its embedded jump
chain and holding times as follows. Let $(X_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be the
jump chain and let $(E_{n})_{n\ge0}$ be i.i.d.\ $\mathrm{Exp}(1)$,
independent of the chain. Given $X_{n}$, define the holding time
\[
\Delta\ell_{n}:=\frac{E_{n}}{X_{n}}\ \sim\ \mathrm{Exp}(X_{n}),
\]
and jump locations $\ell_{0}:=0$, $\ell_{n+1}:=\ell_{n}+\Delta\ell_{n}$.
Then define 
\begin{align}
Y_{\ell} & :=X_{n}\quad\text{for }\ell\in[\ell_{n},\ell_{n+1}),\nonumber \\
X_{n+1} & :=U_{n}X_{n}+Z_{n},
\end{align}
where $(U_{n},Z_{n})$ are i.i.d.\ with $U_{n}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$
and $Z_{n}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1)$. In particular, $(Y_{\ell})$ is almost surely
piecewise constant.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.286124+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c701e0f19379c8e3a94d8c551ad2d0f9d80535cad1c30585cbf2ed22fc6bede1","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma prob0 pure of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Assume that $\xi$ is pure $p$-spin. Let $\varepsilon>0$. Let $u\in(0,1)$, $q\in(0,1)$, $f\in\mathbb{R}$, and let $\zeta\in \mathrm{Prefix}_2(u,q)$ where $\mathrm{Prefix}_2$ is as in Definition (def:nprefix of the paper).
		
		Let $\delta\in[\varepsilon,1)$ and $\mathbf{m}\in[-1+\delta,1-\delta]^N$. Suppose moreover that $q_\mathbf{m}\in (q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon)$ and
		$\mathrm{dist}\!\bigl(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\,\zeta|_{(q,1]}+\zeta([0,q])\,\delta_q\bigr)<\varepsilon$.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item  The gradient $\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})$ is a non-degenerate Gaussian vector in $\mathbb{R}^N$. Its log-density at $0$, tilted by
			\[
			u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right),
			\]
			satisfies
			\begin{multline}
				\log \varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				+u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right)
				\\
				=
				\frac{1}{2}N\xi(q)u^2
				-\frac{1}{2}N\xi''(q)\!\left(\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t\right)^{\!2}
				-\frac{1}{2\xi'(q)}
				\Vert \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})-u\xi'(q)\mathbf{m}\Vert^2
				\\
				-\frac{N}{2}\log(2\pi \xi'(q))
				+\frac{N(p-1)}{2p\,\xi'(q)\,q}
				\!\left(
				\frac{1}{N}\langle \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m}),\mathbf{m}\rangle
				-\xi'(q)\int_0^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				\right)^{\!2}
				\\
				-u\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)+N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)+Nf\right)
				+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right).
			\end{multline}
			
			\item  Suppose moreover that
			\begin{equation}
				\langle \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m}),\mathbf{m}\rangle
				=
				N\xi'(q)\int_0^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t+O(N\varepsilon)
			\end{equation}
			and
			\begin{equation}
				\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(h_\zeta(q,m_i)-\partial_m h_\zeta(q,m_i)m_i\bigr)
				+N\int_0^q t\xi''(t)\zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				+\frac{N}{2}\int_q^1 t\xi''(t)\zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t
				=
				-Nf+O(N\varepsilon).
			\end{equation}
			Then the squared term in (equation eq:pure-prob0-main of the paper) is $O(N\varepsilon)$, so that 
			\begin{multline}
				\log \varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				+u\!\left(\frac1p\langle \mathbf{m},k_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})\rangle-\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)-N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)-Nf\right)
				\\
				=
				\frac{1}{2}N\xi(q)u^2
				-\frac{1}{2}N\xi''(q)\!\left(\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\,\mathrm{d} t\right)^{\!2}
				-\frac{1}{2\xi'(q)}
				\Vert \partial_m h_\zeta(q,\mathbf{m})-u\xi'(q)\mathbf{m}\Vert^2
				\\
				-\frac{N}{2}\log(2\pi \xi'(q))
				-u\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^N h_\zeta(q,m_i)+N\mathcal U_\zeta(q)+Nf\right)
				+O\!\left(N\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right),
			\end{multline}
			and, on the event $\{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0\}$,
			\begin{equation}

		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The allocations are defined along sizes with positive conditioning probability.","0 < nu < lambda and the boundary-tilted law pi has generating-function radius one."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.362761+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c701f819aa156cb392336f5dc77d31cdfefe98e256ab50479dcc6ee2e7e58553","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked; reduction plus asserted conditional, not a solution] Svante Janson's Problem 18.39 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510, asks whether Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability is possible in the condensation regime 0 < nu < lambda. Janson conjectures that it is not possible for the full sequence and, more strongly, that there are always epsilon > 0 and a subsequence along which Y_(1) >= epsilon n w.h.p. (Example 18.36 gives Y_(1)/n -> 0 in probability along a subsequence.) Setting: let w_k >= 0 with w_0 > 0, let Phi(z) = sum_k w_k z^k have radius rho in (0,infinity) with Phi(rho) < infinity, and put pi_k = w_k rho^k/Phi(rho), a law with generating-function radius one and finite mean nu > 0. Let m_n/n -> lambda > nu. (Y_1,...,Y_n) is n i.i.d. pi variables conditioned on sum m_n, Y_(1) = max_i Y_i, and M = (lambda-nu)n. Heuristic rate: carrying M in r = M/a boxes of size a has class weight binomial(n,r) pi_a^r up to the bulk's fluctuation, giving log P = M Lambda(a) + o(M) with Lambda(a) = [log pi_a + log(a/(lambda-nu)) + 1]/a. For pi_k ~ c k^(-beta) and for pi_a = exp(-a^gamma), 0<gamma<1, Lambda increases on large a, so the optimum is a = M (one box), matching the known condensation picture. Since limsup_a Lambda(a) = 0 and Lambda < 0 for large a, Lambda has infinitely many upper records a_1 < a_2 < ... (Lambda(a_j) > Lambda(a) for all a < a_j). The record asserts, as author-checked and with no proof given beyond reference to an analogous step for Problem 18.40 in a companion memo, the following Proposition: if for some epsilon > 0 and every C, along infinitely many records, Lambda(a_j) - max_{a <= epsilon a_j} Lambda(a) > C a_j^(-1/2), then along n_j = a_j/(lambda-nu), P(Y_(1) >= ((lambda-nu)/2) n_j) -> 1, so the conjecture holds. Caveat: the only derivation offered is the heuristic rate with an o(M) error, which is coarser than the order sqrt(a_j) resolution this hypothesis requires, so the record does not establish the Proposition. The record poses the open Question whether, for every law pi on Z_{>=0} with radius one and finite mean, [log pi_a + log a]/a has infinitely many records with gap exceeding a_j^(-1/2) below max_{a <= epsilon a_j} for some fixed epsilon > 0. This is not a proved equivalence with the conjecture. A negative answer would only give a candidate counterexample, still requiring proof that the allocation spreads. The Question's normalisation and fixed threshold also differ from the Proposition's hypothesis. The problem remains open. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.822009+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c73143ec74e424ea68649a830e250439809c11442dd36f075e4edd190adabcb4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:finite-profile-transfer of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $H\geq1$ and $k\geq2$, and let $G$ be a nontrivial torsion-free abelian
group.  The following four collections of truncated profiles are identical:
\[
 \bigl\{(|jA|)_{1\leq j\leq H}:A\subset G,\ |A|=k\bigr\},
 \quad
 \bigl\{(|jB|)_{1\leq j\leq H}:B\subset\mathbb Z,\ |B|=k\bigr\},
\]
\[
 \bigl\{(|P^{\times j}|)_{1\leq j\leq H}:
       P\subset\mathbb Z_{>0},\ |P|=k\bigr\},
 \quad
 \bigl\{(H_{C_B}(j))_{1\leq j\leq H}:
       B\subset\mathbb Z,\ |B|=k\bigr\},
\]
where $P^{\times j}$ is the $j$-fold product set and $C_B$ is the projective
monomial curve attached to $B$ over an arbitrary field.  More strongly,
equip the subgroup generated by an additive realization with a
translation-invariant linear order.  Its complete equality-and-order table
through degree $H$ then has an integer exponent representative.  The
resulting sumset, product-set, and monomial-curve exponent models have
identical ordered tables, active ranks, and relation-birth degrees through
$H$.

Every such table has a primitive integer representative
$B=\{0=b_0<\cdots<b_{k-1}\}$ with
\begin{equation}
 b_{k-1}\leq dH^{d-1}\prod_{i=1}^r p_i
 \leq(k-1-r)H^{k-2},
 \qquad d=k-1-r,
\end{equation}
where $r$ and $p_i$ are its active rank and birth degrees through $H$.
The universal exponent $k-2$ for preserving the complete truncated table is
best possible.","status":"unverified"}

\itemsep\smallskipamount

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.161307+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c76ff01d24ad4f8093e496a7b8036d62b53cda129bbff51ae8e0f650a7bc1740","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 11 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2\ge0$,

\begin{proof} Fix $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2\ge0$.
Recall the notation \eqref{e:lam.mu.delta.ball}, and suppose
$(\lambda',\mu')\in\Lambda$ and 
 $(\lambda,\mu)\in B_\delta(\lambda',\mu')$. Given $\YY'\in S_\star(\lambda',\mu';\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)$, we will construct $\YY\in S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)$ which is $o_\delta(1)$-close to $\YY'$. We set $\vwww$ as in Lemma~\ref{l:D.mu.continuity.w}, so that we have the bound $\|\vwww-\vwww'\|_1 \le \delta/\iota^2$. Recalling Lemma~\ref{l:p.polytope.bd.local.aux}, we see that

The $\Budget$ function is uniformly continuous on the compact domain

	\[\sup\bigg\{
	\begin{array}{l}
	|\Budget(\YY;\mu)
	-\Budget(\YY';\mu')|
	:\YY,\YY'\in[0,9/\iota_0]^{3r+s},
	(\lambda,\mu),(\lambda',\mu')\in\Lambda,\\
	\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad
	\|\mu-\mu'\|_\infty \le \delta,
	\|\YY-\YY'\|_1 \le \delta/\iota^2
	\end{array}
	\bigg\} \le o_\delta(1)\,,
	\]
where $o_\delta(1)$ denotes an error tending to zero as $\delta\to0$. 
For the purposes of this proof, let us abbreviate
	\begin{align*}
	c(\YY;\lambda)
	&\equiv \Cost(\YY;\lambda)
	+ \epsilon_1\alpha^2\iota^2(\|\vBBb\|_2)^2\,,\\
	g(\YY;\lambda,\mu)
	&\equiv c(\YY;\lambda) - \Budget(\YY;\mu) - \epsilon_2\,.
	\end{align*}
Then we can similarly bound
	\[\sup\bigg\{\begin{array}{l}
	|c(\YY';\lambda)
	-c(\YY';\lambda')|
	: \YY'\in[0,9/\iota_0]^{3r+s}, 
	(\lambda,\mu),(\lambda',\mu')\in\Lambda,\\
	\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad
	\|\lambda-\lambda'\|_\infty \le \delta,
	\end{array}
	\bigg\}
	 \le o_\delta(1)\,.
	\]
Combining the above bounds gives
	\beq
	c(\YY';\lambda)
	-\Budget(\YY;\mu) - \epsilon_2
	\le g (\YY';\lambda',\mu') + o_\delta(1)
	\le o_\delta(1)\,,

$\YY,\YY'\in [0,9/\iota_0]^{3r+s}$ within distance $\delta/\iota^2$.

$\YY=(\vBBb',\vvvv',\vUUu',\vwww)$
 to achieve
$g(\YY;\lambda,\mu)\le 0$. If the above left-hand side is

 $\YY=(\vBBb,\vvvv,\vUUu,\vwww)$
 close to 
 $\YY(0)\equiv(\vBBb',\vvvv',\vUUu',\vwww)$ to make $g(\YY;\lambda,\mu)\le 0$.
In this case, consider the path in $\cD_\mu$ given by the line segment joining $\YY(0)\equiv(\vBBb',\vvvv',\vUUu',\vwww)$

	\[\Cost(\YY(t);\lambda)
	-\Cost(\YY(0);\lambda)
	=-(\lambda,\vBBb'+\vUUu')t
	\equiv -A(\YY')t\,.
	\]
Recall from \eqref{e:surplus.small.error.bound} that at the start of the line segment we have $g(\YY(0);\lambda,\mu) \le o_\delta(1)$.  Let $\eta = g(\YY(0);\lambda,\mu)$. We then divide into several cases:

	\[

	\]
and (since $\YY,\YY' \in [0,9/\iota_0]^{3r+s}$) $\|\YY(t_0)-\YY(0)\|_2 \lesssim \eta^{1/2}$. In this case, we can conclude by setting $\YY = \YY(t_0)$.
\item Otherwise, if

assumption~\eqref{e:def-Lambda} implies that 
\[
    \max\Big(\|\vBBb'\|_1,\|\vUUu'\|_1\Big) \le \frac{\eta^{1/2}}{\iota}\,,
\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:26.254877+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c77bb5a91cc58037920a86addf1292d8c1770d1c910fba7b802c9cb510060033","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prp 26 ({\cite[Proposition 6.2) of arXiv:2605.23308, 'Convergence rate estimates for semigroups and heat kernels associated with resistance form'] {Nd24}}]

\begin{itemize}
  \item $\frM_{\bullet}(\tau)$ consists of root-and-measured $\bcm$ spaces,
  \item for any root-and-measured $\bcm$ space $(Y,d^Y,\rho_Y,\mu_Y)$,
