{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:21:52.428087+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c7838ce2b13bbf1628cfb5c1e56b1bb1277468c626e6fbf5d4e4f73929fcf4c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 180 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Let $\nu$ be a complex measure on a surface whose support is a smooth compact curve $\gamma$, which has smooth density with respect to the Lebesgue measure relative to coordinate charts for $\gamma$, and which satisfies

If we have a holomorphic function $z$ on the surface which is a local coordinate near every point of $\gamma$, we can also write $\dd\nu(p) = \mathbbm{1}_{\gamma}(p)\nu(p)\dd z(p)$ for some ``density'' $\nu(p)$ which is a smooth function of $p \in \gamma$.

The Gaussian free field on the surface is such that $\int \textnormal{GFF}(p) \dd \nu(p) = \int_{\gamma} \textnormal{GFF}(p) \nu(p) \dd z(p)$ is a well-defined Gaussian centered random variable. {"assumptions":["DTCS(n), the discrete critical beta-splitting tree of Aldous and Janson","drawn length defined by their recursion (73)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.447284+00:00","domain":"probability, random trees, beta-splitting","id":"claim_c78888704df19cdfa3b168f85d513cd7db6feca3de3217a2ea2693dfd69d957c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Aldous and Janson, The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II (arXiv:2303.02529), Open Problem 14 (pp. 54-55) asks to prove that L_n, the expected drawn length of DTCS(n) under their recursion (73) l(chi_m) = l(chi_i) + l(chi_{m-i}) + 2 + |h(chi_{m-i}) - h(chi_i)|, grows roughly like n log^4 n. For every full binary tree the drawn length is at most the sum of all leaf depths, because the increment 2 + |h_R - h_L| is at most n_L + n_R (a full binary tree with k leaves has height at most k-1); with the authors' own Theorem 3 (the expected depth of a random leaf is asymptotic to (1/(2 zeta(2))) log^2 n = 3 pi^-2 log^2 n) this gives E[drawn length] <= n E[leaf depth] ~ (3/pi^2) n log^2 n = o(n log^4 n). The heuristic's error is a missing factor m: their heuristic (75) uses n a(n,m) as the mean count of size-m subclades where the correct count is (n/m) a(n,m); with the wrong count the conjecture is reproduced exactly, with the right one the scale sum converges (sum log^3 m / m^2) instead of diverging (sum log^3 m / m). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.845469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c81e16d14a6e51fc87da21e030a9ee34388bb31078a04202e7ace736392682c0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi 15 of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] A {\bf Ginibre Brownian motion} of size $N$ is an $\M_N(\C)$-valued diffusion process $Z^N(\cdot)$ of the form
    \[ Z^N(t) \equaldist \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(X^N(t) + \i Y^N(t) ) \]
    where $X^N,Y^N$ are independent Hermitian Brownian motions of size $N$.  Entrywise, this can be described simply: for $1\le i,j\le N$, 
    $\{\sqrt{2N}\,\mathrm{Re}Z_{i,j}^N, \sqrt{2N}\,\mathrm{Im}Z_{i,j}^N\}_{t\ge 0}$ are all independent standard Brownian motions on $\mathbb{R}$.

    The random matrix $Z^N(1)$, whose entries are all i.i.d.\ complex normal random variables, is called a {\bf Ginibre Ensemble} first introduced in \cite{Ginibre1965}. Equivalently, the law of $Z$ has a density with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\M_N(\C)$ which is proportional to $Z\mapsto \exp(-N\mathrm{Tr}_N[Z^\ast Z])$.  Note that this density is invariant under $Z\mapsto UZV^\ast$ for any deterministic unitary matrices $U,V\in\mathrm{U}(N)$; thus, the law of the Ginibre ensemble is unitarily bi-invariant.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(a): f integrable on R","(b): the periodization converges everywhere to a continuous function AND the Fourier transform is absolutely summable over the integers","(c): f continuous with (1+|x|)^{-1-delta} decay of both f and its transform","integrability alone does NOT give the pointwise identity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.263262+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis on Euclidean space","id":"claim_c871045185872c50e3ad107b05bbe60ce99326ffffae1aec8481b784ad7e885a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Convention $\\hat f(\\xi)=\\int_{\\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-2\\pi i x\\xi}dx$. (a) (Always, as an $L^1$ identity) If $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb R)$, the periodization $Pf(x)=\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z}f(x+n)$ converges absolutely for a.e. $x$, $Pf\\in L^1(\\mathbb T)$ with $\\|Pf\\|_{L^1(\\mathbb T)}\\le\\|f\\|_1$, and $\\widehat{Pf}(k)=\\hat f(k)$ for all $k\\in\\mathbb Z$. (b) (Pointwise identity) If in addition $\\sum_nf(x+n)$ converges for every $x$ to a continuous function and $\\sum_k|\\hat f(k)|<\\infty$, then $\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z}f(x+n)=\\sum_{k\\in\\mathbb Z}\\hat f(k)e^{2\\pi i kx}$ for every $x$; taking $x=0$, $\\sum_nf(n)=\\sum_k\\hat f(k)$. (c) (Convenient sufficient condition) If $f$ is continuous and there are $C,\\delta>0$ with $|f(x)|\\le C(1+|x|)^{-1-\\delta}$ and $|\\hat f(\\xi)|\\le C(1+|\\xi|)^{-1-\\delta}$, then (b) applies and both series converge absolutely; this holds for every $f\\in\\mathcal S(\\mathbb R)$. (d) Scaled and multidimensional forms: for $T>0$, $\\sum_nf(nT)=T^{-1}\\sum_k\\hat f(k/T)$; for $f\\in\\mathcal S(\\mathbb R^d)$ and the lattice $\\mathbb Z^d$, $\\sum_{n\\in\\mathbb Z^d}f(x+n)=\\sum_{k\\in\\mathbb Z^d}\\hat f(k)e^{2\\pi i k\\cdot x}$; more generally for a full-rank lattice $\\Lambda$ with dual $\\Lambda^*$ and covolume $|\\Lambda|$, $\\sum_{\\lambda\\in\\Lambda}f(\\lambda)=|\\Lambda|^{-1}\\sum_{\\mu\\in\\Lambda^*}\\hat f(\\mu)$. Classic application (Jacobi theta transformation): $\\sum_ne^{-\\pi n^2t}=t^{-1/2}\\sum_ne^{-\\pi n^2/t}$ for $t>0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.774654+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8733e81386ce57787a3ab51fb9a0075b91a4724e3e22a79b8970f41d9bcbabc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 31 (Combined clumsy-careless collector) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] For fixed $\alpha\in[0,1)$ and $\beta\in(0,1)$,
\[
        \mu_n^{\alpha,\beta}
        \sim
        \frac{1}{(S;S)_\infty}
        \frac{n!}{n^n}Q^nS^{n(n+1)/2}.
\]
If $T_n^{\alpha,\beta}$ is the first post-thinning completion time from the empty collection, then
\[
        \mu_n^{\alpha,\beta}T_n^{\alpha,\beta}
        \Rightarrow \Exp(1).
\]
Moreover, for every fixed $r\ge1$,
\[
        \Ebb\bigl(\mu_n^{\alpha,\beta}T_n^{\alpha,\beta}\bigr)^r\to r!.
\]
Consequently,
\[
        \Ebb T_n^{\alpha,\beta}
        \sim
        (S;S)_\infty
        \frac{n^n}{n!}Q^{-n}S^{-n(n+1)/2},
\]
and
\[
        \Var(T_n^{\alpha,\beta})
        \sim
        (S;S)_\infty^2
        \left(\frac{n^n}{n!}\right)^2
        Q^{-2n}S^{-n(n+1)}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:13:31.904720+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c87a764610fbe61ef1c23644c0f9f4938a21a1f9ccdb4efc4a33ff94d96de279","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:generalcoupling of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $\Omega$ and $\Sigma$ be two finite sets, $\rho$ and $\gamma$ be probability measures on $\Omega$ and $\Sigma$ respectively, and $f: \Omega \to 2^{\Sigma}$ be a function\footnote{Here, $2^{\Sigma}$ is the power set of $\Sigma$.}. For each $\eta \in \Sigma$, let
    $f^{-1}(\eta):=\{\omega \in \Omega \mid \eta \in f(\omega)\}.$
     Suppose that $ \sum_{\omega \in \Omega, \eta \in \Sigma} \rho[\omega] \gamma[\eta] 1\! \!1[\eta \in f(\omega)] > 0$ and then define a coupling probability measure on $\Omega\times\Sigma$ by
	\[\mathscr{P}[\omega,\eta]\propto \rho[\omega] \gamma[\eta] 1\! \!1[\eta \in f(\omega)],~\forall (\omega, \eta)\in\Omega\times\Sigma. \] 

	\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Omega$, denoted by  $\mathscr{P}_{\Omega}$, satisfies $ \mathscr{P}_{\Omega}[\omega]  \propto \gamma[f(\omega)]\rho[\omega]$ for each $\omega \in \Omega$. 
		\item[(b)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$, denoted by $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}$, satisfies $ \mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta] \propto  \rho[f^{-1}(\eta)] \gamma[\eta] $ for each $\eta \in \Sigma$.   

\item[(c)] For each $\omega\in\Omega$ with $\mathscr{P}_{\Omega}[\omega]\neq 0$,  the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\cdot | \omega]$ on $\Sigma$ is $\gamma[\cdot \mid f(\omega)]$.
        \item[(d)]   For each $\eta\in\Sigma$ with $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta]\neq 0$, the conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\cdot|\eta] $ on $\Omega$ is $\rho[\cdot \mid f^{-1}(\eta)]$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543907+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c894786f1b55507dfb078a06491f9f69fe1f01bd76b485d4469c8716a85154c8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a real parameter delta >= 0 the SQUARED BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta started at y >= 0, written BESQ^delta, is the unique strong solution of dY_t = 2 sqrt( |Y_t| ) dW_t + delta dt with Y_0 = y; the solution is nonnegative, and pathwise uniqueness holds despite the non-Lipschitz diffusion coefficient by the Yamada-Watanabe criterion, which requires only Holder continuity of exponent 1/2. The BESSEL PROCESS of dimension delta, BES^delta, is X_t = sqrt(Y_t); for X > 0 it solves dX_t = dW_t + ((delta - 1)/(2 X_t)) dt. When delta = d is a positive INTEGER, BES^d started at |x| has the law of the radial part |B_t| of a d-dimensional Brownian motion started at x - a fact that makes the family the natural interpolation of radial Brownian motion to non-integer dimension. ADDITIVITY: BESQ^delta started at y and an independent BESQ^{delta'} started at y' add to a BESQ^{delta + delta'} started at y + y'; this holds for the SQUARED process and is false for the Bessel process itself. The index nu = delta/2 - 1 is the other common parameterisation and is the one that appears in the modified Bessel functions of the transition density; delta and nu must not be confused. For delta < 2 the boundary point 0 is reached and a boundary convention (absorbing or instantaneously reflecting) must be specified; for delta >= 2 the point 0 is never reached from y > 0 and no convention is needed. [standard; e.g. Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Chapter XI]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:55:57.000374+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8b91c6ad846745543ab01427ecc658f4873f7929768971f718375e64637a53a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Main theorem) of arXiv:2609.02788, '\textbf{Quantized Einstein Metrics on \(S^7\) with \(SU(3)\)-Symmetry}'] For the standard cohomogeneity-one adjoint action of \(SU(3)\) on \(S^7\),
there exist infinitely many pairwise non-isometric smooth invariant Einstein
metrics.  They may be normalized by
\[
 \Ric(g_n)=6g_n,
\]
and have principal orbit \(SU(3)/T^2\) and two singular orbits
\(\mathbb{CP}^2\).

More precisely, the metrics can be chosen so that, if \(b_n\) denotes the
scale of the initial singular orbit and \(\beta_n\) its anisotropy parameter,
then
\[
 b_n\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \beta_n\longrightarrow c_*<0,
\]
where \(c_*\) is the Ricci-flat threshold of
Proposition~\ref{prop:threshold}.  Moreover, the sequence may be indexed so that, for some phase constant
\(\theta_*\in\mathbb R/\pi\mathbb Z\),
\[
 \frac{\sqrt{15}}2\log\frac1{b_n}
 =n\pi+\theta_*+o(1),
\]
and consequently
\[
 \frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}\longrightarrow e^{-2\pi/\sqrt{15}}.
\]
Let \(h_2\) denote the nonnormal Einstein metric on \(SU(3)/T^2\)
whose Ricci-flat cone is
\[
 dr^2+r^2h_2,
 \qquad
 f_1=f_2=\frac r{\sqrt5},\quad
 f_3=\sqrt{\frac25}\,r,
\]
and let \(g_{\RF,*}\) be the complete Ricci-flat threshold metric of
Proposition~\ref{prop:threshold}.  If \(p_n^\pm\) are points on the two
singular orbits, then
\[
 (S^7,b_n^{-2}g_n,p_n^\pm)
 \longrightarrow (M_*,g_{\RF,*},p_*)
\]
in pointed smooth Cheeger--Gromov sense.  On the complementary scale,
\[
 g_n\longrightarrow dt^2+\sin^2t\,h_2
\]
smoothly locally on \((0,\pi)\times SU(3)/T^2\).  Finally, there are
constants \(0<c<C<\infty\) such that
\[
 c b_n^{-2}\le \sup_{S^7}|\Rm(g_n)|\le C b_n^{-2}.
\]
Let \(K_{02}^{(n)}\) denotes the sectional curvature of \(g_n\) in the
two-plane spanned by the radial direction and a unit vector tangent to
the third isotropy summand. At eithe singular orbit,
$$
 b_n^2K_{02}^{(n)}\longrightarrow-\frac{1+2c_*^2}{2}.
$$
Consequently,
$$
 \frac{|K_{02}^{(n+1)}|}{|K_{02}^{(n)}|}

$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.164177+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8dd5d6dbd908dc76ffcd01c3c853b2848ddab7bef6bfcc98f9f6c9096bc819d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 32 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If case \eqref{i:fp-case1} of Remark~\ref{r:fp.cases} does not hold, then in any local
   maximizer $(\vvvv,\xxxx,\vwww)$ of the function $F_\diamond$ defined by \eqref{e:fp-Fdiam}, the vector $\vwww$ must be entrywise positive.
\begin{proof}
    If case \eqref{i:fp-case1} does not hold, we have $\hv_1 > 0$, $\hx > 0$, or $\mu_1 < \alpha$. We assume for contradiction that $\vwww$ is not entrywise positive, and divide the analysis into a few cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item     \emph{Case 1:} $\hv_1 > 0$ or $\hx > 0$. In this case, let  $\www_{j_1}$ be a positive entry of $\vwww$, which must exist due to the constraint $(\mu,\vwww) = 1$. Now suppose for contradiction that we have $\www_{j_2} = 0$. For small positive $\delta$, the replacement
\[(\www_{j_1},\www_{j_2})
\mapsto \bigg(\www_{j_1} - \frac{\mu_{j_2}}{\mu_{j_1}} \delta, \delta
    \bigg)\]
increases the value of the budget
    \[\frac1\alpha
    \bigg( \sum_{j=1}^s \mu_j (\www_j)^{1/2}\bigg)^2\]
by $\Theta(\delta^{1/2})$. It follows that we may replace $\vvv_1$ with $\vvv_1 + \Theta(\delta^{1/2})$, or $\xxxx$ with $\xxxx + \Theta(\delta^{1/2})$, while remaining inside the set $S_\diamond(\lambda,\mu)$. Recalling
\eqref{e:fp-Fdiam}, we can do this in a way which increases the value of $F_\diamond$ by $\Theta(\delta^{1/2})$, contradicting the assumption that we were at a local maximizer.

\item \emph{Case 2:} $\hv_1 < 0$, $\hx \le 0$, and $\mu_1 < \alpha$.
We divide further into two cases:
\begin{itemize}
\item     \emph{Case 2a:} $\vvvv$ is not identically zero.
    As above, let $\www_{j_1} > 0$ and $\www_{j_2} = 0$.
    Further let $\vvv_{j_3} > 0$, and note that $\hv_{j_3} \le \hv_1 < 0$.
    Therefore the replacement
    \[
        (\www_{j_1},\www_{j_2},\vvv_{j_3}) \mapsto
        \lt(\www_{j_1} - \frac{\mu_{j_2}}{\mu_{j_1}} \delta, \delta,
        \vvv_{j_3} - \Theta(\delta^{1/2})\rt)
    \]
    improves \eqref{e:fp-Fdiam} by $\Theta(\delta^{1/2})$ while remaining inside $S_\diamond(\lambda,\mu)$.
    This gives a contradiction.

\item     \emph{Case 2b:} $\vvvv$ is identically zero. Then the constraints defining $S_\diamond(\lambda,\mu)$ reduce to
 \beq
        
        1 + \xxxx \le \frac1\alpha \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^s \mu_j (\www_j)^{1/2}\bigg)^2\,, \quad
        (\mu,\vwww) = 1\,.\eeq
    Since $\mu_1 < \alpha$, we have $\vwww \neq (1/\mu_1, 0, \ldots, 0)$.
   Thus there must exist at least one index $j_1\ge2$ for which $\www_{j_1}$ is positive.
    If $\www_1 = 0$, then the replacement
    \[(\www_1,\www_{j_1}) \mapsto
        \bigg(\delta,\www_{j_1} - \frac{\mu_1}{\mu_{j_1}} \delta\bigg)\] improves the value of \eqref{e:fp-Fdiam}
while remaining inside $S_\diamond$.
    Therefore we must have $\www_1 > 0$.
    Finally, if $\www_{j_2} = 0$ for any $j_2 \ge 2$, the replacement
    \[
        (\www_1,\www_{j_1},\www_{j_2}) \rightarrow
        \lt(\www_1 + \delta^{2/3}, \www_{j_1} - \frac{\mu_1}{\mu_{j_1}} \delta^{2/3} - \frac{\mu_{j_2}}{\mu_{j_1}} \delta, \delta \rt)
    \]
    improves the value of \eqref{e:fp-Fdiam} by $\Theta(\delta^{2/3})$ while remaining inside $S_\diamond$.
\end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
This concludes the proof.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:03:59.374369+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c8e8d5862c639944cb0487f49591d4f0ca638d936f88c94d80bb799ba8187029","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:exist of arXiv:2507.08757, 'Strong existence and uniqueness of the tilt-indexed Busemann process in the planar corner '] {\rm[Jan-Ras-20-aop]} There exists a probability space $(\widehat\Omega,\widehat{\mathfrak{S}},\widehat\mathbb{P})$,  equipped with an additive group of continuous bijections $\widehat{T}=\{\widehat{T}_x:x\in\mathbb{Z}^2\}$ and satisfying the hypotheses of Section (sec:probsp of the paper), on which there exists a stochastic process
\begin{align}    
    \bigl({\widehat B}^{h{\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}}}(x,y) : x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2, h \in -\partial \textup{g}(\mathcal U),\, {\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}} \in \{+,-\}\bigr)

with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}  [label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}]   \itemsep=3pt
\item \textup{(}No $\pm$ distinction at fixed $h$\textup{)} For each $h \in -\partial \textup{g}(\mathcal U)$, 
\[

When ${\widehat B}^{h-}({\widehat\omega},x,y) = {\widehat B}^{h+}({\widehat\omega},x,y)$, call the common value ${\widehat B}^h({\widehat\omega}, x,y)$.
\item \textup{(}Generalized Busemann function\textup{)} For each $h \in -\partial \textup{g}(\mathcal U), {\widehat B}^h \in \widehat{\mathcal{K}}$.  

\item \textup{(}Mean $-h$\textup{)} For each $h \in -\partial \textup{g}(\mathcal U),$ $\widehat\mathbb{E}[{\widehat B}^h(0,e_i)] = -h \cdot e_i.$
\item \textup{(}Monotonicity\textup{)} For $h,h'\in -\partial \textup{g}(\mathcal U)$ with $h \cdot e_1 \leq h' \cdot e_1$, all $x \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, and $\widehat\mathbb{P}$-almost every ${\widehat\omega}$

  \[ \rmetres{V}{x}{y}{\Gamma} = \rmetres{V'}{x}{y}{\Gamma} . \]

The bound is tight as h -> 0. Use: in localization arguments it kills union sites with longitudinal overshoot at a rate no curvature assumption needs to fund, letting curvature windows be quoted only where they are literally assumed. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.691651+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c91bb9984ea148e40ded2a45ac845506a68bfcb1c39e0f6c9edc1af271c4cc7f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 30 (Finite-frequency prefix factorisation) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space with
$\dim V\geq2$, and let
$\gamma\colon[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous bounded-variation path. Set
\[
l=\log S(\gamma),
\qquad
v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0,
\]
and assume that
\[
R(l)=\infty,
\qquad
v\neq0.
\]
Choose $\ell\in V^*$ such that $\ell(v)=1$, put $W=\ker\ell$, and write
\[
\gamma_t-\gamma_0=x_t v+X_t,
\qquad
x_t=\ell(\gamma_t-\gamma_0),
\qquad
X_t\in W.
\]

Let $\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$ be finite and symmetric, so that
$\Lambda=-\Lambda$. Give $W$ an auxiliary Euclidean norm, let $W_{\C}$
be its complexification, and define the real Hilbert space
\[
E_\Lambda
=
\set{(z_\omega)_{\omega\in\Lambda}
\in\prod_{\omega\in\Lambda}W_{\C}:
 z_{-\omega}=\overline{z_\omega}}
\]
with the norm inherited from the Hilbert direct sum. Define the decorated
transverse path
\[
B_t^\Lambda(\gamma)
=
\left(
\int_0^t \e^{i\omega x_s}\dd X_s
\right)_{\omega\in\Lambda},
\qquad 0\leq t\leq T,
\]
and the orthogonal map
\[
T_\Lambda\colon E_\Lambda\to E_\Lambda,
\qquad
(T_\Lambda z)_\omega=\e^{i\omega}z_\omega.
\]
Denote by the same symbol the induced graded automorphism of tensor
series, and set
\[
r_t^\Lambda
=S\bigl(B^\Lambda(\gamma)|_{[0,t]}\bigr),
\qquad
h_\Lambda=r_T^\Lambda.
\]

Then there exists $t_\Lambda\in[0,T]$ such that
\begin{equation}
r_{t_\Lambda}^\Lambda
=h_\Lambda T_\Lambda\bigl(r_{t_\Lambda}^\Lambda\bigr).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, with
\[
a_\Lambda=r_{t_\Lambda}^\Lambda,
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
h_\Lambda
=a_\Lambda T_\Lambda(a_\Lambda)^{-1}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.236802+00:00","domain":"game theory","id":"claim_c9565091907e96d8504914374b1b2370362648e70aac2f39f97cdfa7046dceb0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Solving a finite two-player zero-sum game with m x n payoff matrix A (row player maximizing, column player minimizing the same quantity) is equivalent to solving a pair of dual linear programs. The row player's LP is: maximize v subject to sum_{i=1}^{m} x_i * A_{ij} >= v for all j=1,...,n, x_i >= 0, sum_i x_i = 1. The column player's LP, minimize w subject to sum_{j=1}^{n} A_{ij} * y_j <= w for all i=1,...,m, y_j >= 0, sum_j y_j = 1, is exactly the LP dual of the row player's program. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:51:30.064702+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_c964ae9a508c58bef5e0a37d471ab50227a0a5075609a8cfaa0c7e15fefd9e56","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2606.00586, 'Stein's Method for Convergence Rates of Invariant Measures in the Nonlocal-to-Local Limit'] Let $h \in \sS'(\mR^d)$.

    \item Suppose that $h(\xi)$ is a real-valued function supported in $B_1^c$ and

{"assumptions":["K compact","each f_n continuous","for each x the sequence f_n(x) is monotone in n, in the same direction for every x","the pointwise limit f is continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751214+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_c9b13faaa47bc5e4c48eaac0e195f673c255de2096f3e248b1dfd899c8f459b1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K be a compact topological space and f_n : K -> R continuous. Suppose the sequence is monotone in n at every point (f_n(x) <= f_{n+1}(x) for all n and all x, or the reverse for all n and all x), that f_n -> f pointwise, and that the limit f is continuous. Then f_n -> f UNIFORMLY on K. All four hypotheses carry weight: (a) compactness - on the non-compact [0,1) the sequence f_n(x) = x^n decreases continuously to the continuous limit 0 but not uniformly; (b) continuity of the limit - on the compact [0,1] the same f_n(x) = x^n is monotone and continuous with a discontinuous limit and the convergence is not uniform; (c) monotonicity - the moving bump f_n which is the piecewise-linear tent of height 1 on [1/(n+1), 1/n] and 0 elsewhere on [0,1] converges pointwise to 0 with all data continuous and compact, but sup |f_n| = 1; (d) continuity of each f_n - on [0,1] the indicators of the OPEN intervals, f_n = 1_{(0, 1/n)}, decrease pointwise to the identically zero function, which is continuous, on a compact space, so every hypothesis except the continuity of the f_n holds, yet sup |f_n| = 1 for every n. Monotonicity is required POINTWISE IN THE SAME DIRECTION for all x, not merely that each f_n is a monotone function of x. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 7.13]","status":"unverified"}

\item (Operator van den Driessche--Watmough lift is unnecessary.) On a measurable set E, the restrictions satisfy nu_E << lambda_E if and only if f = 0 mu-almost everywhere on E n Z, with density q 1_E. For nonnegative a, b in L^1(mu), the measures a mu and b mu are mutually absolutely continuous if and only if {a > 0} and {b > 0} agree up to mu-null sets. A common dominating measure is not enough: with mu Lebesgue measure on [0, 1], lambda = 1_[0,1/2] mu and nu = 1_(1/2,1] mu are both << mu, but lambda((1/2, 1]) = 0 while nu((1/2, 1]) = 1/2. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:37:08.954998+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ca0d7ebacf2e9376009eb20f6df8f422c6b2ba7331c4a878f5ae0a04951f9ed2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:explicit_density of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Let $(X_t)_{t\geq 0}$ be an ergodic diffusion with invariant measure $\mu$ whose
symmetric part $\mathcal{L}_S$ satisfies the Poincar\'e inequality~(equation eq:poincare of the paper)
with spectral gap $\lambda_\mathrm{gap}>0$ (by Assumptions~(ass:dynamics of the paper)). 
Let $\overline{\rho}_t(V)$ denote the empirical density according to Definition~(def:empirical_density of the paper)
with ergodic mean $\E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t(V)]=\E^\mu[V]$,
and let $\nu\ll\mu$ with $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu\in L^2(\mu)$.
Then for all $t > 0$ and $a > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{\rho}_t(V) - \E^\mu[\overline{\rho}_t] \geq a\right)
  \leq
  \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}

\begin{align}
  \tilde\sigma_\rho^2 \equiv \frac{2\mathrm{Var}_\mu(V)}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}},
  \qquad
  c_\rho \equiv \frac{\|V - \E^\mu[V]\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}}{\lambda_\mathrm{gap}}.
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

Let $K_1,K_2,K_3>0$ be constants, and let $\mathcal F$ be a sigma-field independent of the Gaussian family $((g_j)_{j\le N},\xi)$. Assume the following conditions.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item For each $N\in\N$ and $\beta\in J$, the random variables $\{X^N_{j,\beta}:1\le j\le N\}$ are $\mathcal F$-measurable and satisfy
\[
  |X^N_{j,\beta}|\le K_1\qquad\text{for all }1\le j\le N,\ \beta\in J.
\]
\item The measurable functions $f_1,f_2:\N\times I\times J\to\R$ satisfy, for all $(N,t,\beta)\in\N\times I\times J$,
\[
  |f_1(N,t,\beta)|\le \frac{K_2}{\sqrt N},
  \qquad
  |f_2(N,t,\beta)|\le K_3.
\]
\item The continuous function $U:\R\to\R$ satisfies, for some $A>0$ and
\[
  0<a<\min\left\{\frac1{8K_1^2K_2^2},\frac1{4vK_3^2}\right\},
\]

\[
  |U(x)|\le A e^{a x^2}\qquad\text{for all }x\in\R.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then there exists a constant $K>0$, depending only on $(A,a,K_1,K_2,K_3,v,I,J)$, such that
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{N\in\N}\sup_{\beta\in J}
  \E_0\left[\sup_{t\in I}\left|U\left(f_1(N,t,\beta)\sum_{j=1}^Ng_jX^N_{j,\beta}+f_2(N,t,\beta)\xi\right)\right|\right]\le K,
\end{equation}
where $\E_0$ denotes conditional expectation with respect to the Gaussian randomness $((g_j)_{j\le N},\xi)$, with $\mathcal F$ fixed. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:01:39.499861+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ca744f91c2d6df8571226151372061360569846065a85fa72e6538cbc23a2476","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:cut_graft of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Let $\mathcal E$ be an event on finite plane trees, and let

{"assumptions":["Dirichlet case: U bounded in at least one direction gives lambda_1 > 0","Neumann case: U bounded, connected, Lipschitz, and the datum must be measured against its mean","Reaction terms shift the rate by sup c"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.107251+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_ca75748799e3142c7793ceaf79dab6a7fc33eb9daceaf19a3c9b6049728cbd2e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The estimate $\\|u(t)\\|_{L^2}\\le e^{-\\lambda_1t}\\|u(0)\\|_{L^2}$ comes from the Poincare inequality $\\|\\nabla v\\|^2\\ge\\lambda_1\\|v\\|^2$ on $H^1_0(U)$, i.e. from a positive spectral gap; it is not a property of the heat equation as such. (1) Unbounded domains: on $U=\\mathbb R^n$ the Dirichlet spectrum is $[0,\\infty)$, $\\lambda_1=0$, and $\\|e^{t\\Delta}\\|_{L^2\\to L^2}=1$ for every $t$, so no rate is uniform over the unit ball of $L^2$; individual solutions do decay, but only algebraically in general -- for $g=\\Phi(\\cdot,1)$ one has $\\|u(t)\\|_{L^2}=(8\\pi(t+1))^{-n/4}$. Half-spaces and cones behave the same way. (2) Neumann boundary conditions: constants solve the Neumann heat equation, $u\\equiv1$ does not decay at all. The correct statement is decay to the mean: for $U$ bounded, connected and Lipschitz (so that $H^1(U)\\hookrightarrow L^2(U)$ is compact and the Neumann spectrum is discrete), $\\|u(t)-\\bar g\\|_{L^2}\\le e^{-\\mu_2t}\\|g-\\bar g\\|_{L^2}$, where $\\bar g$ is the mean of $g$ and $\\mu_2>0$ is the first nonzero Neumann eigenvalue. (3) Zeroth-order terms: for $u_t=\\Delta u+cu$ the decay rate becomes $\\lambda_1-\\sup c$, which is a growth rate as soon as $\\sup c>\\lambda_1$. Auditor's check: whenever an exponential-decay claim appears, identify the eigenvalue being used, verify it is positive on the stated function space, and verify that the domain's geometry (boundedness in at least one direction for Dirichlet, connectedness and mean-zero for Neumann) actually supplies the gap.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.287033+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_caaf82ba26dd526b12d4960d0679adfbfe0cf5e77618ccf990d13e89716944b2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma xxphi of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Let $\zeta\in\mathcal P([0,1])$ and fix $q\in[0,1]$.
		Let $(X_t)_{t\in[q,1]}$ solve the Auffinger--Chen SDE 
		\[
		\mathrm{d} X_t=\xi''(t)\,\zeta([0,t])\,\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,X_t)\mathrm{d} t+\sqrt{\xi''(t)}\,\mathrm{d} B_t.
		\]
		Write $u(t,y):=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,y)$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb{R}$,
		\begin{equation}
			\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,x)
			=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,u(q,x)^2
			-\int_{[q,1]}\mathbb{E}\!\left[u(t,X_t)^2\,\middle|\,X_q=x\right]\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\end{equation}
		Consequently,
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\big[\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,X_q)\big]
		=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,\mathbb{E}\big[u(q,X_q)^2\big]
		-\int_{[q,1]}\mathbb{E}\big[u(t,X_t)^2\big]\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\]
		Moreover, if $\mathbb{E}[u(t,X_t)^2]=t$ for $\zeta$-a.e.\ $t\in[q,1]$
		and also $\mathbb{E}[u(q,X_q)^2]=q$,
		then
		\[
		\mathbb{E}\big[\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(q,X_q)\big]
		=1-\zeta\bigl([0,q)\bigr)\,q-\int_{[q,1]}t\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t)
		=\int_q^1 \zeta([0,t])\mathrm{d} t.
		\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:32:23.741389+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cacc7b69b610a23a1e0040aa6e604bfb5a9801c5189b2cdd44d542ddd54935d2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:main_result of arXiv:2603.24803, 'Critical Spectral Invariants in Random Walks with Geometric Resetting'] Consider a random walk on $\{0,1,\ldots,a\}$ with absorbing boundaries at $0$ and $a$,
transition probabilities $p,q \in (0,1)$ ($p+q=1$), and geometric resetting with
parameter $\gamma \in (0,1]$. Let $q_z(\gamma)$ denote the probability of absorption
at $0$ starting from position $z \in \{1, 2, \ldots, a-1\}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item \textbf{Existence and uniqueness of sign-change point:}
For fixed $\gamma \in (0,1]$, define
$h_z(\gamma) := \partial q_z(\gamma)/\partial\gamma$ for
$z \in \{1, 2, \ldots, a-1\}$.
There exists a unique pair of consecutive integers $(z_0, z_0+1)$ such that
$h_{z_{0}}(\gamma) \cdot h_{z_{0}+1}(\gamma) < 0$. This defines a \emph{sign-change point}
$z^{\dagger}$ satisfying:
\[
h_z(\gamma) > 0 \ \text{for } z < z^{\dagger}, \quad
h_z(\gamma) < 0 \ \text{for } z > z^{\dagger}.
\]

\item \textbf{Midpoint invariance (even $a$):}
If $a$ is even, then $z^{\dagger} = a/2$ for all $p \in (0,1)$, $\gamma \in (0,1]$.
Moreover, the absorption probability at the midpoint is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
q_{a/2}(\gamma)& = \frac{(q/p)^{a/2}}{1 + (q/p)^{a/2}} \quad\\
& \text{for all } \gamma \in (0,1], \; p \in (0,1),
\end{aligned}
\]
and consequently $\partial q_{a/2}(\gamma)/\partial\gamma \equiv 0$.

\item \textbf{Location for odd $a$:}
If $a$ is odd, $z^{\dagger}$ lies between $(a-1)/2$ and $(a+1)/2$, with the
precise location depending on $p$ according to the asymptotic expansion,
valid for $|p-q| \ll 1$:
\[
z^{\dagger}(\gamma,p) = \frac{a}{2} - \frac{C(\gamma,a)}{2}(p-q) + O(|p-q|^2),
\]
where $C(\gamma,a) > 0$ for all $\gamma \in (0,1]$ and satisfies $C(\gamma,a) = \Theta(a)$.

\item \textbf{Approximate invariance for odd $a$:}
When $a$ is odd, no exact invariance exists at integer sites. However, for the
two central positions $z \in \{(a-1)/2, (a+1)/2\}$,
\[
\left|\frac{\partial q_z(\gamma)}{\partial\gamma}\right|
\le \frac{K(\gamma)}{a},
\]
where $K(\gamma) > 0$ is independent of $p$ and may grow moderately with $\gamma$.
Consequently, the sensitivity to resetting at these sites is significantly
reduced compared to bulk positions.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.190810+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb0d9ad222facc8d59b1559d22cc9305191285dcd3ed707c0b3ada8b0bc9e12c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 of arXiv:2606.31287, '\bf Heat kernel lower bound estimates for symmetric pure jump processes via averaged jump '] \rm 
 Let $(\sX,d,m,\sE, \sF)$ be an MMD space.
\begin{enumerate}  
\item[\rm (i)] We say that the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ is conservative if its associated Hunt process is conservative. 

\item[\rm (ii)] We say that the transition density upper bound estimate ${\rm UHK}(\phi)$ holds for the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ if the Hunt process $X$ associated with $(\sE, \sF)$  has a jointly continuous density function
 $p(t, x, y)$ on $(0, \infty )\times \sX \times \sX$ with respect to the measure $m$ and there is a positive constant $c_{\ref{e:2.6}} >0 $ so that 
\begin{equation}
 p(t, x, y) \leq c_{\ref{e:2.6}}\left( \frac{1}{V(x, \phi^{-1}(t))} \wedge
\frac{t}{V(x, d(x,y))\phi (d(x, y))} \right)
\end{equation}
for any $t > 0$ and $x, y \in \sX$.  
Here $\phi^{-1}$ denotes the inverse function of $\phi$.
 
\item[\rm (iii)] We say that the near diagonal lower bound estimate ${\rm NLHK}(\phi)$
 holds for the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ if the Hunt process $X$ associated with $(\sE, \sF)$  has a jointly continuous density function $p(t, x, y)$ on $(0, \infty)\times \sX \times \sX$ with respect to the measure $m$ and there exist constants $\e_{\ref{e:1.9}} \in (0,1)$ and $c_{\ref{e:1.9}} > 0$ such that  
\be 
p(t, x ,y )\ge \frac{c_{\ref{e:1.9}}}{V(x , \phi^{-1}(t))} \quad \hbox{for any } x ,y \in \sX
\hbox{ with }  d(x, y) < \e_{\ref{e:1.9}}\phi^{-1}(t)  .
\ee

 \item[\rm (iv)]  We say that the transition density lower bound estimate for the Dirichlet transition density, ${\rm NDL}(\phi)$ for short, holds for the Dirichlet form $(\sE, \sF)$ if the Hunt process $X$ associated with $(\sE, \sF)$   has a jointly continuous density function $p(t, x, y)$ on $(0, \infty)\times \sX \times \sX$ with respect to the measure $m$ and there exist  $\e_{\ref{e:2.15}} \in (0, 1)$ and $c_{\ref{e:2.15}} > 0$ so that for every $x_0 \in \sX$, $r > 0$, $t\in (0, \phi (\e_{\ref{e:2.15}}r))$ and 
 $B = B(x_0, r)$, 
 \begin{equation}
 p^B(t, x, y) \geq   \frac{c_{\ref{e:2.15}}}{V(x_0, \phi^{-1}(t))}  \quad \hbox{for } x, y \in B(x_0, \e_{\ref{e:2.15}} \phi^{-1}(t)).
 \end{equation}
 Here $p^B(t, x, y)$ is the transition density function of the part process $X^B$ of $X$ killed upon leaving the ball $B$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.350975+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb10364dace7dba743898e874e7664b4dd7421f41ae9cdd370defd519baac0d2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 184 (quenched second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\Ising}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] In addition to Lemma~\ref{l:barD.Ising.second} we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[\max\bigg\{
	\bE\Big[\Delta\bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)^2\Big]
	: 0\le d\le\dmax-1
	\bigg\}
	\le \frac{\SMAX_N(\Ising)^2\BUCKETS\delta}{N}\]
where $\SMAX_N(\Ising)$ is a random variable satisfying the bound
	\[\P\Big(\SMAX^N(\Ising) \ge \log N\Big)
	\le \exp
	\bigg(
	-\frac{(\log N)^2}{L^{O(1)}}
	\bigg)
	\,.\]
The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$ in place of
$\bar{D}^{\Ising}$.

\begin{proof}
Recall that we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.Ising} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)}{(\delta_d)^{1/2}}
	=\frac{1}{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\sum_{i\in B}
	\frac{\be_i}{|B|^{1/2}},
	\by\bigg)
	\equiv \frac{(\be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))}{|B|^{1/2}}\,,
	\]
where we abbreviate $B\equiv B^\Ising$.
If we define the random variable
	\[
	\SMAX_N(\Ising)
	\equiv\max
	\bigg\{
	\Big|( \be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	: 
	0\le d\le \dmax-1, B\in \mathcal{B}^\Ising(q_d)
	\bigg\}\,,
	\]
then we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[
	\bE[\Delta \bar{D}^{\Ising}(q_d)^2]
	= \frac{\delta_d}{N}
	\sum_{B\in \mathcal{B}^\Ising(q_d)}
	(\be_B,\by(q_{d+1}))^2
	\le  \frac{\SMAX_N(\Ising)^2\BUCKETS\delta}{N}\,.
	\]
The bound on $\SMAX_N(\Ising)$ follows by a similar argument as the bound for $\SMAX_N(\RomII)$ from Lemma~\ref{l:barD.II.second.quenched}, with the simplification that $\|\be_B\|=1$ is trivially bounded. 
This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\Ising}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\Ising}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.850549+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb20fbc476e426f62cbb0a29e7dfcaa83cec9e888814ebaa77c1bc7165ffc280","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 of arXiv:2609.02017, 'Optimal girth-dependent bounds for the Bethe approximation of the permanent'] For $\bs{q}=(q_1,\ldots,q_d)\in\Delta_d$, let
\[
  H(\bs{q}):=-\sum_{i=1}^d q_i\log q_i
\]
denote the usual Shannon entropy, and define the complementary entropy functional
\[
  H_{\mr c}(\bs{q}):=-\sum_{i=1}^d(1-q_i)\log(1-q_i).
\]
We call the difference
\[
  S(\bs{q}):=H(\bs{q})-H_{\mr c}(\bs{q})
\]
the local Bethe entropy functional.
If $\mu$ is a
probability distribution on a finite set, we write $H(\mu)$ for the
entropy of its probability vector; for a finite random variable $U$, we write $\mc{L}(U)$ for its law and set $H(U):=H(\mc{L}(U))$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:51:26.589301+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb7cc8fd1114c41bfc16383467dd69f2f04c77f37babab12ced15ff799e959af","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:SaS-measure of arXiv:2606.02003, 'Higher-Order Multifractional Stable Motion:\\ Definition and Fundamental Properties'] Let $(E,\mathcal{E})$ be a measurable space with $\sigma$-finite measure $m$.
Set $\mathcal{E}_0 := \{A \in \mathcal{E} : m(A) < \infty\}$.
A mapping $M_\alpha : \mathcal{E}_0 \to L^0(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$
is a \emph{S$\alpha$S random measure with control measure $m$} if:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item For every $A \in \mathcal{E}_0$:
  $M_\alpha(A) \sim \mathrm{S}\alpha\mathrm{S}(m(A)^{1/\alpha})$, i.e.,
  \begin{equation}
  
  \mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{i\theta M_\alpha(A)}\bigr]
  = e^{-|\theta|^\alpha m(A)},
  \quad \theta \in \mathbb{R}.
  \end{equation}
\item For pairwise disjoint $A_1, A_2, \ldots \in \mathcal{E}_0$,
  the variables $M_\alpha(A_1), M_\alpha(A_2), \ldots$ are independent.
\item For pairwise disjoint $\{A_j\} \subset \mathcal{E}_0$ with
  $\bigcup_j A_j \in \mathcal{E}_0$:
  $M_\alpha\!\left(\bigcup_j A_j\right) = \sum_j M_\alpha(A_j)$
  almost surely.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.644464+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb857d1dad3494a3cf99dabc2cda5ddc7e0cc4e2b95cf9ad1e32505945ce3e4d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 (Wasserstein-1 distance) of arXiv:2605.24445, 'Matrix concentration inequalities for time-inhomogeneous Markov chains'] Let $(\Omega, d)$ be a Polish metric space and let $\mu,\nu$ be two probability measures on $\Omega$ with finite first moment.
The \emph{Wasserstein-1 distance} between $\mu$ and $\nu$ is
\[
    W_1(\mu,\nu)
    \;:=\;
    \inf_{\pi \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)}
    \int_{\Omega\times \Omega} d(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x,y),
\]
where $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ is the set of all couplings of $\mu$ and $\nu$,
i.e., all probability measures $\pi$ on $\Omega\times\Omega$
with marginals $\mu$ and $\nu$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:17:17.062061+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cb874539e13deba5947fe6e95375e80c8e031e1c5d52cdef72f24b040655a49e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 12 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] Consider the birth-death process with immigration introduced above and let
    $A_T=\int_0^T \de s \, X_s$.
For $0<\theta<a/(c-b)$, define $r_\theta=\sqrt{\frac{c\theta}{a+b\theta}}$ and $\beta_\theta
      =br_\theta+\frac{c}{r_\theta}-b-c$.
Moreover, let
\[
    v_\theta
      =\frac{2ac r_\theta^3}{(c-br_\theta^2)^3},
    \qquad
    I_{\mathrm{BDI}}(\theta)
      =\left(
          \sqrt{a+b\theta}-\sqrt{c\theta}
       \right)^2.
\]
Then, for every fixed $n\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$ and $z\in\mathbb R$,
\[
    \bbP_n(A_T\leq\theta T+z)
    \sim
    \frac{
      \psi_{\beta_\theta}(n)
      \langle\psi_{\beta_\theta},\mathbf 1\rangle_{\ell^2(\pi)}
    }{
      \beta_\theta\sqrt{2\pi v_\theta T}
    }
    \exp\!\left(
       -I_{\mathrm{BDI}}(\theta)T+\beta_\theta z
    \right).
\]
On every fixed time interval, the conditioned process converges in total
variation to the birth-death process with rates
\[
    q^{(\theta)}(n,n+1)=r_\theta(a+bn),
    \qquad
    q^{(\theta)}(n,n-1)=\frac{c}{r_\theta}n.
\]
Its invariant law is negative binomial with shape parameter $a/b$ and
mean $\theta$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911677+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_cb9f0a5bfb69e6d801c7f9b4c969831d7a650fa1a7cd92d88cc350fba9aa3034","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $M$ predictors $f_1, \\dots, f_M$ of a target $y$ have errors $e_m = f_m - y$ with error covariance $\\Sigma_E$ (the $M \\times M$ covariance of the vector $(e_1, \\dots, e_M)$ over the population of inputs). An affine stack $\\sum_m w_m f_m + b$ with $\\sum_m w_m = 1$ has error $\\sum_m w_m e_m + b$, so after the intercept removes the mean error its risk is $w^T \\Sigma_E w$, and the optimal weights are the minimum-variance portfolio $w^* = \\Sigma_E^{-1}\\mathbf{1} / (\\mathbf{1}^T \\Sigma_E^{-1}\\mathbf{1})$; without the sum constraint the least-squares stack is the ordinary regression of $y$ on $(f_1, \\dots, f_M, 1)$. Consequently every random-matrix result about the noisy-covariance portfolio problem transfers to ensemble weighting with $q = M / n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$, $n_{\\mathrm{cal}}$ the number of calibration cases the weights are fitted on: the plug-in (least-squares) stack's out-of-sample risk is inflated by the factor $1/(1 - q)$ relative to the optimum, its in-sample risk understates the optimum by $1 - q$, and any cleaning of the covariance must be applied to $\\Sigma_E$. The covariance of the predictions themselves, $\\operatorname{Cov}(f_1, \\dots, f_M)$, is NOT the object to clean: writing $f_m = y + e_m$ it equals $\\operatorname{Var}(y)\\mathbf{1}\\mathbf{1}^T + (\\text{cross terms}) + \\Sigma_E$, a rank-one spike of the size of the signal variance over the error covariance. The stacking weight's departure from equal weights, $w - \\mathbf{1}/M$, is orthogonal to $\\mathbf{1}$, so it lives entirely in the small-eigenvalue subspace of the prediction covariance; a bulk-versus-spike cleaner applied to that matrix (Marchenko-Pastur truncation, shrinkage toward $\\operatorname{tr}/p \\cdot I$, a rotationally invariant estimator floored relative to the top eigenvalue) keeps the signal spike and destroys exactly the directions stacking needs. At $q = 0.025$ (23 members, 932 calibration rows) the whole prize from cleaning $\\Sigma_E$ is bounded by about $2.5$ percent; the prize grows like $q/(1-q)$ as the calibration set shrinks.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["convention with kernel e^{-i x . zeta} (with e^{-2 pi i x . zeta} the exponent becomes 2 pi R |Im zeta|)","support contained in the closed ball of radius R (for a general compact convex K replace R|Im zeta| by the supporting function of K evaluated at Im zeta)","(b): u is a distribution with compact support and finite order; the polynomial exponent equals the order only in the forward direction"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.263692+00:00","domain":"distribution theory and complex analysis","id":"claim_cba247c3ed3e796918e204e741c567b552748af03769e8d7a590344a31b7acf4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Use the convention $\\hat\\varphi(\\zeta)=\\int_{\\mathbb R^d}\\varphi(x)e^{-ix\\cdot\\zeta}dx$ for $\\zeta\\in\\mathbb C^d$, and let $R\\ge0$, $B_R=\\{x\\in\\mathbb R^d:|x|\\le R\\}$. (a) Test functions: $\\varphi\\in C_c^\\infty(\\mathbb R^d)$ with $\\operatorname{supp}\\varphi\\subset B_R$ if and only if $\\hat\\varphi$ extends to an entire function on $\\mathbb C^d$ satisfying, for every $N\\in\\mathbb N$, a bound $|\\hat\\varphi(\\zeta)|\\le C_N(1+|\\zeta|)^{-N}e^{R|\\operatorname{Im}\\zeta|}$. (b) Distributions: if $u\\in\\mathcal E'(\\mathbb R^d)$ has $\\operatorname{supp}u\\subset B_R$ and order at most $N$, then $\\hat u(\\zeta)=\\langle u,e^{-ix\\cdot\\zeta}\\rangle$ is entire on $\\mathbb C^d$ and $|\\hat u(\\zeta)|\\le C(1+|\\zeta|)^{N}e^{R|\\operatorname{Im}\\zeta|}$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:20:07.893906+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cbc56ef58e977fa0d3eb1679ea2b43b004fe83fa10b8d1c4d615dcc2a0fd5466","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lower_bound_weighted_inner_product of arXiv:2608.23765, '\texorpdfstring{Tight Majorizations and Convergence Rates\\ of Nuclear Norm Minimization I'] \mbox{}\\
Let $\varepsilon > 0$
and let $\mathbf{X} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$ 
with SVD given by $ \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}} \diag (\boldsymbol{\sigma}) \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X}}^\top$, where
$\diag (\boldsymbol{\sigma}) \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$ is the rectangular diagonal matrix with the extended vector of nonincreasing singular values $\boldsymbol{\sigma} \in \R^{D}$ of $\mathbf{X}$ on the diagonal.
Consider the weight operator
$ W_{\mathbf{X}, \varepsilon} : \R^{d_1 \times d_2} \to \R^{d_1 \times d_2} $
of (def:optimalweightoperator of the paper) with harmonic-mean core matrix (eq:harmonic:mean of the paper). Define the matrices
$\mathbf{L}_{\mathbf{U}} = \mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}} \diag (\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_{d_1}) \mathbf{U}_{\mathbf{X}}^\top $
and
$ \mathbf{L}_{\mathbf{V}} = \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X}} \diag (\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_{d_2}) \mathbf{V}_{\mathbf{X}}^\top $,
where $ \lambda_i := \max \left( \sigma_i, \varepsilon \right)$
for $1 \le i \le \max \left( d_1, d_2 \right)$ with the convention of $\sigma_i = 0$ for $i > d$.

Let now $\mathbf{Z} \in \R^{d_1 \times d_2}$
be arbitrary with SVD given by $ \mathbf{Z} = \sum_{k=1}^d \sigma_k (\mathbf{Z}) \mathbf{u}_k \mathbf{v}_k^\top $, where $\sigma_k (\mathbf{Z})$
denotes the $k$-th singular value of $\mathbf{Z}$. Then,
it holds that 
\begin{equation*}
    \innerproduct{ \W{\mathbf{X}}{\varepsilon} (\mathbf{Z}), \mathbf{Z} }
    \ge
    \sum_{k=1}^d
    \frac{ \sigma_k^2 (\mathbf{Z})}{ 
        \innerproduct{ \mathbf{L}_{\mathbf{U}}, \mathbf{u}_k \mathbf{u}_k^\top }/2 
        +

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:39:41.443181+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cbe1d106d31bbfccb55cb83bd63076c04f8b9acb51cde99d137a30200c0b3de4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 23 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $n,d$ be any parameters for the Rook's Walk. Then for $\epsilon\in(0,1)$,
   \[t_\text{mix}(\epsilon) \leq \frac{d(n-1)}{2n} \log d + c_u(\epsilon) \frac{d(n-1)}{n}\]
   where $c_u(\epsilon)$ is a constant dependent only on $\epsilon$.
   \begin{proof}
      Let $u=4\epsilon^2+1$. Then,
      \[u^{1/d} =e^{\log(u^{1/d})}=e^{\frac{1}{d}\log(u)}\]
      Now, $e^x$ is concave up so the first order Taylor approximation is a lower bound; That is, $e^x \geq 1+x$. Therefore,
      \[e^{\frac{1}{d}\log (u)} \geq 1+ \frac{1}{d}\log( u)\]
      or equivalently,
      \[u^{1/d} -1 \geq \frac{\log u}{d}\]
      Now, recall our upper bound from Theorem \ref{main1} and substitute,
      \begin{align*}
          t_\text{mix}(\epsilon) &\leq -\frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log\left((4\epsilon^2+1)^{1/d}-1 \right)\\
          &= \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log\left(\frac{1}{(4\epsilon^2+1)^{1/d}-1 }\right)\\
          &\leq \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log\left(\frac{d}{\log (4\epsilon^2 +1)}\right)\\
          &= \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\left(\log(d) -\log\log(4\epsilon^2+1)\right)\\
          &= \frac{d(n-1)}{2n}\log(d) +c_u(\epsilon) \frac{d(n-1)}{n}
      \end{align*}
      as required.
      
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.494629+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cc0dddb7760abf212a455a84f79978f7553eac177655077c985b40a08031c6d8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 25 (Eigenvalue rigidity) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:rigidity}
Let \(A\) be a matrix such that \(A/\sqrt n\) has the distribution of GUE.
Let
\[
\lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_n
\]
denote its eigenvalues, and let \(\gamma_i\) be the corresponding classical
location for the semicircle law, defined by
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\gamma_i}
\frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{(4-x^2)_+}\,dx
=
\frac{i}{n}.
\]
Then for every \(1\leq i\leq n\),
\[
\mathbb P\left(
n^{-1/3}\min(i,n-i+1)^{1/3}
\left|\lambda_i-\sqrt n\,\gamma_i\right|
\geq T
\right)
\ll
n^{O(1)}\exp(-cT^c)
\]
for all \(T>0\), where \(c>0\) is an absolute constant.

In particular, with overwhelming probability,
\[
\lambda_i
=
\sqrt n\,\gamma_i
+
O\!\left(
n^{1/3}\min(i,n-i+1)^{-1/3}\log^{O(1)} n
\right),
\]
and the same estimate holds with \(\lambda_i\) replaced by
\(\mathbb E\lambda_i\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.163974+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cc1b2d0e0e60b2fab206e1bb831beb4f89e5103ec099debaccf925d39496b78b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 30 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall from Lemma~\ref{l:freeprob.V.convex} that $z_{\min}$ is the unique minimizer of $V$ on the interval $[z_0,\infty)$.
    We have $z_{\min} = z_0$ if and only if
    \beq
        
        \alpha \le \mu_1 \textup{ and } \hv_1 < 0\,.
    \eeq
    If \eqref{e:zmin-equal-z0} does not hold, $z_{\min}$ is the unique solution to the equation $V'(z) = 0$ for $z\in(z_0,\infty)$.

\begin{proof}
Recall that if $\hv_1 > 0$, then $V(z)\uparrow\infty$ as $z\downarrow z_0$, so in this case clearly $z_{\min} > z_0$.
If instead $\hv_1 < 0$, then $z_0 = \hw_1$, so we have $z_{\min}=z_0$ if and only if the derivative $V'$ stays nonnegative as $z\downarrow \hw_1$. To this end, recall that as $z\downarrow \hw_1$ we have $m(z)\uparrow\infty$, so
    \[\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j \bigg(
        \frac{\hv_j m(z)}{\alpha - \hv_j m(z)}\bigg)^2
        \longrightarrow \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j = 1\,.\]
We also have $m_2(z)/m(z)^2 \to 1/\mu_1$, and substituting into
\eqref{e:fp-V-pr} gives
    \[
        V'(z)
        \longrightarrow 1 - \frac{\alpha}{\mu_1}
    \]
   as $z\downarrow\hw_1$. This is nonnegative if and only if $\alpha \le \mu_1$, which yields the condition \eqref{e:zmin-equal-z0}. Otherwise, we must have $z_{\min} > z_0$; in this case, since $V$ is strictly convex and twice differentiable, the value $z_{\min}$ must be the unique solution to the equation $V'(z) = 0$ for $z\in(z_0,\infty)$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.162920+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cc7ad3a2d39adf29031059fb6218c5d64b385fbd66d6d353eb47316915f652fa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 of arXiv:2606.29512, '2606.29512'] A $\cV$-valued optional process

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.337196+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccbe3581e05a15199dae907a875ea2d18b230d43198309e129960eccd550e3be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 28 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] The two estimates on which the critical compactness argument rests are the following.

\textup{(i)} Let $\phi_0>0$ be the normalized local Dirichlet principal eigenfunction. For every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\sigma_\varepsilon>0$ such that
\[

for $0<\sigma<\sigma_\varepsilon$. Consequently $\Lp(\cA_{\sigma,2,L})\le\lambda_0+\varepsilon$.

\textup{(ii)} There exist constants $c_J,C_J>0$ such that
\[

Consequently, if $\sigma_n\to0$ and $u_n$ are supported in a fixed bounded interval with $\|u_n\|_2\le C$ and $E_{\sigma_n}(u_n)\le C$, then a subsequence converges strongly in $L^2(\R)$ to a function in $H^1(\R)$ supported in the same interval. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.352896+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ccec066ffa0ec9499357e450b8a09d076a5e7a35b2314061cdccc3fc37f950af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 198 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\cA$ be an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, and let $\bx(q_d)$ be as defined by
\eqref{e:x.q.mean}. Then
    \[
    \P\bigg(\bigg|
    \frac{(\bx(q_d),\bx(q_\ell))}{N}-q_{\min\{d,\ell\}}
    \bigg|\ge
    \frac{1}{N^{1/3}}\bigg) 
    \le \exp(-N^{0.1})\,.
    \]

\begin{proof}
This follows easily from gaussian Lipschitz concentration (see e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}).
Indeed note that $\|\cA(\bG,  \bg^\aux)\|_2\leq N^{1/2}$ almost surely, while by definition $\bx(q_d)$
is an $L$-Lipschitz function of the gaussian vector $(\bG(q_d),\bg^\aux(q_d))$. It follows that for $\ell \le d$, the normalized inner product
    \[\frac{(\bx(q_d),\bx(q_\ell))}{N}\]
is an 
 $O(LN^{-1/2})$-Lipschitz function of 
    \[\Big(\bG(q_\ell),
    \bg^\aux(q_\ell),
    \bG(q_d) - \bG(q_\ell),\bg^\aux(q_d) - \bg^\aux(q_\ell)\Big)\,.\]
 Therefore it concentrates around its mean by Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}, which gives the conclusion.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Counterexample: u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 versus (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 with left state 1 and right state 0","Rankine-Hugoniot: σ = [flux]/[density], so both entries matter","Chain-rule manipulations of the flux are valid only where the solution is C^1"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418709+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_cd2c0cd0a6c998918c8d20dec220a3380322e8bf670c19046ddde117aec30ea3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Rankine-Hugoniot condition, and hence the whole notion of weak solution, is attached to a specific pair (conserved density, flux) — not to the PDE as an equation for smooth functions. Two equations with identical classical solutions can have different weak solutions. Counterexample: for smooth u, Burgers' equation u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 is equivalent to (u^2/2)_t + (u^3/3)_x = 0 (multiply the first by u; conversely divide where u ≠ 0). But a jump from u_l = 1 (left) to u_r = 0 (right) travels with speed [f]/[u] = (1/2 - 0)/(1 - 0) = 1/2 for the first form, and with speed (1/3 - 0)/(1/2 - 0) = 2/3 for the second: the two weak solutions are genuinely different. The same phenomenon makes the nonconservative form u_t + u u_x = 0 meaningless across a shock (the product u u_x is not a distribution for discontinuous u). Physically, the model must specify which quantity is conserved; numerically, only schemes written in the conservative form of the true conserved quantity (Lax-Wendroff theorem) converge to the correct shock speeds. Auditor's check: when a proof rewrites the flux (multiplying the equation by a function of u, changing variables u = φ(v), or using a chain rule), the manipulation is legitimate for smooth solutions only; across discontinuities it changes the answer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.190407+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_cd8b3fd8a8f4ae722c7b30ce5ede1b8d61ec46e770d6d666a20852c38aba2023","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, specifically in homology theory and algebraic topology, cohomology is a way of attaching algebraic invariants to a topological space or other mathematical object that encode its properties in a way that is often computable. Cohomology is often related to questions of whether some local property of the space is obstructed when passing to a global property. For example, the Möbius strip is not the product space of a line segment with a circle, but locally on any segment of the circle it resembles an ordinary rectangle without the global twist. The obstruction to making the product structure global is encoded in the first cohomology of the underlying circle, which classifies the two inequivalent ways a line can twist around a circle. The fact that there are only two inequivalent ways of twisting a line around a circle is encoded in the relevant cohomology group which can be computed as isomorphic to the group where corresponds to an even number of twists, and to an odd number.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.544042+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cdc32c6a7be0c770379c13c38cb0e7ab1ad4655c10de13426f6d3ee3de387d5d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 32 (Monotonicity of angles) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Fix a finite graph $G$, some $\beta\in[0,\infty)$.
    Let $u$ denote some vertex, and let $E_u$ denote the set of edges incident to $u$.
    Pick
    \[
        \tau'=(\alpha',\omega',\eta')\in [0,\pi/2]^{V\setminus\{u\}}\times\{0,1\}^{E\setminus E_u}\times\{0,1\}^{E\setminus E_u},
    \]
    Let $\mu_{\tau'}$ denote the measure
    $\mu_{G,\beta}$ conditioned on \[\{\tau|_{(V\setminus\{u\})\times (E\setminus E_u) \times (E\setminus E_u)}=\tau'\}.\]
    Then the density of $\alpha_u$ on $[0,\pi/2]$ under $\mu_{\tau'}$
      is proportional to
    \begin{align}
        \textstyle
        \left(
        \prod_{\Gamma\in C(\omega')}
        \textstyle
        2\cosh(\beta\cos\alpha_u\sum_{v \in \Gamma}\cos\alpha_v')
        \right)
        \left(
        \prod_{\Gamma\in C(\eta')}
        \textstyle
        2\cosh(\beta\sin\alpha_u\sum_{v\in \Gamma}\sin\alpha_v')
        \right),
\end{align}
where $C(\rho)$ is the partition of $\{v\in V:v\sim u\}$ into $\rho$-connected components.

In particular, if $\mu^{\alpha_u}_{\tau'}$ denotes the law of $\alpha_u$ under $\mu_{\tau'}$, then
\[
    \tau'\preceq\tau''
    \qquad
    \implies
    \qquad
    \mu^{\alpha_u}_{\tau'}\leqstoch\mu^{\alpha_u}_{\tau''}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The conditioning events have positive probability.","The counterexample construction is reported, rather than proved within this record."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363363+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cdd80b44a9454466067d131fab9489ca2a0e9f1127b0248a98cd8979f501f40a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the boundary and condensation part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.3 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Use Janson's balls-in-boxes setting with weights w_j, generating function Phi, radius rho, Psi(t) = t Phi'(t)/Phi(t), nu = lim_{t up to rho} Psi(t), m/n -> lambda, pi the tilted law at tau = rho when lambda >= nu, and N_d the number of boxes with d balls. In the two regimes not covered by the finite-variance mean-conditioning theorem, (c) lambda = nu with sigma^2 = infinity and (d) lambda > nu, the natural analogue of the Gaussian limit has variance sigma_d^2 = pi_d(1-pi_d). In (d) the constraint is absorbed by the condensate rather than by the bulk. The record asserts that this analogue holds under regular variation of the tail, by the argument of Thevenin's Theorem 6.7 in case (d), and fails in general. Assuming those two theorems, a Gaussian limit for the box counts in regimes (c) and (d) does not hold without a further regularity condition on the tail. The record identifies local flatness of the tail at the scale the conditioning must supply as the dividing line. {"assumptions":["T is consistent","T is effectively axiomatized (computably enumerable axiom set)","T interprets Robinson arithmetic Q"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378582+00:00","domain":"mathematical logic","id":"claim_cde8bcbf7d8ce7708f2314743185825fb5c4235f909300f46e471371d1a885c8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a first-order theory satisfying all three hypotheses: (i) T is consistent; (ii) T is effectively axiomatized: its set of axioms is computably enumerable (equivalently, by Craig's trick, computably decidable after re-axiomatization), so theoremhood is computably enumerable; (iii) T interprets enough arithmetic - it suffices that T contains or interprets Robinson arithmetic Q. Then T is incomplete: there is a sentence G in the language of T (arithmetical under the interpretation) such that T proves neither G nor the negation of G. Consequently no consistent, effectively axiomatized theory interpreting Q is complete; in particular Peano arithmetic and ZFC, if consistent, are incomplete. Godel's original 1931 argument additionally assumed omega-consistency to rule out T proving the negation; Rosser's 1936 refinement, stated here, needs only consistency. All three hypotheses are necessary: complete consistent extensions of Q exist but are not effectively axiomatized (e.g. true arithmetic), effectively axiomatized complete consistent theories exist that do not interpret Q (e.g. the theory of dense linear orders, or Presburger arithmetic), and an inconsistent theory proves everything.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A increasing and depending on finitely many coordinates","product measure with a common density p","for general events use the Margulis-Russo form with signed summands"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543078+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce028eff08f7ef08cc636b492788f905d03b4c3fa8e4ee1b14f0bc0ea2dcd3a1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an INCREASING event depending on the states of a FINITE set E of edges, and let P_p be the product measure with density p. Then p -> P_p(A) is a polynomial in p, hence smooth, and d/dp P_p(A) = sum_{e in E} P_p( e is pivotal for A ) = E_p[ N(A) ], where N(A) is the number of pivotal edges. Equivalently the derivative is the TOTAL INFLUENCE. The monotonicity hypothesis matters: for a general event the correct statement is the Margulis-Russo formula d/dp P_p(A) = sum_e [ P_p(A with e open) - P_p(A with e closed) ], whose summands can be negative and which reduces to Russo's formula exactly when A is increasing. Russo's formula is the bridge from influence estimates - Kahn-Kalai-Linial, Talagrand, Friedgut-Kalai - to SHARP THRESHOLDS: a lower bound on the total influence of order log(1/(p(1-p))) forces P_p(A) to rise from eps to 1 - eps over a parameter window of width O(1/log n). [Russo (1981), Margulis (1974); see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.25]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The stated published minimum-location, tail, and limit theorems apply to this Poisson branching walk."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363927+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce056cd6340bc4912f6868fe54fad0f2450076e2feff0e1ef5d3b6511feace21","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the recursion is integrated exactly against two published closed-form values as a control] This is the campaign answer to Conjecture 1 of H. Stepanyants, P. L. Krapivsky, H. Hartle and D. Krioukov, The rank and layer distributions in random recursive trees, arXiv:2608.04303. Let the Poisson-weighted infinite tree have root position zero, with children of each vertex at the points of an independent rate-one Poisson process on (0,infinity), translated by their parent's position. Let M_k be the minimum position of generation k, and set M_0=0. Define s_0(y)=1 for y>=0 and s_k(y)=1-exp(-integral_0^y s_{k-1}(z)dz) for k>=1. Put bar_ell_k=integral_0^infinity s_k(y)exp(-y)dy and ell_k=bar_ell_k-bar_ell_{k+1}. In the source, ell_k is the limiting fraction of vertices in layer k of a random recursive tree, formed by joining each new vertex j uniformly to one of vertices 1,...,j-1; layer zero consists of the initial leaves, and subsequent layers are obtained by successive leaf removals. Let e be the base of the natural logarithm. There is a constant C_star in (0,infinity) such that bar_ell_k exp(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> C_star and ell_k exp(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> (1-exp(-1/e)) C_star. More precisely, if M_star denotes the distributional limit of M_k-[k/e+(3/(2e))log k] furnished by the cited branching-random-walk minimum theorem, then C_star=E[exp(-M_star)]. In particular both tails have order exp(-k/e) k^(-3/(2e)). The proof uses Addario-Berry and Ford's Poisson-Dirichlet branching random walks, Annals of Applied Probability 23 (2013), Theorems 1.1-1.2, and Aidekon's Convergence in law of the minimum of a branching random walk, Annals of Probability 41 (2013), as stated in the record. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_i independent, identically distributed, E X_1 = 0, Var X_1 = 1 (finite variance is essential)","convergence is in distribution in C[0, 1] with the uniform norm (or in D[0, 1] with the Skorokhod topology for the step process)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476597+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce0cd7266679161a8821c7246e4dad6e99fad5e929f3b7da95ca24c19e76a7e9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be independent and identically distributed real random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, and S_k = X_1 + ... + X_k. Then W_n converges in distribution, as a random element of C[0, 1] with the uniform norm, to a standard Brownian motion W on [0, 1]. Consequently, for every functional Phi : C[0, 1] -> R that is continuous almost surely with respect to the Wiener measure, Phi(W_n) converges in distribution to Phi(W): the law of the maximum of the walk, of its time spent positive, of its first hitting time of a level, all converge to the Brownian laws, whatever the increment distribution. Finite variance is essential; with infinite variance the limits are stable processes under different scaling.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.285568+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce2854bc46715b64a84e17e7e82c740cce538870a762eb52c14617533264e705","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 10 of arXiv:2608.21551, '\bf Sparse Separable Factor Analysis in the Complex Domain with an Application to Local Fi'] For $j=1,\ldots,d$, let $\Lambdab_j\in\CC^{p_j\times k_j}$ denote the true loading matrix and $\widehat{\Lambdab}_j$ denote its estimate. Define the orthogonal projectors onto their column spaces by

  \right)^+
  \Lambdab_j^\star,
  \qquad
  \widehat{\Pb}_j

  \left(
    \widehat{\Lambdab}_j^\star
    \widehat{\Lambdab}_j
  \right)^+
  \widehat{\Lambdab}_j^\star,
\end{align*}
where $+$ denotes the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse. The null-space projection error is
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{err}_{\Pb_j}^2
  &=
  \left\|
    \left(
      \Ib_{p_j}-\widehat{\Pb}_j
    \right)
    \Pb_j

\end{align}
Let
\begin{align*}
  r_j
  &=
  \operatorname{rank}(\Lambdab_j),
  \qquad
  \widehat{r}_j
  =
  \operatorname{rank}(\widehat{\Lambdab}_j),
  \qquad
  r_{\min,j}
  =
  \min(r_j,\widehat{r}_j).
\end{align*}
Denote the principal angles between the column spaces of $\Lambdab_j$ and $\widehat{\Lambdab}_j$ by
\begin{align*}
    0
  \leq
  \theta_{(j)1}
  \leq
  \cdots
  \leq
  \theta_{(j)r_{\min,j}}
  \leq
  \frac{\pi}{2}.
\end{align*}
Then,
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{err}_{\Pb_j}^2
  &=

{"assumptions":["Omega open in R^n","a^{ij} = a^{ji}, b^i, c real functions on Omega","lambda|xi|^2 <= a^{ij} xi_i xi_j <= Lambda|xi|^2 for uniform ellipticity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.147082+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations","id":"claim_ce331292e9dfb7e46eae58cc677d147b6511a99448713cb6fd049abdfc239c02","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega in R^n be open. A nondivergence-form operator is Lu = sum_{i,j} a^{ij}(x) D_{ij} u + sum_i b^i(x) D_i u + c(x) u with a^{ij} = a^{ji} real (symmetry is no loss because D_{ij}u is symmetric) and b^i, c real. L is elliptic at x if the matrix (a^{ij}(x)) is positive definite; lambda(x) denotes its smallest eigenvalue. L is uniformly elliptic with constants 0 < lambda <= Lambda if lambda|xi|^2 <= sum a^{ij}(x) xi_i xi_j <= Lambda|xi|^2 for all x (a.e. x for measurable coefficients) and all xi in R^n. Sign convention: here L = +Laplacian when (a^{ij}) = I, b = 0, c = 0, so the maximum principle concerns Lu >= 0 and the favorable sign of the zeroth-order coefficient is c <= 0 (the opposite of the divergence-form convention -div(A grad u) + c u with c >= 0). A classical solution of Lu = f is u in C^2(Omega) with Lu = f pointwise; a strong solution is u in W^{2,p}_loc(Omega) for some 1 <= p <= infinity with Lu = f almost everywhere. If the a^{ij} are C^1 (or Lipschitz), a^{ij} D_{ij} u = D_i(a^{ij} D_j u) - (D_i a^{ij}) D_j u rewrites L in divergence form; for merely measurable a^{ij} the two forms are different theories (De Giorgi-Nash-Moser for divergence form, Krylov-Safonov for nondivergence form).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:59.496825+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ce8217e70fdb06c744eabae51c069fc0b750d8aec4ee06dee28df6c628b24330","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 11 (Conditional first-break law and moments) of arXiv:2605.09641, 'The Ballot Event for Two-Player Coupon Collection: A Renewal--Catalan Asymptotic'] Let $K_d$ be the extended first-break level from

\[
        \E\left[\left(\frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\right)^p\right]

\[
        \E K_d\sim \frac{\sqrt\pi}{2}\sqrt d,
        \qquad
        \operatorname{Var}(K_d)\sim

\]
and the same expectation and variance asymptotics hold conditional on

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:13:22.513826+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cebac43e37aab5fd3a6ff3c520945d3e8cb4b923d1a12460d55a12c8c1761f6a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn H marginal of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] The locally commuting n chordal $\mathrm{SLE}_\kappa$ is a compatible family of measures $\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)}$ on $n$ tuples of continuous non-self-crossing curves $\left(\eta^{(1)}, \eta^{(2)},\ldots,\eta^{(n)}\right)$ for all simply connected domain $\Omega$ with $\left(z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)$, and $\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)$ as above that satisfy additionally the conditions below. 

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Conformal invariance}: If $\varphi: \Omega \rightarrow \Omega^{\prime}$ is a conformal map fixing 0, then the pullback measure
$$
\varphi^* \mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega^{\prime} ; \varphi\left(z_1\right), \varphi\left(z_2\right),\ldots,\varphi\left(z_n),\varphi(u)\right)\right)}^{\left(\varphi\left(U_1\right), \varphi\left(U_2\right),\right)}=\left(\mathbb{P}_{\left(\Omega ; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n\right)}\right) .
$$

Therefore, it suffices to describe the measure when $\left(\Omega ; z_1, z_2,\ldots,z_n,u\right)=\left(\mathbb{H}; z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_n,0\right)$.
We can extend our definition to arbitrary simply-connected domain $\Omega$ with a marked interior point $u$ by pulling back via a conformal equivalence $\phi:\Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$ sending $u$ to $0$.

\item
\textbf{Domain Markov property}: Let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{H} ; x_1, x_2,\ldots,x_n\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots, U_n\right)}$ and we parametrize $\gamma^{(j)}$ by their own capacity in $\mathbb{H}$. Let $\mathbf{t}=\left(t_1, t_2,\ldots,t_n\right)$, such that $t_j$ is a stopping time for $\gamma^{(j)}$ and $\gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}$ is contained in the interior of $U_j$. Let
$$
\tilde{U}_j=U_j \backslash \gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}, \quad \tilde{\gamma}^{(j)}=\gamma^{(j)} \backslash \gamma_{\left[0, t_j\right]}^{(j)}, \quad j=1,2,\ldots,n; \quad \tilde{\Omega}=\mathbb{H} \backslash\left(\gamma_{\left[0, t_1\right]}^{(1)} \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_2\right]}^{(2)} \cup \ldots \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_n\right]}^{(n)}\right) .
$$

Then conditionally on $\gamma_{\left[0, t_1\right]}^{(1)} \cup \gamma_{\left[0, t_2\right]}^{(2)} \cup \ldots \cup  \gamma_{\left[0, t_n\right]}^{(n)}$, we have
$$
\left(\tilde{\gamma}^{(1)}, \tilde{\gamma}^{(2)}, \ldots, \tilde{\gamma}^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\tilde{\Omega} ; \gamma_{t_1}^{(1)}, \gamma_{t_2}^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma_{t_n}^{(n)}\right)}^{\left(\tilde{U}_1, \tilde{U}_2, \ldots,\tilde{U}_n\right)} .
$$

\item \textbf{Absolute continuity with respect to independent SLE($\kappa$)}:
 In $\mathbb{H}$-uniformization, let $\left(\gamma^{(1)}, \gamma^{(2)},\ldots,\gamma^{(n)}\right) \sim \mathbb{P}_{\left(\mathbb{H} ; x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n,u\right)}^{\left(U_1, U_2,\ldots,U_n)\right.}$. 

We assume that there exist smooth functions $b_j: \mathfrak{X}^n(\boldsymbol{x},u) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, where the chamber: $$\mathfrak{X}^n(\boldsymbol{x},u)=\left\{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n,u) \in \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{H} \mid x_1<x_2<\ldots<x_n, u \in \mathbb{H} \right\}$$ 
such that the capacity parametrized Loewner driving function $t \mapsto \theta_t^{(j)}$ of $\gamma^{(j)}$ satisfies
\begin{equation} 
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\mathrm{~d} x_{j}(t)=\sqrt{\kappa} \mathrm{d} B_{j}(t)+b_j\left(x_{1}(t),x_{2}(t),\ldots,x_{n}(t),u\right) \mathrm{d} t \\
\mathrm{~d} x_{k}(t)=\frac{2}{x_{k}(t)-x_{j}(t)} \mathrm{d} t,  k\neq j
\end{array}\right.
\end{equation}
where $B_{j}$ is one-dimensional standard Brownian motion. 

\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:09:43.713102+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cebb0dc53d76d6380a38582e31b823f61940bfcd86841d35d9b8f8c2dbaf09ac","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l.xi-infnity of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $\xi :\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K} \times \hat\mathcal{N}_{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{K}} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a stabilizing marking function satisfying  $R^\xi_\infty(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}})<\infty$ a.s. for all $\tilde{x}\in\tilde{\mathcal{P}}$ and consider $\xi_\infty$ as defined in (equation scoreconvergence of the paper). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:42.300287+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cee543072473629441b91ef51c460c6ff61a63e7f9c8c712992ffa41242103d2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 (Markov Kernels) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Fix $d\ge 1$. Let $I$ be any locally compact additive subgroup of $\mathbb R^d$, for example $I=\mathbb R^d$ or $I=A \mathbb Z^d$ where $A$ is some nonsingular $d\times d$ matrix. Let $\mathcal B(I)$ denote the Borel $\sigma$-algebra on $I$. 
A \textit{Markov kernel} on $I$ is a continuous function from $I\to \mathcal P(I)$, where $\mathcal P(I)$ is the space of probability measures on $(I,\mathcal B(I))$ equipped with the topology of weak convergence of probability measures. 

Any Markov kernel $K$ on $I$ shall be written as $K(   x,A)$, which is identified with the continuous function from $I\to \mathcal P(I)$ given by $x\mapsto K(   x,\cdot)$. We denote by $\mathcal M(I)$ the space of all Markov kernels on $I$.

We equip $\mathcal M(I)$ with the weakest topology under which the maps $T_{f,   x}:\mathcal M(I)\to \mathbb R$ given by $$K\stackrel{T_{f,   x}}{\mapsto}  \int_I f(   y)\;K(   x,\mathrm d   y)$$ 
are continuous, where one varies over all $x\in I$ and all bounded continuous functions $f:I\to \mathbb R$. This topology endows $\mathcal M(I)$ with a Borel $\sigma$-algebra which allows us to talk about random variables taking values in the space of Markov kernels. For $   a\in I$ define the translation operator $\tau_a:\mathcal M(I)\to \mathcal M(I)$ by $(  \tau_{   a} K)(   x,A):= K(x+   a,A+   a)$ which is a Borel-measurable map on this space.","status":"unverified"}
