{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.014637+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cef10872bc2f7d729fa12f1c6c789e180896bd4785f1feb1ccccd89e8218c046","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 12 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] A limiting point \(\xi=(\mu_t)_{t<T}\) is \emph{based at \(q\)} with
respect to the limiting morphism \(\pi\) if
\(\pi_*\mu_t\rightharpoonup\delta_q\).  Such a \(q\) is unique when it
exists, and we denote it by \(q_\pi(\xi)\).  It is
\emph{Type-I based at \(q\)} if there is \(C_\xi<\infty\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \int_Xd_\eta(\pi(x),q)^2\,d\mu_t(x)\le C_\xi(T-t)
 \qquad\text{for every }0\le t<T.
\end{equation}
If \(q\in Y^{\rm rv}\) and \(\rho_q\) is a localized
squared-distance barrier from \cref{def:squared-distance-barrier},
compactness and the defining comparisons for \(\rho_q\) show that this
is equivalent to
\[
 \int_X\rho_q\circ\pi\,d\mu_t\le C'_\xi(T-t).
\]
For an arbitrary holomorphic map, qualitative basing alone need not
imply this rate.  For the semiample K\"ahler--Ricci flow considered here,
\Cref{lem:automatic-label} proves that every limiting point is based at
a unique point \(q_\pi(\xi)\) and is Type-I based there.  Thus
\eqref{eq:label-moment} is never an additional hypothesis below.  When
\(q_\pi(\xi)\in Y^{\rm rv}\), we simply say that \(\xi\) is based at
the regular value \(q_\pi(\xi)\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:57:07.195561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cef74e96596ef283e611f566c0a608052515901afd67e8fb8a1c4e010f1e18a9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:disagree-polymer-len-energy-decor of arXiv:2509.04333, 'The limiting law of the Discrete Gaussian level lines'] Let $(\gamma,\{D_i\},\{h_i\})$ be a labeled disagreement polymer. Its \emph{length} ${\ensuremath{\mathscr N}}(\gamma)$ and \emph{energy} 
		${\ensuremath{\mathscr E}}_\beta(\gamma)$ are defined as
		\[{\ensuremath{\mathscr N}}(\gamma)=\sum_{e\in\gamma}|(\nabla \phi)_e|\quad,\quad 
		{\ensuremath{\mathscr E}}_\beta(\gamma) := \beta\sum_{e \in \gamma} |(\nabla \phi)_e|^2\,.\]
		To describe the law of the disagreement polymer, we will use a family of decoration functions $\Phi$ on subsets ${\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}\subset \mathbb Z^2$---each referred to as a cluster if it is also connected---
        satisfying the following properties.
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item  If ${\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}$ is not connected, then $\Phi({\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}) = 0$.
			
			\item 
			The function $\Phi$ is translation invariant, as well as invariant under a rotation by $\pi/2$ or reflection with respect to one of the axes.
			
			\item There exists a constant $C > 0$ such that for every ${\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}$, we have 
			$
			|\Phi({\ensuremath{\mathsf W}})| \leq \exp(-(\beta - C){\ensuremath{\mathbf d}}({\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}))
			$, 
			where ${\ensuremath{\mathbf d}}({\ensuremath{\mathsf W}})$ is the size of the smallest connected set of bonds in $(\mathbb Z^2)^*$ containing all the boundary bonds of ${\ensuremath{\mathsf W}}$.
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.852191+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf4e894bd3d610bee648403add7690d7b5bd18b2231ba45c128f662a40570b6c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 of arXiv:2609.02017, 'Optimal girth-dependent bounds for the Bethe approximation of the permanent'] For every $e\in E$, define
\begin{align*}

  p_e\KL\bigl(

  \mathsf J_e^-
  &:=

  I(X_\star;E_e)=\mathsf J_e^++\mathsf J_e^-.
\]
For every $v\in V$, define
\[
  \mathsf J_v^+

\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:31:57.879788+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf7ceb7b9f663dd6dd55750949d787415cc1e49ab811d669ae7147b6c3730041","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition d:p-dir-structure of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] Let $p \in (1,\infty)$.
		We say that $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu,\mathcal{E}_p, \mathcal{F}_p, \Gamma_p)$ is a $p$-Dirichlet structure if it satisfies the following properties:
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item			\textbf{Probability space}: $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu)$ is a probability space and $\mathcal{F}_p$ is a subspace of $L^p(X,\mu)$ such that $\mathds{1}_X \in \mathcal{F}_p$.
			\item \textbf{Completeness:} 
			$\mathcal{E}_p$ is a semi-norm on $\mathcal{F}_p$ such that $\mathcal{F}_p$ is a Banach space when equipped with the norm $\norm{f}_{\mathcal{F}_p}=(\norm{f}_{L^p}^p+\mathcal{E}_p(f))^{1/p}$.
			\item \textbf{Homogeneity:} For all $f\in \mathcal{F}_p$ there exists a finite non-negative Borel measure $\Gamma_p \langle f \rangle$ on $X$ such that $\Gamma_p \langle f \rangle(X)= \mathcal{E}_p(f)$   and for all $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$
			\[
			\Gamma_p\langle \lambda f\rangle = |\lambda|^p \Gamma_p\langle f\rangle.
			\]
			\item \textbf{Absolute continuity of energy measure}:  For all $f \in \mathcal{F}_p$, we have $\Gamma_p \langle f \rangle \ll \mu$.
			\item \textbf{Sublinearity:} For every $f,g\in \mathcal{F}_p$ and $A\subset X$, 
			\[
			\Gamma_p\langle f+g\rangle(A)^{\frac{1}{p}}\le \Gamma_p\langle f\rangle(A)^{\frac{1}{p}}+\Gamma_p\langle g\rangle(A)^{\frac{1}{p}}
			\]
			\item \textbf{Chain rule:} For all $f\in \mathcal{F}_p$, $g\in \Lip(\mathbb{R})$ with $g(0)=0$,  we have $g \circ f \in \mathcal{F}_p$ and
			\[
			\Gamma_p\langle g\circ f\rangle  \le \left((\Lip_a[g] \circ f)(x)\right)^p   \,\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle.
			\]
			Note that the measure $\left((\Lip_a[g] \circ f)(x)\right)^p   \,\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle$ is well-defined due to the absolute continuity of energy measure; that is, this measure does not depend on the choice of $f$ from the $\mu$-a.e.~equivalence class.
			\item \textbf{Locality:} For every $f\in \mathcal{F}_p$ and any measurable  set $A\in \mathcal{X}$, if $f|_A=c$ $\mu$-a.e., then $\Gamma_p\langle f\rangle(A)=0$. In particular, $\Gamma_p \langle \mathds{1}_X \rangle$ is the zero measure.
			\item \textbf{Weak lower semicontinuity:} For every $f\in L^p(X)$, and for any sequence of functions $(f_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}\in \mathcal{F}_p$ such that $f_n\to f \in L^p(X)$ with $\sup_{i\in \mathbb{N}} \mathcal{E}_p(f_i)<\infty$, then $f\in \mathcal{F}_p$ and
			\[
			\Gamma_p\langle f \rangle(A)\le \liminf_{i\to \infty} \Gamma_p\langle f_i \rangle(A)
			\]
			for every measurable set $A\subset X$.
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["M a local martingale with M_0 = 0","for 0 < p < 1: M continuous","for p >= 1: cadlag suffices","constants depend on p only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627451+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf80a57cbccec160cd5893a5f18cbdc60f4fa6097c1a6f73d35f5f00697e2593","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let M be a local martingale with M_0 = 0, let M^*_T = sup_{t <= T} |M_t| for a stopping time T, and let [M] be the quadratic variation. There are constants 0 < c_p <= C_p < infinity depending ONLY on p such that c_p E[ [M]_T^{p/2} ] <= E[ (M^*_T)^p ] <= C_p E[ [M]_T^{p/2} ]. The admissible range of p differs by regularity: for CONTINUOUS local martingales the two-sided bound holds for every 0 < p < infinity; for general cadlag local martingales it holds for every p >= 1, and the case 0 < p < 1 genuinely requires continuity (Davis' theorem covers p = 1 in the general case). In discrete time the same holds with [M]_n = sum_{k <= n} (M_k - M_{k-1})^2 the square function, for 1 <= p < infinity. The constants are UNIVERSAL in the sense of depending on p alone - not on the martingale, the filtration, the time horizon or the dimension - and they blow up as p decreases to 0 and as p increases to infinity; explicit admissible choices grow like p for the upper constant. For p = 2 the inequality is an identity with c_2 = C_2 replaced by the Ito isometry together with Doob's L^2 maximal inequality, which is the cheap case one should reach for first. [Burkholder (1973), Davis (1970), Burkholder-Davis-Gundy (1972); see Revuz and Yor, Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion, 3rd ed., Theorem IV.4.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["finite nonempty dataset; n,d>=1,T>=2","fixed real tokens and queries, binary labels, fixed real linear prediction head","selected alpha has feasible unit-margin attention-SVM constraints"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:40:31.344626+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_cf8d74fcc402639c49dd012b15ca4089db49d860df217f5a64f6e8fd2cd32852","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n,d>=1 and T>=2 be integers. For each i in {1,...,n}, let tokens x_it in R^d, query z_i in R^d and label Y_i in {-1,+1} be fixed, and fix a linear prediction head v in R^d. Define token scores gamma_it=Y_i v^T x_it; globally optimal token indices satisfy opt_i in argmax_t gamma_it. Fix selected token indices alpha_i in {1,...,T}. Assume the attention-SVM constraints (x_i,alpha_i-x_it)^T W z_i>=1 for every i and every t!=alpha_i are feasible. Let W_alpha be the unique minimum-Frobenius-norm solution of these constraints, where ||W||_F=(sum_{a,b}W_ab^2)^(1/2). Equivalently it minimizes the squared Frobenius norm, a strictly convex objective. Define support indices T_i={t!=alpha_i:(x_i,alpha_i-x_it)^T W_alpha z_i=1}. The selection alpha is locally optimal exactly when gamma_i,alpha_i>gamma_it for every i and every t in T_i; W_alpha is then called a locally optimal direction. This condition compares the selected token only with support indices. It does not impose comparison with all non-support tokens. This card defines the fixed-head geometry; it makes no gradient-descent convergence assertion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.422230+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cf9d5414ce93b68a7025cbd5fd176c0416f9854412827a86cc46c878d932c689","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eq:fourier-f of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[definition]{def:function-classes}
Let \(\mathcal V_m\) be the class of \(V\in C^{m+1}(\mathbb R)\) such that \(\inf V> -\infty\) and
\[
 \max_{1\le r\le m+1}\norm{V^{(r)}}_\infty<\infty.
\]
Let \(\mathcal F_m\) be the Fourier--Wiener class of real-valued functions
\[
 f(x)=c+\int_\mathbb R e^{itx}\widehat f_0(t)\,\mathrm d t,
 \qquad c\in\mathbb R,
\]
where
\begin{equation}
 \int_\mathbb R(1+\left\lvertt\right\rvert^{m+1})\left\lvert\widehat f_0(t)\right\rvert\,\mathrm d t<\infty.
\end{equation}
Here \(\widehat f_0(-t)=\overline{\widehat f_0(t)}\), so \(f\) is real.

displayed integrability is exactly what the trace-derivative proof uses.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Little: f entire and nonconstant","Great: f holomorphic on a punctured disk about a with an isolated essential singularity at a"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:45:15.353295+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_cfb6b34b04c740458f4aa7f731e3fa6b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Little Picard theorem: if f is entire and nonconstant, then the complement of its image, C minus f(C), contains at most one point; i.e. a nonconstant entire function omits at most one complex value. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < r and has an essential singularity at a, then for every ε in (0,r) the image of the punctured disk 0 < |z - a| < ε is all of C with at most one point removed, and every value so attained (again with at most one exception) is attained infinitely often. Both exceptional values are genuinely possible and the count is sharp: exp(z) is entire and omits exactly the value 0, and exp(1/z) has an essential singularity at 0 and omits exactly 0 near 0. Meromorphic versions: a nonconstant meromorphic function on C omits at most two values of the Riemann sphere, and near an essential singularity a meromorphic function takes every spherical value with at most two exceptions. If f is entire and transcendental (not a polynomial), then f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.355215+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cfd81ecdaa3c5a3c302c41e90469fbd2e1f5ad909d87e45e351384f0a794fd8c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 220 (achievable measures) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $(b,\sigma,p) \in \sS \times \sP$, let $\mu(b,\sigma,p)$ denote the law of $X(1)$ given by the stochastic integral
    \beq

    \eeq
The \textbf{sets of achievable measures} 
for the Ising and spherical problems are defined to be 
    \begin{align*}

$\ocM^{\sph}(\alpha)$,
$\ocM^{\Ising, \concave}(\alpha)$, $\ocM^{\sph, \concave}(\alpha)$
 be the closures of these sets in the

{"assumptions":["consistency of the finite-dimensional distributions under permutation and marginalisation","the state space Polish (or otherwise inner regular by compacts); the theorem fails for general measurable spaces","the conclusion is on the PRODUCT sigma-algebra only"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781981+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_cff4b22d3f4e9f129de820bfc924fd6ae8ae16e1c64314c11984e1f4a5a4588a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be an arbitrary index set and suppose that for every finite subset {t_1, ..., t_n} of T a probability measure mu_{t_1, ..., t_n} on R^n (or on S^n for a Polish space S with its Borel sigma-algebra) is given. Suppose the family is CONSISTENT: (i) permuting the indices permutes the measure correspondingly, and (ii) the marginal of mu_{t_1, ..., t_n, t_{n+1}} on the first n coordinates is mu_{t_1, ..., t_n}. Then there is a probability measure P on the product space S^T equipped with the PRODUCT sigma-algebra whose finite-dimensional marginals are exactly the given family, and P is unique. TWO LIMITATIONS, both routinely forgotten. FIRST, the topological hypothesis is essential: for general measurable spaces the theorem is FALSE, and there are consistent families with no extension (Andersen and Jessen); what is really needed is that the marginals be inner regular in a suitable sense, which Polish spaces provide. SECOND, the resulting measure lives on the PRODUCT sigma-algebra, every member of which is determined by countably many coordinates. When T is uncountable, sets such as {the path is continuous}, {sup_t X_t <= c}, or {the path is bounded} are therefore NOT measurable for that sigma-algebra, so the theorem does not by itself construct Brownian motion as a continuous process; it constructs a process with the right finite-dimensional laws, and a separate regularity theorem - Kolmogorov's continuity criterion - is needed to produce a modification with continuous paths. [Kolmogorov (1933); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 2.1.21, and Billingsley, Probability and Measure, Section 36]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.477019+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d007b509b76b2574e8db1cb4d99bb511beec50788f3846f5da7d43e190951280","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For two probability measures mu and nu on a measurable space (S, A), the total variation distance is d_TV(mu, nu) = sup over A in A of |mu(A) - nu(A)|, a number in [0, 1]. If mu and nu have densities f and g with respect to a common reference measure lambda (which always exists, for instance lambda = mu + nu), then d_TV(mu, nu) = (1/2) integral |f - g| d lambda = 1 - integral min(f, g) d lambda, and the supremum is attained at A = { f > g }. Equivalent characterisations: d_TV is half the supremum of |integral h d mu - integral h d nu| over measurable h with |h| <= 1; and by the coupling characterisation, d_TV(mu, nu) = min P(X not equal to Y) over all couplings (X, Y) with X distributed as mu and Y as nu, the minimum being attained by the maximal coupling. Convergence in total variation is strictly stronger than weak convergence (point masses at 1/n converge weakly to the point mass at 0 but stay at total variation distance 1). The normalisation matters: some texts use the un-halved integral |f - g| d lambda, which lies in [0, 2].","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:18:19.413234+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d01e9fd6f5dc66be51d583a10eeae66e3e2da0fe0e97e13aeb3758562c676ade","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:qRacah_tilings of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] We put a probability measure on the set of all
	nonintersecting path ensembles. The measure depends on the
	geometry of the hexagon (parametrized by $(T,S,N)$), and
	on two parameters $q>0$ and $\kappa\in
	\mathbf{i}\mathbb{R}$.
	The
	probability weight of a nonintersecting path ensemble is
	proportional to
	\begin{equation}
		
		\prod_{\textnormal{holes in the path ensemble}} \mathsf{w}_{q,\kappa}\bigl( x-\tfrac t2+1\bigr),
		\qquad
		\mathsf{w}_{q,\kappa}(j) \coloneqq \kappa q^{j-(S+1)/2}-\frac{1}{\kappa q^{j-(S+1)/2}}.
	\end{equation}
	Here the holes are points $(t,x)$ such that $x\notin X(t)$,
	but $x$ satisfies the inequalities
	(equation eq:hexagon_constraints of the paper). In other words,
	holes are lozenges of the type
	\begin{tikzpicture}[baseline = (current bounding box.south),scale=.25]
		\draw[thick] (0,0)--++(1,1)--++(1,0)--++(-1,-1)--cycle;
	\end{tikzpicture}.
	For example, in (fig:tiling_and_path_picture of the paper), right, the holes are $(1,2),(2,1),(2,4),(3,0),(3,2),(3,5),(4,2),(4,3),(5,3)$.
	The probability weights are normalized so that the total probability of all path ensembles is $1$.
	We call the resulting probability measure the \emph{$q$-Racah measure} on nonintersecting path ensembles
	(equivalently, on lozenge tilings of the hexagon).","status":"unverified"}

\[
\operatorname{div}(f) := \sum_a \operatorname{ord}_a(f)[a]
\]

{"assumptions":["edges are present independently with the same probability p (the binomial model; the uniform model G(n,m) has the analogous statement with m = (n/2)(log n + c))","the statement is about the window p = (log n + c)/n with c fixed as n grows","the Poisson approximation is for the count of isolated vertices; other small components are negligible in this window"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049186+00:00","domain":"random graphs (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_d041dda48ec32c5f52986ec651884b81edb7100fb10f41b597a06330618dfc66","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the binomial random graph G(n,p) with p = (log n + c)/n for a fixed real c, the number of isolated vertices converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable with mean e^{-c} (the method of moments: the factorial moments of the count converge to those of the Poisson law), and the probability that G(n,p) is connected tends to exp(-e^{-c}) (Erdos and Renyi 1959, 1960). The obstruction to connectivity in this window is isolated vertices alone: P(G connected) - P(G has no isolated vertex) tends to 0. Consequently p = log n / n is a sharp threshold: for p = (1 - epsilon) log n / n the graph is disconnected with probability tending to 1 (with a growing number of isolated vertices), and for p = (1 + epsilon) log n / n it is connected with probability tending to 1. Below the threshold at p = c'/n with c' > 1 the graph already has a unique giant component but is disconnected.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["S symmetric positive semidefinite","the feasible set is nonempty (it always is: the simplex)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:16:12.170261+00:00","domain":"portfolio optimization / covariance estimation","id":"claim_d0a23007d09157190578bc34001ca8ab56a2324c0cee39b19878ff5e75ad0f46","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S$ be a symmetric positive semidefinite $M \\times M$ matrix (a sample covariance) and consider the long-only minimum-variance problem $\\min_w w^T S w$ subject to $\\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$ and $w \\ge 0$. Let $w^+$ be a solution and $\\delta \\in \\mathbb{R}^M$, $\\delta \\ge 0$, the Lagrange multipliers of the nonnegativity constraints ($\\delta_m > 0$ only where $w^+_m = 0$). THEOREM (Jagannathan and Ma, 2003). $w^+$ is also the UNCONSTRAINED minimum-variance solution (subject only to $\\mathbf{1}^T w = 1$) for the modified covariance $$\\tilde S = S - \\delta \\mathbf{1}^T - \\mathbf{1}\\delta^T,$$ which is symmetric, positive semidefinite on the relevant set, and differs from $S$ by lowering the covariances of the constrained (excluded) assets with every other asset by $\\delta_m$ and their variances by $2\\delta_m$. Imposing the no-short constraint is therefore equivalent to shrinking the large entries of the sample covariance toward zero by data-determined amounts - which is why the constraint improves out-of-sample risk even when the true covariance would not call for it (\"why imposing the wrong constraints helps\"): it acts as a covariance-shrinkage estimator whose amount is chosen implicitly by the optimisation, without cross-validation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:41:11.649386+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0b953cde21bb02b4b8e3d38e587b807a952d847c7a7db4d0208735c2b3b09c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm summary of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] Let $\gamma_L=(L-1)/\ell$. 
\begin{enumerate}[label={\normalfont(\arabic*)}]
\item The discrete in space processes DITP (resp. DFTP) converge, with quantitative control,  when $L$ tends to infinity, in Skorohod topology towards the continuous-space piecewise deterministic Markov process CITP (resp. CFTP).
\item The processes DITP and DFTP are exponentially ergodic with invariant measures converging as $L$ tends to infinity to the unique invariant measures of the CITP and CFTP.
\item The invariant measures of CITP and CFTP have a positive mass at $\{0\}\times \{-1,0,1\}$ and  $\{\ell\}\times \{-1,0,1\}$.
\item Let us define for a Markov process with semigroup $P_t$ and invariant measure $\pi$ its mixing time as
$t_\text{\normalfont mix}(\epsilon)=\inf\left\{t\ge0\,;\, sup_\mu\|\mu P_t-\pi\|_{TV}\le \epsilon\right\}$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\normalfont (a)] The mixing time $t_\text{\normalfont mix}(\epsilon)$ of CITP is of the order $C'(\epsilon)\frac 1\omega(1+\omega^2l^2)$ for some $C'(\epsilon)$.
\item[\normalfont (b)] The mixing time $t_\text{\normalfont mix}(\epsilon)$ of CFTP is of the order $C'(\epsilon)(\frac1\alpha+\frac1\beta)(1+\alpha^2l^2)$ for some $C'(\epsilon)$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:32:58.366231+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0bd827569040d5647978204537a30a1d9504aab10442edd8df16ffbabae68a0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 33 of arXiv:2506.20146, 'Parabolic Anderson Model in the Hyperbolic Space. Part I: Annealed Asymptotics'] Let $X$ be a locally convex, Hausdorff topological
(real) vector space and let $X^{*}$ be its topological dual. Suppose
that $F:X\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]$ is a lower semi-continuous,
convex function. Define $G:X^{*}\rightarrow(-\infty,\infty]$ by 
\begin{equation}
G(\lambda)\triangleq\sup\big\{_{X^{*}}\langle\lambda,x\rangle_{X}-F(x):x\in X\big\},\ \ \ \lambda\in X^{*}.
\end{equation}
If $F$ is not identically equal to $\infty,$ then one has 
\[
F(x)=\sup\big\{_{X^{*}}\langle\lambda,x\rangle_{X}-G(\lambda):\lambda\in X^{*}\big\},\ \ \ x\in X.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:10.199050+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0c3cb65b15ee11ea412de4476954cc557c6e39ff979512601d6bc2e3837af0a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 5 (Random environment) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] Let $(\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stationary ergodic sequence.

\[
\E[|\ell_0|]<\infty \qquad\text{and}\qquad
\E\!\Big[\bigl|\log\bigl(\p(\xi_{1,0}>0\mid\mathcal E_0)\bigr)\bigr|\Big]<+\infty,
\]
where $\xi_{1,0}$ denotes the number of offspring colonies of a single
colony given the environment $\mathcal E_0$ (see

  \item[(b)] If $\Lambda<0$, extinction is almost sure.

        extinction is almost sure.

{"assumptions":["(X, mu) is a measure space","the sets are measurable"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T07:49:53.248663+00:00","domain":"the symmetric-difference (Frechet-Nikodym) distance on measurable sets","id":"claim_d0da117483c01810993ee9f9b28c742923b9170388b7a408f5aabea94e9531b6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a measure space (X, mu) and measurable sets A, B, d_mu(A, B) = mu(A symmetric difference B), possibly infinite. For an increasing sequence E_1 in E_2 in ... with increments D_k = E_{k+1} minus E_k and union E, d_mu(E_m, E_n) = sum_{k=m}^{n-1} mu(D_k) for m <= n and d_mu(E_m, E) = sum_{k >= m} mu(D_k). Hence the following are equivalent: the sequence is d_mu-Cauchy; sum_{k >= m} mu(D_k) < infinity for some m; d_mu(E_m, E) < infinity for some m; d_mu(E_n, E) -> 0. Consecutive distances tending to zero are not enough: under the measure with weight 1/k at the point k, the chain E_n = {1, ..., n} has d(E_n, E_{n+1}) = 1/(n+1) -> 0 but is not Cauchy.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:57:59.663900+00:00","domain":"differential geometry","id":"claim_d0ded65864a60549061c918d8307a32a1781d949a58034d61d903ebe9b2407be","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let M be a compact, oriented, boundaryless smooth surface with Gaussian curvature K and area element dA. The Gauss-Bonnet theorem states that the integral over M of K dA equals 2 pi chi(M), where chi(M) is the Euler characteristic of M; for instance a topological sphere always has total curvature 4 pi, whatever its metric. If M has a piecewise-smooth boundary with geodesic curvature k_g and exterior angles theta_i at its corners, the formula generalizes to: integral of K dA over M, plus integral of k_g ds over the boundary, plus the sum of the theta_i, equals 2 pi chi(M). Due to Carl Friedrich Gauss and Pierre Ossian Bonnet.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.386594+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d0e74f929ce062ec42ed39aee3972e3d5cfb03147c9f5ca658e0a0b4d6c6e977","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:complexZero of arXiv:2608.18320, 'Asymptotics for Beta-Splitting Trees via Homogeneous Fragmentations and Meromorphic Potent'] Let $\beta>0$ be noninteger and let $      \beta=n_\beta+\theta_\beta$ with $       n_\beta=\lfloor\beta\rfloor$.

If $n_\beta$ is even, then $f_\beta$ has exactly $n_\beta$
nonreal zeros, counted with multiplicity. They occur in conjugate pairs.

Suppose that $n_\beta$ is odd. Let $q_\beta$ be the number of zeros
of $f_\beta$ in the upper half-plane, counted with multiplicity, and,
for $0\leq k\leq n_\beta+1$, let $M_k(\beta)$ be the total
multiplicity of the real zeros of $f_\beta$ in $\mathcal I_k$. Then
each $M_k(\beta)$ is odd and
\begin{equation}
        2q_\beta
        +
        \sum_{k=0}^{n_\beta+1}
        \left[M_k(\beta)-1\right]
        =
        n_\beta+1.
\end{equation}
In particular, $f_\beta$ has at most $n_\beta+1$ nonreal zeros,
counted with multiplicity.

Consequently, for every noninteger $\beta>0$, only finitely many zeros
of $f_\beta$ are nonreal or multiple. All the remaining zeros are real
and simple.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351868+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d12426fdfbbc66523751b41528059a535ae1c7d914220fbadbddbab890b7560a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 190 (quenched first moment bounds on $Q^\sigma$ and $Q^{\sigma,\frozen}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $Q$ as in Definition~\ref{d:Q}, we have
	$\bE[\Delta Q^\RomI(q_d)]
	\le L^{O(1)}(\MAX_N)^2\delta^2$
with $\MAX_N$ as in Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}. We also have
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
	\bE\Delta Q^\sigma(q_d)
	\le L^{O(1)}\bigg\{
	(\MAX_N)^2
	+ \frac{(\SMAX_N)^2 \BUCKETS}{N}
	\bigg\} \delta
	\]
with $\SMAX_N$ as in Proposition~\ref{p:drift.quenched}. The same bound holds for the $Q^{\frozen,\sigma}$ processes.
	
\begin{proof}
Recall that $Q^\sigma=E^\sigma+\tilde{Q}^\sigma$. It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:qv.simplification} that
	\[
	\Big|\Delta E^\sigma(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O\bigg(
	\eta^2
	+\eta\Big(\Delta\tilde{Q}^\sigma(q_d)\Big)^{1/2}
	+\Big( \Delta \bar{D}^\sigma(q_d)\Big)^2\bigg)\,.
	\]
For $\sigma=\RomI$, it follows by combining Lemma~\ref{l:barD.I.second.quenched} with Lemma~\ref{l:tQ.first.quenched} that
	\[
	\bE\Delta Q^\RomI(q_d)
	\le \bE\Delta \tilde{Q}^\RomI(q_d)
		+\bE\Big|\Delta E^\RomI(q_d)\Big|
	\le
	L^{O(1)} \bigg\{
	\eta^2 + (\MAX_N)^2\delta^2 \bigg\}\,.
	\]
For $\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$,
it follows by combining Lemmas~\ref{l:barD.II.second.quenched}--\ref{l:barD.Ising.second.quenched} with Lemma~\ref{l:tQ.first.quenched} that
	\[
	\bE\Delta Q^\sigma(q_d)
	\le\bE\Delta \tilde{Q}^\sigma(q_d)+ \bE\Big|\Delta E^\sigma(q_d)\Big| 
	\le L^{O(1)}\bigg\{
	\eta^2
	+(\MAX_N)^2\delta
	+ \frac{(\SMAX_N)^2 \BUCKETS\delta}{N}
	\bigg\}\,.\]
This proves the claim for the $Q^\sigma$ processes,
using that $\MAX_N\ge1$ and $\eta\ll\delta$. The analogous bound for the $Q^{\frozen,\sigma}$ processes follows by the same argument.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:42.311211+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d15da6a4586260dbc617f335a491888f92f0272d182719666fe63ee7e6afdb52","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] Let $U : \T^d \to \R^d$ with $U \in C^0(\T^d)$ and $y \in \T^d$.     \[R_t(y) := \sup_{X^1,\ X^2 \text{ solutions to~\eqref{eq:main ODE autonomous data}}}  d_{\T^d}(X^1_t, X^2_t).\]
    If, for some $t_0 >0,$ $R_t(y) = 0$ for all $t \in [0,t_0]$, then we say that $U$ is \textit{effectively regular at $y$}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.190977+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d16381197824c4d84ed42265a46bb1166ee1d3ff99103dd8cda53045ededb88d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 7 of arXiv:2606.31287, '\bf Heat kernel lower bound estimates for symmetric pure jump processes via averaged jump '] \begin{enumerate}

for any $x, y \in \sX$.
 

 \item[\rm (ii)]\,\,Let $D$ be an open subset of $\sX$. Define
\[

\[

{"assumptions":["Full-support verification in every variable context including paired S, without orientations","Independent fair algorithmic orientation tie coins; robust source Mis_infinity<=c on every data/coin outcome","All other hypotheses and sample protocol exactly as C013, specialized as stated"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:03:25.815424+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; verified truth supports","id":"claim_d17d974d73b26ffacf67c5e666254e1060bc965f7a41bc88aeee96c154a3cb86","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"OWNER-OWN-WORK DRAFT; proof (unaudited); independent review pending. # Positive-budget global risk differs from expected conditional minimax risk

T379-C014 v2: proof (unaudited), exact rational checks PASS. Target 2;
route-failure of a tempting extension, not a new exact global frontier.

Use the full-verifier, untagged experiment of C013 with d=3,K=2,r=1,
n=1,N>=7. Write lambda=1/(2N), kappa=1/2 and choose robust calibration
budget c=2lambda=1/N. The three pairs are numbered 0,1,2. Conditional
on the verifier output, relabel each certified candidate as 0. Each A
therefore has only candidate 0 true; S has both candidates true. This
relabeling preserves all factual probabilities. Fixed S contexts are
6,...,N-1. The verifier supplies no orientation labels.

One factual sample outside the certified sets resolves exactly one
pair; otherwise all three are unresolved. Thus P(U=3)=1-3lambda and
P(U=2)=3lambda, uniformly in every fixed world and verifier output.
C013's conditional worst-world frontier is zero at U=2 and lambda/2
at U=3. Its expectation is

 E V(c,U)=lambda/2-3lambda^2/2.                         (1)

## Feasible asymmetric algorithm

On U=2, use C013's attainer, removing all posterior mass 2lambda from
the unresolved outside-certificate atoms and adding it to fixed S.
This has zero false mass in every compatible world and Mis<=2lambda.

On U=3, leave pair 0 balanced. For each of pairs 1 and 2, if the factual
sample is a certified candidate in that pair, predict that its context
is A. Otherwise predict either orientation by an independent fair coin.
This is a rule using observed data only. Form two sets of outside-
certificate atoms:

* B1: both atoms of pair 0 and the predicted-S atom of pairs 1 and 2;
* B2: the predicted-A atom of pairs 1 and 2.

Assign g=lambda/4 to each of B1's four atoms, g=0 to B2's two atoms,
g=3lambda/2 to each of the six certified atoms, and
g=lambda+lambda/(N-6) to each of the 2(N-6) fixed S atoms.
These masses sum to lambda+9lambda+2(N-6)lambda+2lambda=1.

For ANY compatible orientation let t be the number of true S atoms
in B1 from pairs 1 and 2. The source mass of B1 is lambda(1+t),
that of B2 is lambda(2-t), and that of the six certified atoms is
9lambda, all with the latter group assigned equal g. The fixed S
group receives exactly 2lambda extra g mass. Uniformly coarsening p
within these four groups gives TV to g equal to

 [t lambda+(2-t)lambda+2lambda]/2=2lambda.

Each group has constant g; the exact score partition can only merge
groups. Uniform averaging is TV-contractive and fixes g, so actual
source Mis_infinity<=2lambda even at N=8 where two scores coincide.
This verifies robust feasibility for every orientation and every coin
realization, without assuming that the orientation predictions are right.

Let E be the number of wrong orientation predictions in pairs 1 and 2.
Exactly one atom of pair 0 is false. Therefore on U=3 the ACTUAL false
mass is

 H=(lambda/4)(1+E).                                   (2)

For example, if both predictions happen to be right, H=lambda/4 is
strictly below the conditional minimax value lambda/2. For the opposite
orientations the same generator has H=3lambda/4. Thus a conditional
worst-world lower bound is not a lower bound in each actual world.

## Expectation in each fixed world

The one-sample categories below are disjoint. Each expected H averages
only the algorithm's independent fair tie coins; their probabilities
are factual sampling probabilities in a fixed actual world.

| Observation | Probability | Expected H |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outside certificate in any S of the three pairs | 3lambda | 0 |
| Certified atom in pair 0 | 3lambda | lambda/2 |
| Certified atom in true A of pair 1 or 2 | 4lambda | 3lambda/8 |
| Certified atom in true S of pair 1 or 2 | 2lambda | 5lambda/8 |
| Fixed S context | 1-12lambda | lambda/2 |

Multiplying and summing gives, in EVERY fixed world and conditional
on EVERY verifier realization,

 E H=lambda/2-7lambda^2/4
     < lambda/2-3lambda^2/2=E V(c,U),                  (3)

with strict gap lambda^2/4=1/(16N^2). Thus the global minimax expected
value is at most the left expression and is strictly below the expected
conditional worst-world value. For N=7 these values are 3/112 versus
11/392, separated by 1/784. No optimality of this algorithm is asserted.

This does not contradict C013, whose exact GLOBAL value was asserted
only at c=0; its positive-budget conditional statement and global bracket
remain intact. This auxiliary-route counterexample is not claimed to
score as a target narrowing. Source calibration definition: Kalai--
Vempala 2311.14648v3, Definitions 1--2 pp.8--9. All other work here is
an owner-own-work unaudited draft. Priority and independent audit pending.

Exact verification: logs/positive_budget_separation_check.json records
13824 compatible-world feasibility checks, 1920 sample/coin outcomes,
32 fixed-world expectation checks and 384 pointwise negative controls.
The runs include N=7,8,9,12; N=8 checks the merged-score case directly.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:36:23.134099+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d194b3d064b052a65f243782076070b4a27cbb94744ff15e5bd7ecc64100ab1c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem MainSeriesKeyLem of arXiv:2506.18207, 'Cartan's Path Development, the Logarithmic Signature and a Conjecture of Lyons-Sidorova'] Let $L_{1},\cdots,L_{r}$ be given vectors
of positive integers and let $n_{0}\geqslant1$. Suppose that $|L_{1}|+\cdots+|L_{r}|+n_{0}=k\leqslant N.$
Then one has 
\begin{align}
 & \sum_{\xi_{0}+\xi_{1}+\cdots+\xi_{r}=l-r}{\rm ad}_{A}^{\xi_{r}}\circ{\rm ad}_{\hat{F}_{w}(H_{L_{r}})}\circ\cdots\circ{\rm ad}_{A}^{\xi_{1}}\circ{\rm ad}_{\hat{F}_{w}(H_{L_{1}})}\circ{\rm ad}_{A}^{\xi_{0}}\big(\hat{F}_{w}(D_{n_{0}}\tilde{L})\big)\nonumber \\
 & =\sum_{i}\sum_{\mu=1}^{r+1}\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}\cdot(b_{i}^{i+n_{0}^{\mu-1}-1})^{l+1-\mu}\nonumber \\
 & \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \sum_{I\in{\cal W}_{\mu,r}}\frac{(-1)^{\varepsilon(I)}\Psi_{I,n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf L}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}\cdot}{b_{(i_{\mu}),n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf n}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}b_{(i_{\mu},i_{\mu+1}),n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf n}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}\cdots b_{I,n_{0}^{\mu-1}}^{{\bf n}_{{\bf p},{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}}}E_{i-|{\bf n}_{{\bf p}}^{\mu,r}|,i+n_{0}^{\mu-1}+|{\bf n}_{{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}|}.
\end{align}
Here \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{W}_{\mu,r}$} denotes the set of words $I=(i_{\mu},i_{\mu+1},\cdots,i_{r})\in\{\pm1\}^{r-\mu+1}$. Given such a word $I$, the vector $\mathbf{p}$
denotes the subword of $(\mu,\cdots,r)$ which records the locations
of $-1$'s in $I$ and ${\bf q}\triangleq(\mu,\cdots,r)\backslash{\bf p}$.
The quantity $\varepsilon(I)$ denotes the length of ${\bf p}$ (i.e.
number of $-1$'s in $I$). The function $\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}$
is defined by 
\[
\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}\triangleq\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0},i}(b_{i},b_{i+1},\cdots,b_{i+k-1}),
\]
where $\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0},i}$ is a suitable meromorphic
function in $m$ complex variables ($m\triangleq n_{0}+|L_{1}|+\cdots+|L_{\mu-1}|$)
whose shape depends on $(L_{1},\cdots,L_{\mu-1}),n_{0}$ and $i$.
The family $\{\Theta_{L_{1},\cdots,L_{\mu-1},n_{0}}^{i}\}$ of functions
satisfy the following property: for any integer $i$, $1\leqslant\nu\leqslant r$
and any sequence of vectors ${\bf V}=(V_{1},\cdots,V_{r})$, under
the one-dimensional reduction $b_{j}\triangleq b_{j}^{*}+w$ the function
\begin{equation}
w\mapsto\sum_{\sigma\in{\cal S}_{\nu}}\Theta_{V_{\sigma(\nu)},\cdots,V_{\sigma(1)},n_{0}}^{i}
\end{equation}
is analytic near $w=0$ and vanishes at $w=0$. When $\mu=1,$ the
function $\Theta_{L_{\mu-1},\cdots,L_{1},n_{0}}^{i}$ depends only
on $n_{0}$ and $i$. As a convention, if $\mu=r+1$ the summation
$\sum_{I\in{\cal W}(\mu,r)}$ in ((lem:MainSeriesKeyLem of the paper)) is
set to be one and $|{\bf n}_{{\bf p}}^{\mu,r}|=|{\bf n}_{{\bf q}}^{\mu,r}|\triangleq0$
. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["1 < p <= q < infinity and e^{-t} <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))","the standard Gaussian measure and the generator normalisation L = Laplacian minus x . gradient","the constant in the contraction is exactly 1 and is dimension-free"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d1cf7dae8a836624c27473f7845ae1273f14a2ce5a18a3ccc841f38670804eeb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (P_t) be the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup on L^p of the standard Gaussian measure on R^n. For 1 < p <= q < infinity, || P_t f ||_q <= || f ||_p for every f, PROVIDED e^{-t} <= sqrt( (p-1)/(q-1) ). The constant is exactly 1 - the semigroup is a contraction from L^p to the strictly larger L^q, not merely bounded - and the condition on t is sharp. Two consequences used constantly: taking p = 2 gives || P_t f ||_q <= || f ||_2 for e^{-t} = 1/sqrt(q-1); and restricting to the n-th Wiener chaos, where P_t acts as multiplication by e^{-nt}, gives the MOMENT COMPARISON || F ||_q <= (q-1)^{n/2} || F ||_2 for every F in the n-th chaos and every q >= 2. That comparison is dimension-free and is the reason all L^q norms on a fixed chaos are equivalent, with a constant depending only on the chaos order and q. GROSS'S THEOREM: hypercontractivity of (P_t) with these exponents is EQUIVALENT to the logarithmic Sobolev inequality Ent(f^2) <= 2 E|grad f|^2 for the same measure; each implies the other by differentiating or integrating the relation at q = q(t). The discrete-cube analogue with the noise operator is the Bonami-Beckner inequality, and the Gaussian case follows from it by the central limit theorem. [Nelson (1966, 1973); Gross (1975); see Bakry, Gentil and Ledoux, Analysis and Geometry of Markov Diffusion Operators, Chapter 5]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:25:12.198226+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d229e7042ba7e7cd9df0d40cc0793788f973a0393f8086f8fd1447474d9abe0f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 46 of arXiv:2510.22783, 'Universality of Cutoff for Riffle Shuffling'] Consider the set $\mathcal M$ of $(N-i+\iota(p)+y_{p,i}-1)\times K$ matrices with entries in $[k]_0$ such that:
        \begin{enumerate}
            \item The first $n^{\rem}$ rows start with $\p$.
            \item The first $n^{\rem}$ rows are lexicographically greater than or equal to $s_i$.
            \item Among the first $n^{\rem}$ rows, at least $y_{p,i}$ are equal to $s_i$.
            \item For every $t\in [K]$ and $j\in [k]_0$, the number of $j$-digits in the $t$-th column is exactly $n_j^{(t),\rem}$ .
        \end{enumerate}
        We then select uniformly at random a matrix from $\widehat{\mathcal{M}}$.
        For each\footnote{Note the fourth condition above with $t=1$ and $j=\p$ implies that \emph{only} the first $n^{\rem}$ rows begin with $\p$; recall $n^{\rem}=n^{(1),\rem}_{\p}$.} $j \in [n^{\rem}]$, denote by $\widehat{s}_j$ the $j$-th row of the selected matrix. 
        If we sort $\{\widehat{s}_j\}_{j \in [n^{\rem}]}$ into increasing lexicographic order, writing the result as $(\overline{s}'_j)_{j \in [n^{\rem}]}$, then we have
        \[
            (\overline s'_{1}, \ldots, \overline s'_{n^{\rem}}) \overset{\mathrm{law.}}{=} (s_{i-y_{p,i}+1},s_{i-y_{p,i}+2},\ldots,s_{\tau(p)})
            \text{\emph{ conditioned on $\mathbf a_i$,}}
        \]
        which gives a natural coupling between the two sequences of strings with $\overline{s}'_{j}=s_{j+i-y_{p,i}}$ for each $j \in [n^{\rem}]$, and thereby between the set $\{\widehat{s}_j\}_{j \in [n^{\rem}]}$ and the sequence $(\overline{s}_{j+i-y_{p,i}})_{j \in [n^{\rem}]}$. 
        We denote this natural coupling by $Q$.
        In particular, the distribution of $\left|\cI(B_x)\right|$ conditioned on $\mathbf a_i$ coincides with that of $\left|\{j \in [n^{\rem}] : \widehat{s}_j \in B_{x}\}\right|$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.172936+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d243b4959dfd7e7460c2fc178f0421f2cd926005a7671c561fb675cb6606f1ba","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 70 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $q_0 \in [0,1)$ and $p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$, 
the mapping $f\mapsto \cM(q_0;p,f)$,
as a function from
 $L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$ to $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$, is uniformly continuous:
    \[
        d_\cH\Big(\cM(q_0;p,f),\cM(q_0;p,\tilde f)\Big)^2
        \le 2 \|f-\tilde f\|_1\,,
    \]
where we recall that $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$ is metrized by the Hausdorff distance \eqref{e:hausdorff}. As a consequence, we have the inclusion  $\sM^{\sv}(\alpha,q_0)\subseteq\sM^{\svi}(\alpha,q_0)$.

\begin{proof}
Let $f,\tilde f \in L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$, and suppose $(b,\sigma)\in\Adm(q_0;p,f)$. Let
	\[
	a(t)
	\equiv \min\bigg\{
	\bigg(\frac{\tilde{f}(t)}
	{f(t)}\bigg)^{1/2}
	,1\bigg\} \in[0,1]\,,
	\]
so in particular if $f(t)=0$ then we take $a(t)=1$. Then define $\tilde{b}_t\equiv a(t) b_t$, and $(\tilde{\sigma}_t-1)\equiv a(t)(\sigma_t-1)$, and note that $\sigma\ge0$ implies
$\tilde{\sigma}_t \ge 1-a(t)\ge0$.  By definition, $(\tilde{b},\tilde{\sigma})$ satisfies condition~\eqref{e:budget-f}, hence it belongs to $\Adm(q_0;p,f)$ as specified by Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}. Let $X,\tilde{X}$ be the 
processes defined by 
\eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(b,\sigma)$ and $(\tilde{b}, \tilde{\sigma})$ respectively, coupled with the same initialization
$X(q_0) =\tilde{X}(q_0) = 0$ and the same Brownian motion $B$. Then, applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality similarly as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:L2-bound-on-stochastic-control}, we have
    \begin{align*}
       &\bbE\Big[(X(1) - \tilde{X}(1))^2\Big]
        \le 2 \bbE\bigg[ \bigg(
            \int_{q_0}^1
            p'(t)^{1/2} |b_t - \tilde b_t|\,dt
        \bigg)^2 \bigg]
        + 2 \int_{q_0}^1 
        s(t)^2
        \bbE\Big[ (\sigma_t
        -\tilde{\sigma}_t
        )^2\Big]\,dt \\
    &\qquad\le 2 \int_{q_0}^1
    \E\bigg[ (b_t - \tilde b_t)^2
    + s(t)^2 
    \Big( (\sigma_t-1)
    -(\tilde{\sigma}_t-1)\Big)^2\bigg]\,dt \\
    &\qquad= 2 \int_{q_0}^1
    (1-a(t) )^2
\E\Big[(b_t)^2 + s(t)^2 
(\sigma_t-1)^2\Big]\,dt \\
&\qquad\le
2 \int_{q_0}^1 (1-a(t) )^2
	 f(t)\,dt
	 \le 2\int_{q_0}^1 \Big(f(t)^{1/2}-\tilde{f}(t)^{1/2}\Big)^2\,dt
\le 2\|f-\tilde{f}\|_1\,.
\end{align*}
This proves the first assertion of the proposition.
For the second assertion, we repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification}:
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tabular}[h]{r|cccccccc}
	\MSRheader\\
	\hline

	\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
The $\sv$ and $\svi$ classes  differ only in the budget constraint: the $\sv$ class satisfies condition~\ref{it:4.1}, while the $\svi$ class satisfies condition~\ref{it:4.3}. Therefore, let us suppose we have 
	\begin{align*}
	&(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta=\delta_0,\zeta^\Ising)
	\in
	\Adm^{\sv}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\,,\\
	&\mu = \mu(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,p,\zeta=\zeta_0)
 \in \cM^{\sv}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\,.\end{align*}
Define the budget functions
        \[
        f(t) = \max\bigg\{
            \bbE\bigg[
            (b_t)^2 + \frac{s(t)^2}{p(t)}(\sigma_t-1)^2\bigg],
            \frac{(\bbE w_t)^2}{\alpha}
        \bigg\}, \quad
        \tilde f(t) =\frac{(\bbE w_t)^2}{\alpha}\,.
    \]
Then, using the notation of
Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}, we have

{"assumptions":["f lower semicontinuous AND bounded below (boundedness below can be relaxed to a linear minorant);","the approximation is from BELOW and increasing.","For an upper semicontinuous f bounded above the dual sup-convolution gives a decreasing sequence of Lipschitz functions."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:01:51.298930+00:00","domain":"real analysis, convex analysis","id":"claim_d260b03e2f3333274936e1cd451507f7f128ecfe5257b820323708fee2f6bbf4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,d) be a metric space and let f : X -> (-infinity, +infinity] be lower semicontinuous and bounded below. For each n define f_n(x) = inf over y in X of ( f(y) + n d(x,y) ). Then each f_n is real-valued and n-Lipschitz, the sequence is nondecreasing, f_n <= f for every n, and f_n(x) increases to f(x) at every x. So a lower semicontinuous function bounded below is the pointwise increasing limit of Lipschitz functions. On a Hilbert space with the quadratic kernel (1/(2t))||x-y||^2 in place of n d(x,y) the same construction gives the Moreau envelope of a convex f, which is convex, differentiable with Lipschitz gradient, and increases to f as t decreases to 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Injectivity of the solution map does not imply continuity of its inverse","The range of the forward solution operator is a proper dense subspace","Conditional (Holder) stability requires an a priori bound at the initial time and degenerates as t tends to 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.107167+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / inverse problems","id":"claim_d293093269857df5a07b55e84088e12c20119ec34fc0008386b758c4e986eecc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Backward uniqueness says the map from $u(\\cdot,T)$ to $u(\\cdot,0)$ is injective; it says nothing about continuity of that map or about its range, and both fail badly -- the backward heat problem is the standard ill-posed problem of Hadamard. (1) No stability: on $U=(0,\\pi)$ with Dirichlet data, $u_k(x,t)=e^{-k^2t}\\sin(kx)$ has $\\|u_k(\\cdot,T)\\|_{C^m}\\le k^me^{-k^2T}\\to0$ for every $m$ while $\\|u_k(\\cdot,0)\\|_{L^2}=\\sqrt{\\pi/2}$ is fixed. Hence there is no estimate $\\|u(\\cdot,0)\\|\\le C\\|u(\\cdot,T)\\|$ in any pair of norms, and numerical backward continuation must be regularized. (2) No solvability: $e^{T\\Delta_D}$ has range $\\{\\psi=\\sum_kc_k\\sin(kx):\\sum_k e^{2k^2T}c_k^2<\\infty\\}$, a dense but meagre subspace of $L^2$; for instance $\\psi(x)=\\sum_{k\\ge1}k^{-2}\\sin(kx)\\in L^2$ is not $u(\\cdot,T)$ for any solution with $u(\\cdot,0)\\in L^2$, since that would require coefficients $e^{k^2T}k^{-2}$ at time $0$. Backward-in-time data must be analytic-like (exponentially decaying spectral coefficients). (3) What does survive is conditional stability of logarithmic or Holder type: under the a priori bound $\\|u(\\cdot,0)\\|_{L^2}\\le M$, log-convexity gives $\\|u(\\cdot,t)\\|_{L^2}\\le M^{1-t/T}\\|u(\\cdot,T)\\|_{L^2}^{t/T}$ for $0<t<T$, with the estimate degenerating exactly as $t\\downarrow0$. An auditor should flag any argument that uses backward uniqueness to produce a bound at the earlier time without such an a priori bound.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:28:31.956427+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d2a9e70959b1c8a582e28d14730d309dc2944262d3b876889a7da3be1d5495f2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 14 of arXiv:2512.01483, 'Scaling Limits of Line Models in Degenerate Environment'] Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$. $$\Phi(\lambda) = \lambda^\alpha, \qquad \lambda \geq 0. $$
We call double-sided stable subordinator of index $\alpha$ the process $(Z(x))_{x \in \mathbb{R}}$ where 
\[Z(x) = \begin{cases}
Z_+(x), \quad &x \geq 0 \\
Z_{-}(-x), \quad &x < 0
\end{cases}\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:19:42.520126+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d2d8c3ccfbbf29bfc118b884d6014c1fda9671c8251a6de5d67b72f021c52116","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2609.03495, 'Spectral Characteristics of Autoencoder Parameters as a Vector Representation of Data'] Let three datasets be given: ${\mathbf{X}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}}$, ${\mathbf{X}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}}$, and ${\mathbf{X}_3 \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}}$; let their singular values be positive: ${\sigma_i^{\text{data}}(\mathbf{X}_c) > 0 ~~~ \forall i \in \overline{1, d}}$.

Let two new datasets be obtained by mixing vectors from the third dataset into each of the first two datasets: ${\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_c = [\mathbf{X}_c, \mathbf{X}_3] \in \mathbb{R}^{(n+m) \times d}, ~~~ c \in \{1, 2\}}$.

Suppose that an autoencoder model with fully connected layers without nonlinear activation functions and latent dimension $k$ is trained on each dataset, minimizing the loss function
${\min_{\boldsymbol{\psi}_c}(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\psi}_c)) = \min_{\boldsymbol{\psi}_c} \|\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_c - \tilde{\mathbf{X}}_c\mathbf{W}_{c}^{enc}\mathbf{W}_{c}^{dec\top}\|_F^2}$
with a regularization term of the form ${\|\text{cov}(\mathbf{h}) - \mathbf{I}\|^2}$, which decorrelates the vectors $\mathbf{h}$ in the latent space, i.e., ${\text{cov}(\mathbf{h}) \sim I}$.

Then the mean squared difference between the singular values of the parameters of the autoencoders with parameters $\mathbf{W}^{enc}_1$, $\mathbf{W}^{dec}_1$, $\mathbf{W}^{enc}_2$, $\mathbf{W}^{dec}_2$ decreases as $m$ increases:
\[
\|\sigma_i^{\text{model}}(\mathbf{W}^{enc}_1) - \sigma_i^{\text{model}}(\mathbf{W}^{enc}_2)\|_2 \underset{m \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} 0,
\]
Consequently, as the datasets converge, both their singular values and the singular values of the parameters of the autoencoders trained on these datasets converge as the number of rows $m$ tends to infinity. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:47:40.724893+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d2e426de2a9c0d1dbe287a9371a28ce378b2e17f3678959dc89051396af941a4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:cluster_expansion of arXiv:2604.18558, 'Uniform analyticity of local observables in FK-percolation and analyticity of the Ising sp'] Assume that for $\epsilon > 0$ small enough, there exists a constant $C_\epsilon > 0$, going to 0 when $\epsilon$ tends to 0, such that for any $|z| < \epsilon$, for every polymer $\gamma \in \mathsf{P}^L_N$, 
\[
|\mathsf{w}_z(\gamma)| \leq C_\epsilon \exp( - |\gamma|(1 + c(d))).
\]
Then, there exists $\epsilon > 0$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
\item For all $|z| < \epsilon$, the following equality is true, and the sum appearing in the right-hand side converges absolutely:
\[
\Xi(\mathsf{w}_z) = \exp\big( \sum_{n\geq 1}\sum_{\gamma_1, \cdots, \gamma_n \in \mathsf{P}_N^L} \varphi_n(\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_n) \prod_{k = 1}^{n} \mathsf{w}_z(\gamma_k) \big). 
\]
We then say that $\Xi(\mathsf{w}_z)$ admits a \textit{convergent cluster expansion}.
\item Moreover, there exists $c_\epsilon > 0$, going to 0 when $\epsilon$ goes to 0 such that for any $|z| < \epsilon$, and all $N \in \mathbb N$,
\[
\sum_{n\geq 1}\sum_{\gamma_1, \cdots, \gamma_n \in \mathsf{P}_N^L} \big|\varphi_n(\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_n)\big| \prod_{k = 1}^{n} \big|\mathsf{w}_z(\gamma_k)\big| \leq c_{\epsilon} |\mathbb T_N^L| . 
\]
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:48:30.920892+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d2ee27e3fff78f733aab52028fa5098ce9d2e317533b205d04d28538bd7ce8b0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 12 (Partial Fraction Decomposition, {\cite[Theorem 2) of arXiv:2609.00974, 'On Algebraic Integrability\\ of Vector Fields \\ with Rational Function Coefficients\\ tha'] {PFD_euclidean_1989}}]
    Let $k$ be a field of any characteristic.
    Let $f\in k(x)$ be a rational function. Let $f=\frac{a}{b}$ be a presentation of $f$, where $a,b\in k[x]$ and $(a,b)=1$. Let $b=\prod_{i=1}^n p_i^{m_i}$ be a decomposition into pairwise distinct irreducible factors. Then, there exists the \textbf{partial fraction decomposition} (PFD) of $f$:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item A polynomial $Q\in k[x]$.
        \item For each $1\le i\le n$ and $1\le j\le m_i$ a polynomial $s_{ij}\in k[x]$ with $\op{deg}(s_{ij})<\op{deg}(p_i)$.
    \end{itemize}
    These polynomials are\textbf{ unique} such that the following equality holds:
    \[
    f=Q+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^{m_i} \frac{s_{ij}}{p_i^j}.
    \]
    In particular, if $k$ is algebraically closed, then, without any loss of generality, we can assume that $p_i=x-a_i$, so $s_{ij}\in k$ and we define:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Polynomial Part: $P(f)=Q$
        \item Logarithmic Part: $L(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{s_{i1}}{x-a_i}$, and we call $s_{i1}$ the residue of $f$ at $a_i$.
        \item Higher Part: $H(f)=\sum_{i>1}^n\sum_{j=1}^{m_i} \frac{s_{ij}}{{(x-a_i)}^j}$
    \end{enumerate}
    In total, we have $f=PFD(f)=P(f)+L(f)+H(f)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:05:57.774401+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d33191c1458e93b51dc31850206d53134b261e002ea7837d2f27736aa08d6b12","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2608.30549, '\vspace{-1cm}Maximally Spread Out Measures and Implications\\{} for Phase Transitions in A'] Let $(\XX, d)$ be a quasi-metric space and let $\emptyset \neq \SC \subset \XX$ be bounded.
  Then, writing $\AR^\ast := (\umd(\SC))^{-1}$, the following holds:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item (A suitable family of controlled complexity achieves every rate below $\AR^\ast$)
          There exists a family $(\CalA_n^\ast)_{n \in \N}$ of subsets
          $\emptyset \neq \CalA_n^\ast \subset \XX$
          of controlled complexity in $\XX$ such that for every $0 \leq \AR < \AR^\ast$,
          there exists $C(\AR) > 0$ satisfying
          \[
            \sup_{x \in \SC} \,\, \dist(x, \CalA_n^\ast) \leq C(\AR) \cdot n^{-\AR}
            \qquad \forall \, n \in \N.
          \]

    \item (No family of controlled complexity can achieve a rate above $\AR^\ast$
          uniformly over $\SC$)
          Let $(\CalA_n)_{n \in \N}$ be a family of controlled complexity in $\XX$.
          If
          \begin{equation}
            \sup_{x \in \SC} \,\, \dist(x, \CalA_n) \leq C(\AR) \cdot n^{-\AR}
            \qquad \forall \, n \in \N
            
          \end{equation}
          holds for some $\AR \geq 0$ and some constant $C(\AR) > 0$, then $\AR \leq \AR^\ast$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Now, set $\AR^\sharp := \bigl( \lmd (\SC) \bigr)^{-1}$ and
  assume that $\mu$ is a probability measure on $\XX$ that is critical for $\SC$.
  Then the following holds:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),resume]
    \item (Any rate above $\AR^\sharp$ is only achievable on a $\mu$-null set)
          For every $\AR > \AR^\sharp$ and every family $(\CalA_n)_{n \in \N}$
          of subsets $\emptyset \neq \CalA_n \subset \XX$ of controlled complexity in $\XX$,
          the set
          \[
            \CalR^\AR \bigl( (\CalA_n)_{n \in \N}, \SC, \XX\bigr)
            := \Bigl\{
                 x \in \SC
                 \,\,:\,\,
                 \sup_{n \in \N}
                 \bigl(
                   n^\AR \cdot \dist (x, \CalA_n)
                 \bigr)
                 < \infty
               \Bigr\}
          \]
          is a $\mu$-null set, i.e.,
          $\mu^\ast \bigl( \CalR^\AR \bigl( (\CalA_n)_{n \in \N}, \SC, \XX\bigr) \bigr) = 0$.
          In fact, we even have
          \[
            \mu^\ast
            \biggl(\,\,
              \bigcup_{\AR \in (\AR^\sharp, \infty)}
                \CalR^\AR \bigl( (\CalA_n)_{n \in \N}, \SC, \XX\bigr)
            \biggr)
            = 0
            .
          \]
  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:09.864425+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d36a2ef583dd20283c0ebf6fd083d59b8a7907d9648dfc3b17689e6dbbec56cb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 5 of arXiv:2605.21638, 'Markov renewal theory for transfer operators and point processes on the line'] Let $P$ be the transition kernel of a positive Harris chain with state space $\R^k$ and invariant probability measure $\pi$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.298544+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d36aadf58ab0d13884210791987860ff7ccf3a869661d3036493ad47e1a35ca8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Fixed-measurement posterior information budget) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Fix a measurement value $r$ with $0<p_R(r)<\infty$ and define
\[
q_t^r(x):=p_t(x\mid r),
\qquad
\mathcal K_t(r):=\KL(q_t^r\|p_t).
\]
Let $0<s<t<\infty$.  Assume $\mathcal K_s(r)<\infty$, the relative Fisher
information
\[
\int q_u^r(x)
\left\|\nabla\log\frac{q_u^r(x)}{p_u(x)}\right\|^2\dd x
\]
is integrable over $u\in[s,t]$, and the integration-by-parts boundary terms
vanish.  Then
\begin{equation}

\mathcal K_s(r)-\mathcal K_t(r)
=
\int_s^t
\E_{X_u\mid r}\|g_u(X_u,r)\|^2\,\dd u.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for almost every $t>0$ (and at every differentiability point),
\begin{equation}

-\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\mathcal K_t(r)
=
\E_{X_t\mid r}\|g_t(X_t,r)\|^2.
\end{equation}
Averaging over the measurement gives
\begin{equation}

\MI(R;X_s)-\MI(R;X_t)
=
\int_s^t\E\|g_u(X_u,R)\|^2\,\dd u,
\qquad
-\frac{\dd}{\dd t}\MI(R;X_t)
=
\E\|g_t(X_t,R)\|^2
\end{equation}
whenever the derivative exists.  Thus force energy is the forward-time
dissipation rate of posterior--prior relative entropy, or the corresponding
reverse-time assimilation rate. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.501734+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d38ed9fc1e17f4dfce2eb8e15ab63c4dd61992ec0cfb8abeae8bc29607040e8f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition eq:general-mixture of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:general-moment-correction}
Fix \(q\ge1\).  Let \(Q\) be any symmetric probability law with finite
moments through order \(2q\).  For all sufficiently small
\(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a symmetric compactly supported
\(C^\infty\) density \(\nu_\varepsilon\) such that

 \mu_\varepsilon=\varepsilon Q+(1-\varepsilon)\nu_\varepsilon
\end{equation}
matches the standard Gaussian moments through order \(2q\).  If \(\nu_\varepsilon\) is supported in \([-R,R]\), then
\[
 \mu_\varepsilon(A)=\varepsilon Q(A)
 \quad\text{for every Borel }A\subset\mathbb R\setminus[-R,R].

If \(Q\) has a strictly positive \(C^\infty\) density, then so does

{"assumptions":["ferromagnetic pairwise interactions; the exponential-decay conclusion needs finite-range (or exponentially decaying) couplings, since G(x,y) >= tanh(beta J_xy) by Griffiths' inequality","finite volume, or an infinite-volume Gibbs state for which the relevant correlation inequalities (e.g. Griffiths inequalities) hold","existence of a family of finite sets separating the two points of interest","the model's symmetry, such as spin-flip Z_2 symmetry, used in the classical derivation of the inequality"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d393890b51a665689a58b52bbeacddfa45ba308a4e92ffc9e53fce0dc9def944","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the Ising model, or more generally ferromagnetic spin systems with finite-range interactions (with merely summable long-range couplings G(x,y) >= tanh(beta J_xy) by Griffiths' inequality, so exponential decay can fail), let G(x,y) = <sigma_x sigma_y> be the two-point function. The Simon-Lieb inequality bounds G(x,y) across any finite set Lambda separating x from y (x in Lambda, y outside Lambda) by G(x,y) <= sum_{u in Lambda, v not in Lambda} G_Lambda(x,u) beta J_{uv} G(v,y), with G_Lambda the two-point function of the model restricted to Lambda (free boundary condition) and beta the inverse temperature (forms with tanh(beta J_{uv}) in place of beta J_{uv} are also used), a one-step recursive bound relating the two-point function across a separating surface to the two-point function up to the boundary of Lambda times the coupling crossing it. Iterating the inequality over a sequence of nested separating sets, such as concentric boxes, yields exponential decay of G(x,y) once the associated generating function drops below its self-consistency threshold, giving a classical route, predating and complementary to the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, to sharpness of the phase transition and analyticity of the free energy in the high-temperature regime. It does not determine the exact critical temperature directly, only characterizing it implicitly through the inequality's self-consistency condition, and it applies specifically to ferromagnetic spin systems with a workable notion of finite separating surfaces; it does not transfer automatically to percolation, which uses combinatorially different, though philosophically related, inequalities. Typical failure: Iterating the Simon-Lieb inequality across many nested separating surfaces while implicitly assuming a geometric decay rate that has not actually been verified to be summable; turning the one-step recursive bound into exponential decay requires checking that the relevant generating function, summing G times J over the boundary, lies strictly below its self-consistency threshold, and this check is exactly where the difficulty of locating beta_c resides, so skipping it silently assumes the conclusion. Canonical reference: Simon, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Lieb, 1980, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a specified target distribution with a known, workable Stein characterizing operator or equation","an auxiliary coupling structure connecting to W, such as an exchangeable pair, a size-biased coupling, or a dependency graph","sufficient smoothness or explicit derivative bounds on the solution f of the Stein equation for the specific target distribution","control of the resulting expectation bound in terms of the coupling's own closeness or error parameters"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.996944+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d39aa2bb9e25135cdd42c23538dfcea568834d63bc2b2b834c74380b75fd1b82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). To bound the distance, in Kolmogorov, Wasserstein, or total variation metric, between the law of a random variable W and a target distribution, classically the standard normal but also Poisson, exponential, and other targets, Stein's method characterizes the target law via a characterizing (Stein) equation: for the normal, E[f'(Z) - Zf(Z)] = 0 for all sufficiently smooth f if and only if Z is standard normal. Given a test function h, one solves the associated Stein equation f'(x) - xf(x) = h(x) - E[h(Z)] for f, and then bounds E[f'(W) - Wf(W)] directly using structural information about W, typically supplied by an auxiliary coupling such as an exchangeable pair, a size-biased coupling, or a dependency-graph/local-dependence construction, without going through characteristic functions or moment matching. This yields explicit, often near-optimal-rate, quantitative bounds on distributional distance for sums of dependent or weakly dependent random variables and for counts in combinatorial structures, settings where classical central limit theorem machinery is difficult to apply directly because of dependence. It does not automatically give a good bound for an arbitrary random variable, since constructing the right coupling matched to the problem's dependence structure is the substantive and typically hardest step, and the quality of the final bound is entirely determined by the quality of that coupling. Typical failure: Treating Stein's method as an automatic black box that produces a good rate on its own, when in fact the rate is entirely determined by the quality of the coupling constructed for the specific problem, such as an exchangeable pair with a large error term or a dependency graph with high maximum degree; a poorly constructed coupling yields a valid but far-from-optimal, or even useless, bound, and this construction step, rather than the abstract Stein equation itself, is where nearly all the technical difficulty and risk of error lies. Canonical reference: Stein, 1972, Proceedings of the Sixth Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability; Chen, Goldstein and Shao, Normal Approximation by Stein's Method, 2011, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f real analytic on an open set U in R^n","x solves the gradient flow x' = -grad f(x) on [0, infinity)","the trajectory has compact closure in U (precompact; bounded is enough when U = R^n)"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:12:37.001254+00:00","domain":"real-analytic gradient flows, optimization dynamics","id":"claim_d3b09a78eebe9d043b33f43006ca699084a5e2f256ecfc3a1bfc55dbccdda3be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Lojasiewicz gradient inequality. Let U be an open subset of R^n, f: U -> R real analytic, and p in U. There are an open neighbourhood W of p in U and constants theta in (0,1) and c > 0 such that |f(x) - f(p)|^theta <= c |grad f(x)| for every x in W. Consequence (finite length and convergence of bounded gradient trajectories). Let x: [0, infinity) -> U solve x'(t) = -grad f(x(t)) and suppose the trajectory {x(t): t >= 0} has compact closure in U. Then x has finite length, int_0^infinity |x'(t)| dt < infinity, and x(t) converges as t -> infinity to a single critical point a of f. Near a, the tail length obeys int_t^infinity |x'(s)| ds <= (c/(1-theta)) (f(x(t)) - f(a))^(1-theta), with c and theta the constants of the inequality at a. Critical points need not be isolated; smoothness alone is not enough (there are smooth functions with bounded gradient trajectories that spiral forever without converging).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The uniform growth bound with constants M and omega, which every C_0-semigroup has by the uniform boundedness principle.","The renorming changes the geometry of the space - the new norm need not be, for instance, a Hilbert norm even if the original was, so any argument relying on inner-product structure must be checked rather than assumed to survive."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.871401+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, semigroup theory","id":"claim_d3dac9e684fa7cee76a6e64a5e95a24fd4a86841256053c866427af3587cab08","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (T(t)) be a C_0-semigroup on a Banach space X satisfying the growth bound ||T(t)|| <= M exp(omega t). Then there is an EQUIVALENT norm on X, namely |||x||| = sup over t >= 0 of exp(-omega t) ||T(t) x||, in which the semigroup satisfies |||T(t) x||| <= exp(omega t) |||x||| - that is, the constant M is normalised away and the semigroup becomes a quasi-contraction. The new norm satisfies ||x|| <= |||x||| <= M ||x||, so it is equivalent and the generator, its domain and its spectrum are unchanged; only the operator NORMS and the numerical range move. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:41:29.024738+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d3e2c77622f8024859707cc8bf75fa031012b848d26a17bad25860cbfb4c5410","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2608.26490, 'Bayesian methods and Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms for curve reconstruction and poin'] For a fixed $n=1,\dots,N$, let $r_n$ be a random position generated according to the sampling scheme in \cref{eq:un,eq:sn,eq:pi,eq:L}. Then \cref{eq:rn} follows.
\begin{proof}
Given a geometry $G$, the position $r_n$ specifies and is specified by a global coordinate $v_n$ that equals the arc-length from $h^1$ along the curve $\mathcal{G}$ encoded by $G$. Consequently, it suffices to show that $v_n$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,L^G]$ where $L^G=\sum_{k=1}^K L_k^G$ is the total arc-length of $\mathcal{G}$.

Conditional on $s_n$ and $u_n$, such global coordinate $r_n$ is obtained deterministically by
\begin{align*}
v_n|s_n,u_n
&\sim\delta_{C^G_{s_n-1}+u_nL_{s_n}^G},
\end{align*}
where the cumulative segment lengths are defined by
\begin{align*}
C^G_0&=0,
\\
C^G_k&=\sum_{k'=1}^K L^G_{k'},
&
k&=1,\dots,K.
\end{align*}
According to the law of total probability, we obtain the marginal
\begin{align*}
p(v_n)
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
p(v_n|s_n,u_n)p(s_n,u_n),
\end{align*}
and, because of independence in \cref{eq:sn,eq:un}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
p(v_n)
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
p(v_n|s_n,u_n)p(s_n)p(u_n)
\\
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{C^G_{s_n-1}+u_nL_{s_n}^G}(v_n)\pi_{s_n}^G
\\
&=
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\frac{1}{L_{s_n}^G}\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)\frac{L_{s_n}^G}{L^G}
\\
&=\frac{1}{L^G}
\sum_{s_n=1}^K\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)
\\
&=\frac{1}{L^G}
\end{align*}
indicating that, indeed, $v_n$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,L^G]$ which completes our proof. Here, the last equality holds because, from the $K$ different summands $\int_0^1du_n\,
\delta_{u_n}\left(\frac{v_n-C^G_{s_n-1}}{L_{s_n}^G}\right)$, only one integrates over the singularity.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.642574+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d401a3cd427a7085cf62848e53807cfe68398c4334970a00a4c1b8b0218f8704","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 11 of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] Let \(Y\) be a subordinator with L\'evy measure \(\nu\) and Laplace exponent \(\psi\).
Let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), let \(c\ge0\), and let \(K\) be a slowly varying function at \(\infty\).
Define
\[
h(x):=\frac{x^\alpha}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)K(x)}
\quad (x>0),
\]
and let \(g\) be the right-continuous inverse of \(h\), that is,
\[
g(\lambda):=\inf\{y\ge0 \mid h(y)>\lambda\}.
\]
Let \(Z^{(\alpha)}\) be the \(\alpha\)-stable subordinator characterized by
\[
E[e^{-qZ^{(\alpha)}_t}]=e^{-tq^\alpha}
\quad (q,t\ge0).
\]
Then the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(\left(\frac{Y_{\lambda t}}{g(\lambda)}\right)_{t\ge0}
  \xrightarrow[\lambda\to\infty]{d}
  \bigl(c^{1/\alpha}Z^{(\alpha)}_t\bigr)_{t\ge0}\) on \(D([0,\infty),\bR)\).
  \item
  \(\nu(x,\infty)\sim c x^{-\alpha}K(x) \quad (x\to\infty)\).
  \item
  \(\psi(q)\sim c \Gamma(1-\alpha) q^\alpha K(1/q) \quad (q \to 0)\).
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:32:56.100267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d418d5c7eb52ca818ca1e9c4347b8a9a10fdde559c2dab7d205f0e3ac6e5705f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2411.13030, 'Classification of the limit shape for 1+1-dimensional FPP'] Let $G$ be non-deterministic and $B>t_{0}(G)$. For any edge $e$ of the lattice, we define the \emph{detour height} as the distance to an edge with small passage time:
\[
k_B(e):=\min\left (k\ge 1 | \,  \min( \tau(e+(0,k)),\tau(e-(0,k)))< B\right).
\]
The \emph{detour} of $e$ is the path that starts at one edge of $e$, goes $k_B(e)$ edges upwards or downwards, passes the horizontal edge with weight less than $B$ and goes $k_B(e)$ edges down back to the other endpoint of $e$. The \emph{detour time} $dt_B(e)$ is the passage time of the detour.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:35:05.844828+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d4b78a2c290f68647eba7acb0d2569cf54c5a373e88460fa1847b2c5c8e4abe5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:spectral-upper of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] For a reversible chain with stationary distribution $\pi$,
\[
  I(X_0;X_1)
  =\sum_{x\in S}\pi(x)\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P(x,\cdot)\|\pi)
  \;\le\;\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
  \bar r_\pi\;\le\;
  \frac{\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2}{\log(1/\pi_{\max})},
\]
where $\pi_{\max}=\max_x\pi(x)$.
If $\pi$ is uniform, then
\[
  \bar r_\pi
  \;\le\;
  \frac{\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i^2}{\log n}
  \;\le\;
  \frac{(n-1)(1-\gamma)^2}{\log n}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:10.196851+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d4bbd0876f392fb250cd171a850d9811a55edc13374830a7ef0551cc08c624b4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 28 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Visibility, relaying scheme.}

Let $\landsc$ be a landscape.

Let $(a_1, b_1)$ and $(a_2, b_2)$ be two buildings of $\landsc$. We say that $(a_2, b_2)$ is visible from $(a_1, b_1)$ if it is in range and there are no buildings above the segment from $(a_1, b_1)$ to $(a_2, b_2)$. In other words, if the following conjunction of events holds true:
\[\{(a_2, b_2)\text{ is in range from } (a_1, b_1)\} \cap \below{[a_1, a_2]}{(a_1, b_1)}{\frac{b_2-b_1}{a_2-a_1}}.\]

Thanks to this, we can define the relaying scheme $\tau$ as
\[\tau_{\mathrm{R}} (x, y, \landsc) = (x_b, y_b) := \underset{\substack{(a, b) \in \landsc\cap \mathrm{R}+(x, y) \\(a, b) \text{ visible from }(x, y)}}{\text{argmax}} \frac{b-y}{a-x}.\]
When this is well defined, and $\tau (x, y, \landsc) = (-\infty, -\infty)$ otherwise.

The blockage angle and its tangent are defined as usual in this context","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.993827+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d4de95b7e4d71378aa4c48b750c7c3459932fb397a66afbb74404473f39d36a3","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 37 (Symmetric feedback closes the primitive criterion) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $q\ge2$, $x\in H^{\odot q}$ and
$F=I_q(x/\sqrt{q!})$.  Put

\begin{align}
 \kappa_4(F)
 &=\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}\binom qs^2\norm{x\otimes_sx}^2
 \notag\\
 &\quad+\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}\frac{q^2}{s^2}\,
 b_{q,q,s}\norm{x\wtensor_sx}^2.
 
\end{align}
If $\norm x\le R$, then
\begin{equation}
 |\kappa_4(F)|
 \le 3^{q+1}R^2
 \left(\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}
 b_{q,q,s}\norm{x\wtensor_sx}^2\right)^{1/2}.
 
\end{equation}
In fact the carré-du-champ defect and the fourth cumulant satisfy the

\begin{align}
 \kappa_4(F)
 &=3q\sum_{s=1}^{q-1}\frac{b_{q,q,s}}s
   \norm{x\wtensor_sx}^2,
 \\
 \frac1{3q}\kappa_4(F)
 &\le
 \Var\bigl(\Gamma(F,F)\bigr)
 \le\frac{q-1}{3q}\kappa_4(F).
 
\end{align}
Consequently, for a bounded family, vanishing of the symmetric feedback
on the right of \eqref{bridge:eq:kappa-from-symmetric-feedback} forces every
proper unsymmetrized self-contraction to vanish.","status":"unverified"}
