{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:57:28.725379+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d537d3ff9908c551b174be0816f534f466c2ed0a3a84ff44d09efc5670c6c38f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 24 (Discrete local sewing) of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $\theta\in (0,1)$ and let $\Pcal=\{S = U_0<U_1<\ldots<U_N = T\}$ (with $N\in\Nsf$, $N\geq 2$) be a partition of the interval $[S,T]$ satisfying the following condition:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=($P_\theta$)]
	\item
		Whenever $s,t\in\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket$ satisfy $\llbracket s+1,t-1\rrbracket\neq \emptyset$, there exists $u\in\llbracket s+1,t-1\rrbracket$ such that 
            \[
                \omega_{s,u}\leq \theta \omega_{s,t}.
            \]
	\end{enumerate}
Let $K:\Delta\Pcal\to\Rsf^m$ be a function and denote 
	\[
		K_{s,t}:=K(U_s,U_t), \quad (s,t)\in\Delta\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket.
	\]
Assume that the following condition is satisfied:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=($K$)]
	\item
		It holds that $K_{s,s}=0$ for all $s\in\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket$ and $K_{s,s+1}=0$ for all $s\in \llbracket 0,N-1\rrbracket$. Additionally, there exist $C,M\in (0,\infty)$ such that the estimate
	\[
		| K_{s,t} - K_{s,u} - K_{u,t}| \leq C |K_{s,u}|\,\omega_{u,t}^\frac{1}{p} + M\omega_{s,t}^\frac{3}{p}
	\]
holds for every $(s,u,t)\in\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket^3$ satisfying $s\leq u\leq t$ and $\omega_{s,t}\leq 1$.
	\end{enumerate}
Then there exist $\delta \in (0,1)$ and $L\in (0,\infty)$ such that the estimate
	\[
		|K_{s,t}| \leq L M \omega_{s,t}^\frac{3}{p}
	\]
holds for every $s,t\in\Delta\llbracket 0,N\rrbracket$ satisfying $\omega_{s,t}<\delta$. Constant $\delta$ depends only on $p$, $\theta$, and $C$ while constant $L$ depends only on $\theta$ and $p$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.301835+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d546f3a1f6e280eeb44776b614a793b582af78b1f028496f1a80d5917861a304","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:stealthiness-criterion of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $(P_z)_{z\in Z}$ be a Borel $\Gamma$-equivariant uniformly
Delone family, and let $Y_P$ be the associated cross-section.
Suppose that there are $\rho>0$ and an open neighborhood
$\Omega$ of the origin such that
\[
    \widehat{\delta}_{P_z}
    =
    \rho\delta_0
    \qquad\text{on }\Omega
\]
for $\nu$-almost every $z$, in the sense of tempered
distributions. Then the associated cross-section system has intensity $\rho$.
Moreover, for every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfying
\[
    \operatorname{supp}\widehat f\subset\Omega,
\]
one has
\[

    =
    \rho\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d
\]
for $\mu_{\Gamma,Z}$-almost every $x$. Consequently,
\[
    \sigma_{Y_P,\mu_{\Gamma,Z}}(\Omega)=0.
\]
In particular, the cross-section system is stealthy.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["D_mu>0.","This concept records the endpoint and threshold-rigidity claims without certifying missing limiting steps."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.365373+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d55645e860cf4706ac4c1c86c0536aabee8b3bfc87ea02dfaa532e346ccc362b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; the criterion reproduces the source's worked example, and every algebraic step was confirmed symbolically] Problem 3.3 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240), asks for the optimal universal C>0 such that mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for every t>=C D_mu^2 and every compactly supported probability measure mu. Here D_mu=sup{|x-y|: x,y in supp(mu)}, S(0,t) is the centered semicircle law of variance t, and boxplus is additive free convolution. The source proves C<=4. The record answers C=1. Sufficiency is the proved bound that mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for all t>=D_mu^2. Optimality is the source's Example 2.1: mu=(delta_{-1}+delta_1)/2, with D_mu=2, is not unimodal for any t<4=D_mu^2. Let t*(mu) be the least t_0 such that mu boxplus S(0,t) is unimodal for every t>=t_0. Then t*(mu)<=D_mu^2, and equality holds for every symmetric two-point law (equal weights at two points) by Example 2.1 and scaling. The record further claims (Corollary) that equality holds only for symmetric two-point laws. That direction rests on the record's unproved assertion that t*(mu)=D_mu^2 requires a separating local minimum of value exactly 1/D_mu^2, a limiting step not written out. It is retained here as a claim, not certified. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.161511+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d595f6e2ed6ee8c526511a13862ba9d97f8c5f841ce447757b85a65986f3311f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 12 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon\ge0$, 
and for $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, 
the mapping
$(\lambda,\mu)\mapsto S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)[\epsilon]$,
is continuous with respect to the Hausdorff metric $d_H$.

\begin{proof}
Fix $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\epsilon\ge0$ and $\delta'>0$. By Lemma~\ref{l:S.star.cts.dH}, there exists $\delta>0$ such that if 
$(\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda$ and 
$(\lambda',\mu')\in B_\delta(\lambda,\mu)$, then the sets
\begin{align*}
K&\equiv S_\star(\lambda,\mu;\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)\,,\\
K'&\equiv S_\star(\lambda',\mu';\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2)
\end{align*}
lie within Hausdorff distance $\delta'$ of one another.
For any $\hat{\YY}\in K[\epsilon]$, there exists $\YY\in K$ with
$\|\hat{\YY}-\YY\|_2\le\epsilon$, and then there exists $\YY'\in K'$ with
$\|\YY-\YY'\|_2\le\delta'$. By Lemma~\ref{l:D.mu.continuity.w}, 
since $\hat{\YY}\in\cD_\mu$,
there exists $\tilde{\YY}\in\cD_{\mu'}$
with $\|\hat{\YY}-\tilde{\YY}\|_1\le\delta/\iota^2$. Then
	\[
	\|\tilde{\YY}-\YY'\|_2
	\le\|\tilde{\YY}-\hat{\YY}\|_2
	+ \|\hat{\YY} - \YY\|_2
	+ \|\YY - \YY'\|_2
	\le \epsilon + \delta' + \frac{\delta}{\iota^2}
	\le \epsilon + 2\delta'\,,
	\]
where the last inequality can be arranged by taking $\delta$ small enough (depending on $\delta'$).
Since $\YY'$ and $\tilde{\YY}$ both lie in $\cD_{\mu'}$, it follows by convexity of $\cD_{\mu'}$ that $\tilde{\YY}$ lies within distance
$2\delta'$ of a vector $\hat{\YY}' \in K'[\epsilon]$. We then finally have
	\[
	\|\hat{\YY}-\hat{\YY}'\|_2
	\le \|\hat{\YY}-\tilde{\YY}\|_2
		+ \|\tilde{\YY}-\hat{\YY}'\|_2
	\le\frac{\delta}{\iota^2} + 2\delta'
	\le 3\delta'\,.
	\]
This implies that $K[\epsilon]$ and $K'[\epsilon]$ lie within Hausdorff distance $3\delta'$ of one another, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.826381+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d5a3d191409b48031dea830f8f42d4a2b03d5c48f637fb77a8271a60b16461dc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:kappasize of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] There are absolute constants $c_0,C_0>0$ such that
\[
 c_0r\leq\kappa_r\leq C_0r\qquad(r\geq2).
\]
Consequently
\[
 K_h:=\sum_{r=2}^h\kappa_r\asymp h^2.
\]
More precisely, using the real-variable functions $\delta$ and $w$ just
defined, put
\[
 \Omega=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\delta(x)\leq1,
 \ \min_i x_i<0<\max_i x_i\},
 \qquad I=\int_\Omega w(x)\,dx.
\]
Then $0<I<\infty$ and
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\ K_h\sim\frac{I}{2\zeta(3)}h^2.\ }
\end{equation}
Writing $\mathfrak K:=I/(2\zeta(3))>0$, one has
$K_h\sim\mathfrak K h^2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:09:43.711585+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d5a9fae84efbbb8c48108887d143dbb6a52666f75dd6368a31645991ada63f32","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thmIPS of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let  the input process to the interacting particle system be

\item  A {\em score function} $\xi = \xi^{(h, \Phi, \Psi)}(\tilde{x},\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_n) := h(M_n[x])$ defined in~(equation xiU of the paper), satisfies the {\em $p$-moment condition}~(equation momh of the paper) for all $p \in [1, \infty)$.

we have
$$
({\rm Var}[\mu_n^{\xi}(f)])^{-1/2} \big(\mu_n^{\xi}(f) - \mathbb {E} [\mu_n^{\xi}(f)]\big)  \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z,$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.160484+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d5c69f5a9def5c43ebde26912fc4597acbdf2cf9f029a385ff2b04326fee72b7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 5 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\YY = (\vBBb,\vvvv,\vUUu,\vwww)$ be the random vector defined in \eqref{e:freeprob.random.YY}, and $\mu(\bG,\omega)$ be defined in \eqref{e:lambda-mu-random}.
    For any $\epsilon'' > 0$ there exists $c = c(\alpha,\iota,\epsilon'') > 0$ such that
    \[
        \P\bigg(
            \inf\big\{
                \|\tilde \YY - \YY\|_2 : \tilde \YY \in \cD_{\mu(\bG,\omega)}
            \big\} \le \epsilon''
        \bigg)
        \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
    \]
\begin{proof}
Throughout the proof, we abbreviate $(\lambda,\mu) = (\lambda(\bG,\omega),\mu(\bG,\omega))$, although we keep in mind that they are permitted to depend on $(\bG,\omega)$. We will construct $\tilde\YY = (\tilde\vBBb,\tilde\vvvv,\tilde\vUUu,\tilde\vwww) \in \cD_\mu$ such that $\|\tilde \YY - \YY\|_2 \le \epsilon''$ on an event with probability $1-e^{-cN}$.
    We set $(\tilde\vBBb,\tilde\vUUu) = (\vBBb,\vUUu)$, and $\tilde\vvvv = \max(\vvvv,\vUUu)$ where the maximum is taken entrywise.
    Note that for all $j\in [r]$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
    \baln
        \vUUu_j - \vvvv_j
        &=
        \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})}{N}
        \bigg)^2
        - \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
        \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N} \\
        &\le 
        \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N}
        \bigg)
        \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j} \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})^2}{N} - 1
        \bigg)\,,
    \ealn
from which it follows that
    \[
        |\tilde\vvvv_j - \vvvv_j|
        = (\vUUu_j - \vvvv_j)_+
        \le \bigg(
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
            \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N}
        \bigg)
        \bigg|
            \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j} \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})^2}{N} - 1
        \bigg|\,.
    \]
    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc} and \eqref{e:wishart.bound.repeated}, with probability $1-e^{-cN}$,
    \[
        \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j}
        \frac{(\barbg^a,\hat{\by})^2}{N}
        \le \frac{\|\hat{\by}\|^2 \|\bG\|_\op^2}{N|B_j|}
        \le \frac{(2N^{1/2})^2 (CN^{1/2})^2}{NM 
		\lambda_j}
        \le \frac{4C^2}{\alpha \iota}\,.
    \]
Set $\delta > 0$ small enough that
    \[
        [(1-\delta)^2,(1+\delta)^2] \subseteq \bigg[
            1 - \frac{\epsilon''\alpha\iota^2}{8C^2},
            1 + \frac{\epsilon''\alpha\iota^2}{8C^2}
        \bigg]\,.
    \]
    Since $(\bmeta^a : 1\le a\le M)$ are standard gaussians in $\bbR^N$ independent of $\bar{\bx}$ and $B_j$, we have
    \[
        \frac{1}{|B_j|} \sum_{a\in B_j} \frac{(\bmeta^a,\bar{\bx})^2}{N}
        \stackrel{d}{=}
        \frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} \cdot \frac{\|\bz\|^2}{|B_j|}
    \]
    where $\bz$ is a standard gaussian in $\bbR^{|B_j|}$.
    By Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc} and a standard gaussian tail bound,
    \[
        \max\bigg\{
            \bigg|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1\bigg|, 
            \bigg|\frac{\|\bz\|^2}{|B_j|} - 1\bigg|
        \bigg\} \le \delta
    \]
    with probability $1-e^{-cN}$.
It follows from the assumption on $\delta$ that
    \[
        \bigg| \frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} \cdot \frac{\|\bz\|^2}{|B_j|} - 1 \bigg|
        \le \frac{\epsilon''\alpha\iota^2}{8C^2}\,.
    \]
Combining the above bounds gives
    \beq
        |\tilde\vvvv_j - \vvvv_j|
        \le \frac{4C^2}{\alpha \iota}
        \cdot \frac{\epsilon''\alpha\iota^2}{8C^2}
        = \frac{\epsilon'' \iota}{2}\,.
    \eeq

{"assumptions":["Y = (1/3) sum_{k>=0} B_k (2/3)^k with fair i.i.d. bits B_k in {0,1} (the Bernoulli convolution at ratio 2/3)","mu_n = law of frac(2^n Y); hat_mu the Fourier transform of the law of Y"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.970329+00:00","domain":"probability/Bernoulli convolutions","id":"claim_d6179c4cc4d147afa7a0e105cd32a45d","kind":"proof_attempt","schema_version":1,"statement":"For Y = (1/3) sum_{k>=0} B_k (2/3)^k with fair independent bits B_k, the Fourier transform of its law mu (the Bernoulli-2/3 measure) has the exact closed form hat_mu(xi) = prod_{k>=0} (1 + exp(-2 pi i xi (2/3)^k / 3))/2, agreeing with an independent stationary-density solver's Fourier coefficients to 1e-11 at xi = 1,2,3,5,8,16,32. Writing mu_n for the law of frac(2^n Y), hat_mu_n(k) = hat_mu(2^n k) for every integer k, so every level of a 'fibre-bias' deficit ladder is the same measure evaluated at a doubled frequency; an explicit Fourier lower bound (Cauchy-Schwarz against a unimodular test function, the k=0 term vanishing by the Y -> 1-Y symmetry) reproduces 14-39 pct of the numerically measured fibre bias at ladder levels n=0..6 using 20,000-term sums, independently of any density solver. Along the lacunary orbit 2^n, |hat_mu(2^n)| reduces to the exact arithmetic product prod_{k>=0} |cos(pi 2^{n+k}/3^{k+1})|, each factor depending only on 2^{n+k} mod 2 * 3^{k+1} (verified digit-for-digit against the direct Fourier product for n=0..16), with only k up to about 1.71n contributing; because 2 is a primitive root mod every 3^j, the exact period-average of log|cos(pi u/3^{k+1})| over units u equals -log 2 for every k, predicting an average decay of about 1.185 per level n, while the MEASURED slope of log|hat_mu(2^n)| over n=0..16 is about 1.0 per level - the decay itself is bursty (0.31 at n=0, 4.1e-8 at n=7, back up to 1.7e-5 at n=10, 4.3e-9 at n=15), the small factors being exactly the k where 2^{n+k+1} lands near an odd multiple of 3^{k+1}, though the trend matches the prediction; the exchange of sums behind the prediction is rigorous only for k up to about log_3 n, where the window covers the period 2 * 3^k. For the rational, non-Pisot ratio lambda=2/3, the currently PROVED decay rate of hat_mu is only logarithmic in the frequency (giving deficits of order n^{-c}, not summable - the family a related paper bound n^{-13/25} belongs to), while the measured/predicted decay is vastly faster; the gap between the proved logarithmic rate and the faster measured rate is exactly the missing ingredient - a lacunary Fourier estimate for the 2/3 Bernoulli convolution better than logarithmic - and closing it requires simultaneous equidistribution of 2^{n+k} mod 3^{k+1} across k up to about 1.71n, an unproved, Erdos-Kahane-barrier-type statement (a literature check found proved Fourier decay for rational lambda=p/q is logarithmic-power in general, and known absolute-continuity results for algebraic parameters reach down to about lambda=0.7995, above 2/3=0.667). {"assumptions":["independence of the matrix entries or summands, each with finite moments up to the order being matched, typically four","matching of the first four (or the relevant number of) moments between the actual entry distribution and the Gaussian reference, up to a specified small error","sufficient smoothness, typically several bounded derivatives, of the test function F used in the swapping argument","a separate mechanism, such as local relaxation flow or a priori rigidity estimates, to transfer from smooth-test-function statements to the actual eigenvalue statistics of interest"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.997682+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d62d01195d629cfaace32a339dd8b3931fc1ee479898a520c29aeefdbd2472a7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The Lindeberg exchange (swapping) principle proves distributional limit theorems by replacing the summands or matrix entries of a random object one at a time with Gaussian (or other reference) analogues, bounding the resulting change in E[F] for a sufficiently smooth test function F via a Taylor expansion at each swap, provided the relevant moments, typically up to third or fourth order depending on the smoothness assumed of F, agree between the original and replacement distributions. In random matrix theory, the Tao-Vu four-moment theorem states that for Wigner matrices, local eigenvalue statistics such as gap distributions at a fixed bulk location are universal, independent of the specific entry distribution, provided the first four moments of the off-diagonal entries match those of the Gaussian (GOE/GUE) case up to a small, quantified error, with a weaker three-moment matching sufficing for some global statistics; this is the primary technical engine behind Wigner-Dyson-Mehta universality results beyond the exactly solvable Gaussian ensembles. It does not apply directly to test functions or statistics that are insufficiently smooth, requiring a separate regularization step, typically via a local relaxation flow or Dyson Brownian motion argument, to pass from smooth test functions to eigenvalue counting functions or individual eigenvalue locations, and it requires the specific moment-matching order assumed, with fewer matched moments giving correspondingly weaker conclusions. Typical failure: Applying the four-moment theorem's universality conclusion directly to a non-smooth statistic, such as the exact location or gap of a specific eigenvalue or an indicator-type event, without the additional Green's function comparison or local relaxation machinery needed to pass from smooth test functions to such statistics; the raw Lindeberg swapping argument by itself only controls E[F(eigenvalues)] for smooth F, and asserting the full local universality conclusion from moment matching alone skips this substantial extra step. Canonical reference: Lindeberg, 1922, Mathematische Zeitschrift; Tao and Vu, 2011, Acta Mathematica; Erdos and Yau, A Dynamical Approach to Random Matrix Theory, 2017, American Mathematical Society (Courant Lecture Notes).","status":"unverified"}

For a finite (or countable, with finite entropy) measurable partition $\\xi = \\{A_1, \\dots, A_k\\}$ put $H_\\mu(\\xi) = -\\sum_i \\mu(A_i) \\log \\mu(A_i)$ (with $0 \\log 0 = 0$), and $\\xi^n_0 = \\bigvee_{j=0}^{n-1} T^{-j}\\xi$, the partition into sets $A_{i_0} \\cap T^{-1}A_{i_1} \\cap \\dots \\cap T^{-(n-1)}A_{i_{n-1}}$ (the $n$-step itineraries). The entropy of $T$ relative to $\\xi$ is $h_\\mu(T, \\xi) = \\lim_{n\\to\\infty} \\frac1n H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ (the limit exists because $n \\mapsto H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ is subadditive; it also equals $\\inf_n \\frac1n H_\\mu(\\xi^n_0)$ and $\\lim_n H_\\mu(\\xi \\mid \\xi^n_1)$). {"assumptions":["free entries independent standard Gaussian, H = W/sqrt(n)","f Lipschitz; no other regularity","the bound is around the mean, which is not identified here"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544234+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d6862b4e3c8c63b6e20e398a7e0d94968e582011da1837ac900c1fbb41e8f5be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let W be a real symmetric n by n matrix whose entries W_{ij} for i <= j are independent standard Gaussians, and let H = W / sqrt(n) with eigenvalues lambda_1, ..., lambda_n. Let f be Lipschitz with constant ||f||_L. Then for every t > 0, P( | (1/n) sum_{i=1}^n f(lambda_i) - E (1/n) sum_i f(lambda_i) | >= t ) <= 2 exp( - n^2 t^2 / (4 ||f||_L^2) ). The exponent scales like n^2 t^2, not n t^2: linear eigenvalue statistics are FAR more concentrated than an average of n independent samples would be, and their fluctuations are of order 1/n rather than 1/sqrt(n). This is a consequence of the eigenvalue repulsion built into the matrix model, and it is one of the few places where a naive independence heuristic gives the wrong exponent by a whole power of n. The result needs only Lipschitz f - no smoothness, no boundedness - and it is a statement about concentration around the MEAN, not about identifying the mean, which is the separate content of Wigner's theorem. The constant 4 in the denominator is tied to the stated normalisation (independent standard Gaussians for the free entries, then divided by sqrt(n)); a different convention rescales it. [standard; the argument is Hoffman-Wielandt plus Gaussian Lipschitz concentration, e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Theorem 2.3.5]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a metric space","Y is a topological space (metric suffices, and is the usual case)","f: X x Y -> R is separately continuous: continuous in each variable with the other held fixed","for the residual-set-of-continuity-points consequence, X x Y is a Baire space (e.g. X, Y complete metric)","values are real (or in a metric space in which the partition-of-unity averaging makes sense, e.g. a locally convex space)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.815145+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Baire classes, separate continuity","id":"claim_d6a3e76764dc5394e33eca6c37c02af4c15a58c1386d4a14e4041123cff48df9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Recall that a real function g on a topological space Z is of BAIRE CLASS ONE if it is the pointwise limit of a sequence of continuous real functions on Z. THEOREM (Baire for R x R; Rudin in this generality): let X be a METRIC space, let Y be a topological space (in particular a metric space), and let f: X x Y -> R be SEPARATELY CONTINUOUS, i.e. for each fixed y the map x -> f(x,y) is continuous on X and for each fixed x the map y -> f(x,y) is continuous on Y. Then f is of Baire class one on X x Y: there is a sequence of continuous functions f_n: X x Y -> R with f_n(x,y) -> f(x,y) for every (x,y). CONSEQUENCE (Baire's theorem on functions of the first class): if in addition X x Y is a Baire space - for instance if X and Y are both complete metric, or both locally compact Hausdorff - then the set of points at which f is JOINTLY continuous is a dense G_delta subset of X x Y, and its complement is meagre. So a separately continuous function is jointly continuous at 'most' points, in the sense of category. CLASSICAL EXTENSION: a function of n variables that is separately continuous in each variable is of Baire class n - 1 (Lebesgue); the case n = 2 is the theorem above. SHARP EDGES. (a) Separate continuity does NOT give joint continuity: f(x,y) = xy/(x^2 + y^2) with f(0,0) = 0 is separately continuous on R^2, indeed continuous on each line through the origin, and is discontinuous at the origin (it equals 1/2 on the diagonal). The theorem therefore cannot be strengthened to continuity anywhere in particular, only to a residual set of continuity points. (b) The metric structure of the first factor is essential to the proof, which builds a locally finite partition of unity on X; for arbitrary topological factors the statement requires extra hypotheses and should not be quoted in that generality. (c) The consequence about continuity points needs X x Y to be a Baire space; on a non-Baire domain 'dense G_delta' carries no information, and the conclusion is vacuous. (d) Baire class one is a statement about POINTWISE limits; it gives no uniform convergence, and the limit functions f_n constructed in the proof are not monotone in n. (e) The converse is false and is not being claimed: plenty of Baire class one functions on a product are not separately continuous.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:47:22.242693+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d6ac7136845286d61c1202883e37bac1aeb09d5b24bcbffa27ae07a618126421","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 6 of arXiv:2605.25762, 'Brownian Convergence of Planar Domains and Stability of the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Pro'] The Hilbert transform of a real valued $2\pi$- periodic function
$f$ is defined by 
\[
H\{f\}(x):=PV\left\{ \frac{1}{2\pi}\int^{\pi}_{-\pi}f(x-t)\cot(\frac{t}{2})dt\right\} =\lim_{\eta\rightarrow0}\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\eta\leq|t|\leq\pi}f(x-t)\cot(\frac{t}{2})dt

{"assumptions":["the spiked covariance model with a detected spike, i.e. a sample eigenvalue above the Marchenko-Pastur edge","gamma = p/n in (0, 1]"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:37:33.911177+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_d6c76d948bf22c5f46b571c1b55ac0c5ab6172b42a25b010a67337b1c7b3fc7a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the spiked covariance model with noise level $\\sigma^2$ and ratio $\\gamma = p/n$, let $\\hat\\lambda$ be a sample eigenvalue lying above the bulk edge, $\\ell := \\hat\\lambda / \\sigma^2 > (1 + \\sqrt{\\gamma})^2$. Then the unique $\\theta > \\sqrt{\\gamma}$ with $(1 + \\theta)(1 + \\gamma/\\theta) = \\ell$ is $$\\hat\\theta = \\tfrac{1}{2}\\Big( (\\ell - 1 - \\gamma) + \\sqrt{(\\ell - 1 - \\gamma)^2 - 4\\gamma} \\Big),$$ and $\\sigma^2 (1 + \\hat\\theta)$ is the consistent estimate of the population eigenvalue behind $\\hat\\lambda$. The discriminant is nonnegative exactly when $\\ell \\ge (1 + \\sqrt{\\gamma})^2$, so the formula is defined precisely for eigenvalues at or above the edge. The population value $\\sigma^2(1 + \\hat\\theta)$ is always strictly less than $\\hat\\lambda$ (a sample spike is debiased downward), by the amount $\\sigma^2 \\gamma (1 + 1/\\hat\\theta)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:09:59.299744+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d6f29a6841e41be5378eec1bc15b94989400ec777035a848e170aed8277b1c90","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn contFV of arXiv:2608.06500, 'Free energy of Ising models under a spectral condition'] For $\alpha>0$, an \emph{$\alpha$-good potential} is a
    function $V:\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$,  $(h,\varphi)\mapsto V_h(\varphi)$ 
    which is twice continuously differentiable 
    
    with 
    \[
        \sup_{\substack{|h|\le C \\ \varphi\in\mathbb{R}}}
        \left| \frac\partial{\partial h} V_h'(\varphi)\right| < \infty
    \]
    for all $C>0$ and $V_h''(\varphi)\in[\alpha,\alpha^{-1}]$
    for all $h,\varphi\in\mathbb{R}$ (where  $V_h'$ and $V_h''$ are the first and
     second  derivatives of $V_h$ with respect to $\varphi$). In other words, this family of potential
    functions is smooth and uniformly strongly convex with Lipschitz
    gradient, and furthermore $V_h'$ is Lipschitz in $h$. For
    $\text{\boldmath $h$}\in\mathbb{R}^N$, we define the potential

    \begin{align*}
V_\text{\boldmath $h$}(\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}):=\sum_{i=1}^NV_{h_i}(\varphi_i)\, .
\end{align*}

    Given an $\alpha$-good potential $V$ and
    a weighted graph $G=(\text{\boldmath $B$},\text{\boldmath $h$})$ on $[N]$ with $\text{\boldmath $B$}\succ-\alpha\text{\boldmath $I$}$,
    we consider the Gibbs measure on $\mathbb{R}^N$ with base measure
    $e^{-V_\text{\boldmath $h$}(\text{\boldmath $\varphi$})}{\rm d}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}$ and quadratic Hamiltonian
    $-\frac12\<\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}, \text{\boldmath $B$}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}\>$ and denote its free energy density
    by

    \begin{align*}
F_V(G)=F_V(\text{\boldmath $B$},\text{\boldmath $h$})=\frac1N \log \int_{\mathbb{R}^N} \exp\left( -\frac12
\<\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}, \text{\boldmath $B$}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}\> \right) e^{-V_\text{\boldmath $h$}(\text{\boldmath $\varphi$})} {\rm d}\text{\boldmath $\varphi$}.
\end{align*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:50:27.053857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d734ef006c17a22dac77fd1f3f955c1530993a066722f0a550cb03c4e3518b5c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:ergo of arXiv:2505.14012, 'Ergodicity for stochastic neural field equations'] \phantom{ }
\begin{enumerate}
\item An invariant measure $\mu\in{\mathcal M}_1(H)$ for the semigroup $\{P_t\}_{t\ge 0}$ is called \emph{ergodic} if
\[Q_T(v,\cdot) \rightharpoonup \mu\]
as $T\to\infty$ for any $v\in H$ in the sense of weak convergence of probability measures.
\item An invariant measure $\mu\in{\mathcal M}_1(H)$ for the semigroup $\{P_t\}_{t\ge 0}$ is called \emph{strongly mixing} if
\[P_t(v,\cdot)\rightharpoonup \mu\]
as $t\to\infty$ for any $v\in H$ in the sense of weak convergence of probability measures.
\item An invariant measure $\mu\in{\mathcal M}_1(H)$ for the semigroup $\{P_t\}_{t\ge 0}$ is called \emph{exponentially ergodic} if there exists $\beta>0$ and a positive function $c:H\to\mathbb{R}$ such that for any $\varphi\in\operatorname{Lip}_b(H)$, all $t>0$, and all $v\in H$,
\[\left|P_t\varphi(v)-\int_H\varphi(z)\,\mu(dz)\right|\le c(v)e^{-\beta t}\operatorname{Lip}(\varphi).\]
\item An invariant measure $\mu\in{\mathcal M}_1(H)$ for the semigroup $\{P_t\}_{t\ge 0}$ is called \emph{exponentially mixing} if there exists $\beta>0$ and a positive function $c:H\to\mathbb{R}$ such that for all $t>0$, and all $v\in H$,
\[\|P_t(v,\cdot)-\mu\|_{F-M}\le c(v)e^{-\beta t},\]
where
\[\|\nu\|_{F-M}:=\sup\left\{\left|\int_H\varphi(z)\,\nu(dz)\right|\;\colon\;\varphi\in \operatorname{Lip}_b(H),\;\|\varphi\|_{\operatorname{Lip}_b}\le 1\right\}\]
is the \emph{Forter-Mourier norm} (also called \emph{bounded Lipschitz norm}) of a signed measure $\nu$ on ${\mathcal B}(H)$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Real compatible factors; differentiable loss depending only on the product","Constant-step summation is conditional on the stated sufficient decrease and lower bound"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T20:54:55.722211+00:00","domain":"LoRA factor gradient descent","id":"claim_d76476f244c48b4335361c25d6818f6fe34988dbd5c9e5aa0346ab1ea240500d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For real factors B of size m-by-r and A of size r-by-p, and differentiable product loss F(BA), put G_B=grad F(BA) A^T, G_A=B^T grad F(BA), and D=AA^T-B^TB. If a fixed eta>0 additionally satisfies the sufficient-decrease inequality f_next<=f-a eta ||grad f||F^2 for f(B,A)=F(BA), some a>0, and f is bounded below by f_star along the iterates, summation gives ||D_t-D_0||F<=(eta/a)(f_0-f_star). This implication assumes descent; it does not establish it or prove arbitrary-step convergence. The trace identity (||B||F^2+||A||F^2)^2<=r[||AA^T-B^TB||F^2+4||BA||F^2] then converts bounds on imbalance and product into a factor bound. Du-Hu-Lee, Algorithmic Regularization in Learning Deep Homogeneous Models: Layers are Automatically Balanced, arXiv:1806.00900, Theorem 2.2 gives continuous-time Gram invariance; Appendix B, Claim B.1 expands the discrete square-loss update. The conditional constant-step summation and trace inequality here are elementary method consequences, not their full GD convergence theorem. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.784061+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d770fd00e3be841d57d0052ff66900cc13317779c3f82c6c82309eeeb0bc3c20","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 29 (Geometric estimates from initial data) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] \bse
Fix an admissible Navier--Stokes triple $(\mathscr F,\chi,\mathscr B)$ as defined in \autoref{def-pot-admissible-triple}.
Let $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$ with $\Phi=(\Jperp,\Jpar,\Pbb,\Qbb)$ and $\Psi=(\ell,\log\Omega,\Kpar)$ be a sufficiently regular dissipated-energy or particle-production Einstein--Navier--Stokes areal flow $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$ on $[t_0,t_1]\times\Tbb^3$.  Denote the values at time $t=t_0$ by
\be
(\mathring\Phi,\mathring\Psi,\mathring\zeta) \coloneqq (\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)(t_0,\cdot) \quad \text{on } \Tbb^3 .
\ee
Then the following estimates hold, where implied constants depend on the Navier--Stokes potential $\chi$ and on $t_0,t_1$, but not on the relaxation structure~$\mathscr B$ nor on the solution $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$.
\bei
\item \emph{Spatial energy.} The fluid variables, and the first-order geometric variables $\Pbb,\Qbb$ have
  \bel{estimate-SE}
    \int_{\{t\}\times \Tbb^3} \Bigl( T_\chi^{00} + \Ebf_0(\Pbb,\Qbb) \Bigr) \dVtrois
    \lesssim \|\mathring\Phi\|_{\mathrm{energy}} , \qquad t\in[t_0,t_1] .
  \ee

\item \emph{Conformal length and volume.}
  \bel{estimate-LV}
  \aligned
  & \mathcal L(t) \leq \mathcal L(t_0) , \quad \mathcal V(t) \leq |t/t_0|^{3/4} \mathcal V(t_0) , \qquad t_0 \leq t \leq t_1 < 0 \quad \text{(future-contracting regime)},
  \\
  & \mathcal L(t) \geq \mathcal L(t_0) , \quad \mathcal V(t) \geq |t/t_0|^{3/4} \mathcal V(t_0) , \qquad 0 < t_0 \leq t \leq t_1 \quad \text{(future-expanding regime)}.
  \endaligned
  \ee
  Furthermore, the minimum conformal length $\mathcal L_{\min}=\min_{t\in[t_0,t_1]} \mathcal L(t)\geq 0$ is reached at $t=t_1$ in the future-contracting regime and at $t=t_0$ in the future-expanding regime.
\eei
In the future-contracting regime, subsequent estimates require the assumption that $\mathcal L_{\min}>0$ and depend on $1/\mathcal L_{\min}$, which is \emph{not bounded} by the initial data.  In the future-expanding regime $\mathcal L_{\min}>0$ is part of the initial data.
The constants $C_1,C_2,\dots$ below depend on $\mathcal L_{\min}$ and on the finite-energy and bounded-variation norms of initial data.
\bei
\item \emph{Both-sided bounds on conformal length and volume.}
  \bel{both-sided-LV}
  (C_1)^{-1} \leq \mathcal L(t) \leq C_1 , \qquad (C_2)^{-1} \leq \mathcal V(t) \leq C_2 .
  \ee

\item \emph{Bounded variation in space.} The lapse, twist and conformal length measure satisfy
  \bel{spatial-bv}
    \|\ell\|_{\BVac(0,1)} + \|(\log\Omega,\Kpar)\|_{\BVac(\Tbb^3)}
    \leq C_3 , \qquad t \in [t_0,t_1] .
  \ee

\item \emph{Temporal integrals.} The (not necessarily positive) spatial stress~$T_\chi^{11}$ admits integrals on constant-$x$ slices
\bel{temporal-stress}

Altogether, under the assumed coercive stress condition, the finite-energy and bounded-variation norms \eqref{equa-flow-energy-norm}--\eqref{equa-flow-variation-norm} of the areal flow are bounded by a function of its initial data and, in the future-contracting regime, of~$\mathcal L_{\min}$.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
    \item \textbf{Random regular graphs.}
    Let \(G_n\) be the random \(d\)-regular graph on \([n]\), with law \(p_{d,n}\).
    If $d>2c_{\theta,u}$, then there exist \(\eta>0\), \(s>0\), and \(c>0\) such that for every \(a\ge 0\),
    \[
    p_{d,n}\!\left(
    \frac1s\int_a^{a+s}\Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\,\dd t \ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi graphs.}
    Let \(G_n\sim G(n,\lambda/n)\). If $\lambda>2c_{\theta,u}$,
    then there exist \(\eta>0\), \(s>0\), and \(c>0\) such that for every \(a\ge 0\),
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \frac1s\int_a^{a+s}\Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\,\dd t \ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]

    \item \textbf{Simple bounded-degree configuration model.}
    Let \(G_n\) be the simple graph obtained from the configuration model with
    degree sequence \((d_i^{(n)})_{i=1}^n\). Assume that
    \[
    1\le d_i^{(n)}\le \Delta
    \qquad\text{for all }i,n,
    \]
    and $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n d_i^{(n)}\to \rho$. If $\rho>2c_{\theta,u}$,
    then there exist \(\eta>0\), \(s>0\), and \(c>0\) such that for every \(a\ge 0\),
    \[
    \Pbb\!\left(
    \frac1s\int_a^{a+s}\Pbb^{G_n}_{\theta,t,u}(A_\eta)\,\dd t \ge c
    \right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
    \]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:11:02.370219+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d7869535a4c1dc4341bba41ff9e33b837ad20e1d78007ed5e4cfb961277d2aed","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition middle terms strategy of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] Let $n$ be even. Then, $I_{\frac{n}{2}}^*=I_{\frac{n}{2}+1}^*=\{n-1,n\}$, i.e. the player should guess card $n-1$ or card $n$ in positions $\frac{n}{2}$ and $\frac{n}{2}+1$. If $n$ is odd, card $n-1$ or card $n$ should be guessed in position $\frac{n+1}{2}$.
    \begin{proof}
        By Proposition $(guessing strategy symmetry of the paper)$ and Lemma $(last two rows are equal of the paper)$, it suffices to show that $n\in I_{\frac{n}{2}}^*$ and $k\notin I_{\frac{n}{2}}^*$ for $k\leq n-2$. We compute 
        \[p_{i,\frac{n}{2}}=\frac{\binom{i-1}{\frac{n}{2}-1}+\binom{i-1}{\frac{n}{2}}}{2^i}=\frac{\binom{i}{\frac{n}{2}}}{2^i}\]
        where the second equality is a consequence of Pascal's identity. Consider the sequence 
        \[a_i=\frac{\binom{i}{\frac{n}{2}}}{2^i}\]
        We note that $a_i=0$ for all $i\leq \frac{n}{2}-1$ and $a_i>0$ for all $i\geq \frac{n}{2}$. Now we examine the ratio of consecutive terms. Canceling factorials, we obtain
        \[R_i:=\frac{a_{i+1}}{a_i}=\frac{i+1}{2(i+1-\frac{n}{2})}\]
        Immediately, we have $R_{n-1}=1$ and $R_{i}<1$ for all $i\leq n-2$. This shows that $a_i$ is strictly increasing for all $\frac{n}{2}\leq i\leq n-1$ with $a_{n-1}=a_{n}$. This implies $a_{n-1}$ and $a_n$ are the unique maxima. But $a_n=p_{n,\frac{n}{2}}$, and the result follows. The construction for odd $n$ is nearly identical.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f ∈ C^2 with f'' ≥ θ > 0 (uniform convexity); mere convexity gives the formula in a weaker form without the 1/(θt) rate","u0 ∈ L^∞(R) (no continuity or BV assumption is needed)","one space dimension","L = f*, so L' = (f')^{-1} is the inverse of the characteristic speed map"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.417891+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: scalar conservation laws in one dimension","id":"claim_d7a257d997d536db52cf3c6032a0f57ab1de869ebcb3ceea2438b6ddd1fd22e4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f ∈ C^2(R) be uniformly convex, f''(s) ≥ θ > 0 for all s, and let u0 ∈ L^∞(R). Put L := f* (the Legendre transform of f), h(y) := ∫_0^y u0(r) dr (so h is Lipschitz), and for t > 0 consider the minimization of y ↦ t L( (x-y)/t ) + h(y). Then: (i) for each t > 0 a minimizer exists for every x, is unique for all but at most countably many x, and, denoting it y(x,t), the map x ↦ y(x,t) is nondecreasing; (ii) the function u(x,t) := (f')^{-1} ( ( x - y(x,t) ) / t ) = L'( (x - y(x,t))/t ), defined for a.e. x and every t > 0, is the unique Kruzhkov entropy solution of u_t + f(u)_x = 0 with u(·,0) = u0; (iii) u satisfies Oleinik's one-sided estimate u(x + z, t) - u(x,t) ≤ z/(θ t) for all z > 0 and t > 0 — so the solution can jump down but never up, and jumps are exactly the points where the minimizer y(·,t) is discontinuous; (iv) u = w_x where w is the Hopf-Lax solution of the Hamilton-Jacobi equation w_t + f(w_x) = 0 with w(·,0) = h.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:25:41.597731+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d7dc728e4f45aa1bb5e1654709fbed1a4422baded7a647ef548d66d29c62a225","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition defn:axiomatic_shf of arXiv:2608.11603, 'Continuous-time directed polymers to the Critical SHF via moments'] {}
	A process $\mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}$ is called a Stochastic Heat Flow with strength $\theta_{\star}$, or $\mathsf{SHF}(\theta_{\star})$, if
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}, ref=\thedefinition\textup{(\roman*)}]
    	\item
    	 \textbf{(Continuity)} $\mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}} = \{\mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{s,t}\} \in C(\mathbb{R}_{\leqslant}^{2}, \measspace{\mathbb{R}^2 \times \mathbb{R}^2})$. 
    	\item
    	\textbf{(Chapman--Kolmogorov)} For all $t_{0} < t_{1} < t_{2}$, there exists a sequence $\{u_{\ell}\}$ in $\mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^2)$ for which the operator $\psi \mapsto u_{\ell} \ast \psi$ converges strongly to the identity, such that the difference $\mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{t_{0},t_{1}} \bullet_{\ell} \mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{t_{1},t_{2}} - \mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{t_{0},t_{2}}$ is well-defined and converges to $0$ vaguely, in probability as $\ell \to \infty$.
    	\item 
    	\textbf{(Independent increments)} For all $ t_{0}  < \cdots < t_{k}$, the random variables $\mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{t_{0},t_{1}},  \ldots \mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{t_{k-1}, t_{k}}$ are independent.
    	\item
    	\textbf{(Delta-Bose Moments)} For $n = 1,2,3,4$, $s<t$ and $h, h' \in \mathcal{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}^2)$, the following holds:
    	\begin{equation*}
    		\mathbf{E} \Big(\Big\langle h, \mathcal{Z}^{\theta_{\star}}_{s,t} h' \Big\rangle \Big)^{n} = \Big\langle h^{\otimes n}, \mathcal{Q}^{[\![n]\!], \theta_{\star}}(t-s) h'^{\otimes n} \Big\rangle \, .
    	\end{equation*} 
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751964+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_d808bc15a0303b9690e36c075fb8407e6aa1c7ddf475cac89c2eb1a5636847d8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The monotone convergence theorem for an INCREASING sequence 0 <= f_1 <= f_2 <= ... needs no integrability hypothesis at all: integral f_n dmu increases to integral (lim f_n) dmu in [0, infinity]. The downward statement is FALSE without an extra hypothesis. On R with Lebesgue measure, f_n = 1_{[n, infinity)} decreases pointwise to 0, yet integral f_n = infinity for every n. The correct downward version requires f_1 in L^1 (equivalently, on a finite measure space with a bounded f_1): if f_n decreases pointwise to f and f_1 is integrable then integral f_n -> integral f, which follows from applying upward monotone convergence to f_1 - f_n. FATOU'S LEMMA, integral liminf f_n <= liminf integral f_n for f_n >= 0, is strict in general and its strictness is exactly the escaping-mass and concentrating-mass phenomena: with f_n = 1_{[n, n+1]} on R, liminf f_n = 0 pointwise so the left side is 0 while the right side is 1; with f_n = n 1_{(0, 1/n)} on [0,1] the left side is 0 and the right side is again 1. Reverse Fatou, limsup integral f_n <= integral limsup f_n, requires an integrable UPPER bound f_n <= g in L^1, and fails without one: for f_n = n 1_{(0, 1/n)} on [0,1] the pointwise limsup is 0 with integral 0, while limsup integral f_n = 1, so the inequality is violated - and no integrable g dominates all the f_n. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorems 2.14 and 2.15]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.345721+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d811d5a4f342b2ca990a543b016e9be538d352a4041c33ed5bb124df76084441","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 139 (IAMP mimicking BOGP SDE) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall from Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} 
  the initial conditions $X(q_0)\sim\zeta$ and $Y(q_0)\sim\zeta^\Ising$. Now let
  \[
  \breve{X}(q_0)\equiv0\,,\quad
  \breve{Y}(q_0)\equiv
    \frac{Y(q_0) \sqrt{q_0}}{(\bbE[Y(q_0)^2])^{1/2}}\,.\]
If $Y(q_0)\equiv0$ then we (somewhat arbitrarily) set $\breve{Y}(q_0)\sim\cN(0,q_0)$.
Then $\E[\breve{Y}(q_0)^2]=q_0$ in either case,
and it follows from
assumption~(\ref{i:IAMP-main-init}) of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} 
that
  \beq
    \bbE\bigg[
      \Big(
  Y(q_0)-\breve{Y}(q_0)
  \Big)^2\bigg]
  =\Big(
   \E[Y(q_0)^2]^{1/2}
   -  (q_0)^{1/2}\Big)^2
    \leq \Big|
    \bbE[Y(q_0)^2]-q_0\Big|
    \leq \epsilon\,.
    \eeq
We initialize vectors $\bx^0,\prxbx^0\in\R^M$ and 
$\by^0,\prxby^0\in\R^N$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item The coordinates of $\prxby^0$ are sampled i.i.d.\ from $\Law(Y(q_0))=\zeta^\Ising$. If $\bbE[Y(q_0)^2]>0$, then we set 
	\[\by^0 = \bigg(
	\frac{q_0}{\bbE[Y(q_0)^2]}
	\bigg)^{1/2} \prxby^0\,.\]
If $\bbE[Y(q_0)^2]=0$, then we let $\by^0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_0 I_N)$. 

\item the coordinates of $\prxbx^0$ are sampled i.i.d.\ from $\Law(X(q_0))=\zeta$, and we set $\bx^0 = \bzero \in \R^M$.
\end{itemize}
For fixed $\delta$ we abbreviate $ b^\ell(x)\equiv b_{q_0+\ell\delta}(x) \equiv b(q_0+\ell\delta,x)$, etc. We then introduce the vectors
\beq
\begin{aligned}
\bb^{\ell}
&\equiv
b^\ell(\prxbx^{\ell})
\equiv
b_{q_0+\ell\delta}(\prxbx^{\ell}) \in \bbR^M\,,\\
\bsig^{\ell}
&=
\sigma^\ell(\prxbx^{\ell})
\equiv
\sigma_{q_0+\ell\delta}(\prxbx^{\ell}) \in \bbR^M,
\\
\bw^{\ell}
&\equiv
w^\ell(\prxby^{\ell})
\equiv w_{q_0+\ell\delta}(\prxby^{\ell})
 \in \bbR^N, 
\end{aligned}\eeq
where the functions $b^\ell,\sigma^\ell,w^\ell$ are applied coordinate-wise. Let 
  \beqc_\ell(\epsilon)
  \equiv
  \bigg[\alpha\delta
  \Big( \budget(q_0+\ell\delta)+\epsilon-\Cost(q_0+\ell\delta) \Big)
    \bigg]^{1/2}\,.
  \eeq
As in \eqref{eq:IAMP-fully-general-fixed}, each $\bar{\bg}^\ell$ is an independent standard gaussian vector in $\R^N$. We let $\gamma(\ell,\delta)$ and $\prxgamma(\ell,\delta)$ be certain positive scalars, defined in \eqref{eq:proxy-C-ell-delta-def} below.  The IAMP iterates are as follows, with $\bu^0=\bzero \in \R^N$ and $\bm^{-1} = \bm^0=\bzero\in\R^M$: 
\begin{align}

  \prxby^{\ell+1}
  -
  \prxby^{\ell}
  &=
  \prxgamma(\ell,\delta)^{-1}
  \bw^{\ell}\odot(\bu^{\ell+1}-\bu^{\ell})
  \in\bbR^N,
  \\

  \by^{\ell+1}
  -
  \by^{\ell}
  &=
  \gamma(\ell,\delta)^{-1}
  \bw^{\ell}\odot(\bu^{\ell+1}-\bu^{\ell})\in\bbR^N\,,
  \\

  \bu^{\ell+1}
  -
  \bu^{\ell}
  &\equiv
  (\bA_\ell)^{\top}
  \big(
    \bm^{\ell}
    -
    \bm^{\ell-1}
  \big)
  + \delta^{1/2}
  (\bJ_{\ell+1})^\top\bb^\ell
  + c_\ell(\epsilon)
  \bar{\bg}^{\ell}
  -
  \ons_{\bu,\ell}
  \in\R^N\,,\\

  \bv^{\ell}&=\bA_{\ell}\by^{\ell}-\ons_{\bv,\ell-1}\in\bbR^M\,,
  \\

  \bm^{\ell+1}-\bm^{\ell}
  &=p(q_0+\ell\delta)^{-1}
  \big(\bsig^{\ell}
  -
  1
  \big)
  \odot
  \big(\bv^{\ell+1}-\bv^{\ell}\big)
  \in \bbR^M\,,
  \\

  \prxbx^{\ell+1}
  -
  \prxbx^{\ell}
  =
  \bx^{\ell+1}
  -
  \bx^{\ell}
  &=
  \bsig^{\ell}\odot
  \big(\bv^{\ell+1}-\bv^{\ell}\big)
  +
  \delta
  p'(q_0+\ell\delta)^{1/2}
  \,
  \bb^{\ell}
  \in 
  \bbR^M
  \,.
\end{align}
The Onsager terms $\ons_{\bu,\ell}$ and $\ons_{\bv,\ell-1}$ will be defined in \eqref{e:u.combined.ons} and \eqref{e:v.combined.ons} below. 
\textbf{We denote the above iteration by $\IAMP_N(\sigma,b,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising,\delta)$.} 
In the notation of Remark~\ref{rmk:omega-general-seed}, 
this algorithm will have random seed given by
	\beq
	\omega= \Big(
	\bG_\circ,
	(\bar\bg^\ell)_{1\le\ell\le\ubl},
	\bx[0], \by[0]\Big)\,.
	\eeq
For a fixed realization of $\omega$, this IAMP iteration will be a $C(L,\epsilon)$-Lipschitz function of the random matrix $\bG$ on an event with probability $1-e^{-cN}$, and the algorithm witnessing Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main} is its globally Lipschitz extension.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are topological spaces and X x Y carries the product topology","for the equality: both X and Y are second countable (a countable base of open sets); separable metric suffices","B(X) tensor B(Y) denotes the sigma-algebra generated by measurable rectangles, not its completion","the inclusion B(X) tensor B(Y) inside B(X x Y) needs no countability hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402216+00:00","domain":"measure theory and topology, Borel structures on products","id":"claim_d85e091e5868ae9cbf056305f26be57cebf2da93d681eeb18aff1182d687f85d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be topological spaces and give X x Y the product topology. Write B(Z) for the Borel sigma-algebra of a space Z and B(X) tensor B(Y) for the product sigma-algebra, i.e. the sigma-algebra on X x Y generated by the measurable rectangles A x B with A in B(X) and B in B(Y). Then: (i) ALWAYS B(X) tensor B(Y) is contained in B(X x Y), because the two coordinate projections are continuous, hence Borel measurable. (ii) If X and Y are both SECOND COUNTABLE (each has a countable base of open sets), then equality holds: B(X x Y) = B(X) tensor B(Y). In particular this applies to separable metric spaces, so B(R^(m+n)) = B(R^m) tensor B(R^n), and to Polish spaces and to countable products of second countable spaces. Practical consequence: for second countable targets, a map into X x Y is Borel measurable exactly when both components are, and Borel functions of two variables are jointly measurable in the product sense - which is what lets Fubini-Tonelli be applied to Borel functions. WHERE IT FAILS: second countability is not a technicality. Let X be a set of cardinality strictly greater than the continuum equipped with the discrete topology, so that B(X) is the full power set and X x X is discrete. The diagonal {(x,x)} is closed, hence Borel in X x X, but by a classical theorem (B. V. Rao) the diagonal of X belongs to P(X) tensor P(X) if and only if the cardinality of X is at most the continuum. So B(X x X) strictly contains B(X) tensor B(X). The underlying reason is structural: every set in a product sigma-algebra is already measurable with respect to a countably generated pair of sub-sigma-algebras, so a product sigma-algebra can only see countably many 'coordinates' at a time, while the product topology of a non-second-countable space produces open sets that need uncountably many. A second warning of the same kind: for Lebesgue sigma-algebras the analogous equality is FALSE - the Lebesgue sigma-algebra of R^(m+n) is strictly larger than the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras of R^m and R^n; it is its completion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["All restricted four-point, unit-norm centered-ReLU teacher and paired nonzero initialization assumptions of C010","Independent label noise amplitude sigma_e=c_e sqrt(kappa) eta_e^(1/4)~sqrt(kappa)e^(9/4)","Noise-averaged clean risk; simultaneous both-layer GD step 1/2; fixed nu in (0,1]","Even width limit precedes feature-scale limit; local windows only; eta_e is spectral ratio, not GD step size"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:50.829441+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_d89b9de19b9c660b1053843fd221195d71bd568e8a0d66ceffe03289fef81a6d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Joint low-noise central-window bifurcation

T267 / Target 2 / C012 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.
This is a local, rescaled noise-onset result in C010's restricted model.
It is not an exact global two-critical-noise-level theorem.

## 1. Precise scaling and result

Use C010's four-point stratified design, centered unit-norm ReLU teacher,
paired nonzero initialization with fixed nu in (0,1], both-layer GD with
step 1/2, and label-noise-averaged clean risk Q. Let alpha=alpha_e and
let b_h denote C009's full-kernel rates. Set

eta_e=(b2+b12)/b1 ~ e,
rho_e=kappa sqrt(eta_e), kappa>0 fixed,
sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e),
t0_e=log(1/sqrt(eta_e)).

Here sigma_e is the amplitude of independent symmetric label noise.
It is asymptotic to sqrt(kappa) e^(9/4). The network step size remains
1/2; eta_e in this proof is a spectral ratio, not that step size.

Let F_e(z) be the continuously interpolated frozen risk divided by
alpha^2. Define its central-time version
G_e(s)=F_e((t0_e+s)/b1). Then, uniformly on compact real s intervals,

G_e'(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa(s)
       =kappa exp(-s)-exp(-2s)-1,
G_e''(s)/(2 eta_e) -> H_kappa'(s)
       =-kappa exp(-s)+2exp(-2s).

Equivalently, the normalized value differences converge locally uniformly:

[G_e(s)-G_e(0)]/(2 eta_e) -> V_kappa(s)-V_kappa(0),
V_kappa(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(1/2)exp(-2s)-s.

If kappa>2, define z_+=(kappa+sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2 and
z_-=(kappa-sqrt(kappa^2-4))/2. The frozen curve has a central strict local
minimum at scaled time tending to s_min=-log z_+, and a subsequent strict
local maximum at scaled time tending to s_max=-log z_-.
In small fixed neighborhoods of those two points there is exactly one
frozen stationary point of the indicated type for sufficiently small e.
The actual nonlinear discrete-GD risk has strict descent-rise-descent
witnesses near these points, with probability tending to one in the
iterated even-width-then-feature-scale limit. Its interval minimizers and
maximizers on these separate neighborhoods have the same scaled limits.
Its resulting central local peak obeys

b1 k_peak-t0_e -> s_max,
k_peak ~ (2pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e),

in that iterated probabilistic sense. The first assertion refers to every
maximizer in a chosen sufficiently small neighborhood of s_max; it does
not assert that all actual extrema are unique.

For 0<kappa<2, the FROZEN interpolated risk is strictly decreasing on any
fixed compact central s window for sufficiently small e. No monotonicity
of actual finite-width risk is asserted. At kappa=2 the leading derivative
has a degenerate zero; this proof does not resolve its finite-e unfolding.
Thus 2 is a threshold for this limiting central-window shape, not a proved
global critical noise level or a global absence theorem.

## 2. Uniform derivative limit

The exact frozen curve is
F_e(z)=rho_e(1-exp(-b0 z))^2
      +sum_(h=1,2,12)[exp(-2b_h z)+rho_e(1-exp(-b_h z))^2].
Its nonconstant h derivative with respect to z is
2 b_h q_h [rho_e-(1+rho_e)q_h], q_h=exp(-b_h z).
At z=(t0_e+s)/b1, q1=sqrt(eta_e)exp(-s). Therefore its contribution to
G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) is exactly
kappa exp(-s)-(1+kappa sqrt(eta_e))exp(-2s).

For h=2,12, b_h/b1=O(eta_e) and
q_h=1+O(eta_e log(1/eta_e)), uniformly on compact s sets. Their combined
contribution to G_e'(s)/(2eta_e) tends to -1, since their b_h/b1 weights
sum to eta_e. Differentiating with respect to s makes their contribution
tend to zero: the extra b_h/b1 factor is O(eta_e).
The constant-mode term and its s derivatives tend to zero after division
by eta_e. Indeed b0/b1 is of order 1/e, t0_e is of order log(1/e), and
exp[-(b0/b1)(t0_e+s)] decays faster than every power of e on compact s
sets. These exact formulas prove both uniform derivative limits.
Integration from zero proves the uniform value-difference limit.

## 3. Limiting stationary points and risk witnesses

Writing z=exp(-s)>0, H_kappa=kappa z-z^2-1.
For kappa>2 its roots are z_+>1 and z_-<1 with product one.
At s_min=-log z_+, H_kappa'=z_+ sqrt(kappa^2-4)>0;
at s_max=-log z_-, H_kappa'=-z_- sqrt(kappa^2-4)<0.
Thus V has a strict minimum then a strict maximum. Compact uniform
convergence of H and H' gives a unique frozen critical point near each,
of the same type; the derivative is bounded away from zero outside small
root neighborhoods inside a fixed central compact window.

Choose delta>0 sufficiently small. The four scaled times
s_min-delta, s_min, s_max, s_max+delta are increasing and have strict
limiting value inequalities descent-rise-descent. Rounded integer times
floor((t0_e+s)/b1) have scaled grid error at most b1, which tends to zero.
The associated frozen risk differences therefore have strictly positive
margins of order alpha^2 eta_e. The same value convergence provides a
strict gap away from the unique minimum or maximum in each separate
small neighborhood.

For 0<kappa<2, completion of the square gives
H_kappa=-(z-kappa/2)^2+kappa^2/4-1<0 for every z>0.
Its maximum is strictly negative, so compact uniform derivative
convergence implies the stated frozen decrease on each fixed compact
s window. This does not control scaled times escaping all compacts.

## 4. Actual nonlinear GD and order of limits

For each fixed e, rho_e, alpha_e and all interval endpoints are fixed
numbers, and all involved integer times lie below T_e=ceil(e^(-5/2))
for sufficiently small e. Labels remain bounded. C010's independent-pair
finite-horizon comparison therefore controls every involved actual risk
uniformly through T_e as width grows, including all sixteen noise
patterns. Multiplication of the error by the fixed positive factor
1/(alpha_e^2 eta_e) preserves convergence to zero for this FIXED e.
It follows, first taking width to infinity then e to zero, that the
actual risk value differences converge to the same V differences and
inherit the strict four witnesses. The positive local value gaps transfer
the interval minimizers and maximizers to s_min and s_max. No derivative
comparison for the actual nonlinear network is needed or claimed.

Finally eta_e~e, b1~nu^2 e/(4pi), so t0_e~(1/2)log(1/e) and the displayed
peak time follows. This theorem concerns a different joint-noise regime
from C011's fixed-rho phase comparison; neither proof exchanges limits.

## 5. Exact concrete witness certificate, kappa=5/2

Here z_+=2, z_-=1/2. Use z values 3,2,1/2,1/4 in decreasing order,
so the corresponding s=-log z and integer times increase. The primitive
values are respectively

-3+log 3, -3+log 2, -9/8-log 2, -19/32-2log 2.

Their required margins are
log(3/2), 15/8-2log 2, log 2-17/32, all strictly positive.
For fully checkable bounds, log(3/2)>1/3 and
7/12<log 2<3/4 follow from integrals of 1/t: the lower bound splits
[1,2] into [1,3/2] and [3/2,2] and uses right-endpoint rectangles.
For the upper bound write t=1+x and use
1/(1+x)<=1-x/2 on [0,1], strict in the interior, since the difference
has numerator x(1-x)/2. The margins exceed 1/3,3/8,5/96 respectively.
This certifies a specific joint-noise witness choice by exact rational
bounds, not a floating-point estimate of a bifurcation.

## Remaining scope

The exact finite-e global onset, the degenerate kappa=2 case, interaction
with the initial constant-mode transient, iid sampling, fixed-positive
noise and all-time nonlinear dynamics remain open. These restrictions
matter: a central-window derivative result cannot imply that no other
double-descent pattern occurs elsewhere in time. Pairing and finite
support remain as in C010. Dependencies C009/C010 and this argument
await independent mathematical review; specialist novelty is unestablished.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:43:55.606917+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d8ec3ef31db884761237fab40059b78b21c5ffd265553aa72e7dc1b883d52f2f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theoremi thm_planar_ordering of arXiv:2604.04672, 'Connected components and topological ends of stationary planar forests'] Let $\Gamma$ be a set of topological lines of the plane, such that for all distinct $\gamma,\gamma'\in\Gamma$, the difference $\gamma\setminus\gamma'$ is a portion of $\gamma$. Then, for all distinct $\gamma,\gamma'\in\Gamma$, denoting by $\triangle$ the symmetric difference operator, the set
        \[J(\gamma,\gamma')\coloneqq\overline{\gamma\triangle\gamma'}\]
    is a Jordan curve. Furthermore, setting
        \[(\gamma,\gamma')_\Gamma\coloneq\{\sigma\in\Gamma\setminus\{\gamma,\gamma'\}:J(\gamma,\sigma)\subset\overline{\mathrm{Int}} J(\gamma,\gamma')\}\]
    for all distinct $\gamma,\gamma'\in\Gamma$, the ternary relation $\cdot\in(\cdot,\cdot)_\Gamma$ induces a \emph{betweenness} structure on $\Gamma$, that is, there exists a strict total order $<_\Gamma$ on $\Gamma$, unique up to reversal, such that for all distinct $\gamma,\gamma',\sigma\in\Gamma$,
        \[\sigma\in(\gamma,\gamma')_\Gamma\iff[\gamma<_\Gamma\sigma<_\Gamma\gamma'\text{ or }\gamma'<_\Gamma\sigma<_\Gamma\gamma].\]
    Finally, for all distinct $\gamma,\gamma',\sigma\in\Gamma$, $\sigma\notin(\gamma,\gamma')_\Gamma\iff J(\gamma,\sigma)\subset\overline{\mathrm{Ext}} J(\gamma,\gamma')$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Its density is invariant and hence constant under the second ergodic law; ergodicity of the first forces its absolutely continuous mass to be either zero or one. Nonzero overlap therefore forces equality. Check: The singular and absolutely continuous parts are preserved by the action by uniqueness of Lebesgue decomposition; this is the load-bearing invariance step. Obstruction: This handles forest laws admitting such an ergodic common action. Arbitrary networks may lack it; two distinct probability laws need not be singular in general.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726283+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis / dispersive PDE","id":"claim_d948b0ea69eecd49bd6d6367620cfaf6003daf10d9fece613e380a2beca5623f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Christ–Kiselev lemma passes from an untruncated space-time bound L^p_t → L^q_t to its causal truncation ∫_{s<t} only when p < q strictly. At p = q the truncation can be unbounded even when the full operator is bounded. Concrete counterexample on L²(R): let K(t,s) = sin(t−s)/(t−s) (continuous, locally bounded). The full operator is convolution with the sinc kernel, whose Fourier multiplier is π·1_{[−1,1]}(ξ) (up to normalization), so it is bounded on L² with norm ≈ π. Its causal truncation is convolution with k(u) = 1_{u>0} sin(u)/u, whose multiplier is m(ξ) = ∫_0^∞ e^{−iuξ} sin(u)/u du; using ∫_0^∞ sin(u) sin(uξ)/u du = (1/2) log |(1+ξ)/(1−ξ)|, the imaginary part of m is −(1/2) log|(1+ξ)/(1−ξ)|, which is unbounded as ξ → ±1. A convolution operator on L²(R) is bounded if and only if its multiplier is in L^∞, so the truncated operator is unbounded on L²: p = q = 2 fails. Consequence for PDE: the retarded (Duhamel) Strichartz estimate at the double endpoint q = q̃ = 2 cannot be obtained from the untruncated estimate by Christ–Kiselev; it is exactly the case Keel–Tao had to prove directly. Any proof that claims the double-endpoint inhomogeneous estimate 'by Christ–Kiselev' is misapplying the lemma.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["for the smoothing transform: existence of alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 in the admissible range, plus regularity conditions such as E[sum_i T_i^alpha log^+ T_i]<infinity from Durrett-Liggett/Biggins theory","for Poisson-Dirichlet: a well-defined subordinator, or fragmentation/coalescent structure, whose ranked, normalized jump sizes are being studied","independence of (T_i) from the i.i.d. copies (W_i) in the smoothing transform equation","non-degeneracy conditions ruling out the trivial Dirac-mass-at-0 solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.998030+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d95edc3570f77641129fb8247438ed5ea704bbccb6be4cad5233917af61c0692","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The smoothing transform concerns fixed points of the distributional equation W =_d sum_i T_i W_i, where (T_i) is a given, typically random, sequence of nonnegative weights and (W_i) are i.i.d. copies of W independent of (T_i); such fixed points arise as limits of branching random walk martingales, including derivative martingale limits, or of Mandelbrot multiplicative cascades, and their tail behavior, characterized by a power-law index alpha solving E[sum_i T_i^alpha]=1 or a related equation, governs the limit's regular variation. Durrett and Liggett characterized the solution set of the smoothing transform equation, establishing existence, uniqueness up to a scaling constant, and the precise tail index under moment conditions on (T_i), a result foundational for analyzing branching random walk boundary and derivative martingale limits and related models such as the random energy model. Separately, Poisson-Dirichlet distributions PD(alpha,theta) arise as the limiting law of ranked, normalized jump sizes of a subordinator, of ranked cycle lengths in random permutations, or of ranked masses in fragmentation and coalescent processes, characterized via the stick-breaking (GEM) construction or via a Poisson process of jumps of a stable subordinator normalized by its total mass. Neither result gives an explicit closed-form density for the general fixed point or limit; the smoothing transform's fixed point is typically characterized only implicitly, through its tail index and functional equation, and both results require specific moment or regular-variation conditions on the input weights or subordinator to hold. Typical failure: Assuming the smoothing transform has a unique nontrivial fixed point up to scale without checking that the characteristic equation E[sum T_i^alpha]=1 actually has a solution in the admissible range, or without the Durrett-Liggett/Biggins regularity conditions, particularly in boundary cases such as the critical branching random walk where the derivative martingale, rather than the ordinary martingale, is the relevant object; applying the generic smoothing-transform tail behavior in a boundary or degenerate parameter regime without re-deriving it is a common source of incorrect tail-index claims. Canonical reference: Durrett and Liggett, 1983, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Biggins and Kyprianou, 2005, Electronic Journal of Probability; Pitman and Yor, 1997, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.493241+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d9619f115929734baab046145a93d1ace1842cc7f20f5d61cfb6bb39e4756f86","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 10 (Gelfand-Tsetlin facts, {\cite[Proposition 2) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] {NarSheffTao}}]
Let \(\lambda=(\lambda_1\geq \cdots \geq \lambda_n)\in\Spec_n\).  For
\(a\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}\) denote the real
Gelfand-Tsetlin polytope of triangular arrays
\[
        \Gamma=\{\lambda^{(k)}_i:1\leq i\leq k\leq n\}
\]
satisfying
\[
        \lambda^{(k+1)}_i
        \geq
        \lambda^{(k)}_i
        \geq
        \lambda^{(k+1)}_{i+1},
        \qquad
        1\leq i\leq k<n,
\]
with top row \(\lambda^{(n)}=\lambda\), and diagonal boundary condition
\[
        \sum_{i=1}^k \lambda^{(k)}_i
        =
        \sum_{i=1}^k a_i,
        \qquad 1\leq k\leq n.
\]
Let \(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel *}:=\bigcup_a\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}\).
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] If \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), then the Schur--Horn relation
\(\diag(\lambda)\rel a\) holds if and only if
\(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}\) is nonempty.
\item[(ii)] The \(\binom n2\)-dimensional volume of
\(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel *}\) is \(V_n(\lambda)/V_n(\tau_n)\).
\item[(iii)] If \(A\) is Haar-uniform on the unitary orbit with spectrum
\(\lambda\), then the eigenvalues of the northwest principal minors of
\(A\) form a uniformly distributed point of
\(\GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel *}\). Its boundary vector \(a\) is the diagonal of
\(A\).
\item[(iv)] If \(\Lambda\in\Spec_n\) has large gaps,
\[
        \min_{1\leq i<n}(\Lambda_i-\Lambda_{i+1})
        >
        \lambda_1-\lambda_n,
\]
then for every \(a\in\mathbb R^n\) there is a volume-preserving linear
bijection
\[
        \GT_{\diag(\lambda)\rel a}
        \longleftrightarrow
        H_n(\Lambda,\lambda;\Lambda+a).
\]
Under this bijection, a Gelfand-Tsetlin pattern
\((\lambda^{(k)}_i)_{1\leq i\leq k\leq n}\) is sent to the hive \(h:T_n\to
\mathbb R\) given by
\[
        h(i,j)
        =
        \Lambda_1+\cdots+\Lambda_j
        +
        \lambda^{(j)}_1+\cdots+\lambda^{(j)}_i .
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-02T00:34:53.675639+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_d97be235d01df4d78b67ce6366ce4d108aa22374e33abc12f3ab6cb220eb967c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In calculus and real analysis, absolute continuity is a regularity property of functions that is stronger than uniform continuity, and hence continuity. The notion of absolute continuity allows one to obtain generalizations of the relationship between the two central operations of calculus—differentiation and integration. This relationship is commonly characterized in the framework of Riemann integration, but with absolute continuity it may be formulated in terms of Lebesgue integration. For real-valued functions on the real line, two interrelated notions appear: absolute continuity of functions and absolute continuity of measures. These two notions are generalized in different directions. The usual derivative of a function is related to the Radon–Nikodym derivative, or density, of a measure. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:23:03.034516+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d98feba1bb71e6e4d6980179a25205901c9d83096617fcde4b9b35c89fed88d3","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 20 (SDE for the second Malliavin derivative) of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Assume that Assumptions \ref{ass:smooth},
and \ref{ass:second-malliavin-uniform} hold. Fix
$ 0 \le r \le s \le t $, $ u \in [s,t] $,
$ i,j,k \in \left\{ 1,\dots,N \right\} $, and
$ \alpha,\beta \in \left\{ 1,\dots,m \right\} $.
Then, the process $\left(
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
\right)_{u \in [s,t]}$ solves the SDE
\begin{align}

D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_u^{i,N}
&=
\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\left(
\partial_x b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
+
G_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
+
R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
\right)
d\rho
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\int_s^u
\left(
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
+
H_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
+
S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
\right)
dB_\rho^i ,
\end{align}
where $\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}$ denotes the initial
condition given by
\begin{align*}
\mathcal I_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}
&=
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}}
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} X_s^{i,N}
e_\alpha
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ r=s \right\}}
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=k \right\}}
\partial_x \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_s^{i,N}e_\beta
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=j \right\}} \frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\left( X_s^{\ell,N} \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} X_s^{\ell,N} e_\alpha
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ r=s \right\}}
\mathbf{1}_{\left\{ i=k \right\}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu \sigma\left( X_s^{i,N},\mu_s^N \right)\left( X_s^{\ell,N} \right)
D_s^{j,\alpha} X_s^{\ell,N} e_\beta ,
\end{align*}
with $ e_\alpha $ denoting the $ \alpha $-th vector of the canonical basis of $ \R^m $,
\begin{align}

G_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
&=
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
D_r^{k,\beta} D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N},
\end{align}
and $H_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho) $ is defined by the same formula, with
$ b $ replaced by $ \sigma $, while
\begin{align}

R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)
&=
\partial_{xx}^2 b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_\mu\left[ \partial_x b \right]
\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_x\left[
\partial_\mu b\left( \cdot,\mu_\rho^N \right)\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\right]\left( X_\rho^{i,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\partial_v\left[
\partial_\mu b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\right]\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right]
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\frac1{N^2}\sum_{\ell=1}^N \sum_{q=1}^N
\partial_{\mu\mu}^2 b\left( X_\rho^{i,N},\mu_\rho^N \right)
\left( X_\rho^{\ell,N}, X_\rho^{q,N} \right)
\left[
D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{q,N}, D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}
\right],
\end{align}
and $ S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho) $ is defined by the same formula, with
$ b $ replaced by $ \sigma $. Finally, there exists a constant $ C > 0 $, independent of
$ r,s,t,\rho,N,i,j,k,\alpha,\beta $, such that, for every $ \rho \in [s,t] $,
\begin{align}

\norm{R_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)}
+
\norm{S_{r,s}^{i,j,k,\alpha,\beta}(\rho)}
&\le
C \Bigg(
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}}
+
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}
\nonumber\\
&\quad
+
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{i,N}}
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_s^{j,\alpha} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}
+
\frac1N \sum_{\ell=1}^N
\norm{D_r^{k,\beta} X_\rho^{\ell,N}}","status":"unverified"}

Then
\[
\alpha d\,\cH\!\left(\frac{c}{\alpha d}\right)-\sup_\R V
\le\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)\le
\alpha d\,\cH\!\left(\frac{c}{\alpha d}\right)-\inf_\R V.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\frac{\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)}{|\log\alpha|}\longrightarrow\frac{c}{R_+}
\qquad(\alpha\downarrow0).
\]
Under the edge hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:heteroHamiltonian},
\[
\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)
=\frac{c}{R_+}\left[\log\frac{c}{\alpha d}
+p\log\log\frac{c}{\alpha d}-p\log R_+-\log(R_+A)-1\right]+O(1).
\]
If, in addition, $V\equiv a_0$, then
\[
\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)=\alpha d\,\cH\!\left(\frac{c}{\alpha d}\right)-a_0
=\sup_{s\in\R}\{cs-\alpha d(M(s)-1)\}-a_0.
\]
If $s_\alpha>0$ is the optimizer, then $\alpha dM'(s_\alpha)=c$ and
\[
(\Lambda_D^\R)'(\alpha)=-d(M(s_\alpha)-1)<0,\qquad
(\Lambda_D^\R)''(\alpha)=\frac{c^2}{\alpha^3dM''(s_\alpha)}>0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)=-a_0+\frac{c^2}{2\alpha dD_2(J)}
-\frac{D_4(J)c^4}{24\alpha^3d^3D_2(J)^4}+O(\alpha^{-5})
\qquad(\alpha\to+\infty),
\]
and, under the edge hypothesis,
\[
\Lambda_D^\R(\alpha)=\frac{c}{R_+}\left[\log\frac{c}{\alpha d}
+p\log\log\frac{c}{\alpha d}-p\log R_+-\log(R_+A)-1+o(1)\right]-a_0
\]
as $\alpha\downarrow0$. Finally, for
$\cA_{\sigma,m,\R}u=\sigma^{-m}(J_\sigma*u-u)+cu'+a_0u$,
\[
\Lp(\cA_{\sigma,m,\R})=\sigma^{-m}\cH(c\sigma^{m-1})-a_0.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["n>=2 and K>0","All 2n coordinates of x and y are mutually independent and each has a Lebesgue density bounded a.e. by K","Z,u,v,w are deterministic real coefficients","rank(Z)>=2"],"created_at":"2026-10-07T01:09:09+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_d9f3dbc365ca4e0870b0925e5f01e8fe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n>=2, K>0, and let x=(x_1,...,x_n) and y=(y_1,...,y_n) be real random vectors whose 2n coordinates are mutually independent, each with a Lebesgue density bounded almost everywhere by K. Let Z be a deterministic real n by n matrix, u,v deterministic real n-vectors, and w a deterministic real scalar. Write sigma_1(Z)>=...>=sigma_n(Z)>=0 for its singular values, and assume r=rank(Z)>=2. Then Q=x^T Z y+x^T u+v^T y+w has a Lebesgue density satisfying ||p_Q||_infinity <= 2(C_RV K)^2 sqrt(2e*pi) min_{2<=j<=r} [j^(-1/2) (product_{i=1}^j sigma_i(Z))^(-1/j)], where C_RV is the universal constant in the Rudelson-Vershynin bounded-density projection theorem. Equivalently one may minimize over 2<=j<=n, interpreting terms with zero singular-value product as infinity. This is the k=1 corollary of Banks, Garza-Vargas, Kulkarni and Srivastava, arXiv:2005.08930. No bounded-density bound is available in general at rank one: if U,V are independent uniform(0,1), UV has density -log(t) on 0<t<1, which is unbounded near zero. Independence only between the two vectors is insufficient even at rank two: x=(U,U), y=(V,V), Z=diag(1,-1) gives Q=0 almost surely. A quadratic-form application must independently verify the coordinate independence and rank hypotheses.","status":"unverified"}

with masses $s_0=s_3=s_6=s_7=\frac1{4(1+2\varepsilon)}$ and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T16:46:51.518941+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_d9f8d662691360ba70c27634d29157ba859e2c7184c720c68306842f109cf517","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the pigeonhole principle states that if n items are put into m containers, with n > m, then at least one container must contain more than one item. For example, of three gloves, at least two must be right-handed or at least two must be left-handed, because there are three objects but only two categories of handedness to put them into. This seemingly obvious statement, a type of counting argument, can be used to demonstrate possibly unexpected results. For example, given that the population of London is more than one unit greater than the maximum number of hairs that can be on a human head, the principle requires that there must be at least two people in London who have the same number of hairs on their heads.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.235220+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dab15ba146eefad594bfb1127aa334a49aadee8418addb6be53fcfc3f5cb9226","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 of arXiv:2609.00567, 'Hodge--Tate splitting and Akizuki--Nakano vanishing in positive characteristic'] Let \(\iota \colon X \to S\) be a morphism of $\F_p$-stacks.

\[
