\[
F_{X/S}\colon X \to  X^{(1)}
\]
be the relative Frobenius.
  \begin{itemize}
      \item   The \emph{(absolute) de Rham stack} of \(X\) is defined as a functor
  \begin{equation*}
    X^{\dR} \colon \CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p} \to \Ani; \  R \mapsto X(W(R)/^L p),
  \end{equation*}
  where \(W(R)\) is the ring of Witt vectors of \(R\), \(-/^L p\) is the derived quotient by \(p\), and \(X(W(R)/^L p)\) is the mapping space \(\Map_{\dSch_{\setF_p}}(\Spec(W(R)/^L p), X)\) in the \(\infty\)-category of derived schemes over \(\setF_p\).
  Since this is isomorphic to the relative Hodge--Tate stack \((X/\setZ_p)^{\HT}\) of \(X\) relative to the crystalline prism \((\setZ_p, (p))\) introduced in \cite{bhatt2022Prismatization}*{Construction 7.1}, this is a stack on \(\CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p}\) (\cite{bhatt2022Prismatization}*{Lemma 7.3}).

  This is equipped with natural morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    \pi_{X} \colon X \to X^{\dR} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu_X \colon X^{\dR} \to X
  \end{equation*}
  of \(\setF_p\)-stacks: For each \(R \in \CAlg^{an}_{\setF_p}\), each morphism is given by precomposition of morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    R \xrightarrow{\Phi_R} W(R)/^L p \quad \text{and} \quad W(R)/^L p \xrightarrow{\res} R,
  \end{equation*}
  where \(\Phi_R\) is the animation of the morphism \(a \mapsto [a^p] \bmod p\) and \(\res\) is the restriction morphism.
  Note that the composition \(\nu_X \circ \pi_X\) is the absolute Frobenius morphism \(F_X \colon X \to X\) of \(X\).
\item The \emph{de Rham stack} of $X$ over $S$ is defined by
\[
(X/S)^{\dR} \defeq X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR},\pi_S} S.
\]
We define natural morphisms
  \begin{equation*}
    \pi_{X/S} \colon X \to (X/S)^{\dR} \quad \text{and} \quad \nu_{X/S} \colon (X/S)^{\dR} \to X^{(1)}
  \end{equation*}
  of \(\setF_p\)-stacks as follows:
The morphism $\pi_{X/S}$ is defined by
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
X \arrow[r,"\pi_{X/S}"'] \arrow[rd,bend right,"\iota"] \arrow[rr,bend left,"\pi_X"] & X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR}} S \arrow[r,"\pr_1"] \arrow[d,"\pr_2"] & X^{\dR} \arrow[d,"\iota^{\dR}"] \\
& S \arrow[r,"\pi_S"] & S^{\dR}.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
The morphism $\nu_{X/S} \colon (X/S)^{\dR} \to X^{(1)}$ is induced by the following commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
X^{\dR} \times_{S^{\dR}} S \arrow[r,"\pr_1"] \arrow[d,"\pr_2"] & X^{\dR} \arrow[d,"\iota^{\dR}"] \arrow[r,"\nu_X"] & X \arrow[d,"\iota"] \\
S \arrow[r,"\pi_S"] \arrow[rr,bend right,"F"] & S^{\dR} \arrow[r,"\nu_S"] & S.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\item We assume that $\iota$ is smooth representable.
Then the cotangent complex \(L_{X/S}\) is a locally free \(\cO_X\)-module concentrated in degree \(0\).  
We set
\[
\Omega^1_{X/S} \defeq L_{X/S},
\qquad
\Omega^i_{X/S} \defeq 
\bigwedge_{\cO_X}^i\Omega^1_{X/S}.
\]
The universal \(S\)-derivation
\[
d_{X/S}\colon \cO_X \to  \Omega^1_{X/S}
\]
extends uniquely to the relative de Rham complex
\[
\Omega^\bullet_{X/S}
=
\left[
\cO_X
\xrightarrow{d_{X/S}}
\Omega^1_{X/S}
\xrightarrow{d_{X/S}}
\Omega^2_{X/S}
 \to \cdots
\right].
\]

We define a morphism of complexes of $\cO_{X^{(1)}}$-modules
\[
F^{\dR}_{X/S} \colon \cO_{X^{(1)}} \to F_{X/S,*}\Omega^{\bullet}_{X/S}
\]
as follows:
We have
\[
d_{X/S}\circ F_{X/S}^{\sharp}=0
\]
by checking smooth locally on \(X\).  
Therefore, the morphism
\[
F_{X/S}^{\sharp}\colon
\cO_{X^{(1)}} \to  F_{X/S,*}\cO_X
\]
defines a morphism of complexes
\[
F_{X/S}^{\dR}\colon
\cO_{X^{(1)}}
 \to 
F_{X/S,*}\Omega^\bullet_{X/S},
\]
whose degree \(0\) component is \(F_{X/S}^{\sharp}\) and whose
positive-degree components are zero.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:55:27.258728+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dabd2d8a9c94c17b6e66ae3a98f56a0c89349c4f708e8d59a99c1a6e168d952a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:dg of arXiv:2410.23509, 'Dynkin Games for L\'evy Processes'] Let 
$G_1(x)\leq G_2(x)$
be two real continuous payoff functions.
Consider a L\'evy process $X$ and a discount factor $r>0$, 
such that conditions (equation eq:ic of the paper) and (equation eq:limit of the paper) above hold.
Given two stopping times $\sigma$ and $\tau$, define the expected payoff

$$
{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)=\operatorname{\mathbf{E}}_x\left(
e^{-r\tau}G_1(X_{\tau})\mathbf{1}_{\{\tau\leq\sigma\}}
+
e^{-r\sigma}G_2(X_{\sigma})\mathbf{1}_{\{\sigma<\tau\}}
\right).
$$

The Dynkin game (DG) problem consists
in finding the value function $V(x)$ and two optimal stopping rules ${\sigma^*}$ and ${\tau^*}$ such that
\begin{align}
V(x)&=\inf_{\sigma}\sup_{\tau}{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)=\sup_{\tau}\inf_{\sigma}{\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma,\tau)={\operatorname{\mathbf{M}}_x}(\sigma^*,\tau^*).

\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149110+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_db0bd50e4b1d3185e597734ebdf3437ca5f83b01bff6e16e23fd7c464aeb3f41","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: Omega bounded. The proofs use boundedness twice - the auxiliary function exp(gamma x_1) must be bounded on Omega, and the maximum must be attained on a compact set. On unbounded domains the conclusion is false even for harmonic functions with zero boundary data. Unbounded counterexample: on the half-space {x_n > 0} the function u(x) = x_n is harmonic and vanishes on the whole boundary, yet u > 0 inside; sup u = infinity while sup over the boundary of u = 0. Bounded counterexample (so boundedness of u does not rescue the statement in general): for n >= 3 let Omega = {|x| > 1} and u(x) = 1 - |x|^{2-n}. Then u is harmonic in Omega, continuous up to the boundary, bounded with 0 <= u < 1, u = 0 on the boundary sphere, and sup over Omega of u = 1 > 0 = sup over the boundary of u^+. In the plane, u(x) = log|x| on {|x| > 1} is an unbounded version of the same phenomenon. What restores the principle: treat infinity as a boundary point, i.e. assume limsup of u(x) as |x| tends to infinity is <= 0 (then the principle holds on any unbounded Omega, by exhausting with large balls), or impose a Phragmen-Lindeloef growth restriction adapted to the geometry. The admissible growth is set by the opening of the domain, and a thinner domain permits faster growth, not slower: in a plane sector of opening pi/a the threshold is exp(|x|^a), so a narrow sector allows faster growth than a half-plane, and in a strip of width d the threshold is exp(pi|x|/d), the extremal being exp(pi x_1/d) cos(pi x_2/d). The same caution applies to the H^1 weak maximum principle: its proof uses the Sobolev inequality together with the fact that the level sets have finite measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583768+00:00","domain":"algebraic geometry","id":"claim_db5eb654cfadf445fa059f8bceb44a8415837ad88ca812a4513a0ade0f74de10","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a smooth projective curve of genus g over an algebraically closed field, equivalently a compact Riemann surface, and let D be a divisor on X. Write l(D) for the dimension of the space of meromorphic functions on X whose poles are bounded by D and which have no other poles, and let K be a canonical divisor of X. The Riemann-Roch theorem states l(D) - l(K - D) = deg(D) + 1 - g, where deg(D) is the sum of the coefficients of D. Once deg(D) > 2g - 2 this gives l(D) = deg(D) + 1 - g exactly, since l(K-D) then vanishes. Proved by Riemann and Roch in the 1850s-60s; vastly generalized by Hirzebruch and Grothendieck.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:35:56.961006+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db6f1f3f67070692d1b6450d41e2d7f9f5137d013b008fc1d32aeb790cb14589","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma main_lemma of arXiv:2604.05921, 'Simplicity of random hypergraphs'] Let $\delta_1,\delta_2 \in \mathds{N}$. Given (possibly non-unique) vertices $v_1,v_2,\hdots,v_{\delta_1} \in V$, let the unique vertices be denoted by $v'_1,v'_2,\hdots,v'_{u(\vb*{v})}$, for some $u(\vb*{v}) \in \mathds{N}$. Similarly, let the unique vertices in $w_1,w_2,\hdots,w_{\delta_2}$ be denoted by $w'_1,w'_2,\hdots,w'_{u(\vb*{w})}$. Let $D(\vb*{v})=\frac{\delta_1!}{\prod_{i=1}^{u(\vb*{v})} m_{v'_i}(\vb*{v})!}$ and $D(\vb*{w})=\frac{\delta_2!}{\prod_{i=1}^{u(\vb*{w})} m_{w'_i}(\vb*{w})!}$. Let $\hat{R}(\cdot)$ be as in (equation def:B_hat of the paper) and let $U$ denote a uniformly chosen vertex in $V$. For any functions $f_1^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N}$, $f_2^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N}$ and $w \in \mathds{N}$,
    \begin{align}
        
        &\sum_{\vb*{v} \in V^{\delta_1}}  \sum_{\vb*{w} \in (V\backslash\{v_1,\hdots,v_{\delta_1}\})^{\delta_2}} (D(\vb*{v})D(\vb*{w}))^w \prod_{i=1}^{u(\vb*{v})} f_1^{(m_{v'_i}(\vb*{v}))}(v'_i) \prod_{j=1}^{u(\vb*{w})} f_2^{(m_{w'_j}(\vb*{w}))}(w'_j) \nonumber \\
        &=\sum_{\substack{\vb*{a} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}:\\ \sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} ia_i = \delta_1}}  \frac{\delta_1!^{1+w}}{\prod_{k=1}^{\delta_1} k!^{(1+w)a_k}} \sum_{\substack{\vb*{b} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}:\\ \sum_{i=1}^{\delta_2} ib_i = \delta_2}}  \frac{\delta_2!^{1+w}}{\prod_{k=1}^{\delta_2} k!^{(1+w)b_k} } \nonumber \\
    &\hspace{1cm} \times \sum_{\gamma(\cdot) \in \hat{R}(\vb*{a},\vb*{b})} (-1)^{\sum{\vb*{g} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}, \vb*{h} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}}( \sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} g_i + \sum_{j=1}^{\delta_2} h_j -1) \gamma(\vb*{g},\vb*{h})} \nonumber \\
    &\hspace{1cm} \times  \prod_{\substack{\vb*{y} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_1}\\ \vb*{z} \in \mathds{N}^{\delta_2}}} \Bigg( \frac{1}{\gamma(\vb*{y},\vb*{z})!} \Big(\frac{n\mathds{E} \big[\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_1} (f_1^{(i)}(U))^{y_i} \prod_{j=1}^{\delta_2} (f_2^{(j)}(U))^{z_j} \big] \big(\sum_{i=1}^{\delta_1} y_i + \sum_{j=1}^{\delta_2} z_j-1 \big)!}{\prod_{i=1}^{\delta_1} y_i! \prod_{j=1}^{\delta_2} z_j!} \Big)^{\gamma(\vb*{y},\vb*{z})} \Bigg).
    \end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:53:00.814024+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db722a684036d88d3fed8ad5ff1061549c4e967a0edae2aee9aeb8f24e21e943","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Type forest, type rays and paths of arXiv:2607.16911, 'Multipartite random graphs with given degrees: local limit, revisiting the giant, distance'] Consider the \\emph{Ulam-Harris forest} $\\mathscr{F}_S$ on the set of types $S$. That is to say, $\\mathscr F_S$ is an infinite forest, consisting of $|S|$ many infinite tree components $\\{\\mathscr T(s):s\\in S\\}$. For any fixed $s_0 \\in S$, the root of the tree $\\mathscr T(s_0)$ is $s_0$, and for any $v\\in \\mathscr T(s_0)$, it has $|S|$ many offspring $\\{vs:s\\in S\\}$. Observe that any $v\\in \\mathscr T(s)$ has the form of a word $v=s_0s_1\\dots s_k$. We call the forest $\\mathscr F_S$ the \\textit{type forest} corresponding to the set of types $S$. \n    \n    Furthermore any directed infinite path $\\pi=(s_0\\rightarrow s_0s_1 \\rightarrow s_0s_1s_2\\rightarrow \\dots)$ starting at the root $s_0$ is called a \\emph{type ray} in $\\mathscr T(s_0)$, and a finite directed path of the form $(s_0\\rightarrow s_0s_1 \\rightarrow \\dots \\rightarrow s_0s_1s_2\\dots s_k)$ is called a \\emph{type path} started at $s_0$. By $|\\pi|$ we denote the length of $\\pi$. Thus, if $\\pi$ is a type ray, $|\\pi|=\\infty$, while for $\\pi=(s_0\\rightarrow s_0s_1 \\rightarrow \\dots \\rightarrow s_0s_1\\dots s_k)$, $|\\pi|=k$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:04.961469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db75c2f89cf0c0e5614bf6efc2acc163da629893662959afc861c32c88072a49","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2604.00642, 'Quantitative central limit theorem for an integrated periodogram via the fourth moment the'] Let
\[
f_\alpha(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{-\alpha}L(\lambda),
\qquad \lambda\in(-\pi,\pi),\quad \alpha\in\mathcal A,
\]
where $\mathcal A=[a,b]\subset[0,1)$, and assume that the true parameter value $\alpha_0$ belongs to $\mathcal A$. Suppose that $L\in \mathcal C^1([-\pi,\pi]\setminus\{0\})$ is positive on $[-\pi,\pi]$ and slowly varying at $0$.

Define the Whittle contrast by
\[
Q_n(\alpha)
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
\left[
\log f_\alpha(\lambda)+\frac{I_n(\lambda)}{f_\alpha(\lambda)}
\right]\dd\lambda,
\qquad \alpha\in\mathcal A.
\]
Let
\[
\widehat\alpha_n\in \arg\min_{\alpha\in\mathcal A} Q_n(\alpha)
\]
be any measurable minimizer of $Q_n$ over $\mathcal A$. Then
\[
\widehat\alpha_n \xrightarrow{\mathbb P} \alpha_0,
\]
and
\[
\sqrt n\,(\widehat\alpha_n-\alpha_0)
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{4}{\sigma_0^2}\right),
\]
where
\[
\sigma_0^2
=
\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \bigl(\log|\lambda|\bigr)^2\,\dd\lambda.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:25:41.600281+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db7d364cb00afeb71df457227830316d3af03b3c823ffcc7ab835243f64266b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:mass-no-killing of arXiv:2608.11931, '\texorpdfstring{Nonlinear parabolic characterizations of stochastic completeness at infini'] Let $G$ be a graph with $\kappa=0$ and \(\mu(X)<\infty\).
Let $\phi\in\mathcal{I}$ with $\phi^{-1}(\mathbb R_+)\neq\emptyset.$ Then \(G\) satisfies
\hyperref[def:SC]{\textup{(SC)}}{} if and only if one, and hence all, of the
statements {\rm(ii)}--{\rm(iv)} of
Theorem~(thm:generalized-mass-characterization of the paper) hold, with the
generalized mass identity~\hyperref[eq:nonlinear-generalized-mass]{\textup{(MB)}}{} reducing
to the conservation of mass:
\[
    \mathsf M_u(t)=\mathsf M_{u_0}
    \qquad \text{for } t\in[0,T].
\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_db9918fbc671f11eee90cd6406606fa76cc6077e21fc89d28df52ffb173bfd87","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 237 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\alpha,L,\epsilon,K>0$ and any sequence of $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_N)_{N\ge 1}$,
	\[
		\lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big) 
		= \lim_{N\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu_{\sym}(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha;\epsilon)\Big)
		= 0\,.
	\]

\begin{proof}
	We only prove that the first limit is zero, as the second limit is proved analogously.
	Suppose for contradiction that there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $\bbW_2(\mu(\cA_{N[K]}), \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta$ for infinitely many $N$.
	By \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4} from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}, there exists $C = C(\alpha,L,K) > 0 $ such that for sufficiently large $N$, $\mu(\cA_{N[K]}) \in \cP_4(\R,C)$.
Then, for infinitely many $N$, we have
	\[\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\in
		S_\delta 
		\equiv \Big\{ \mu \in \cP_4(\R,C) : \bbW_2(\mu, \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)) \ge \delta 
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_4(\R,C)$ endowed with the $\bbW_2$ metric is compact.
	The set $S_\delta$ is closed with respect to the $\bbW_2$ metric, hence also compact. Therefore
 we may find $\mu \in S_\delta$ and a subsequence $(N_j)_{j\ge 1}$ such that
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} \bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big) = 0\,.
	\]
	As noted in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, we have $\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j[K]}) = \mu^{\Ising}(\cA_{N_j})$: thus, since each $\cA_{N_j}$ is an $\epsilon$-approximate $L$-Lipschitz algorithm, so is each $\cA_{N_j[K]}$. It follows by omitting finitely many $j$'s that we have
	\[
	\WERR(\cA_{N_j[K]},\mu)
	=\max\bigg\{
	\bbW_2\Big(\mu(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\mu\Big),
	\bbW_2\Big(
		\mu^\Ising(\cA_{N_j[K]}),
		\cP(\{\pm1\})
		\Big)
	\bigg\}\le\epsilon
	\]
for all $j$. Recalling the definition \eqref{e:cM.Lip} of  $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon)$, this implies
	\[
		\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;\epsilon)\,,
	\]
	which contradicts that $\mu \in S_\delta$.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

\[

where the supremum is over stopping times for Brownian motion. Then, for every $T>0$,
\[

\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726371+00:00","domain":"hyperbolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dbf122d5a238489aa083fdb44f89336d4d034fb877e0be5e3ba3b1dc4f1ae3c4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'the solution at (t,x) depends only on the data on the sphere ∂B(x,t)', i.e. sharp propagation on the light cone with no tail, holds only in odd space dimensions n ≥ 3. Finite speed of propagation (support in {|x| ≤ t + R}) holds in every dimension; the sharp inner edge does not. Counterexample n = 1: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{[−1,1]}, d'Alembert's formula gives u(t,x) = (1/2)∫_{x−t}^{x+t} u1, so u(t,0) = 1 for every t ≥ 1 — the disturbance never leaves the origin. Counterexample n = 2: with u0 = 0 and u1 = 1_{B(0,1)}, Poisson's formula gives u(t,0) = (1/2π)∫_{|y|<1} (t² − |y|²)^{−1/2} dy > 0 for every t > 1 — a decaying tail behind the wavefront (this is why a splash on a pond is felt long after the front passes, while a sound pulse in three dimensions is heard once). Practical consequence: statements like 'the data inside B(x,t) do not matter' or 'the solution vanishes after the front passes' are valid only for odd n ≥ 3, and any argument that tacitly extends them to n = 1, 2 or to even dimensions (or to variable-coefficient / curved-background wave equations, where strong Huygens generally fails even in odd dimensions) is unsound.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.845617+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc6b41a2e65e311eaddb446d8f516a18f90158f9f11f93d80d67fed31fc2a608","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi 17 (Elliptical Brownian motions) of arXiv:2511.10535, 'Eigenvalues of Brownian Motions on $\mathrm{GL}(N,\mathbb{C})$'] Let $\rho>0$ and let $\zeta\in\C$ with $0<|\zeta|\le\rho$.  Define
\begin{equation}
    
    \theta = \frac12\arg \zeta \qquad a = \sqrt{\frac12(\rho+|\zeta|)} \qquad b = \sqrt{\frac12(\rho-|\zeta|)}. 
\end{equation}
Then $a^2+b^2=\rho$ and $e^{2\i\theta}(a^2-b^2)=\zeta$, so that $(a,b,\theta)$ satisfy \eqref{eq.rho.zeta}.  This yields a bijective mapping
\begin{equation} \{(\rho,\zeta)\colon 0<|\zeta|\le\rho\}\mapsto\{(a,b,\theta)\colon a>b\ge 0, \theta\in[0,\pi)\}. \end{equation}
We may extend the definitions of $a,b$ to allow $\zeta=0$, in which case $a=b$; here $\theta$ is undefined.

Let $(X^N(t))_{t\geq 0}$, $(Y^N(t))_{t\geq 0}$ be independent Hermitian Brownian motions of size $N$. 
We define the general {\bf elliptical Brownian motion} $(W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t))_{t\ge0}$ by
	\[ W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t) = e^{\i \theta} \left(aX^N(t) + \i b Y^N(t)\right). \]
    Similarly, if $(x(t))_{t\geq 0}$ and $(y(t))_{t\geq 0}$ are freely independent free semicircular Brownian motion, the {\bf free elliptical Brownian motion $(w_{\rho,\zeta}(t))_{t\ge0}$} is defined as
    \[ w_{\rho,\zeta}(t) = e^{\i \theta} \left(a x(t) + \i b y(t)\right). \]
In both cases, when $a=b$ (i.e.\ $\zeta=0$), all values of $\theta$ yield the same distribution for the right-hand-side, so we may take canonically $\theta=0$ in this case.

Note that the laws of $W^N_{\rho,\zeta}(t)$ and $w_{\rho,\zeta}(t)$ are invariant under $a\mapsto-a$, $b\mapsto-b$, and $(a,b,\theta)\mapsto(b,a,\theta+\frac{\pi}{2})$.  It then follows from \eqref{eq.bijection} that $\rho>0$, $|\zeta|\le\rho$ paramaterize the laws of all possible elliptical Brownian motions.

To lighten notation we will often drop the subscripts $\rho,\zeta$ if there can be no confusion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:23:58.616383+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc75c05103e56e836dc8a7c9b6a2b507af99d8e9e30200a0d1c57c3dbb785083","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 138 (Basic properties of the flow map of $\newL$) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] Let $\newL$ be the null vectorfield defined in \eqref{E:DOUBLENULLEIKONALFUNCTIONNORMALIZEDNULLVECTORFIELDS},

	$\newL$ with respect to the double-null coordinates
	$(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3)$, i.e., the solution to

	\begin{align} 
		\nullgeop{\ubar}
		\FlowmapnewL(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3)
		& = 
		\newL \circ \FlowmapnewL(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3),
		&
		\FlowmapnewL(\leftubar,u,x^2,x^3)
		& = (\timefunction_0,u,x^2,x^3).

	Then for $A = 2,3$ there exist functions 
	$\FlowmapnewLarg{A}
	: [\leftubar,\ubarboot] \times [\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2] \times \mathbb{T}^2
	\rightarrow \mathbb{T}$
	such that:
	\begin{align}

	=
	\left(
		\ubar,u,
		\FlowmapnewLarg{2}(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3),
		\FlowmapnewLarg{3}(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3)
	\right).
	\end{align}
	Moreover, $\FlowmapnewL$
	is a $C^{0,1}$ Lipeomorphism
	from $[\leftubar,\ubarboot] \times [\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2] \times \mathbb{T}^2$
	onto $[\leftubar,\ubarboot] \times [\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2] \times \mathbb{T}^2$

	\begin{align}

			\FlowmapnewL

		& \lesssim \auxbootsmall,
		& 
		\left\|
			\InverseFlowmapnewL
			-
			\mbox{\upshape I}
		\right\|_{C_{\textnormal{null}}^{0,1}([\leftubar,\ubarboot] \times [\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2] \times \mathbb{T}^2)}
		& \lesssim \auxbootsmall,
	\end{align}
	where $\mbox{\upshape I}(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3) \eqdef (\ubar,u,x^2,x^3)$
	is the identity map on double-null coordinate space and $\InverseFlowmapnewL$ 
	is the inverse function of $\FlowmapnewL$.
	In particular, for each fixed $(\ubar,u) \in[\leftubar,\ubarboot] \times [\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]$,
	the map 
	$(x^2,x^3) 
	\mapsto 
	\left(\FlowmapnewLarg{2}(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3),\FlowmapnewLarg{3}(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3) \right)$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:19:42.478187+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dc7f92a47f72e853d6ed6052ff3725a3345f24c23d06c222b2e1bdf27fc0359c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 11 (Parametric weighted lattice-corner expansion) of arXiv:2609.03466, 'Least-Favorable Location for Binomial Top-$t$ Selection'] Let $U$ be a compact interval. For each $p\in U$, let $Z_p$ be a random vector supported by a fixed finite subset of $\Zz^d$, with masses that are positive and $C^{r+2}$ in $p$. Assume that the additive group generated by differences of support points is $\Zz^d$. Put
\[
 M_p(\lambda)=\Ee e^{\langle\lambda,Z_p\rangle}.
\]
Suppose there is a $C^{r+2}$ map $\lambda:U\to(0,\infty)^d$ satisfying
\[
 \nabla_\lambda\log M_p(\lambda(p))=0.
\]
Let
\[
 I(p)=-\log M_p(\lambda(p)),
 \qquad
 \Sigma(p)=\nabla_\lambda^2\log M_p(\lambda(p)).
\]
Let $w:\Zz_+^d\to\Rr$ be bounded and define
\[
 W(p)=\sum_{z\in\Zz_+^d}
 w(z)e^{-\langle\lambda(p),z\rangle}.
\]
For independent copies $Z_{p,1},\ldots,Z_{p,n}$, put $S_{n,p}=\sum_{i=1}^nZ_{p,i}$ and
\[
 \mathcal T_n(p)=\sum_{z\in\Zz_+^d}w(z)\Pp(S_{n,p}=z).
\]
Then, for $\varepsilon_n=n^{-1/2}(\log n)^{3r+6}$,
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n(p)
 =\frac{e^{-nI(p)}n^{-d/2}}
 {(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p)}}
 \left[W(p)+O_{C^r(U)}(\varepsilon_n)\right].
 
\end{equation}
If $r\ge1$ and $I'(p_0)\ne0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n'(p_0)
 =n^{1-d/2}e^{-nI(p_0)}
 \left\{-I'(p_0)
 \frac{W(p_0)}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p_0)}}+o(1)\right\}.
 
\end{equation}
If in addition $W(p_0)\ne0$, this may equivalently be written with a relative factor $\{1+o(1)\}$. If $r\ge2$, $I'(p_0)=0$, $I''(p_0)>0$, and $W(p_0)>0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_n''(p_0)
 =-I''(p_0)
 \frac{W(p_0)}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\sqrt{\det\Sigma(p_0)}}
 n^{1-d/2}e^{-nI(p_0)}\{1+o(1)\}.
 
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:23:58.630342+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dcb9755e3b78d02e1ec93b76039e5957f028e8053edea20d6ae234b5f42a125f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 240 (Existence and continuation criteria for the characteristic initial value problem; \cite{speckyucharacteristicIVP}) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] \hfill

\medskip
	
\noindent \underline{\textbf{Local existence for the characteristic IVP}}. 
Recall that the classical solution is $C^{\infty}$ on $\twoargMrough{[\timefunction_0,0],[- \rightu,\leftu]}{0}$
and therefore induces $C^{\infty}$ data on the characteristic surfaces
$\ingoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\leftubar}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}, \, \outgoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\moreinterestingu_1}{[\leftubar,0]}$; see Appendix~\ref{A:DATASSUMPTIONS}.
Then there exists a  
$\ubarlocal \in (\leftubar,0)$, depending on the data, such the characteristic data launch a unique $C^{\infty}$ solution
on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarlocal)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$,

{"assumptions":["U open with lambda_1 > 0 on H^1_0(U) (e.g. U bounded, or bounded in one direction, or of finite measure)","g in L^2(U)","u the weak solution of the Dirichlet heat equation with u(0) = g","the equality case requires the infimum defining lambda_1 to be attained, e.g. U bounded"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.105957+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_dccca23e6eedae7c488796bf4490a59edff019e1d479e546a6dbd3a3e781c655","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $U\\subset\\mathbb R^n$ be open with $\\lambda_1=\\inf\\{\\|\\nabla v\\|_{L^2}^2/\\|v\\|_{L^2}^2:v\\in H^1_0(U),v\\ne0\\}>0$; this positivity holds in particular when $U$ is bounded, when $U$ is merely bounded in one direction, and when $U$ has finite measure. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.176507+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dce2c5f1ca2ba7f115f24e4985d485e0ea81fbf2f9568b8bd5140a67410b7be1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 71 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For fixed $q_0 \in [0,1)$ and $f \in L^\infty([q_0,1];[0,1/\alpha])$, the mapping $p \mapsto \cM(q_0;p,f)$, viewed as a function from $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ to  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$, is uniformly continuous:
    \[
        d_\cH\Big(\cM(q_0;p,f),\cM(q_0;\tilde p,f)\Big)^2
        \le 6(1+\|f\|_\infty) \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1\,.
    \]
Here $\incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ is metrized by  $\mathsf{dist}(p,\tilde p) = \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1$, and we recall that  $P(\cP_2(\bbR))$ is metrized by the Hausdorff distance \eqref{e:hausdorff}. 

\begin{proof}
Let $p,\tilde p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with $\|p'-\tilde p'\|_1 = \delta$.
Since $p(1) = \tilde p(1) = 1$, it follows by integrating that $|p(t) - \tilde p(t)| \le \delta$ for all $t\in [q_0,1]$, and so certainly we have $\|p-\tilde{p}\|_1\le\delta$. Recalling the notation of Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}, let $(b,\sigma)\in \Adm(q_0;p,f)$. We will construct modified controls $(\tilde b,\tilde \sigma) \in \Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$ such that the corresponding solutions to \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} approximate each other. Recall $s(t)\equiv (tp)'(t)^{1/2}$, and similarly denote
$\tilde{s}(t)\equiv (t\tilde{p})'(t)^{1/2}$.
We set $\tilde{b}=b$, and let $\hat \sigma$ be defined by the relation
	\[\hat{\sigma}_t-1
	= a(t) 
	(\sigma_t-1)\,,\quad
	a(t)
	\equiv 
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	\frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{\tilde{s}(t)}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_0,1]$. We note that 
	\[
	\frac{s(t)}{p(t)^{1/2}}
	= \frac{[p(t) + tp'(t)]^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}} \ge 1\,,
	\]
so the ratio $a(t)$ can only be large if $p'(t)$ is very large, which occurs on a set of times of small measure. It is clear from the construction that $(\tilde b,\hat{\sigma})$ satisfies the budget constraint \eqref{e:budget-f} defining $\Adm(q_0;\tilde p,f)$, with the exception that $\hat{\sigma}$ is not necessarily non-negative. Let $X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(b,\sigma)$, and $\hat X$ be given by \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} with controls $(\tilde b, \hat \sigma)$. We couple these processes with the same initialization $X(q_0) = \hat{X}(q_0) = 0$ and the same Brownian motion $B$. We will first show the endpoint laws of $X(1)$ and $\hat{X}(1)$ are close, then address the issue of $\hat{\sigma}$ being possibly negative. To this end, we recall from \eqref{e:formal.sde.main} that
  \[
        X(1) = \int_{q_0}^1 p'(t)^{1/2} b_t\,dt
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t)\,dB(t)
        + \int_{q_0}^1 s(t) (\sigma_t-1)\,dB(t)
        \,,
    \]
and similarly for $\hat{X}(1)$. This gives us a decomposition
$X(1)-\hat{X}(1) = \textup{(a)}+\textup{(b)}+\textup{(c)}$, and we proceed to bound each of the three terms:
    \begin{align*}\E[\textup{(a)}^2]
    &= \E \bigg[
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 \Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big) b_t\,dt\bigg)^2\bigg]
    \le \bigg(
     \int_{q_0}^1\Big(
        p'(t)^{1/2}
        - \tilde{p}'(t)^{1/2}\Big)^2\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg( \int_{q_0}^1 \E[(b_t)^2]\,dt\bigg) \\
    &\le\bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 |p'(t)-\tilde{p}'(t)|\,dt\bigg)
    \bigg(\int_{q_0}^1 f(t)\,dt\bigg) 
    =  \delta \|f\|_1 \,,
    \end{align*}
having used the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality along with the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f}. Next,
    \[\E[\textup{(b)}^2]
    = \int_{q_0}^1 \Big( s(t)-\tilde{s}(t) \Big)^2\,dt
    \le \int_{q_0}^1 \Big|s(t)^2 - \tilde{s}(t)^2\Big|\,dt
    \le \|p-p\|_1+\|p'-p'\|_1 \le 2\delta\,.\]
Lastly, using the above definition of $\hat\sigma$, we have
	\begin{align*}
	\E[\textup{(c)}^2]
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \Big( s(t) (\sigma_t-1)-\tilde{s}(t)(\hat{\sigma}_t
    -1)\Big)^2\,dt\\
    &= \int_{q_0}^1
    \frac{s(t)^2}{p(t)}
    \E[(\sigma_t-1)^2]
    \cdot p(t)
    \bigg( 1- 
    	\frac{\tilde{s}(t)}{s(t)} a(t)
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt\\
	&\le
	\|f\|_\infty
	\int_{q_0}^1
	p(t)
    \bigg( 1- \frac{\tilde{p}(t)^{1/2}}
		{p(t)^{1/2}}
    	 \bigg)^2
	\,dt 
	\le \|f\|_\infty \delta\,,
	\end{align*}
having used the budget constraint~\eqref{e:budget-f} along with the calculation from the bound on (a) above. Collec (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:54:53.443469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd038426f703dde2403154a36724715d1981820c0aa7f4d5dc7cdb10eb9bd4aa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Multispecies mixed Ising model) of arXiv:2606.15432, 'A Concavity Theorem for the Parisi PDE'] Let $N\geq 1$, $D\geq 1$ and $\Sigma_N=\{\pm 1\}^N$.
For all $\bmx\in\mathbb R^D$, define the covariance function
\[
    \xi(\bmx)
    =
    \sum_{k\geq 1}
    \xi_k(\bmx)
    =
    \sum_{k\geq 1}
    \sum_{\substack{\bm p\in\mathsf P_k}}
    \Delta_{\bmp}^2\prod_{d=1}^D x_d^{p_d}.
\]
where $\bmDelta=(\Delta_{\bmp}^2:\bmp\in\mathsf P_k,\, k\geq 1)$ is a family of nonnegative coefficients and
where
\[
    \mathsf P_k
    =
    \{\bmp=(p_1,\ldots,p_D)\in\mathbb Z_+^D:
      |\bmp|:=p_1+\cdots+p_D=k\}.
\]
We also assume that $\xi((1+\varepsilon)\bm{1})<\infty$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.

For \(\sigma,\tau\in\SigN\), define the species overlap vector by
\[
    R_{N,d}(\sigma,\tau)
    =
    \frac1N\sum_{i\in I_{N,d}}\sigma_i\tau_i,
    \qquad
    \bmR_N(\sigma,\tau)=(R_{N,d}(\sigma,\tau))_{d=1}^D,
\]
where \(\bmI_N=\{I_{N,1},\ldots,I_{N,D}\}\) is a partition of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$.

The Hamiltonian of the \emph{multispecies mixed Ising model} is a centered Gaussian process
 \(H_N=(H_N(\sigma))_{\sigma\in\SigN}\)
with covariance
\[
    \mathbb E H_N(\sigma)H_N(\tau)
    =
    N\xi(\bmR_N(\sigma,\tau)),
    \qquad \sigma,\tau\in\SigN.
\]","status":"unverified"}

\[
        \sigma_g^2

\]
In particular, if the local gap defined in (equation gap definition invariant subspace of the paper)

\[
        \sigma_g^2
        =
        2\operatorname{Re}\langle g,-L_K^{-1}g\rangle .
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces","T is a bounded linear operator X -> Y","compactness of I - ST and I - TS (not merely boundedness) is what makes the criterion work"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.572195+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_dd902b48ae729c20df07599e1a8e793996632d7377d0e8bd78774bcd906c51d0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y). Then T is Fredholm if and only if T is invertible modulo compact operators, i.e. there is S in B(Y,X) with I_X - S T in K(X) and I_Y - T S in K(Y). Moreover, if T is Fredholm one may choose S (a Fredholm regularizer, or parametrix) so that I_X - S T and I_Y - T S have finite rank, namely the projection onto ker T along a closed complement and the projection onto a finite-dimensional complement of ran T along ran T; any such S is itself Fredholm with ind S = -ind T. For X = Y this says: T is Fredholm if and only if its class in the Calkin algebra B(X)/K(X) is invertible.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.764803+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dd9208166dd05484a23daf9673b9aef5c8e7dea3fc0576c4ede0e2f0feef7150","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 of arXiv:2512.04807, 'Existence and uniqueness of the canonical Brownian motion in non-simple conformal loop ens'] Consider the setup described just above where we let $\Gamma^\C$ be a nested whole-plane~\clekp{}. There exists a unique (up to a deterministic factor) collection of resistance forms $\rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = ((\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C}))_{k \in \N}$ that is measurable with respect to $\Gamma^\C$ and satisfies the following properties. There is a further collection of resistance forms $((\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^\C}))_{V \in \metregions}$ such that the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[I.]
 \item For each $k \in \N$ we have that $(\rformres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}, \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C})$ is a local, regular resistance form on $\Upsilon_k$. Its associated resistance metric $\rmetres{k}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C}$ is topologically equivalent to $\dpathY[\Upsilon_k]$.
 \item Let $V_1,\ldots,V_n \in \metregions[k]$, $n \in \N$, such that $V_i \cap V_j = \emptyset$ for $i \neq j$ and $\bigcup_i \ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k = \Upsilon_k$. Then
 \begin{align*}
  \rfdomainres{\Upsilon_k}{\Gamma^\C} &= \{ f : f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V_i}{\Gamma^\C} \text{ for each } i \} ,\\
  \text{and}\quad
  \rformres{k}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} &= \sum_i \rformres{V_i}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{f|_{\ol{V_i} \cap \Upsilon_k}}{\Gamma^\C} .
 \end{align*}
\item If $V,V' \in \metregions[k]$, $V \subseteq V'$, and $f\colon \ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \to \R$ is a continuous function that is constant on each $\dpathY$-connected component of $\ol{V'} \cap \Upsilon_k \setminus \ol{V}$, then
\begin{align*}
 & f \in \rfdomainres{V'}{\Gamma^\C} \text{ if and only if } f|_{\ol{V} \cap \Upsilon_k} \in \rfdomainres{V}{\Gamma^\C} \\
 \text{and}\quad & \rformres{V'}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} = \rformres{V}{f}{f}{\Gamma^\C} .
\end{align*}
 \item For each open set $U \subseteq \C$, the collection of forms $(\rformres{V}{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C})_{V \in \metregions[U]}$ is a.s.\ a measurable function of $\Gamma^\C|_U$.
\item For each $z \in \C$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = \rform{T_{z}\cdot}{T_{z}\cdot}{\Gamma^\C+z} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $T_{z} f = f(\cdot -z)$ denotes translation by $z$.
\item There exists a constant $\resexp > 0$ so that for each $\lambda > 0$, we have
\[ \rform{\cdot}{\cdot}{\Gamma^\C} = \lambda^{\resexp}\rform{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{S_{\lambda}\cdot}{\lambda\Gamma^\C} \quad\text{a.s.,} \]
where $S_{\lambda} f = f(\lambda^{-1}\cdot)$.
\end{enumerate}
The analogous statement holds for the \clekp{} Brownian motion. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space over R or C","K: X -> X is compact","lambda is a nonzero scalar (for lambda = 0 every assertion can fail)","in the Hilbert-space form, H is a Hilbert space and K* is the Hilbert adjoint, so the relevant homogeneous adjoint equation uses the complex conjugate of lambda"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.572093+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory, integral equations","id":"claim_ddaa1329528122fb80376912c0e3927070e563e1860806c39b21c8299d538814","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space over R or C, let K in K(X) be compact, let lambda be a nonzero scalar and set T = lambda I - K. Then: (i) ker T is finite-dimensional; (ii) ran T is closed; (iii) dim ker T = dim ker T' = dim(X / ran T) < infinity, where T' = lambda I - K' on the dual X'; in particular T is Fredholm with ind T = 0; (iv) ran T = {y in X : f(y) = 0 for every f in ker T'}. Consequently exactly one of the following holds: either lambda x - K x = y has a unique solution for every y in X (and the solution depends continuously on y), or the homogeneous equation lambda x - K x = 0 has a nonzero solution, in which case the solution space is finite-dimensional of dimension d, the adjoint homogeneous equation lambda f - K' f = 0 also has a d-dimensional solution space, and lambda x - K x = y is solvable exactly for those y annihilated by every solution f of the adjoint homogeneous equation (solutions then form an affine space of dimension d). In a Hilbert space H with K compact, the adjoint condition reads: lambda x - K x = y is solvable iff y is orthogonal to ker(conj(lambda) I - K*).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:50:48.848317+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ddbd361e7cd5ae1a97210c3759252a0a1a2c90c9e97f3b20d921b81cd1419b6c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:n2 of arXiv:2607.08551, 'Weighted-threshold Coupon Collection'] Consider the Zipf family with $N=2$:

{"assumptions":["Standard Borel covariate; strictly positive measurable score almost surely, finite mean score.","Fixed retention fraction strictly between zero and one.","Conditional unbiasedness and the mean positive-weight retention budget; no claim about estimator asymptotics."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:24:15.363712+00:00","domain":"Statistical data selection and inverse-probability weighting","id":"claim_ddd5fc36f48265162995ac3142dd2378fa412c120b9b084e148942e78dec54b7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon optimal unbiased selection, strictly positive-score specialization. Let X take values in a standard Borel space, let Z(X)>0 almost surely be measurable with E Z(X)<infinity, and fix 0<gamma<1. Among nonnegative randomized weights S satisfying E[S|X]=1 and E[P(S>0|X)]=gamma, the minimum of J(S)=E[S^2 Z(X)] is attained by S_star=I/pi_star(X), where I conditional on X is Bernoulli(pi_star(X)) and pi_star(X)=min(1,c*sqrt(Z(X))). There is a unique c>0 such that E pi_star(X)=gamma. The minimum is E[Z(X)/pi_star(X)]=E[max(Z(X),sqrt(Z(X))/c)]<infinity. Every minimizer has this same retention probability almost surely and has constant weight 1/pi_star(X) on its retained observations, conditional on X. Uniform random retention has objective E Z/gamma; the optimal objective is strictly smaller unless Z is almost surely constant. This is the convex allocation problem in Proposition4.2 and AppendixB of Kolossov-Montanari-Tandon, with the strict-positive-score restriction stated explicitly to avoid zero-score conventions. {"assumptions":["(X, B, mu, T) is a measure-preserving system on a standard (Lebesgue) probability space","G is a compact metrizable group, m its normalized Haar measure","phi : X -> G is Borel measurable","the fibre action is by left translation, T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, phi(x) g)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.731878+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, skew products and cocycles","id":"claim_ddecdf9c38acba7f9d1a20280128c4273217092304e304e1c131cecbf3f30d61","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu, T) be a measure-preserving system on a standard probability space, let G be a compact metrizable group with normalized Haar measure m, and let phi : X -> G be measurable (the cocycle generator). The G-extension, or skew product, is the transformation

  T_phi(x, g) = (T x, phi(x) g)   on   (X x G, B x Borel(G), mu x m).

It preserves mu x m: for fixed x the fibre map g -> phi(x) g is a left translation, and Haar measure on a compact group is left invariant (compactness is what makes Haar a probability measure, so that mu x m is a probability measure). Iterating, T_phi^n(x, g) = (T^n x, phi_n(x) g) with the cocycle phi_n(x) = phi(T^{n-1} x) * ... * phi(T x) * phi(x), which satisfies the cocycle identity phi_{n+k}(x) = phi_k(T^n x) * phi_n(x).

Two standard obstructions to ergodicity are built into the definition. (i) If phi takes values in a proper closed subgroup H of G, then every set of the form X x (union of right cosets H g) is T_phi-invariant, so T_phi is not ergodic. (ii) More generally if there is a measurable u : X -> G with phi(x) = u(T x)^{-1} h(x) u(x) for h taking values in a proper closed subgroup, the same conclusion holds after the measurable change of coordinates (x, g) -> (x, u(x) g); cocycles differing in this way are called cohomologous, and ergodicity of T_phi depends only on the cohomology class. Note the sides: with the convention above the cocycle acts by LEFT translation and the invariant objects are RIGHT cosets; the opposite convention T_phi(x,g) = (Tx, g phi(x)) swaps them, and mixing the two conventions is the usual source of sign/side errors in the ergodicity criteria.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.746107+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de12232140b00c54f654a321a766291084b9267f14677bea219692b0e6f96eed","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Define 5 of arXiv:2506.10522, 'On the Law of the Iterated Logarithm for $m$-dependent stationary random variables under s'] \begin{description}
  \item[ \rm (i)] ({\em Identical distribution}) Let $\bm X_1$ and $\bm X_2$ be two $n$-dimensional random vectors defined
respectively in sub-linear expectation spaces $(\Omega_1, \mathcal{H}_1, \mbE_1)$
  and $(\Omega_2, \mathcal{H}_2, \mbE_2)$. They are called identically distributed, denoted by $\bm X_1\overset{d}= \bm X_2$  if
$$ \mbE_1[\varphi(\bm X_1)]=\mbE_2[\varphi(\bm X_2)], \;\; \forall \varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^n). $$
 A sequence $\{X_n;n\ge 1\}$ of random variables is said to be identically distributed if $X_i\overset{d}= X_1$ for each $i\ge 1$.
\item[\rm (ii)] ({\em Independence})   In a sub-linear expectation space  $(\Omega, \mathcal{H}, \mbE)$, a random vector $\bm Y =
(Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)$, $Y_i \in \mathcal{H}$ is said to be independent to another random vector $\bm X =
(X_1, \ldots, X_m)$ , $X_i \in \mathcal{H}$ under $\mbE$  if for each test function $\varphi\in C_{b,Lip}(\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n)$
we have
$ \mbE [\varphi(\bm X, \bm Y )] = \mbE \big[\mbE[\varphi(\bm x, \bm Y )]\big|_{\bm x=\bm X}\big].$
 \item[\rm (iii)] ({\em Independent random variables}) A sequence of random variables $\{X_n; n\ge 1\}$
 is said to be independent, if  $X_{i+1}$ is independent to $(X_{1},\ldots, X_i)$ for each $i\ge 1$.
 \item[\rm (iv)](m-dependence) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be $m$-dependent if there exists an integer $m$ such that for every $n$ and every $j\geq m+1$, $(X_{n+m+1},\cdots,X_{n+j})$ is independent of $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)$. In particular, if $m=0$, $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is an independent sequence.
\item[\rm (v)](stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $(X_1,\cdots,X_n)\overset{d}{=}(X_{1+p},\cdots,X_{n+p})$.
\item[\rm (vi)](linear stationary) A sequence of random variables(or random vectors) $\{X_n;n\geq 1\}$ is said to be linear stationary if for every positive integers $n$ and $p$, $X_1+\cdots+X_n\overset{d}{=}X_{1+p}+\cdots+X_{n+p}$.
 \end{description}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain with row-stochastic transition matrix P","Fixed finite real matrices A_i, vectors b_i and constant step alpha","Finite second moment of xi_0","Conditional independence of z_(k+1) and xi_k given z_k","Columnwise vectorization and stacking by chain state"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:05:57.431397+00:00","domain":"reinforcement learning; Markov jump linear systems","id":"claim_de1b5940314d04a7ddcbc45caa566cc8e834b108f83b393e8aa92596fbff4e17","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let z_k be an exogenous time-homogeneous Markov chain on {1,...,N}, with p_ij=P(z_(k+1)=j|z_k=i). Assume xi_0 has finite second moment and that, conditional on z_k, the next chain state is independent of xi_k (in particular deterministic initial xi_0 with the natural chain filtration suffices). Define p_k^i=P(z_k=i), q_k^i=E[xi_k 1_{z_k=i}], Q_k^i=E[xi_k xi_k^T 1_{z_k=i}]. Then p_(k+1)=P^T p_k, q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i q_k^i+alpha p_k^i b_i], and Q_(k+1)^j=sum_i p_ij[H_i Q_k^i H_i^T+alpha(H_i q_k^i b_i^T+b_i(q_k^i)^T H_i^T)+alpha^2 p_k^i b_i b_i^T]. For stacked q_k and v_k=(vec(Q_k^1),...,vec(Q_k^N)), columnwise vectorization gives q_(k+1)=H11 q_k+alpha(P^T diag(p_k) tensor I_d)b and v_(k+1)=H22 v_k+H21 q_k+alpha^2(P^T diag(p_k) tensor I_(d^2))b2, where b stacks b_i, b2 stacks b_i tensor b_i, H11_(j,i)=p_ij H_i, H22_(j,i)=p_ij(H_i tensor H_i), and H21_(j,i)=alpha p_ij[b_i tensor H_i+H_i tensor b_i]. In particular H22=(P^T tensor I_(d^2))diag_i(H_i tensor H_i); the update factor uses the departure state i. The raw second moment is sum_i Q_k^i and E||xi_k||^2=sum_i trace(Q_k^i); these Q_k^i are not centered conditional covariances. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627278+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_de27015aaa0fed8be3e6e4717dc3b361b73aac1ab1054852f520fd6389b23345","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A linear operator T: X -> Y between Banach spaces is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball is relatively compact in Y; equivalently, every bounded sequence (x_k) in X has a subsequence along which (T x_k) converges in Y. A compact operator is bounded. Facts: (1) the compact operators K(X, Y) form a closed linear subspace of the bounded operators B(X, Y), and compositions of a compact operator with bounded operators on either side are compact, so K(X) = K(X, X) is a closed two-sided ideal of B(X); (2) every finite-rank bounded operator is compact, and a norm limit of finite-rank operators is compact; when Y is a Hilbert space (more generally when Y has the approximation property) every compact operator is such a limit - for Banach spaces in general this fails (Enflo, 1973); (3) the identity of an infinite-dimensional Banach space is not compact (Riesz's lemma: the unit ball is not compact), so a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is never invertible; (4) Riesz-Schauder theory: for compact T on an infinite-dimensional Banach space the spectrum sigma(T) is a countable (possibly finite) set whose only possible accumulation point is 0, 0 belongs to sigma(T), every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue with finite-dimensional generalised eigenspace, and for lambda != 0 the operator lambda - T is injective if and only if it is surjective (the Fredholm alternative: either (lambda - T) x = y has a unique solution for every y, or the homogeneous equation has a nontrivial solution, and then the inhomogeneous one is solvable exactly for y annihilated by the kernel of the adjoint); (5) a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues tending to 0 (the spectral theorem); (6) integral operators (Kf)(x) = integral k(x, y) f(y) dy with a continuous kernel on a compact domain, or with an L^2 kernel (Hilbert-Schmidt operators), are compact, and so is every diagonal operator on l^2 whose entries tend to 0. Compact perturbations preserve the essential spectrum and the Fredholm index (Atkinson).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356404+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_de6ed04e0e0829407fc76e9f9053d5e379c62e487fac745c92001f9f22aa70f4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 233 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Suppose $\cA_N$ is a $L$-Lipschitz algorithm.
	Then there exists $C(\alpha) > 0$ depending on only $\alpha$ and $c = c(\alpha,L) > 0$ such that
	\beq
		\P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
			 \le C(\alpha)
			\,\,\text{and}\,\,
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \le 2
		\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
	Furthermore, for any $k\ge 1$, there exists $C(\alpha,k)$ such that for all sufficiently large $N$,
	\beq
		\max\bigg\{
			\frac{\E[(\|\bG\|_{\op})^k]}
				{N^{k/2}}, 
			\frac{\E[\|\bx\|^k]}{N^{k/2}}
		\bigg\} \le C(\alpha,k)\,.
	\eeq
\begin{proof}
	By Lemma~\ref{l:wishart}, there exists $C(\alpha)$ such that 
	\beq
		
		\P\bigg(
		\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}}
		 \le C(\alpha)
		\bigg) \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq
Since the mapping $(\bG,\bg^\aux) \mapsto \|\bx\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, the random variable $\|\bx\|$ is $L$-subgaussian.
	Combined with the equality $\E[\|\bx\|^2] = N$ from Definition~\ref{d:Lip}, this readily implies
	\[
		\P\bigg(
		\frac{\|\bx\|}
			{N^{1/2}}
		 \le 2\bigg) 
		 \ge 1-e^{-cN}\,,
	\]
which gives \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail}.
	By Jensen's inequality,
	\[
		\frac{\E\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}}
		\le 
		\frac{\E[\|\bx\|^2]^{1/2}}
			{N^{1/2}}
		 = 1
		 \,.
	\]
Since $\|\bx\|$ is $L$-subgaussian, for any $u\ge1$ we have
	\[\P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg)
		\le \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\| - \E\|\bx\|]}{N^{1/2}} \ge u - 1
		\bigg) 
		\le \exp\bigg(
			-\frac{(u-1)^2 N}{2L^2}
		\bigg)\,.\]
Integrating this bound gives
	\begin{align*}
		\E\bigg[\frac{\|\bx\|^k}{N^{k/2}}\bigg]
		&\le 2^k + \int_{2^k}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|^k}{N^{k/2}} \ge t
		\bigg) \,dt
		= 2^k + \int_2^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bx\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du \\
		&\le 2^k + \int_2^\infty \exp\bigg(-\frac{(u-1)^2 N}{2L^2}\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du 
		\le 2^k + 1\,,
	\end{align*}
	where the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	Since the mapping $\bG \mapsto \|\bG\|_{\op}$ is $1$-Lipschitz, the random variable $\|\bG\|_{\op}$ is $1$-subgaussian.
	Then \eqref{e:confinement.wishart.restated} implies that $\E[\|\bG\|_{\op}] \le C(\alpha) N^{1/2}$. Then, by a similar calculation as above, we obtain
	\begin{align*}
		\E\bigg[\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}^k}{N^{k/2}}\bigg]
		&\le (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)^k}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}^k}{N^{k/2}} \ge t
		\bigg) \,dt \\
		&= (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)}^\infty \P\bigg(
			\frac{\|\bG\|_{\op}}{N^{1/2}} \ge u
		\bigg) ku^{k-1} \,du \\
		&\le (2C(\alpha))^k + \int_{2C(\alpha)}^\infty
		\exp\bigg(
			-\frac{(u-C(\alpha))^2 N}{2}
		\bigg) ku^{k-1}\,du
		\le (2C(\alpha))^k + 1\,,
	\end{align*}
	where the last inequality holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	This proves \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.moment}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.495274+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dec1f14d27a1db30a6d8dabe2fe80c84dc4cfadfc7e265da9ef866b4244aced3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Let
\[
\mathcal R(u):=
\frac{\displaystyle\int_\Omega|\nabla u|^2\,dx}
{\displaystyle\int_\Omega|u|^2\,dx},
\qquad
\mathcal A:=
\{u\in H_0^1(\Omega)\setminus\{0\}:M(u)\geq0\}.
\]
Suppose that \(\bar u\in\mathcal A\) is a local minimizer of
\(\mathcal R\) on \(\mathcal A\). Then there exist
\(\mu_0,\mu_1\geq0\), with \(\mu_0+\mu_1>0\), such that
\begin{equation}
	\mu_0D\mathcal R(\bar u)=\mu_1DM(\bar u),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
	\mu_1M(\bar u)=0.
\end{equation}
If \(DM(\bar u)\neq0\), then \(\mu_0>0\), and consequently there exists
\(\mu\geq0\) such that
\begin{equation}
	D\mathcal R(\bar u)=\mu\,DM(\bar u),
	\qquad
	\mu M(\bar u)=0.
	
\end{equation}
Thus, under the constraint qualification \(DM(\bar u)\neq0\), the
Fritz John conditions \cite{John} reduce to the usual Kuhn--Tucker
conditions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:13:49.974155+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dec516930bba9db6dd4e2b2facaf1814e8cf8f8e593d06d54f06d2a35b357538","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:forests of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] Define $\mathcal{T}_{1,2}\eqdef\mathcal{T}\times\{0,1\}\times\{0,1,2\}$, and denote by $\tilde\tau=(\tau,r,u)$ an element of $\mathcal{T}_{1,2}$. 
We introduce a set of (ordered, unlabelled) forests
\begin{equs}
\text{$   \widehat\mathcal{T}$}\eqdef
\Big\{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}=(\tilde {\tau}_1,\dots,\tilde{\tau}_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})})
=
\Big( (\tau_1,r_1,u_1), \dots, (\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},r_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},u_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}) 
\Big)\in\text{$\mathcal{T}$}_1^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}:p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\in[P]
\Big\}\,. 
\end{equs}

For two forests ${\boldsymbol{\tau}},{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\in\widehat\mathcal{T}$ and a tuple $I=(i_1,\dots,i_{|I|})$ consisting of distinct elements of $[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]$, we define the forest ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{I}$ by
\begin{equs}    {\boldsymbol{\tau}}_I\eqdef\big(\tilde\tau_{i_1},\dots,\tilde\tau_{i_{|I|}}\big)\,,
\end{equs}
and we define the forest  ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}\sqcup{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$, the concatenation of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$, by
\begin{equs}    {\boldsymbol{\tau}}\sqcup{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\eqdef(\tilde\tau_1,\dots,\tilde\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})},\tilde\sigma_1,\dots,\tilde\sigma_{p({\boldsymbol{\sigma}})})\,.
\end{equs}
Fix ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}=(\tilde\tau_1,\dots,\tilde\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})})\in\widehat\mathcal{T}$ and
suppose that for every $i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]$, we are given tuples of times $(t_{i},s^{\tau_i})\in(-\infty,1]\times\R^{\mathfrak{s}(\tau_i)}$.
We then write
\begin{equs}
    t_{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}\eqdef (t_{\tau_1},\dots,t_{\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}})  \in (-\infty,1]^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})} \,,\;\text{and}\;s^{{\boldsymbol{\tau}}}\eqdef(s^{\tau_1},\dots,s^{\tau_{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}}) \in \R^{\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})} \,,
\end{equs}
where $\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}\text{$\mathfrak{s}$}(\tau_i)$ is the \textit{size} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$. We also write $\mathfrak{l}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})+\mathfrak{s}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})$. 

Finally, we define the \textit{scaling} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ by
\begin{equs}    |{\boldsymbol{\tau}}|\eqdef\big(p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})-1\big)+\sum_{i=1}^{p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})}|\tau_i|\,,
\end{equs}
the \textit{order} of ${\boldsymbol{\tau}}$ by $\text{${\mathfrak{o}}$}({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef \sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}\text{${\mathfrak{o}}$}(\tau_i) $, and set $r({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}r_i$ and $u({\boldsymbol{\tau}})\eqdef\sum_{i\in[p({\boldsymbol{\tau}})]}u_i$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.642694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dedb47cb49ca03e3d809abd5685ffdbcbde13bd9575f46646317a0119f60760b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 13 of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] Let \(Z\) be a subordinator with Laplace exponent \(\psi\), and let \(\mu_Z\) be the random measure on \([0,\infty)\) induced by \(Z\), namely
\[
\mu_Z((a,b]) := Z_b-Z_a
\quad (0\le a<b<\infty).
\]
Let \(A\subset [0,\infty)\) be a Borel set with \(\lambda(A)<\infty\), where \(\lambda\) denotes the Lebesgue measure.
Then
\begin{align}
  E[e^{-q\mu_Z(A)}]=e^{-\lambda(A)\psi(q)}
\quad (q\ge0). 
\end{align}
In particular,
\[
\mu_Z(A)\overset{d}{=} Z_{\lambda(A)},
\]
and if \(A,B \subset [0,\infty)\) are disjoint, \(\mu_{Z}(A)\) and \(\mu_{Z}(B)\) are independent.
More generally, if \(A\) is a random Borel set independent of \(Z\), then
\[
E[e^{-q\mu_Z(A)}\mid A]=e^{-\lambda(A)\psi(q)}
\quad (q\ge0),
\]
and hence, if \(\lambda(A)=a\) almost surely for some \(a\ge0\), then
\[
\mu_Z(A)\overset{d}{=} Z_{a}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

A norm induces a metric d(x, y) = ||x - y||, and all topological notions (convergence, continuity, completeness) on a normed space refer to this metric. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.198334+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df26d27bad5c5d1eeef1c6602c0d167196e97df45a91ccf2597a76b1fb895a00","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 125 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $J\equiv J(p,2\tep,\lambda/2)$ as  defined by \eqref{e:bad.times.J}. Then the coefficients from Definition~\ref{d:cts.coeffs} satisfy the estimates 
	\[
	\max\left\{
	\begin{array}{c}
	|\tbbb(t,y)^2
		-\Tbbb(t,y)^2|,\\
	|\tvvv(t,y)-\Tvvv(t,y)|,\\
	|\tuuu(t,y)^2-\Tuuu(t,y)^2|
	\end{array}
	\right\}
	\le \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} \lambda
	\]
for all $(t,y)\in( [q_*,1]  \setminus J)\times\R$. 

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{l:limit.coefs} gives
	\[\begin{aligned}
	\tB(t,y)&=\tB^N(t,y)+o_N(1)\,,\\
	\Tbbb(t,y)&=\Tbbb^N(t,y)+o_N(1)
	\end{aligned}\]
for all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times\R$. Recall that $(p^N)'(t)$ converges to $p'(t)$ for almost every $t$. Therefore, for \emph{every} $t$, we can find $s\in[t-\tep,t+\tep]$ such that $(p^N)'(s)$ converges to $p'(s)$. If $t\notin J$, then $t\notin J^N$ for sufficiently large $N$ by Lemma~\ref{l:bad.times.JN.J}, so $p'(s)$ differs from $p'(t)$ by at most $\lambda/2$, while $(p^N)'(s)$ differs from $(p^N)'(t)$ by at most $\lambda$. Therefore, for $t\in[q_*,1]\setminus J$, we have
	\[
	\Big|\tbbb(t,y)-\tbbb^N(t,y)\Big|
	=\bigg|\frac{\tB(t,y)}{p'(t)^{1/2}}
	-\frac{\tB^N(t,y)}{(p^N)'(t)^{1/2}}\bigg|
	\le o_N(1)
	+ \bigg( \frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)}(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda\,,
	\]
using the bounds on $\tB^N$ and $\tB$ implied by Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg} and Corollary~\ref{c:reg.in.limit}.
Additionally, since $t\notin J^N$,
Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} bounds the discrepancy between $\tbbb^N(t,y)$ and $\Tbbb^N(t,y)$.
Sending $N\to\infty$ gives the claimed bound on the discrepancy between $\tbbb(t,y)$ and $\Tbbb(t,y)$. The other bounds follow by similar arguments:
	\begin{align*}
	\Big|\tvvv(t,y)-\tvvv^N(t,y)\Big|
	&=\bigg|
	\frac{\tV(t,y)}{p(t)}
	-\frac{\tV^N(t,y)}{p^N(t)}\bigg|\,,\\
	\Big|\tuuu(t,y)-\tuuu^N(t,y)\Big|
	&=\bigg|\frac{\tU(t,y)}{[ p(t)
		\cdot t p'(t)]^{1/2}}
		-\frac{\tU^N(t,y)}{[ p^N(t)
		\cdot t (p^N)'(t)]^{1/2}}
		\bigg|\,.
	\end{align*}
Note in these cases that in the factor $L^{O(1)}$ appearing in the final bound, the $O(1)$ exponent can depend on the constant $\breve{c}$ from \eqref{e:breve.q.bounds}. We will remark on this point again in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:Lipschitz-SDE-approx}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356532+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df2ec02ab8113e2c74344a7c95930cb4ecc1735b76c9be1b5407fe24fca67876","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 234 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exist $C(\alpha) > 0$ and $C(\alpha,L,K) > 0$, such that the following holds for all sufficiently large $N$.
	If $\cA_N$ is an $L$-Lipschitz algorithm and $\cA_{N[K]}$ is as in Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, then 
	\begin{align}
		
		\max\{ 
		\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
		,\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^2}^2
		\}
		 &\le C(\alpha)\,, \\
		
		\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^4}^4 &\le C(\alpha,L,K)\,.
	\end{align}
	Furthermore, for $\mu_\bG(\bx)$ defined in \eqref{eq:proj-pursuit-def}, there exists $c = c(\alpha,L) > 0$ such that
	\beq
		\P\bigg(\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2 \le C(\alpha)
			\bigg) \ge 1 - e^{-cN}\,.
	\eeq

\begin{proof}
	Throughout this proof $c > 0$ is a constant depending on $\alpha,L$ which may change line by line. Recall that we abbreviate $\bx\equiv\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 
	We prove \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} first. Recalling the definition of $\fm$ from Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, note that
\beq
		\|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2
		=\frac{\|\fm\|^2}{M} 
		= \frac{1}{M} \bigg\|\frac{\bG \bx}{N^{1/2}}\bigg\|^2
		\le \frac{(\|\bG\|_{\op} \|\bx\|)^2}{MN} \,.
	\eeq
	By \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.tail} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, with probability $1-e^{-cN}$ the above is
	\[
	\le \frac{C(\alpha)^2 N \cdot 4N}{MN} 
		= \frac{4C(\alpha)^2}{\alpha}\,.
	\]
	This proves \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.tail} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$.
	Next, note that
	\[
		\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
		= \E \|\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux))\|_{L^2}^2
		= 
		\frac{\E[\|\fm\|^2]}{M} 
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.step1}}{\le} 
		\frac{\E[(\|\bG\|_{\op} \|\bx\|)^2]}{MN} \,.
	\]
By H\"older's inequality and the bound \eqref{e:confinement.subgaussian.basic.moment} from Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}, the above is
	\[\le
		\frac{\E [(\|\bG\|_{\op})^4]^{1/2} \E[\|\bx\|^4]^{1/2}}{MN} 
		\le \frac{C(\alpha,4)N^2}{MN} 
		= \frac{C(\alpha,4)}{\alpha}\,,
	\]
	for $C(\alpha,4)$ defined in Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.subgaussian.basic}.
This proves the first part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$. For the second part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2}, we split into cases depending on whether $a\in S_K(\cA_N)$. Recall that the truncated algorithm $\cA_{N[K]}$ resamples the rows indexed by $S_K(\cA_N)$. If $a\notin S_K(\cA_N)$, then $\tilde{\fm}_a$ is equidistributed as $\fm_a$, so they have the same second moment. If $a\in S_K(\cA_N)$, then 
	\[\tilde{\fm}_a
		= \frac{(\bg^a, \tilde{\bx})}{N^{1/2}}\,.
	\]
where $\bg^a$ is independent of $\tilde{\bx}$, as $\cA_{N[K]}$ does not use the input $\bg^a$.
	Thus, the distribution of $\tilde{\fm}_a$ conditional on $\tilde{\bx}$ is a (one-dimensional) centered gaussian random variable with standard deviation $\|\tilde{\bx}\| / N^{1/2}$. It follows in this case that
	\[
	\E[(\tilde{\fm}_a)^2]
	= \frac{\E[\|\tilde{\bx}\|^2]}{N}=1\,.
	\]
Altogether this gives
	\[
	\|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|^2
	=\frac{ \E[\|\tilde{\fm}\|^2]}{M}
	\le
	\frac{ \E[\|\fm\|^2 + M]}{M}
	\le C(\alpha)+1\,.
	\]
This proves the second part of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} after adjusting $C(\alpha)$.

Finally we turn to the proof of  \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4}. Recalling the notations of Definition~\ref{d:truncated.lip.alg}, let
	\[
	\tilde{\fm}_a
	\equiv
	\fm_a\Big(\bG,\bg^{\aux+}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:29:21.897970+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df3e6ebb290d7b0f2ea7bfc5e4c3bc16082f28eb79826863386b3b49d7f365fc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 2 of arXiv:2608.00449, 'First-order phase transitions in the hard-core model'] \label[definition]{def:orders}
    Suppose that $G$ is an infinite graph such that a phase transition occurs at $\lambda^*>0$. 
    For $\lambda>0$ and a vertex $u$ of $G$, let $D_{G,u}(\lambda)$ be defined as 
    \[ D_{G,u}(\lambda) = \sup_{\mu,\nu}\left| \mu(u) - \nu(u) \right|, \]
    where the supremum is over all pairs of hard-core measures $\mu,\nu$ on $G$ at fugacity $\lambda$.
    Suppose also that for each vertex $u$, the one-sided limit from above $\ell_{G,u}(\lambda^*) = \lim_{\lambda\downarrow \lambda^*} D_{G,u}(\lambda)$ exists.
    
    If there exists a vertex $u\in V(G)$ such that $\ell_{G,u}(\lambda^*)>0$, then we say that $\lambda^*$ is a \emph{first-order} phase transition.
    If, on the other hand, $\ell_{G,u}(\lambda^*)=0$ for all $u\in V(G)$, then we say that $\lambda^*$ is a \emph{second-order} phase transition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["t>0.","The classical Ibragimov characterization for nondegenerate absolutely continuous laws."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364956+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_df81d86c41a2e859c5a707fc5ae34d83a64ca8c89b34f2c04e48ecc49cc1f09a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked] This is a proved special case of Problem 3.11 of Takahiro Hasebe and Yuki Ueda's Large time unimodality for classical and free Brownian motions with initial distributions, ALEA 15 (2018), 353-374, DOI:10.30757/ALEA.v15-15 (arXiv:1710.08240). A probability measure is unimodal if, for some mode m, it is an atom at m plus an absolutely continuous measure whose density is nondecreasing to the left of m and nonincreasing to the right. Write boxplus for additive free convolution, the distribution of a sum of freely independent self-adjoint variables with the indicated laws, and * for classical convolution of independent real variables. Call lambda freely strongly unimodal if lambda boxplus nu is unimodal for every unimodal probability measure nu. For every t>0 the centered Cauchy distribution C_t with density t/[pi(t^2+x^2)] is not freely strongly unimodal: some unimodal nu makes nu boxplus C_t nonunimodal. The proof combines the Cauchy convolution identity with Ibragimov's characterization of classical strong unimodality by log-concavity of the density; the Cauchy density is not log-concave. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","a one-parameter family of unitaries or an exponential e^{itT} is being used","the continuity and self-adjointness hypotheses are the ones at issue"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772569+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, quantum dynamics","id":"claim_df9328ea820c9b58103e280388d82cc43f63148f9a76b0b2e1fdd63f459b8d1b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: (i) U(t) is unitary for every t ∈ ℝ and satisfies the group law on all of ℝ; (ii) t ↦ U(t)x is continuous (weak continuity or, on a separable space, weak measurability suffices, but some regularity is required); (iii) the generator is self-adjoint. What fails. Without any continuity: pick a discontinuous additive function φ: ℝ → ℝ (a Hamel basis construction) and set H = ℂ, U(t) = e^{iφ(t)}. This is a one-parameter group of unitaries with U(0) = 1, but φ is non-measurable and unbounded on every interval, so U(t) is not of the form e^{ita} for any real a; no generator exists. Hence 'one-parameter unitary group' without a continuity hypothesis carries no spectral information. Overshooting in the other direction: if one assumes t ↦ U(t) is continuous in operator norm, then the generator is necessarily bounded, so norm continuity is the wrong hypothesis for Schrodinger evolutions, where A is unbounded. With a symmetric but not self-adjoint generator: on L²(0, ∞) the right translation semigroup (T(t)f)(x) = f(x − t) for x > t, 0 for x ≤ t, is a C_0-semigroup of isometries that is not a group (T(t) is not surjective), and its generator is A = −d/dx on {f ∈ H¹(0, ∞) : f(0) = 0}, i.e. A = −iS with S = −i d/dx closed and symmetric with deficiency indices (1, 0). There is no unitary group whose generator extends S, so exponentiating a symmetric operator to 'e^{itS}' is not legitimate: only self-adjointness (or essential self-adjointness followed by taking the closure) licenses the unitary group. Audit rule: in quantum dynamics arguments, check that the Hamiltonian has been shown self-adjoint on a stated domain before using e^{itH}, unitarity, conservation of norm, or invariance of D(H).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["M is a compact Riemannian manifold and f a C^1 diffeomorphism of M","mu is an f-invariant Borel probability measure (compactness makes the Oseledets integrability condition automatic)","the exponents, multiplicities and subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; constant a.e. when mu is ergodic","the Oseledets splitting is measurable, generally not continuous, and the Pesin blocks are not invariant"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732600+00:00","domain":"smooth ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents","id":"claim_dfb0e656c58d4f14dd665a85b8ce62d25a662a2455b987541fa0436ab64565e1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a C^1 diffeomorphism of a compact Riemannian manifold M and mu an f-invariant Borel probability measure. Since M is compact, log of the norm of Df and of Df^{-1} are bounded, hence integrable, so Oseledets' multiplicative ergodic theorem applies: for mu-a.e. x there are finitely many numbers lambda_1(x) > lambda_2(x) > ... > lambda_{k(x)}(x) (the LYAPUNOV EXPONENTS at x) and a Df-invariant splitting of the tangent space

  T_x M = E_1(x) + ... + E_{k(x)}(x),   Df_x E_i(x) = E_i(f x),

such that for every nonzero v in E_i(x) the limit of (1/n) log |Df^n_x v| as n -> +-infinity exists and equals lambda_i(x). The functions x -> lambda_i(x), the multiplicities dim E_i(x), and the subspaces are measurable and f-invariant; if mu is ergodic they are constant almost everywhere. The splitting is in general only MEASURABLE, not continuous, and the convergence is not uniform in x.

Two structural facts that every application uses. (1) TEMPEREDNESS: any measurable positive function that is subexponential along orbits -- such as the angle between the Oseledets subspaces, or the norm of the change to Lyapunov (adapted) coordinates -- can be chosen tempered, meaning (1/n) log of its value at f^n x tends to 0; this is what lets one build Lyapunov charts in which Df is uniformly contracting on the negative-exponent bundle at the cost of a chart size that shrinks subexponentially along the orbit. (2) PESIN BLOCKS: for each l one collects the points where the Oseledets estimates hold with uniform constants depending on l; the resulting sets Lambda_l are COMPACT (after discarding a null set and restricting the subbundles continuously), increase in l, exhaust a full-measure set, and carry uniform hyperbolic-like estimates. They are NOT f-invariant -- an orbit wanders between blocks -- which is exactly why non-uniformly hyperbolic statements are local-and-measurable rather than uniform.

A point x is called (non-uniformly) hyperbolic when no exponent at x is zero; the stable bundle E^s(x) is the sum of the E_i(x) with lambda_i(x) < 0 and the unstable bundle the sum of those with lambda_i(x) > 0. Zero exponents are the obstruction: nothing in this framework says anything about directions with zero exponent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:03:59.375619+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_dff9bffa0ab891c73511e0184790ef06096f22a114fc8353137b035d6e8368dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:stexist of arXiv:2507.08757, 'Strong existence and uniqueness of the tilt-indexed Busemann process in the planar corner '] There exists a stochastic process 
\begin{align}
    \bigl(B^{h{\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(x,y) : x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\, h \in \mathcal{H},\, {\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}} \in \{+,-\}\bigr)
\end{align}
on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}  [label={\rm(\alph*)}, ref={\rm\alph*}]   \itemsep=3pt
\item \textup{(}No $\pm$ distinction at fixed $h$\textup{)} For each $h \in \mathcal{H}$, 
\[
\mathbb{P}\{B^{h-}= B^{h+}\}=1.
\]
When $B^{h-}(\omega) = B^{h+}(\omega)$, call the common cocycle $B^h(\omega)$.
\item \textup{(}Forward measurable Busemann function\textup{)} For each $h\in \mathcal{H}, B^h \in \mathcal K_c^+$.
\item \textup{(}Mean $-h$\textup{)} For each $h \in \mathcal{H}$ and $i\in\{1,2\}$, $\mathbb{E}[B^h(0,e_i)] = -h \cdot e_i.$
\item \textup{(}Monotonicity\textup{)} For $h,h'\in \mathcal{H}$ with $h \cdot e_1 \leq h' \cdot e_1$, all $x \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, and $\mathbb{P}$ almost every $\omega$
\[ 
    B^{h-}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h+}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_1) \geq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_1)  
\]
and
\[ 
    B^{h-}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h+}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_2) \leq  B^{h'-}(x,x+e_2).
\]
\item \textup{(}Left-/right-continuity\textup{)} For $\mathbb{P}$-almost all $\omega$, all $h\in \mathcal{H}$, and all $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}^2$,
\begin{equation*}\begin{aligned}
B^{h-}(x,y) = \lim_{\substack{\mathcal{H}\hspace{0.5pt}\hspace{0.5pt}\ni\hspace{0.5pt} \hspace{0.5pt} h' \to h\\ h'\cdot e_1 \nearrow h \cdot e_1}} B^{h\pm}(x,y) \,\text{ and }\, B^{h-}(x,y) = \lim_{\substack{\mathcal{H}\hspace{0.5pt}\hspace{0.5pt}\ni\hspace{0.5pt} \hspace{0.5pt} h' \to h\\ h'\cdot e_1 \searrow h \cdot e_1}} B^{h\pm}(x,y).
\end{aligned}\end{equation*}
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, this process is unique in the sense that any two processes satisfying the above conditions are equal almost surely. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:28:49.056837+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e02df6e7008de2572a83edb0462c226bcad4b7a0dff7276dbd117a9e18dd763b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:first-order-interval-correspondence of arXiv:2608.16119, 'Fully nonlinear parabolic equations under a fixed reference diffusion: weighted \texorpdfs'] Suppose that Assumption~(ass:reference-diffusion of the paper) holds.  For every $\alpha\geq0$,
every regular weight $w$ of order $\alpha$, every interval $I=(r_0,r_1)$,
every integer $m\geq1$, and
\begin{equation*}
 F\in L_w^2(I;\mathbb R^m),\qquad \eta\in L^2(\mu_{r_1};\mathbb R^m),
\end{equation*}
there is a unique first-order occupation-energy solution in the sense of
Definition~(def:first-order-occupation-solution of the paper), denoted by
$\mathcal U_I^w(F,\eta)$.  In the following BSDE, $D_xu$ is the $m\times d$
Jacobian and
\begin{equation*}
 \mathsf Z u:=(D_xu)\sigma\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}.
\end{equation*}
For $m=1$, its single row is identified with the column vector
$\sigma D_xu$ in (equation eq:reference-operators of the paper).  For every
$s\in(r_0,r_1)$, the composition of $u$ has a continuous version on
$[s,r_1]$ and
\begin{equation}
 u(t,X_t)=\eta(X_{r_1})+\int_t^{r_1}F(r,X_r)\,\mathrm d r
 -\int_t^{r_1}\mathsf Z u(r,X_r)\,\mathrm d W_r.
 
\end{equation}
Moreover, for $\kappa\geq1$,
\begin{equation}
 \kappa\left\lVert u\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
 +\left\lVert \mathsf Z u\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
 \leq e^{\operatorname{osc}_{\alpha,I}(w)}\left(
  \kappa^{-1}\left\lVert F\right\rVert_{w_\kappa;I}^2
  +w_\kappa(r_1)\norm\eta_{L^2(\mu_{r_1})}^2\right).
 
\end{equation}
The construction is independent of the weight: if the same data belong to
the spaces associated with two regular weights $w_1,w_2$, then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal U_I^{w_1}(F,\eta)=\mathcal U_I^{w_2}(F,\eta)
 \quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(I\times\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^m).
 
\end{equation}
Thus the superscript may be omitted and the solution written as
$\mathcal U_I(F,\eta)$; the full-interval notation is $\mathcal U(F,\eta)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:06:39.320429+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e0591a8f177295dd9b78ddf50bd06a308d4e4040b19920696ab99bffde067828","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:local_solutions_NSE of arXiv:2607.15140, 'On the absence of blow-up in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations with transport noise'] Suppose that (equation eq:ass_caccioppoli1 of the paper) and (equation eq:ass_caccioppoli4 of the paper) are satisfied.
Let $Q=I\times B$ be a parabolic cylinder with center $(t_0,x_0)$ and radius $\varrho>0$, i.e., 
$$
Q_{\varrho}(t_0,x_0)=(t_0-\varrho^2,t_0)\times B_{\varrho}(x_0).
$$ 
We say that $(v,\pi,(\widetilde{\pi}_n)_n)$ is a local solution to (equation eq:turbulent_stokes_caccioppoli of the paper) if the following are satisfied.
\begin{enumerate}[{\rm(1)}]
\item The processes 
$$
v:I \times \Omega\to H^1(B;{\mathbb R}^d), \quad \pi:I \times \Omega\to L^2(B) \ \ \text{ and }\ \  (\widetilde{\pi}_n)_n:I \times \Omega\to H^1(B;\ell^2), 
$$
are progressively measurable, and a.s.,
\begin{align*}
v&\in C(\overline{I};L^2(B;{\mathbb R}^d))\cap L^2(I;H^1(B;{\mathbb R}^d)) \\
\pi&\in L^2(Q),\quad \text{ and }\quad  (\widetilde{\pi}_n)_n \in L^2(I;H^1(B;\ell^2)).
\end{align*}

\item The following conditions hold.
\begin{itemize}
\item a.s.\ for all $t\in I$, and all $\phi\in C^\infty_{{\rm c}}(B;{\mathbb R}^d)$:
\begin{align*}
\int_{B} v(t)\cdot \phi
&=
\int_{B} v(t_0-\varrho^2)\cdot \phi\\
&+\int_{t_0-\varrho^2}^t  \int_{B} \Big[ 
\pi\,\nabla \cdot \phi+ \Big(-F -\nu \nabla v+\frac{1}{2} \sum_{n} (\nabla \widetilde{\pi}_{n}\otimes \zeta_n)\Big):\nabla \phi\Big]\\
&+\int_{t_0-\varrho^2}^t \Big(\int_{B} \big[(-\nabla \widetilde{\pi}_n + (\zeta_n\cdot \nabla) v) +G_n\big]\cdot \phi \Big)_{n} \, \mathrm{d} \mathcal{W}_{\ell^2},
\end{align*}
\item a.e.\ on $I\times \Omega$, 
in $\mathscr{D}'(B)$,
\begin{align*}
\nabla \cdot v&=0,\\
\Delta \pi
&= \nabla^2 :F - \frac{1}{2} \nabla \cdot \sum_{n}\nabla \cdot(\nabla \widetilde{\pi}_{n}\otimes \zeta_n )  ,\\
\Delta \widetilde{\pi}_n
&= \nabla \cdot [(\zeta_{n}\cdot \nabla)v]+\nabla \cdot G_n.
\end{align*}
\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:55:18.060628+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e05b91a1c5270332be7572b9980f8499073e2f5c7e468d516e6039c7f73ed5ab","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 2 of arXiv:2606.17381, 'Large deviation principle for friendship-biases\\ in Galton--Watson trees'] {\bf [Type characterisation lemma]}

Consider a Galton--Watson tree with the offspring law $(p_k)_{k\in\N_0}$ satisfying $p_1 =p\in (0,1)$ and $p_2= 1 -p$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[\rm{(a)}] 
The root can only be either positive or neutral. It is neutral if and only if it is a branching point and its two children are branching-linear points.
\item[\rm{(b)}] 
A linear point is negative if and only if it is the child of the root and is not the parent of a branching point. It is positive if and only if it is the parent of a branching point and is not the child of the root.
\item[\rm{(c)}] 
A branching-linear point is neutral if and only if its parent is the root and its child is a linear point, otherwise, it is positive.
\item[\rm{(d)}] 
A branching point that is not the root is either negative or neutral. It is neutral if and only if its parent and both of its children are also non-root branching points.
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
