{"assumptions":["(X,d) is a compact metric space","T: X -> X is a homeomorphism","T is expansive with expansive constant c > 0 for the metric d","alpha is a finite Borel partition with diam(A) < c for every A in alpha","for the cover statement, U is a finite open cover with mesh(U) < c","for the entropy consequence, mu is a T-invariant Borel probability measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814532+00:00","domain":"topological and ergodic dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_e0991e6f5703dfafed9b8ef66c327d54b46c44f7e1c7b2d0847a9c270a85228d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X,d) be a compact metric space and let T: X -> X be a homeomorphism which is EXPANSIVE with expansive constant c > 0, meaning: for every pair of distinct points x, y in X there exists an integer n with d(T^n x, T^n y) > c. Let alpha = {A_1, ..., A_k} be a finite Borel partition of X whose mesh is below the expansive constant, i.e. diam(A_i) < c for every i. CONCLUSION: alpha is a two-sided generator. Precisely, the smallest sigma-algebra containing T^{-n}(A_i) for all n in Z and all i is the full Borel sigma-algebra of X. Consequently, for EVERY T-invariant Borel probability measure mu, alpha is a generator mod mu, and the Kolmogorov-Sinai theorem gives h_mu(T) = h_mu(T, alpha) = lim_n (1/n) H_mu(alpha v T^{-1}alpha v ... v T^{-(n-1)}alpha): the measure-theoretic entropy is already computed by that one fixed finite partition, with no refinement over scales. TOPOLOGICAL COUNTERPART, same hypotheses: if U is a finite OPEN cover of X with mesh(U) < c, then h_top(T) = h_top(T, U); in particular an expansive homeomorphism of a compact metric space has finite topological entropy, and the entropy is reached at one fixed finite scale. SHARP EDGES. (a) Expansiveness is indispensable, not a convenience: for the identity map on [0,1] (which is not expansive) every finite partition alpha satisfies alpha v T^{-n}alpha = alpha for all n, so the generated sigma-algebra is the finite algebra generated by alpha and never the Borel sigma-algebra, however small the mesh. More generally, for a non-expansive system no bound on the mesh forces the generator property. (b) The constant c depends on the metric even though expansiveness itself does not: on a compact metric space expansiveness is independent of the choice of compatible metric, but 'mesh below c' must be read in the SAME metric for which c is an expansive constant. (c) The conclusion is about the TWO-SIDED sigma-algebra, using T^{-n} for all n in Z. For a one-sided generator (only n >= 0), which is what is needed for one-sided entropy statements and for non-invertible maps, one needs POSITIVE expansiveness (some n >= 0 with d(T^n x, T^n y) > c); a homeomorphism of an infinite compact metric space is never positively expansive, so that strengthening is not available here. (d) The theorem says the entropy is captured by alpha; it does NOT say h_mu(T) = H_mu(alpha) or that alpha is independent under T.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.671932+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e09bdeb89af170e687f698b66b53450bff40ae034a1df56a10e06ed6422f2823","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 35 (Finite-cover descent) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let
\[
 \pi_{\mathrm{fin}}:M_{\mathrm{fin}}\longrightarrow M
\]
be a connected, \(d\)-sheeted finite regular cover of closed connected
manifolds, with deck group \(\Gamma\).  Let \(g(t)\), \(t\geq T\), be a
\(C^0\)-continuous family of Riemannian metrics on \(M\), let
\(g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t)=\pi_{\mathrm{fin}}^*g(t)\), and let \(a(t)>0\) be
continuous.  Put
\[
 \widehat g(t)=a(t)g(t),\qquad
 \widehat g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t)=a(t)g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t).
\]
Then the following conclusions hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
At every time,
\[
 \diam(M,\widehat g(t))
 \leq \diam(M_{\mathrm{fin}},\widehat g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t))
 \leq 2d\,\diam(M,\widehat g(t)).
\]
Consequently, any \(O(1)\), \(o(1)\), or two-sided positive diameter bound
for either normalized family transfers to the other, with constants depending
only on \(d\).

\item
If
\[
 (M_{\mathrm{fin}},\widehat g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t))\longrightarrow\pt
\]
in the Gromov--Hausdorff sense, then
\((M,\widehat g(t))\to\pt\).

\item
Suppose that
\[
 (M_{\mathrm{fin}},\widehat g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t))\longrightarrow C_L
\]
for a metric circle of length \(L>0\).  Then
\((M,\widehat g(t))\) has a full Gromov--Hausdorff limit.  It is either a
metric circle of length \(L/m\) or a closed interval of length \(L/(2m)\),
for some positive integer \(m\) dividing \(|\Gamma|\).  The limit is a circle
if every limiting action of \(\Gamma\) on \(C_L\) is orientation preserving;
it is a closed interval if a limiting action contains an
orientation-reversing isometry.

\item
The manifolds \(M_{\mathrm{fin}}\) and \(M\) have the same universal cover,
and the lifts of \(g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t)\) and \(g(t)\) to it agree.  Hence every
pointed Cheeger--Hamilton limit of one lifted family is the corresponding
limit of the other.

\item
Suppose, for an integer \(m\geq0\), that
\(\widehat g_{\mathrm{fin}}(t)\) converges in a fixed-coordinate
\(C^m\)-norm to a Riemannian metric \(g_{\mathrm{fin},\infty}\).  Then the
limit is \(\Gamma\)-invariant, descends to a metric \(g_\infty\) on \(M\),
and \(\widehat g(t)\to g_\infty\) in \(C^m\).  A uniform exponential rate
on the cover descends with the same exponent.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:38:36.830346+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e0a65af24f67596daca271b5090e101206d886a00bd633a311924e7a3983a8a7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:master of arXiv:2606.28869, '\bfseries A General Theory of Paths:\\ \large Signatures, Jump Lifts, and Expected Signatu'] The constructions in the paper assemble into the following six-layer representation theorem, each layer being valid under the hypotheses stated in the cited results.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.25em]
\item \textbf{Algebraic path layer.} Bounded-variation signatures satisfy Chen multiplicativity and the shuffle identity; group-like signatures have Lie logarithms, and reduced bounded-variation paths are characterized by their signatures modulo tree-like equivalence.
\item \textbf{Jump and stream layer.} Finite-variation c\`adl\`ag{} paths admit forward It\^o{} and Marcus lifts. The forward lift fails shuffle by the jump bracket, while the Marcus correction restores geometricity. For pure-jump paths, the forward lift is the iterated-sums signature and the Marcus lift is Hoffman's exponential image.
\item \textbf{Geometricity-defect layer.} The two canonical failures of shuffle multiplicativity are second order: quadratic covariation for non-geometric conventions and coordinate covariance for expected signatures. Consequently, an expected signature is group-like only in the deterministic reduced-path case.
\item \textbf{Probabilistic and geometric layer.} Truncated signature kernels yield MMDs equal to Euclidean distances between truncated expected signatures, while the truncations of geometric signatures form a central tower of free nilpotent groups whose forgotten layers have Witt dimensions.
\item \textbf{Self-exciting layer.} Affine processes have finite linear closures for truncated expected signatures after state-weight augmentation. Scalar exponential Hawkes clocks admit the explicit systems (equation eq:hawkes-matrix of the paper) and (equation eq:A2 of the paper), local parameter recovery through (equation eq:ident-reconstruct of the paper), and a directional cross-area detecting two-channel excitation asymmetry to first order.
\item \textbf{Boundary and continuation layer.} Raw expected signatures have intrinsic heavy-tail moment thresholds, normalized expected signatures provide bounded characteristic replacements under the hypotheses of [chevyrev2022], reversal acts by the tensor antipode, and signature large deviations follow by contraction from rough-path large deviations.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356673+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e10d86a0e5ae172fc845f728151fa8a6f3e5bef5b0cd722074bd9020ffc74a17","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 235 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exists $C(\alpha) > 0$ such that for all $\fq\in [1,2)$ and any sequence of $L$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA_N)_{N\ge 1}$, the following holds.
	For all sufficiently large $N$,
	\[
		\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu(\cA_N), \mu(\cA_{N[K]})\Big)
		\le \frac{C(\alpha)}{K^{2/\fq-1}}\,.
	\]
\begin{proof}
	Consider $N$ large enough that the conclusion of Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound} holds: this gives
	\[
	C(\alpha)
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2} }{\ge}
	\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2
	= \frac{\E[\|\fm\|^2]}{M}
	\ge \frac{\|\E\fm\|^2}{M}
	\ge \frac{|S_K(\cA_N)| K^2}{M}\,.
	\]	
We can thus couple $x\sim \mu(\cA_N)$ and $y\sim \mu(\cA_{N[K]})$ such that 
$\P(x\neq y) \le C(\alpha) / K^2$. It follows from  the first assertion of  Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound} that 
	\[
		\E[|x-y|^2]
		\le 2\E[x^2+y^2]
		= 2(\|\mu(\cA_N)\|_{L^2}^2 + \|\mu(\cA_{N[K]})\|_{L^2}^2)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l2}}{\le} 4C(\alpha)\,.\]
Applying H\"older's inequality then gives
	\begin{align*}
		&\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu(\cA_N), \mu(\cA_{N[K]})\Big)^\fq
		\le \E[|x-y|^\fq]
		\le \P(x\neq y)^{1-\fq/2} \E[|x-y|^2]^{\fq/2}
	\\
	&\qquad
		\le \bigg(\frac{C(\alpha)}{K^2}\bigg)^{1-\fq/2} (4C(\alpha))^{\fq/2}
		= \frac{2^\fq C(\alpha)}{K^{2-q}}
		\le \bigg(\frac{2\max\{1,C(\alpha)\}}{K^{2/\fq-1}}\bigg)^\fq\,.
	\end{align*}

{"assumptions":["the optimism theorem for weighted least squares; weights normalised to sum to one","regime (2) beyond the Loewner bounds uses row exchangeability given the weights as a first-order approximation of the two moment matrices"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T11:47:28.060880+00:00","domain":"regression / model assessment","id":"claim_e133d7fdae691c4a0638ff9a8fb3a814a36acd27f937ccf5fa74ff1dd0aeeb11","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the setting of the optimism theorem for weighted least squares, normalise the weights to sum_i s_i = 1. (2) Concentrated weights with homoscedastic errors: the Loewner bounds s_min X'SX <= X'S^2 X <= s_max X'SX give 2 sigma^2 m s_min <= optimism <= 2 sigma^2 m s_max, and when the rows are exchangeable given the weights (E[x x'] = G for every row) the two moment matrices are (sum s_i) G and (sum s_i^2) G to first order, so the optimism is 2 sigma^2 m sum_i s_i^2 = 2 sigma^2 m / n_eff with Kish's n_eff = (sum s)^2 / sum s^2; relative to the noise level sigma^2 of the loss the gap is 2 m / n_eff, and a concentrated weighting behaves as a small sample. (3) Variance-stabilising weights s_i = c / sigma_i^2 (Aitken's weights) give S^2 Sigma = c S, the trace collapses to c m, the optimism is 2 c m whatever the concentration of the weights, and relative to the noise level c n of the loss it is 2 m / n again: under Aitken weights a small Kish n_eff is not a small sample but the balanced sample of the stabilised problem. Which regime a weighted fit is in is therefore an empirical question about how the error variance scales with the weights; an additive error floor sigma_i^2 = a + b/s_i mixes the two, the summand becoming s_i (a s_i + b), and the concentration re-enters through the floor on the heavily weighted rows.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:35:10.793966+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e14e9bfbe2a49764f58470cb6fbe67e3df3743f29fabf836ad6bbb51d835b6e6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defin 31 (Level change, step up, step down) of arXiv:2604.00635, 'Large deviations of the periodic Toda chain'] Let $\bs{\sg}_{N-1} \in \{ 0,1\}^{N-1}$.  One says that $\sigma_j$ with $j \in  \intn{1}{N-2}$
is a "level change" if $\sigma_j \neq \sigma_{j+1}$. Level changes come in two forms:

\begin{itemize}

\item "steps up" corresponding to $(\sigma_j, \sigma_{j+1}) = (0,1)$

\item "steps down" corresponding to $(\sigma_j, \sigma_{j+1}) = (1,0)$.

\end{itemize}

There is a natural identification $\bs{\sg}_{N-1} \mapsto \big(\sigma_1, X(\bs{\sg}_{N-1}) \big)$
where $X(\bs{\sg}_{N-1}) \subset \intn{1}{N-2}$ is the set of level changes.  That is, $\sigma_1$ is the first element in the sequence and

$$X(\bs{\sg}_{N-1}) \,  = \, \big\{ j \in \intn{1}{N-2} \, : \,  \sigma_j \neq \sigma_{j+1} \big\} \, .$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.198217+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e1755027b6b72bacceb84a2948a53af4813916207fa89947be3d5506f36530d0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 124 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the definition \eqref{e:bad.times.J}. 
If $(p^N)'$ converges to $p'$ in the L\'evy--Prohorov metric in the sense of Definition~\ref{d:levy.prohorov.derivs}, then  we have
	\[
	J^N\equiv
	J(p^N,\tep,\lambda)
		\subseteq 
		J\bigg(p,2\tep,\frac{\lambda}{2}\bigg)
	\equiv J
	\] for all $N$ large enough. 

\begin{proof}
The function $(p^N)'$ is nonincreasing, so there exists a nonnegative measure $\nu_N$ on $[q_0,1]$ with
	\[
	\nu_N( (s,t]) = -\Big[(p^N)'(t)-(p^N)'(s)\Big]
	\]
for all $q_0 \le s\le t\le1$, and with $\nu_N(\{0\})=0$. Define analogously the measure $\nu$ corresponding to the limiting function $p$.
The L\'evy--Prohorov convergence assumption implies that for all $N\ge N(\tep)$ we have
	\[
	\nu_N(A) \le \nu(A^{\tep})+\tep
	\]
where $A\subseteq[q_0,1]$ is any Borel set, and $A^{\tep}$ is the $\tep$-fattening of $A$. (The same inequality also holds with $\nu$ and $\nu_N$ exchanged.) It follows that
	\begin{align*}
	&-\Big[(p^N)'(t+\tep)-(p^N)'(t-\tep)\Big]
	= \nu_N([t-\tep,t+\tep])\\
	&\qquad\le \nu([t-2\tep,t+2\tep]) + \tep
	=-\Big[p'(t+2\tep)-p'(t-2\tep)\Big]+ \tep
	\le \frac{\lambda}{2}+\tep\,,
	\end{align*}
where the last bound holds provided $t\notin J$. Since $\tep\ll\lambda$ by Assumption~\ref{a:params}, this shows that if $t\notin J$ then $t\notin J^N$, as claimed.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.164974+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e1ab87659c9828464b5b9edeaac9c25323ecc986248336539b1663089ed6c98c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 55 of arXiv:2608.30059, 'Multihomogeneous Measures and Stochastic Polar Representations'] Let \(\nu\in M_{\chi,\sigma}(E)\) and consider:
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item
\(\nu=\nu_Z\) for some \(E\)-valued random element \(Z\).

\[
L_h=1\quad\nu\text{-almost everywhere}.
\]

\item

\[
0<K_f<\infty\quad\nu\text{-almost everywhere}.

Conditions \textup{(ii)} and \textup{(iii)} are always equivalent.
If \(\rho\not\equiv1\), all three conditions are equivalent.

there is an \(h\) as in \textup{(ii)} satisfying

total mass, and a probability representing measure exists precisely

We say that

When an estimate holds for all \(0\le t<T\), as will be the case for
the estimates proved below, we use the same notation.  Condition

base coordinates, whereas \((\mathrm Q)_U\) is the lower differential

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:56:17.365327+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e1bc1c93d17ac8382e28d7da3e397a756e3b42e7d640cc512f1f6b71d4e6d4b8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:sepstatdetcon of arXiv:2606.02472, 'Correlated uniform attachment trees'] From two sequences $(X_j^{i})_{j\geq 1}$, $i=1,2$ with $X_j^{i} \in \{0,1,\ldots, j-1\}$, generate a paired tree sequence $(T_k^{1}, T_k^{2})_{k\geq 1}$, where the edges of $T_k^{i}$ are $\{\{j, X_j^{i}\}\}_{j=0}^k$.
    Fix a sequence of time steps $0<K_0<K_1<\cdots< K_\ell< m<n$, and assume  $(X_j^{1},X_{j}^{2})_{j\geq 1}$  are such that the following hold. 
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
        \item For all $j=0,\ldots, \ell$, the $K_j$ most central nodes of $(T_k^{i})_{k\geq 1}$, $i=1,2$, do not change after step $m$, meaning
        \[
        A_{K_j}^{i}(N) = A_{K_j}^{i}(m) \text{ for all } N \geq m, \, i=1,2, \, \text{and } j=0,\ldots, \ell.
        \]
        \item After time step $m$, the differences in the number of nodes connecting to $A_{K_j}^{i}$ in each of the two trees has the following uniform bound
        \ba{
         \max_{j \in \{0,\ldots, \ell \}} \left| \sum_{k=m+1}^{n} \mathbbm{1}_{ \left\{ X_k^{1} \in A_{K_j}^{1}(m) \right\} }  - \sum_{k=m+1}^{n} \mathbbm{1}_{ \left\{ X_k^{2} \in A_{K_j}^{2}(m)\right\} } \right| \leq \log(n)^{2/3}.
        }
         \item After time step $m$, the weighted sum of squares of the differences in the number of nodes connecting to $A_{K_j}^{i}(m)$ in each of the two trees satisfies the bound
        \[
        \frac{1}{\ell + 1} \sum_{j=0}^{\ell} \frac{1}{K_j} \bbbclr{  \sum_{k=m+1}^{n} \mathbbm{1}_{ \left\{ X_k^{1} \in A_{K_j}^{1}(m) \right\} }  - \sum_{k=m+1}^{n} \mathbbm{1}_{ \left\{ X_k^{2} \in A_{K_j}^{2}(m) \right\} } }^2 > C\log(n),
       \]
       for some fixed  $C>0$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then
    \ban{
        \frac{1}{(\ell + 1)\log(n)} \sum_{j=0}^{\ell} \frac{1}{K_j} &\bbbclr{ \sum_{x \in A_{K_j}^{1}(n)} \deg_{T_n^{1}}(x) -  \sum_{x \in A_{K_j}^{2}(n)} \deg_{T_n^{2}}(x)  }^2
            \\
         &> C  - \frac{1}{(\ell + 1)\log(n)} \sum_{j=0}^{\ell} \frac{2(m+1) \log(n)^{2/3} + (m+1)^2}{K_j}. \notag
    } (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Lebesgue measure on [0,1] for the counterexample","0 < p < 1"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553704+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_e1f1d09dab661f59168150611995537e63e0f249b26c9ceb645e324eb84a1360","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For 0 < p < 1 the functional ||f||_p = (int |f|^p)^{1/p} is NOT a norm and the triangle inequality is false. Counterexample: on [0,1] with Lebesgue measure take f = 1_{[0,1/2]} and g = 1_{(1/2,1]}. Then ||f+g||_p = ||1_{[0,1]}||_p = 1, while ||f||_p + ||g||_p = 2 * (1/2)^{1/p} = 2^{1 - 1/p} < 1 for every p < 1 (e.g. 2^{-1} = 0.5 at p = 1/2). What survives: (i) the reverse inequality ||f+g||_p >= ||f||_p + ||g||_p for nonnegative f, g when 0 < p < 1; (ii) the quasi-triangle inequality ||f+g||_p <= 2^{1/p - 1}(||f||_p + ||g||_p); (iii) the p-th power is subadditive, int |f+g|^p <= int |f|^p + int |g|^p, so d(f,g) = ||f - g||_p^p is a complete translation-invariant metric and L^p (0 < p < 1) is a complete metric topological vector space - but it is not locally convex on a nonatomic space, and its dual is {0}. Related trap: the generalized Hölder inequality with 1/r = sum 1/p_i remains valid for r < 1, but the TWO-exponent Hölder inequality with a negative conjugate exponent (0 < p < 1, q = p/(p-1) < 0) points the other way under the appropriate positivity and finiteness hypotheses, so the standard direction may not be quoted when p < 1.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:31:20.864288+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e2069d1afb6f67b3701640a860faeb5ff84d4044d1c572cc42e53b268a42a291","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 11 of arXiv:2506.10856, 'The space of multifurcating ranked tree shapes: enumeration, lattice structure, and Markov'] The space $\mathcal{T}_{N,K}$ of ranked tree shapes with $N$ leaves and $K$ internal nodes is in bijection with the space $\mathcal{F}_{N,K}$ of $K\times K$ lower triangular matrices with non-negative integer entries that obey the
following constraints:
\begin{enumerate}[label={F\arabic*.}]
    \item The diagonal elements $F_{i,i}$ are strictly increasing: $F_{1,1}< F_{2,2}<...<F_{K,K}$ with $F_{K,K}=N$. The subdiagonal elements satisfy $F_{i+1,i} = F_{i,i}-1$ for all $i=1,...,K-1$.
    \item The elements $F_{i,1}, i=3,...,K$ in the first column satisfy \[ \max\{0, F_{i-1,1}- 1\} \leq F_{i,1} \leq F_{i-1,1}\] This just implies the column elements are decreasing by at most 1 if $F_{i-1,1}$ is non-zero.

        \item $F_{i-1, j}-1 \leq F_{i,j} \leq F_{i-1, j}$: Column-wise change is either 1 or 0.
        \item $0\leq (F_{i-1, j} - F_{i,j}) - (F_{i-1, j-1}- F_{i,j-1}) \leq 1$: in any $2\times 2$ grid, sum of off-diagonal elements minus sum of on-diagonal elements is 1 or 0.

\end{enumerate}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.299975+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e24889e4fd5825bc288daedce508a877706cdda9e02cf792d8e1985c8e632777","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 14 (Aligned anisotropic Gaussian allocation) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Let $X_0\sim\calN(0,\Sigma)$, where
\[
\Sigma=V\diag(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)V^\top,
\qquad \lambda_i>0.
\]
Let $A\in\R^{d_y\times d}$ have full row rank and suppose the measurement
is aligned with the prior eigenbasis,
\[
A=U\begin{bmatrix}\diag(s_1,\ldots,s_{d_y})&0\end{bmatrix}V^\top,
\qquad
\Gamma=\sigma_y^2\Id_{d_y},
\]
with $s_i=0$ for $i>d_y$.  Define
\begin{equation}

B_{i,t}=a_t^2\lambda_i+\Delta_t,
\qquad
v_{i,t}=\frac{\lambda_i\Delta_t}{B_{i,t}},
\qquad
\tau_i^2=\left(\lambda_i^{-1}+s_i^2/\sigma_y^2\right)^{-1},
\qquad
\widetilde B_{i,t}=a_t^2\tau_i^2+\Delta_t,
\end{equation}
where $\tau_i^2=\lambda_i$ when $s_i=0$.  Under the joint law of $(X_t,R)$,
\begin{equation}

\E|s_{t,i}^{\rm prior}(X_t)|^2=\frac1{B_{i,t}},
\qquad
\E|g_{t,i}(X_t,R)|^2
=
\frac{a_t^2s_i^2\lambda_i^2}
{B_{i,t}^2(s_i^2v_{i,t}+\sigma_y^2)},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}

\rho_i(t)
=
\frac{a_t^2s_i^2\lambda_i^2}
{B_{i,t}(s_i^2v_{i,t}+\sigma_y^2)}
=
\frac{B_{i,t}}{\widetilde B_{i,t}}-1.
\end{equation}
Consequently:
\begin{enumerate}
\item As $a_t\to0$,
\[
\rho_i(t)=
\frac{a_t^2s_i^2\lambda_i^2}{s_i^2\lambda_i+\sigma_y^2}+O(a_t^4).
\]
\item For $s_i>0$, $\rho_i(t)$ is strictly increasing along the reverse
trajectory, with low-noise limit $s_i^2\lambda_i/\sigma_y^2$, and
\begin{equation}

\rho_i(t)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\widetilde B_{i,t}=\frac12B_{i,t}.
\end{equation}
Thus, within this aligned linear-Gaussian model, $\rho_i=1$ is a
variance-halving, equal-Fisher-energy reference level.  It is crossed at a
unique interior noise level iff $s_i^2\lambda_i>\sigma_y^2$; when
$s_i^2\lambda_i=\sigma_y^2$, it is attained only at the clean endpoint.
\item Since the exact force is null on unmeasured aligned coordinates,
\begin{equation}

\rho_t^{\rm global}=\omega_t\rho_t^{\rm row},
\qquad
\omega_t=
\frac{\sum_{i:s_i>0}B_{i,t}^{-1}}{\sum_{i=1}^dB_{i,t}^{-1}}.
\end{equation}
For an isotropic prior, $\omega_t=d_y/d$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

In the critical beta-splitting random tree on n leaves, closed into a cycle, take a uniformly random leaf and the leaf r places further round the cycle. Aldous and Janson (The critical beta-splitting random tree II: overview and open problems, arXiv:2303.02529, Section 3.9, Open Problem 1) asked for a proof that the correlation of the two leaf heights tends to 1 - alpha when log r_n / log n tends to alpha in [0, 1]. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:37:15.062605+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e290d389ee1d213943133d51282ad804808edce692d39fdb23f6883f94eb7031","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 21 of arXiv:2607.11756, 'Full replica symmetry breaking in the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model'] Suppose that
\[
 0<a<b\le1,

\]
Set
\[
 T=\beta^2(b-a),

 U(t,x)=u(\sigma(t),x),
 \qquad 0\le t<T.
\]
Let $\widehat X_t=X_{\sigma(t)}$, denote its density by $p(t,\cdot)$,
and define
\begin{equation}
 f(t,x)=p(t,x)\e^{-mU(t,x)},
 \qquad
 V(t,x)=-\log f(t,x).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 U_t=-\frac12(U_{xx}+mU_x^2),

on $(0,T)\times\R$, and
\begin{equation}

 \qquad V_{xx}\ge0,

 \qquad\text{on }(0,T)\times(0,\infty).

For $0\le B<1$, let $x=x(t,B)\ge0$ be the inverse slope coordinate
\[
 B=U_x(t,x),
\]
and set
\[
 C(t,B)=U_{xx}(t,x(t,B)).
\]
Define
\begin{align}

 &R_V&=\frac12(V_x^2-V_{xx}),                     \\
 R_0&=2CJ-\frac m2C-\frac12z^2,

 L&=CJ-z(N+z),                                    \\
 w(t,B)&=2p(t,x(t,B))C(t,B).                      
\end{align}
Every derivative of $V$ appearing in slope coordinates is evaluated at
$(t,x(t,B))$.

Fix a compact interval $I\subset[0,T)$, so that $\max I<T$. There are constants
$c_I,C_I>0$ such that, for every $t\in I$ and $x\in\R$,
\begin{align}
 c_I\e^{-C_Ix^2}

{"assumptions":["H is a Hilbert space","a is bounded sesquilinear on H × H","the claimed coercivity constant α > 0 must hold on all of H"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772311+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, elliptic PDE, finite element analysis","id":"claim_e2aa108ac361aa69126eca86591b9d8beaedd4bc7bdd886699f31c317c3ce026","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: Re a(u, u) ≥ α‖u‖² for all u in the Hilbert space H, with a fixed α > 0 and the norm of H itself (the trial and test space). What fails: strict positivity a(u, u) > 0 for u ≠ 0, or injectivity of the associated operator, is not enough - the solution operator need not be bounded and the problem need not be solvable. Counterexample 1: H = ℓ², a(u, v) = Σ_{n ≥ 1} n^{-1} u_n conj(v_n). Then a is bounded (C = 1), Hermitian, and a(u, u) > 0 for every u ≠ 0, but the associated operator is the injective compact diagonal operator with entries 1/n, whose range is not closed. For f = (1/n)_n ∈ ℓ², the equation a(u, v) = ⟨f, v⟩ for all v forces u_n = 1 for all n, which is not in ℓ²: no solution exists. Counterexample 2 (the practical one): on a bounded connected Lipschitz domain Ω, a(u, v) = ∫_Ω ∇u·∇v̄ on H = H¹(Ω) is bounded and positive semidefinite but not coercive, since a(1, 1) = 0; the Neumann problem −Δu = f, ∂_ν u = 0 is solvable only under the compatibility condition ∫_Ω f = 0, and is never uniquely solvable in H¹(Ω) (constants can be added). Coercivity is recovered only on the subspace {u ∈ H¹(Ω) : ∫_Ω u = 0} via the Poincaré-Wirtinger inequality; on H_0^1(Ω) it is recovered via the Poincaré inequality, which is why the Dirichlet problem is the easy case. Other silent hypotheses: H must be complete (a coercive bounded form on a dense non-closed subspace gives no existence), and the coercivity constant α must be uniform, not depending on u. Note a is not assumed symmetric - that part is genuinely unnecessary. For non-coercive but well-posed problems (e.g. mixed or saddle point formulations, convection dominated problems, different trial and test spaces), the correct replacement is the Banach-Necas-Babuska inf-sup theorem: an inf-sup condition on a plus injectivity of the adjoint form, of which coercivity is only a sufficient condition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.095016+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e2bdc304174e9fecc0b830e21a47837cec922f95e7efd160273f5cec30664a8e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:paired-resource of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] A safe gate and its $C$-degree are as in
(def:circuit-primitives of the paper); the amplified estimate is proved in
(lem:safe of the paper).

For an active eigenframe of an arbitrary self-adjoint pure-Weyl $C$, put
\[
 (F_Cx)_a=\lambda_aA_a^Tx,
 \qquad
 F_C^*F_C=Q_2:=-\sum_a\lambda_a^2A_a^2,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Tr} Q_2=2\|C\|_2^2.
\tag{2.2.1}
\]
A concrete carrier for these two fronts is obtained as follows.  Let
$E_C=\ell^2(I_C)$ be the active label space,
$J_C:E_C\to\Lambda^2H$ the isometry $J_Ce_a=A_a$, and
\[
 \iota_\wedge A=2^{-1/2}\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}e_i\otimes e_j,
 \qquad
 \mathsf W_C=(\iota_\wedge J_C)\otimes I_H,
\]
and define the one-hole column
\[
 (T_Cx)_{ijk}=\sum_\ell C_{ij,k\ell}x_\ell.
\tag{2.2.2}
\]
With the ordered-pair convention
$C_{ij,k\ell}=\sum_a\lambda_a(A_a)_{ij}(A_a)_{k\ell}$,
one has the exact typed identity
\[
 \mathsf W_CF_C=-2^{-1/2}T_C,
 \qquad
 \mathfrak q_C^{\rm hole}
 :=\mathsf W_CF_CF_C^*\mathsf W_C^*
 =\frac12T_CT_C^*.
\tag{2.2.3}
\]
Thus the open token is a specified three-strand operator, up to the signed
leg permutations recorded by its port state; it is not defined merely by
having a prescribed scalar cap.  Moreover
\[
 T_C^*T_C=2Q_2,
 \qquad
 T_C=P_{[2,1]_0}T_C,
\tag{2.2.4}
\]
where $P_{[2,1]_0}$ is the trace-free hook projection on the first three
indices.

A paired-front atom contains the two correlated Hilbert--Schmidt fronts
of this single $F_C$ pair, equivalently the concrete hole
$\mathfrak q_C^{\rm hole}$ in (eq:2.2.3 of the paper), any safe left and right gates, and
an untouched typed ancillary boundary $E$.  Let $\mathfrak M_C^{\rm alg}(E)$ be

We quantify the speed of this convergence in the case of the KPZ equation. \]

    \qquad (s,x)\in[0,1]\times\mathbb R .
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:52:51.763133+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e3223d8c3fad1c6c8b05cff9dce34e7d45416a97ea810ebf9d22dca071224981","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:classicalStochStab of arXiv:2604.28068, 'Mean-square Stability and Bifurcations for Dissipative SDEs'] Suppose that $x^*$ is an equilibrium of the SDE (equation eq:main_d of the paper) and let
$X$ be a global solution with initial data $X_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$. Then $Y=X-x^*$ is a solution of the centered SDE (equation eq:main_YSDE of the paper) with $Y_0=X_0-x^*$. We say that the equilibrium  $x^*$ is
\begin{enumerate}
\item stable in probability for $t\geq 0$ if  for any  $s\geq 0$ and $\varepsilon>0$,
\[
\lim_{Y_0\to 0}\mathbb{P}\left[\sup_{t>s}\|Y(t)\|>\varepsilon\right]=0;
\]
\item asymptotically stable in probability if  it is stable in probability and 
\[
\lim_{Y_0\to 0}\mathbb{P}\left[\lim_{t\to\infty}\|Y(t)\|=0\right]=1;
\]
\item pth-moment stable if for any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a $\delta> 0$ such that
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[\|Y(t)\|^p\right]<\varepsilon,\quad t\geq 0,
\]
whenever $\|Y_0\|^p<\delta$; if $p=2$, the equilibrium is said to be mean-square stable;
\item globally pth-moment asymptotically stable if  it is pth-moment stable, and for all $Y_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$,
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[\|Y(t)\|^p\right]=0;
\] 
if $p=2$, the equilibrium is said to be mean-square asymptotically stable;
\item a.s.~stable if  for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\delta> 0$ such that
\[
\|Y(t)\|<\varepsilon,\quad t\geq 0,\quad a.s,
\] 
whenever $\|Y_0\|<\delta$;
\item globally a.s.~asymptotically stable if  for all $Y_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$, 
\[
\lim_{t\to \infty}\|Y(t)\|=0\quad a.s.
\]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.350731+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e33a70d0d09cf4f2fb54d7c01ab85e5224355e2dc6d011ae8099d05660c96c11","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 182 (quenched second moment bounds for 
$\bar{D}^{\RomII}$ and 
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] In addition to Lemma~\ref{l:barD.II.second} we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[\max\bigg\{
	\frac{\bE[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{p(q_d)}
	: 0\le d\le \dmax-1\bigg\}
	\le \frac{\SMAX_N(\RomII)^2 \BUCKETS \delta}{M}\,,\]
where $\SMAX_N(\RomII)$ is a random variable satisfying the bound
	\[\P\Big(\SMAX_N(\RomII) \ge \log N\Big)
	\le\exp\bigg(-\frac{(\log N)^2}{L^{O(1)}}\bigg)\,.\]
The same bound holds with $\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ in place of
$\bar{D}^{\RomII}$.

\begin{proof} Recall that
we can rewrite \eqref{e:drift.error.II} as
	\[
	\frac{\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)}{(p_d)^{1/2}}
	= 
	\frac{(\delta_d)^{1/2}}{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{1/2}}\sum_{a\in B}
	\frac{\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)}{|B|^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1})\bigg)
	\equiv
	\frac{(\delta_d)^{1/2}}{|B|^{1/2}}
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)\,.
	\]
If we define the random variable
	\[
	\SMAX_N(\RomII)
	\equiv\max
	\bigg\{
	\bigg|
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)
	\bigg|
	: 
	0\le d\le \dmax-1,
	B\in \mathcal{B}(q_d)
	\bigg\}\,,
	\]
then we have the quenched second moment bound
	\[
	\frac{\bE[\Delta\bar{D}^{\RomII}(q_d)^2]}{p_d}
	= \frac{\delta_d}{M}\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d)}
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by \bigg)^2
	\le \frac{\SMAX_N(\RomII)^2\BUCKETS\delta}{M}\,,
	\]
Note that for any $B\subseteq[M]$ we have
$\bar{\bg}^B= \bar{\bG}^\st \be_B$, so $\|\bar{\bg}^B\| \le\|\bar{\bG}\|_\textup{op}$. It then follows from Lemma~\ref{l:wishart} that for $C(\alpha)$ large enough, we have 
	\beq
	\P\Big(\|\bar{\bg}^B\|^2 \ge 
	C(\alpha) N \textup{ for any }B\subseteq[M]\Big)
	\le \frac{1}{2^N}\,.
	\eeq
The vectors $(\bar{\bg}^B : B\in\mathcal{B}(q_d))$ are measurable with respect to $\cG(q_d)$, so applying Lemma~\ref{l:y.subgaus} gives
	\begin{align*}
	&\P\Big(\SMAX_N(\RomII) \ge \log N\Big)
	=\P\bigg(
	\bigg|
	\bigg( \frac{\bar{\bg}^B(q_d)}{N^{1/2}},\by(q_{d+1}) \bigg)
	\bigg|
		\ge \log N
	\textup{ for any } 0\le d\le \dmax- 1, B \in \mathcal{B}(q_d)
	\bigg)\\
	&\qquad\le
	\dmax\BUCKETS
	\bigg\{ \frac{1}{2^N}
	+ \exp\bigg(-\frac{(\log N)^2}{L^{O(1)}}\bigg)
	\bigg\}
	\le\exp\bigg(-\frac{(\log N)^2}{L^{O(1)}}\bigg)
	\,,
	\end{align*}
where the $1/2^N$ in the second line comes from \eqref{e:II.union.bound}, and the final simplification uses Assumption~\ref{a:params}. This proves the claim for $\bar{D}^{\RomII}$, and the claim for
$\bar{D}^{\frozen,\RomII}$ follows by using \eqref{e:barD.vs.plus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:36:49.928517+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e347ff1c8563c534518f837e5edb616a903a413aaa066bbb80a24db7a809b259","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Openproblem op:mather-measures of arXiv:2609.01557, '$L^\infty$ Variational Approximation of the Aubry Set'] Conceptually, (equation eq:AtoM of the paper) shows that the Mather set can, in principle, be recovered from the projected Aubry set $\mathcal A$ together with the limiting function $u_\infty$. However, this characterization is not particularly convenient from a numerical point of view. It is therefore natural to ask whether Evans' variational approximation also provides a more direct way to recover the projected Mather set $\mathcal M$, or equivalently the full Mather set $\widetilde{\mathcal M}$.

Let
\[
\sigma_k(x)
:=
\frac{e^{kH(Du_k(x),x)}}
{\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb T^n}
e^{kH(Du_k(y),y)}\,dy}.
\]
The pair \((u_k,\sigma_k)\) is also the logarithmically coupled stationary mean-field game associated with Evans' variational approximation; see [GY20].
Thanks to [Evans03, Evans04], along a subsequence,
\[
\sigma_{k_j}\rightharpoonup \sigma
\qquad\text{weakly in the sense of measures},
\]
where \(\sigma\) is a projected Mather measure. In dimension one, under a
suitable nondegeneracy condition, \(\operatorname{spt}(\sigma)\) coincides
with the whole projected Mather set (i.e., $\operatorname{spt}(\sigma)=\mathcal M$),  whereas degeneracy may lead to further
selection ([GISMY10]). What is the corresponding picture in higher dimensions? In
particular, under what conditions does
\[
\operatorname{spt}(\sigma)=\mathcal M,
\]
and what determines the subset of \(\mathcal M\) selected when this equality
fails? (Stated as a problem by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:35:57.003752+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e37836a89c6daf091382bfc6c4ed6f0cd7343b9694cdc60e9d2e6e6e3fb81078","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:general_order of arXiv:2604.05921, 'Simplicity of random hypergraphs'] For any functions $f^{(i)}(v):V \rightarrow \mathds{N}$ and $w \in \mathds{N}$, if

{"assumptions":["conditioned Galton-Watson (simply generated) tree with n vertices","N_d = number of vertices of outdegree d"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.318625+00:00","domain":"probability/random trees","id":"claim_e3850e9afeb448f99ec9561d012acf69","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Janson's Problem 20.2 (Probability Surveys 2012, Section 20.2) asks whether the outdegree counts N_d of a conditioned Galton-Watson (simply generated) tree are asymptotically normal. (a) nu = 1 with finite variance: yes, jointly with the covariances (Janson, Random Structures Algorithms 48 (2016), Theorem 1.13 with Example 2.2 and Section 8). (b) nu = 1 with infinite variance and (c) nu < 1: yes when the offspring law is regularly varying (Thevenin, Electron. J. Probab. 25 (2020), Theorems 6.2 and 6.7, variance pi_d(1 - pi_d)), but not in general. A subcritical law whose bulk sits on {0, 1}, with two rare atoms at (1 - q - c) n_r +/- A sqrt(n_r), each of probability n_r^{-4}, makes the conditioned tree carry exactly one of the two with probability tending to 1/2 each, so N_1 = n pi_1 -/+ A sqrt(n) up to smaller terms, a near two-point law (Theorem A, full proof); the critical infinite-variance case is the same construction with the pair straddling the missing mass of an absent rarer atom (Theorem B, a sketch that still needs a lattice local moderate-deviation expansion). Thevenin's conjecture that normality holds for every such law is therefore false. The regularly varying case survives because the giant's law is locally flat at scale sqrt(n).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["product measure on a FINITE index set","BK: both events increasing","Reimer: no monotonicity hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542992+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e3854fb8e108d83f54f7a2c762956ced396b14b16573131eabefa9f8eab4f84b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^E with E FINITE. For events A and B define the DISJOINT OCCURRENCE A box B as the set of configurations omega for which there exist DISJOINT sets of coordinates K and L such that every configuration agreeing with omega on K lies in A and every configuration agreeing with omega on L lies in B - informally, A and B occur for disjoint reasons. VAN DEN BERG-KESTEN: if A and B are both INCREASING then P(A box B) <= P(A) P(B). REIMER: the same inequality holds for ARBITRARY events A and B, with no monotonicity hypothesis. The direction is opposite to Harris-FKG, which is the point: increasing events are positively correlated, but requiring them to occur on disjoint witnesses destroys that correlation and more. The finiteness of E is a genuine hypothesis of the standard statements; infinite index sets are handled by approximation, and the definition of disjoint occurrence itself needs care there. Typical use: bounding the probability of two disjoint open crossings, or of a self-avoiding open path of length n, by a product. [van den Berg and Kesten (1985); Reimer (2000), Combin. Probab. Comput. 9; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Theorem 2.12]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.487280+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e3be3c9182f994af2806f0d42922ebf649a4ecf9e795918fbcd91230f3fe9f9f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn Coulomb gas correlations for a divisor on the Riemann sphere of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let the divisor
$$
\boldsymbol{\sigma}=\sum \sigma_j \cdot z_j,
$$
where $\left\{z_j\right\}_{j=1}^n$ is a finite set of distinct points on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$.
The Coulomb gas correlation $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ is a differential of conformal dimension $\lambda_j$ at $z_j$, given by

\begin{equation}
\lambda_j=\lambda_b\left(\sigma_j\right) \equiv \frac{\sigma_j^2}{2}-\sigma_j b ,
\end{equation}

where $\lambda_b(\sigma)=\frac{\sigma^2}{2}-\sigma b \quad(\sigma \in \mathbb{C})$
whose value is given by

where the product is taken over all finite $z_j$ and $z_k$.

\]
In general, the function is multivalued, and one must choose a single-valued branch for each factor $(z_j-z_k)^{\sigma_j\sigma_k}$, except in special cases where all $\sigma_j$ are integers. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869358+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_e3fe93c1b93e4bf1bae09cdb537c1446b11a7eef12cc45dbf8842efaebdec015","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"FIRES WHEN you are about to prove a convex-order dominance for a Markov-modulated inter-event time by conditioning on the modulating state and calling the result a mixture of exponentials. THE ROUTE: conditionally on the chain's stationary sojourn structure the inter-event time is exponential with a state-dependent rate, and a MIXTURE of exponentials always dominates the matched exponential in the convex order by Jensen applied to t -> E[exp(-lambda t)]. WHERE IT FAILS: only when the chain does NOT move during the inter-event interval. MINIMAL WITNESS that the simplest sufficient condition also fails: the source's own four-state example has a NON-MONOTONE hazard rate, so the decreasing-hazard-rate criterion does not apply either. CONDITION OF FAILURE: any modulating transition inside an inter-event interval. The route that worked instead was Palm inversion - see the E0078 result node.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:19:46.227892+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e40608a37e4de12076c5bc6e9e448876a6b9b555bdd13c5118d52fc6908afd03","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 5 (Large deviations principle) of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] The sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ obeys the \textbf{large deviations principle} (`\textbf{LDP}') with \textbf{rate function} $I$ if the following hold:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item[i.] (Upper bound) If $x \in \X$ and $a < I(x)$, then there is a neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ such that
		\[\mu_n U \le e^{-an + o(n)}.\]
		\item[ii.] (Lower bound) If $x \in \X$ and $I(x) < a < \infty$, then any neighbourhood $U$ of $x$ satisfies
		\[\mu_n U \ge e^{-a n - o(n)}.\]
		\item[iii.] (Exponential tightness) For every $a > 0$ there is a compact subset $K$ of $\X$ such that
		\[\mu_n (\X\setminus K) \le e^{-an + o(n)}.\]
	\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:07:56.656860+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e40d3f350c8d318f0c66cccca44dc7c116ccf56efaf13103a6135068d8412d5b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:drift of arXiv:2411.04773, 'Meeting of squared Bessel flow lines and application to the skew Brownian motion'] An $\mathcal F$-predictable process $\overline{\delta}:{\mathbb R}\to{\mathbb R}$ is called a drift function if there exists a deterministic vector $(\delta_i)_{1\le i\le n} \in {\mathbb R}^n$ and $\mathcal F$-stopping times $-\infty=\tilde{t}_1<\tilde{t}_2<\ldots<\tilde{t}_{n+1}=\infty$ such that $\overline{\delta}=\delta_i$ on $A_i:=(\tilde{t}_{i},\tilde{t}_{i+1})$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.163857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e444a01e4404c33f58e4f4f48ec3e8fbc8498651ff93b0fc01e5ff4adf5a47a1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 29 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The function $V$ defined by \eqref{e:freeprob.V} is strictly convex on the interval $(z_0,+\infty)$, with $V(z)\to\infty$ as $z\to\infty$.
As a consequence, $V$ has a unique minimizer on the interval $[z_0,+\infty)$, which we denote $z_{\min}$.

\begin{proof} For $z>z_0$, we calculate
    \beq
        
        V'(z)
        = 1 - \alpha \frac{m_2(z)}{m(z)^2} \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j
            \bigg(\frac{\hv_j m(z)}{\alpha - \hv_j m(z)}\bigg)^2\,.
    \eeq
Recall that $m:(\hw_1,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ is strictly decreasing, and we have
$\alpha - \hv_j m(z) > 0$ for all $z>z_0$. It follows that, on  the interval
$(z_0,\infty)$, the function
    \[
    \frac{m(z)}{\alpha-\hv_j m(z)}
    = \frac{1}{\alpha/m(z)-\hv_j}
    \]
is strictly decreasing, \emph{regardless of the sign of $\hv_j$}. Consequently, in \eqref{e:fp-V-pr}, each term
    \[      \bigg(\frac{\hv_j m(z)}{\alpha - \hv_j m(z)}\bigg)^2\]
is strictly decreasing on $(z_0,\infty)$, again \emph{regardless of the sign of $\hv_j$}. In the special case $s=1$, we have $m_2(z)=m(z)^2$, so we conclude in this case that $V'$ is strictly increasing on the interval $(z_0,\infty)$. For $s\ge2$, we note that $m_2(z)/m(z)^2$ is positive, and
    \[
        \frac{d}{dz}\bigg[ \frac{m_2(z)}{m(z)^2}\bigg]
        = \frac{2}{m(z)^3} \Big(m_2(z)^2 - m(z)m_3(z)\Big)
        < 0
    \]
by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. It therefore follows in this case as well that $V'$ is strictly increasing, and so $V$ is strictly convex, on the interval $(z_0,\infty)$.
Finally, as $z\to\infty$, $m(z) \to 0$. Therefore the first term of $V(z)$ tends to $\infty$ while the second term remains bounded, and so $V(z) \to \infty$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.424875+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e48d1c31ee50e160fa1e46d567717236adb315c63688f5abb4b567b9c82f86e6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 3. dfn: Polish functor of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Polish functor}] 
  We say that a functor $\tau$ is \textit{Polish} if there exist a functor $\tilde{\tau}$
  and, for each $(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}$,
  a sequence $(\tilde{\tau}_{k}(S))_{k=1}^{\infty}$ of open subsets in $\tilde{\tau}(S)$
  satisfying the following conditions.
  \begin{enumerate} [label = (P\arabic*), leftmargin = *]
    \item 
      The functor $\tilde{\tau}$ is complete, separable and continuous. 
    \item 
      The functor $\tau$ is a topological subfunctor of $\tilde{\tau}$.
    \item 
      For every $(S, d^{S}, \rho_{S}) \in \mathfrak{M}$,
      it holds that $\tau(S) = \bigcap_{k \geq 1} \tilde{\tau}_{k}(S)$.
    \item 
      Let $f: S_{1} \to S_{2}$ be a root-and-distance-preserving map
      between $(S_{i}, d^{S_{i}}, \rho_{S_{i}}) \in \mathfrak{M},\, i=1,2$.
      Then, $\tilde{\tau}_{f}^{-1}(\tilde{\tau}_{k}(S_{2})) = \tilde{\tau}_{k}(S_{1})$
      for each $k \geq 1$. 
      In particular,
      $\tilde{\tau}_{f}^{-1}(\tau(S_{2})) = \tau(S_{1})$.
  \end{enumerate}
  We call $(\tilde{\tau}, (\tilde{\tau}_{k})_{k \geq 1})$ a \textit{Polish system} of $\tau$.","status":"unverified"}

operator $T:H\to H$, that is, the eigenvalues of

\[
    \sum_{j\geq1}s_j(T)<\infty,
\]

\[

\]

values of its eigenvalues $\{\lambda_j(T)\}_{j\ge 1}$, and hence these conditions are equivalent

\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.754498+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e4ee7b1b0c19bb8b82285bdfeda4e24623277fdb17afbb02be376dc92a798f9b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Df 34 of arXiv:2609.03836, 'Koszul Orlik--Solomon Algebras from Non-supersolvable Arrangements'] Let $E$ be a finite set.
    Let $E = E_0 \sqcup E_1 \sqcup E_2$ be a tripartition of $E$.
    Write $E_{01} = E_0 \cup E_1$ and $E_{12} = E_1 \cup E_2$.
    Suppose $M$ is a matroid on $E_{01}$ and $N$ is a matroid on $E_{12}$ such that
    $E_1$ is a modular flat of $M$ and
    $M|_{E_1} = N|_{E_1}$.
    
    One defines the \textbf{generalized parallel connection} of $M$ and $N$ along $E_1$---denoted $P_{E_1}(M, N)$---to be the unique matroid on $E$ whose flats are the subsets $F \subseteq E$ such that 
    $F \cap E_{01}$ is a flat of $M$ and 
    $F \cap E_{12}$ is a flat of $N$.
    The rank of this matroid is $\rk P_{E_1}(M, N) = \rk M + \rk N - \rk_M E_1$.
    When $E_1$ is modular in $N$ also, we say (following Ziegler) that $M$ is the \textbf{modular join} of $M$ and $N$ along $E_1$.
    In this case, $P_{E_1}(N, M)$ also exists and is equal to $P_{E_1}(M, N)$.","status":"unverified"}

by the common one-variable Green series, admissibility in
$\{1,\ldots,m\}$ is
\[
 a+(h-1)+q\le m.
\]

\[
 M(a)=m-h+1-a,
 \qquad M(a+1)=M(a)-1.

\]

multiplicity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.693476+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e53b29e59e81738e45376b2c2bf7cd67a9e4cec7a398428857e3bc2fd0e42ba8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:two-vortex of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $\boldsymbol\kappa=(\kappa_1,\kappa_2)$ satisfy
$\kappa_1>0>\kappa_2$, and let
$(\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})\in\Lambda_2(D)$ be a strict local
minimum point of $W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}$.  Choose $\rho>0$ such that
\[
  B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,1})\times B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,2})
  \Subset\Lambda_2(D),
\]
and
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
  W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)
  &>W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}
  (\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})\\
  &\quad\text{for every }(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)\in
  \overline{B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,1})\times
  B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,2})}
  \setminus\{(\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})\}.
  \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Fix $M_i,R_i>0$ for $i=1,2$.  Then there exist positive constants
$C$, $\eta_0$, and $\varepsilon_0$, depending only on
$D,\rho$, and $\mathbf a_{*,i},\kappa_i,M_i,R_i$, $i=1,2$,
such that the following holds.

For every $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0$, let
$(\mathbf a_{1,\varepsilon},\mathbf a_{2,\varepsilon})
\in B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,1})\times B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,2})$, and let
$\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}\in L^\infty(D)$ be nonnegative and satisfy
\[
  \int_D\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}\,\mathrm d\mathbf x=|\kappa_i|,
  \qquad
  \|\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}\|_\infty
  \leq M_i\varepsilon^{-2},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}
  \subset B_{R_i\varepsilon}(\mathbf a_{i,\varepsilon}),
  \quad i=1,2.
\]
Set
$\omega_{\varepsilon,0}
:=\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,0}-\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,0}$.
Let $\omega_{\varepsilon,t}$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the corresponding Yudovich
solution of (equation eq:euler-intro of the paper), and let
$\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,t}$ denote the transport of
$\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0}$ by the associated Euler flow map.
If
\begin{equation}
  \eta^{(2)}_{\varepsilon,0}
  :=\sum_{i=1}^2\mathcal D(\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,0})
  +\Bigl[W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}
  (\mathbf a_{1,\varepsilon},\mathbf a_{2,\varepsilon})
  -W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}
  (\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})\Bigr]
  +\varepsilon
  \leq\eta_0,
\end{equation}
then, for every $t\in\mathbb R$,
\begin{equation}
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,t})
  \times\mathsf C(\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,t})
  \subset B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,1})\times
  B_\rho(\mathbf a_{*,2}),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{align}
  &\sum_{i=1}^2\mathcal D(\zeta_{i,\varepsilon,t})
  +\sup_{(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)\in
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{1,\varepsilon,t})\times
  \mathsf C(\zeta_{2,\varepsilon,t})}
  \Bigl[
  W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}(\mathbf b_1,\mathbf b_2)
  -W_{\boldsymbol\kappa}^{(2)}
  (\mathbf a_{*,1},\mathbf a_{*,2})
  \Bigr] \leq C\eta^{(2)}_{\varepsilon,0}.
  
\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["P is a set of partial computable functions","P is nontrivial: neither empty nor all partial computable functions"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378848+00:00","domain":"computability theory","id":"claim_e566adf01a15158b9f7ce6ec58f8cd9ca5acbd8ecb4145e42d80266d80928187","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Every nontrivial semantic property of programs is undecidable. Precisely: let P be any set of partial computable functions that is nontrivial, meaning some partial computable function belongs to P and some does not. Then the index set {encodings of Turing machines M : the partial function computed by M belongs to P} is undecidable. 'Semantic' is essential: the property must depend only on the function computed, not on the machine's text (syntactic properties such as 'has fewer than 100 states' are decidable). Only the two trivial semantic properties (satisfied by all machines, or by none) have decidable index sets. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:17:17.061688+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e5687ee2014797e01ddd176afbf0325910953c5ec57a43f11b7388e3882bb4e4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 11 of arXiv:2608.19744, 'Conditioned Brownian motion and local equivalence of path ensembles'] Let $X$ be the CIR process above, take
$A_T=\int_0^T \de s \, X_s$
and fix $0<\theta<\eta$.  With $r_{\beta_\theta}=\frac{\kappa\eta}{\theta}$ and $\beta_\theta
      =\frac{\kappa^2}{2\sigma^2}
        \left(\frac{\eta^2}{\theta^2}-1\right)$,
put
\[
    I_x^{\mathrm{CIR}}(\theta)
      =\frac{\kappa^2(\eta-\theta)^2}{2\sigma^2\theta},
    \qquad
    v_\theta
      =\frac{\sigma^2\theta^3}{\kappa^2\eta^2}.
\]
Then, for every fixed $x>0$ and $z\in\mathbb R$,
\[
\begin{split}
    \bbP_x^{\mathrm{CIR}}(A_T\leq\theta T+z)
    \sim{}&
    \frac{1}{\beta_\theta\sqrt{2\pi v_\theta T}}
    \left(
       \frac{2r_{\beta_\theta}}
            {\kappa+r_{\beta_\theta}}
    \right)^\alpha
    \exp\!\left(
       -\frac{(r_{\beta_\theta}-\kappa)x}{\sigma^2}
    \right)
    \exp\!\left(
       -I_x^{\mathrm{CIR}}(\theta)T+\beta_\theta z
    \right).
\end{split}
\]
On every fixed time interval, the conditioned process converges in total
variation to the CIR process
\[
    \de Y_t
      =r_{\beta_\theta}(\theta-Y_t)\,\de t
       +\sigma\sqrt{Y_t}\,\de B_t,
    \qquad Y_0=x.
\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.096857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e5ace840b7a802a63627f4607d2573244712aad61251eef12fdf70c6287c7bb4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:ribbon-majorant of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Fix a ribbon record $\Gamma$, a circuit state $\tau$, and a designated

trace-class costs.  No endpoint weight or debit in $\mathcal E$ is

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:18:19.220034+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e5da1f660a5af8df7096bc9240824b67d25a665e411ceb9d2690023e730a6afd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 of arXiv:2608.29075, 'The 2-Monoidal Structure of Symmetric Sequences'] Let $(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ be a 2-monoidal category. A \textit{bimonoid} in $\catname{C}$ is a quintuple $(H,\mu,\iota,\Delta,\epsilon)$ where $(H,\mu,\iota)$ is a monoid in $(\C,\square,I)$, $(H,\Delta,\epsilon)$ is a comonoid in $(\C,\circ,J)$, and the two structures are compatible in the sense that the following four diagrams commute.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{(H \circ H)\square (H \circ H)} && {(H\square H)\circ (H \square H)} \\
	{H \square H} & H & {H \circ H}
	\arrow["{\zeta_{H,H,H,H}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow["{\mu \circ \mu}", from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\Delta \square \Delta}", from=2-1, to=1-1]
	\arrow["\mu"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\Delta"', from=2-2, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{H \square H} & {J \square J} && I & H \\
	H & J && {I \circ I} & {H \circ H}
	\arrow["{\epsilon \square \epsilon}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\mu"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\mu_J}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\iota", from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow["{\Delta_I}"', from=1-4, to=2-4]
	\arrow["\Delta", from=1-5, to=2-5]
	\arrow["\epsilon"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\iota \circ \iota}"', from=2-4, to=2-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& H \\
	I && J
	\arrow["\epsilon", from=1-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow["\iota", from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\iota_J = \epsilon_I}"', from=2-1, to=2-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    A morphism of bimonoids is a morphism of the underlying monoids and comonoids.

{"assumptions":["Conclusion is constancy on the closure of U x [0,t_0] only","U must be connected","The maximum must be attained at a point with x_0 in U and t_0 > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106923+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_e5db45cf444dc11d943ed80dd9009a1a1904ce853e38b9031ae8a4e06c9b3559","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"If a solution of the heat equation attains its maximum over $\\overline{U_T}$ at an interior point $(x_0,t_0)\\in U_T$, the conclusion is that $u$ is constant on $\\overline U\\times[0,t_0]$ -- the past of $t_0$ -- and nothing at all is claimed for $t>t_0$. Heat is not time-reversible, and the mean value property over heat balls only looks backwards. Counterexample: on $U=(0,\\pi)$, $T=2$, let $h(t)=1$ for $t\\le1$ and $h(t)=1-e^{-1/(t-1)}$ for $t>1$ (smooth, $h\\le1$, $h<1$ for $t>1$), and let $u$ be the solution of $u_t=u_{xx}$ with $u(\\cdot,0)\\equiv1$ and $u(0,t)=u(\\pi,t)=h(t)$. On $[0,1]$, $u\\equiv1$ by uniqueness; the weak maximum principle gives $\\max_{\\overline{U_T}}u=1$, attained at the interior point $(\\pi/2,1)\\in U_T$; but for $t>1$, $u$ is not constant (its boundary values are $<1$ while, by continuity, $u$ stays near $1$ in the middle). So constancy holds exactly up to $t_0=1$ and fails afterwards. A second load-bearing hypothesis is connectedness of $U$: for $U=(0,1)\\cup(2,3)$ the solution equal to $1$ on the first component and to $e^{-\\lambda_1t}\\phi_1$ on the second attains its maximum at an interior point of the first component and is not constant on $U$. Finally, the interior maximum must be attained in $U_T$, i.e. at a point with $x_0\\in U$: a maximum on the lateral boundary says nothing about constancy (that is the Hopf lemma's domain, which asserts instead that the outward normal derivative is strictly positive there).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The counterexample uses H(p) = p^2 (smooth, uniformly convex) and zero data, so no exotic Hamiltonian is needed","'Solution a.e.' means Lipschitz plus the equation at points of differentiability","Uniqueness is restored by the viscosity property or, equivalently for convex superlinear H, by the semiconcavity bound of the Hopf-Lax solution"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418105+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: Hamilton-Jacobi equations","id":"claim_e6002f2b1fb67f105d5effe237759fa92f79220ba532358144c459114f6ad305","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in any uniqueness statement for u_t + H(Du) = 0 the solution must be a VISCOSITY solution (equivalently, for convex superlinear H, a Lipschitz a.e. solution satisfying the one-sided semiconcavity estimate). Satisfying the equation at almost every point plus the initial condition is far too weak. Counterexample (n = 1): H(p) = p^2, initial datum g ≡ 0. Both u ≡ 0 and v(x,t) := min(0, |x| - t) are Lipschitz on R × [0,∞), vanish at t = 0, and satisfy v_t + v_x^2 = 0 at every point of differentiability: for |x| < t one has v = |x| - t, v_t = -1, v_x = ±1; for |x| > t one has v ≡ 0. Only u ≡ 0 is the viscosity solution (it is also what the Hopf-Lax formula gives, since L(q) = q^2/4 and min_y ( |x-y|^2/(4t) ) = 0). Why v fails: at a point (0,t) with t > 0, v has a local minimum in x with a convex kink, so φ ≡ v(0,t) + c(t'-t) touches from below with φ_x = 0, φ_t = -1, and the supersolution inequality φ_t + φ_x^2 ≥ 0 reads -1 ≥ 0. Equivalently v violates semiconcavity: v(z,t) - 2v(0,t) + v(-z,t) = 2|z|, which is not O(|z|^2). Auditor's check: whenever a proof concludes 'u is the solution' from 'u is Lipschitz and solves the PDE a.e.', the argument is incomplete unless viscosity, semiconcavity, or a variational (Hopf-Lax) representation is verified.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:59.496248+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6248aa0074ed65c0cb416759fb98cfbee64e1b86f405d7a62cdf77ef9f92b0d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 (First-break localization and tails) of arXiv:2605.09641, 'The Ballot Event for Two-Player Coupon Collection: A Renewal--Catalan Asymptotic'] Let $K_d$ be the extended first-break level defined by
\[
        \Prob(K_d=k)=\pi_{d,k}\quad(1\le k\le d-1),
        \qquad
        \Prob(K_d=d)=\rho_d,
\]
where
\[
        \rho_d:=\prod_{r=1}^{d-1}\frac{d-r}{d+r}
\]
is the probability that no one-sided tie-break occurs before simultaneous completion.  Thus the value $K_d=d$ records this exceptional terminal event.  Then
\[
        \frac{K_d}{\sqrt d}\Rightarrow X,
        \qquad
        \Prob(X\in \dd x)=2x e^{-x^2}\Ind_{\{x>0\}}\dd x .
\]
In particular,
\[
        K_d\to\infty,
        \qquad
        \frac{K_d}{d}\to0
\]
in probability.  More precisely, for $k=o(d)$,
\[
        \prod_{r=1}^{k-1}\frac{d-r}{d+r}
        =\exp\left(-\frac{k(k-1)}{d}+O\left(\frac{k^4}{d^3}\right)\right),
\]
and there are absolute constants $C,c>0$ such that, for every $R\ge1$ and all sufficiently large $d$,
\begin{equation}
        \sum_{k\ge R\sqrt{d\log d}}\pi_{d,k}
        \le C d^{-cR^2}+e^{-cd}.
\end{equation}
More generally, for every $M\ge1$ and all sufficiently large $d$,
\begin{equation}
        \sum_{k\ge M\sqrt d}\pi_{d,k}
        \le C e^{-cM^2}+e^{-cd}.
\end{equation}
In particular, for $R$ large enough the tail in
\eqref{eq:first-break-tail} is $o(d^{-1})$.","status":"unverified"}

(1).    For $H\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, sample the walk  $W(t)$ in $\tilde{\mathcal{W}}(\cdot,H,L;N)$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149207+00:00","domain":"functional analysis for elliptic PDE","id":"claim_e668a967db6b2df1576259501b51767438bb0d124e237c2d8edd4b1aa48d5602","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: there is beta > 0 with B[u,u] >= beta ||u||^2 for every u in the Hilbert space H. Strict positivity (B[u,u] > 0 for u nonzero) is not enough, and neither is injectivity of the associated operator. Counterexample: H = l^2, B(u,v) = sum_k u_k v_k / k. This form is bounded (|B(u,v)| <= ||u|| ||v||), symmetric and strictly positive, but B(e_k, e_k) = 1/k tends to 0, so it is not coercive. The bounded functional F(v) = sum_k v_k / k is represented by the sequence (1/k) in l^2, yet B(u, .) = F forces u_k = 1 for all k, which is not in l^2: the equation has no solution. PDE instances of the same failure: (i) on H^1_0(Omega) the form B[u,v] = integral (grad u . grad v - lambda_1 u v) satisfies B[u,u] >= 0 with equality exactly on the first eigenfunction, and the Dirichlet problem for -Laplacian - lambda_1 is not solvable for general right-hand sides (the Fredholm orthogonality condition appears); (ii) on H^1(Omega) the Neumann form integral grad u . grad v annihilates constants, and integral f = 0 is necessary for solvability; (iii) on an unbounded Omega the Poincare inequality may fail, so integral (grad u . grad v) is not coercive for the full H^1 norm. Two further points a careful reader should keep straight: coercivity is sufficient but not necessary (for lambda strictly between two Dirichlet eigenvalues the form of -Laplacian - lambda is indefinite, yet the problem is uniquely solvable by the Fredholm alternative), and Lax-Milgram does not require B to be symmetric - symmetry only turns the solution into the minimizer of a quadratic energy (Riesz representation / Dirichlet principle).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.351711+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6789d4681558e1453083424208786d0dc56c6880309cc2396d52ceae8d18ee8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 189 (error between $Q$ and $\tilde{Q}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $Q^{\sigma,\tau}=E^{\sigma,\tau}+\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ as given by \eqref{e:qv.covar} and \eqref{e:tQ.notIs}. Then
	\[\Big|
	\Delta E^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O(1)\bigg\{
	\eta^2
	+
	\sum_{\rho\in\{\sigma,\tau\}}
	\bigg[
	\eta\bigg(
	\min\Big\{
	\Delta Q^\rho(q_d),
	\Delta\tilde{Q}^\rho(q_d)\Big\}
	\bigg)^{1/2}
	+ \Big( \Delta \bar{D}^\rho(q_d)\Big)^2
	\bigg]
	\bigg\}\]
for all $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$.
The same bound holds with $Q^\frozen$, $\tilde{Q}^\frozen$, $E^\frozen$
in place of $Q$, $\tilde{Q}$, $E$.

\begin{proof} Recall that $\vZ\equiv \vY-\vD$, so we can rewrite \eqref{e:qv.covar} as
	\[
	\Delta Q^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)
	= \bE \bigg[
		\Big( \Delta Y^\sigma(q_d)
			-\Delta D^\sigma(q_d)
			\Big)
		\Big(
		\Delta Y^\tau(q_d)
		-\Delta D^\tau(q_d)
		\Big)
		\,\bigg|\, \cG(q_d)
		\bigg]\,.
	\]
For simplicity of exposition, let us consider the case $\sigma=\tau=\RomI$.
Similarly to the argument for
Lemma~\ref{l:D.barD.discrep},
let $B=B(q_d,a(q_d))$ denote the bucket at time $q_d$ that contains $a(q_d)$. Lemma~\ref{l:X.Y.discrep} then tells us that $\Delta Y^\RomI(q_d)$ is within $2\eta$ of $\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$, where
$a(q_{d+1})$ is a uniformly random sample from
$B$. Thus define $\bar{Q}^{\RomI}$ to be the process with increments
	\beq
	\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	= \frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Big(
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)-\Delta D^\RomI(q_d)
	\Big)^2
\,.
	\eeq
 It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:X.Y.discrep} that
	\[
	\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d)
	=\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\bigg\{
	O(\eta)
	+\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a) 
	- \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\bigg\}^2\,,\]
which allows us to bound
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	&\Big|\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d)
	-\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O(\eta^2)
	+ O(\eta)
	\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\bigg|
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a) 
	- \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\bigg|
	\\ \nonumber
	&\qquad\le O(\eta^2)
	+ O(\eta) 
	\bigg[\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Big(
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a) 
	- \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d) \Big)^2\bigg]^{1/2}\\
	&\qquad\le
	O(1)\bigg\{ \eta^2+\eta 
		\Big( \Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d) \Big)^{1/2}\bigg\}\,.
	
	\end{align}
This shows that increments of
$Q^{\RomI}$ and $\bar{Q}^{\RomI}$ are close. We can further bound
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	&\Big|
	\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	-\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| 
	=\bigg| \frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\bigg\{
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)-\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\bigg\}^2
	- \frac{1}{|B|}\Big(\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)\Big)^2\bigg|
	\\ \nonumber
	&\qquad=\bigg|
	\Big(\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)^2
	- 2
	\Big( \Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)
	\frac{1}{|B|}
	\sum_{a\in B}
	\Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a)
	\Big)
	\bigg|\\ \nonumber
	&\qquad=\bigg|
	\Big(\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)^2
	-2\Big(\Delta D^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)
	\Big(\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)
	\bigg|\\
	&\qquad\le O(1)  
	\bigg\{
	\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2
	+ \eta\Big|\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| + \eta^2\bigg\}
	\le O(1)
	\max\bigg\{\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2,\eta^2\bigg\}
	
	\,,\end{align}
having used the definition of $\bar{D}$ from \eqref{e:barD}, together with Lemma~\ref{l:D.barD.discrep}. Combining the bounds gives
	\[
	\Big|
	\Delta E^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le  O(1)
	\bigg\{ \eta^2 
	+\eta\Big( \Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d) \Big)^{1/2}
	+\Big(\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)\Big)^2
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
Next note that \eqref{e:barQ.to.tildeQ} implies
	\[\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\le O(1)\max\bigg\{ 
	\Delta \bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d),
	\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2,
	\eta^2
	\bigg\}\,.\]
Meanwhile \eqref{e:Q.to.barQ} implies that either 
$\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d) \le O(\eta^2)$, in which case
$\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d) \le O(\eta^2)$ also,
or $\Delta\bar{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)$ is much larger than $\eta^2$, in which case it is of the same order as
 $\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d)$. It follows that
	\[\Delta\tilde{Q}^{\RomI}(q_d)
	\le O(1)\max\bigg\{ 
	\Delta Q^{\RomI}(q_d),
	\Delta \bar{D}^{\RomI}(q_d)^2,
	\eta^2
	\bigg\}\ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.103264+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_e68f193186254c789712f4d9509a62ad","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, specifically in homology theory and algebraic topology, cohomology is a way of attaching algebraic invariants to a topological space or other mathematical object that encode its properties in a way that is often computable. Cohomology is often related to questions of whether some local property of the space is obstructed when passing to a global property. For example, the Möbius strip is not the product space of a line segment with a circle (i.e., a cylinder), but locally on any segment of the circle it resembles an ordinary rectangle (product of two line segments) without the global twist. The obstruction to making the product structure global is encoded in the first cohomology of the underlying circle, which classifies the two inequivalent ways a line can twist around a circle (an even number of twists or an odd number of twists). The fact that there are only two inequivalent ways of twisting a line around a circle is encoded in the relevant cohomology group $H^{1}(S^{1},\\{+1,-1\\})$ which can be computed as isomorphic to the group $\\{+1,-1\\}$ where $+1$ corresponds to an even number of twists, and $-1$ to an odd number.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.285897+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e69ce9a9193dcd224bc7a66db7e2a67e23fd8a7e452dc938eec983f2b0dee69b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma KacRice of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Let $\zeta$ be a probability measure on $[0,1]$ with a $2$-atom prefix
		$\{0,q\}$ for some $q\in(0,1)$, and let $\varepsilon\in(0,q/2)$.
		Let $\mathcal N_\varepsilon(f,\zeta,q)$ be the number of critical points $\mathbf{m}$ of
		$F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}$ such that
		\[
		\mathbf{m}\in \mathrm{SUSY}_1(\zeta,\varepsilon)
		\qquad\text{and}\qquad
		\frac1N F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})\in(f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon).
		\]
		For $\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N$, write $q_\mathbf{m}:=\frac1N\|\mathbf{m}\|^2$.
		
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item \textup{(Mixed case.)}
			Assume that for every $\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N$ with
			$q_\mathbf{m}\in(q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon)$, the Gaussian vector
			\[
			\bigl(\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}),\,F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})\bigr)
			\]
			is non-degenerate.  In particular, this holds for a genuine mixed
			$p$-spin Hamiltonian, i.e.\ when
			\[
			\xi(t)=\sum_{p\ge 2}\beta_p^2 t^p
			\]
			has at least two non-zero coefficients.
			Then
			\begin{multline}
				\mathbb{E}[\mathcal N_\varepsilon(f,\zeta,q)]
				=N\int_{[-1,1]^N}\int_{(f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon)}
				\mathbb{E}\!\left[
				|\det(\nabla^2 F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))|
				\,\middle|\,
				\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0,\,
				F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=Nf'
				\right]
				\\
				\times
				\varphi_{(\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}),\,F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))}(0,Nf')\,
				\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{SUSY}_1(\zeta,\varepsilon)}(\mathbf{m})\,
				\mathrm{d}\mathbf{m}\,\mathrm{d} f'.
			\end{multline}
			
			\item \textup{(Pure case.)}
			Assume that $\xi(t)=\beta_p^2 t^p$ is pure $p$-spin for some $p\ge2$.
			Recalling the notation~(equation eq:def-Rex-KR of the paper),
			\begin{multline}
				\mathbb{E}[\mathcal N_\varepsilon(f,\zeta,q)]
				=
				\int_{[-1,1]^N}
				\mathbb{E}\!\left[
				|\det(\nabla^2 F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m}))|
				\,\middle|\,
				\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})=0
				\right]
				\varphi_{\nabla F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})}(0)
				\\
				\times
				\mathbf{1}_{\mathrm{SUSY}_1(\zeta,\varepsilon)}(\mathbf{m})\,
				\mathbf{1}_{(f-\varepsilon,f+\varepsilon)}
				\!\left(\frac1N\mathcal R^{\rm ex}_\zeta(\mathbf{m})\right)
				\mathrm{d}\mathbf{m}.
			\end{multline}
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f in L^2(R^d)","the Plancherel transform is the L^2 extension of the L^1 transform"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264524+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_e6a7de372efdb69b5dda51fbcd54ebeef72e1430e1bd848aa9b086939563f833","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing distinction: for $f\\in L^1$ the transform is an honest absolutely convergent integral, bounded, continuous, defined at every $\\xi$; for $f\\in L^2\\setminus L^1$ it is defined only as the $L^2$-limit $\\hat f=\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\widehat{f\\mathbf 1_{\\{|x|\\le R\\}}}$ (the unique continuous extension from the dense subspace $L^1\\cap L^2$), hence is an equivalence class defined only almost everywhere. Example: $f(x)=\\sin(\\pi x)/(\\pi x)\\in L^2\\setminus L^1$, whose Plancherel transform is $\\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ a.e.; the truncated integrals converge to $1$ for $|\\xi|<1/2$, to $0$ for $|\\xi|>1/2$ and to $1/2$ at $\\xi=\\pm1/2$, but no value at $\\pm1/2$ is meaningful for the $L^2$ transform. Consequences an auditor should check: (i) claims like '$\\hat f(\\xi_0)=0$' or '$\\hat f$ is continuous' are meaningless for $L^2$ data without naming a representative (the usual legitimate versions are 'a.e.' statements or support statements up to null sets); (ii) $\\|\\hat f\\|_\\infty\\le\\|f\\|_1$ is unavailable; (iii) that $\\lim_{R\\to\\infty}\\int_{-R}^Rf(x)e^{-2\\pi ix\\xi}dx$ exists for a.e. $\\xi$ when $f\\in L^2(\\mathbb R)$ is a deep result (the Fourier-integral form of Carleson's theorem), not a corollary of Plancherel, which only gives $L^2$ convergence and hence a.e. convergence along some subsequence of radii. On $L^1\\cap L^2$ the two definitions agree a.e., which is what makes the extension consistent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:57:51.740922+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6ac89e65302e15edf34ba94c568cc943b432d4e6be5b799ba5cafd0e6f728c5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 15 of arXiv:2608.30120, 'Graphs of operators as points in the Grassmann manifold'] If $T\\in\\k(\\h)$, then $P_{Gr(T)}\\in\\p_{res}^0(\\h\\times\\{0\\})$ for the decomposition given by $\\h\\times\\h=\\h\\times\\{0\\}\\oplus \\{0\\}\\times\\h$. \n\nConversely, if $T$ is closed and $P_{Gr(T)}\\in \\p_{res}(\\j_+)$, then $T$ is compact.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the joint law of the points is invariant under reflection of any subset through the origin","the points are almost surely in general position (every d or fewer are linearly independent)","independence of the points is not required"],"created_at":"2026-10-14T12:08:18+00:00","domain":"geometric probability","id":"claim_e6ae446cd6fd7036517cf71cccaaa1cb4fa2b1cf94cd433f14ec3cf8acbcb1e8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $x_1,\\dots,x_N$ be random points in $\\mathbb{R}^d$ whose joint law is invariant under reflection of any subset of them through the origin, and which are almost surely in general position. Then the probability that all of them lie in a single open halfspace whose boundary contains the origin, equivalently the probability that the origin is not in their convex hull, equals $2^{-N+1}\\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\\binom{N-1}{k}$. In particular this probability is $1$ whenever $N \\le d$. Note that symmetry alone does not suffice: general position is needed, since for instance two points i.i.d. uniform on $\\{\\pm e_1\\} \\subset \\mathbb{R}^2$ are symmetric (their joint law is invariant under reflection of any subset of them through the origin) but not in general position, and they lie in a common open halfspace whose boundary contains the origin with probability $1/2$ (exactly when the two points coincide; $e_1$ and $-e_1$ lie in no such halfspace, and the origin is in their convex hull), whereas the formula gives $2^{-1}\\left(\\binom{1}{0}+\\binom{1}{1}\\right)=1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:54:57.568178+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6ccd3bfb0bebac58eb198b65ce853be21569a59e5c13f54c485fca3321989c4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2412.03366, 'Regularity of Weighted Tensorized Fractional Brownian Fields and associated function space'] Let $\psi$ denote a Lemari\'e-Meyer  wavelet  and $\varphi$ the associated scaling function. The hyperbolic wavelet basis is defined as the system $$\{\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2} :  \, (j_1, j_2) \in (\mathbb{N}\cup \{-1\})^2, \, (k_1, k_2) \in \mathbb{Z}^2\}$$
where
\begin{itemize}
\item if $j_1,j_2\geq 0$,
$$
\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \psi(2^{j_1}x_1-k_1)\psi(2^{j_2}x_2-k_2)\; ,
$$
\item if $j_1=-1$ and $j_2\geq 0$
$$
\psi_{-1,j_2,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \varphi(x_1-k_1)\psi(2^{j_2}x_2-k_2)\; ,
$$
\item if $j_1\ge 0$ and $j_2=-1$
$$
\psi_{j_1,-1,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \psi(2^{j_1}x_1-k_1)\varphi(x_2-k_2)\;,
$$
\item if $j_1=j_2=-1$
$$
\psi_{-1,-1,k_1,k_2}(x_1,x_2)= \varphi(x_1-k_1)\varphi(x_2-k_2)\;.
$$
\end{itemize}
For any $f\in\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$, one then defines its hyperbolic wavelet coefficients by
\begin{eqnarray*}
c_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}&=&2^{j_1+j_2}<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1,j_2\geq 0\;,\\
c_{j_1,-1,k_1,k_2}&=&2^{j_1}<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1\geq 0\mbox{ and }j_2=-1\;,\\
c_{-1,j_2,k_1,k_2}&=&2^{j_2}<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1=-1\mbox{ and }j_2\geq 0\;,\\
c_{-1,-1,k_1,k_2}&=&<f,\psi_{j_1,j_2,k_1,k_2}>\mbox{ if }j_1=j_2=-1\;.
\end{eqnarray*}","status":"unverified"}
