{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:04:59.433035+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6e52dfefc826fecfc9e941613dba88a029b6b84c724b1b3fc1e41c47966fad7","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:ito-expansion-Lp of arXiv:2605.20697, 'Uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for \\ Second-Order Consensus-Based Optimization'] Let \(p>2\), and recall that 
\[
    L_p(t)
    :=
    \frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J
    \phi_{a,p}(Y_t^j,\hat Z_t^j),
    \qquad
    \phi_{a,p}(y,z)
    :=
    a|y|^p+|z|^p+\frac m\gamma |y|^{p-2}\langle y,z\rangle \,,
\] and $\Delta_\alpha(t):=m_X(\mu_{X_t^J})-\mathcal M_\alpha(t)$. Hence, $ X_t^j-\mathcal M_\alpha(t)=Y_t^j+\Delta_\alpha(t)\,,$
and
\[
    \mathrm d\hat Z_t^j
    =
    (-K_Z\hat Z_t^j-K_YY_t^j)\mathrm d t+\mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}},
\]
where
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}}
    :=
    \frac{\sigma}{m}
    \left[
        \left(1-\frac1J\right)
        S(Y_t^j+\Delta_\alpha(t))\,\mathrm d W_t^j
        -
        \frac1J\sum_{k\ne j}
        S(Y_t^k+\Delta_\alpha(t))\,\mathrm d W_t^k
    \right].
\end{equation}
The stochastic differential of \(L_p(t)\) is
\begin{align}
    \mathrm d L_p(t)
    &=
    \frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J
    \Bigg\{
    \left[
        \left(\frac{ap}{\gamma}-\frac m\gamma K_Y\right)|Y_t^j|^p
        -
        pK_Z|\hat Z_t^j|^p
    \right]\mathrm d t
    \notag\\
    &\quad
    +
    \left[
        \left(
            ap-\frac m\gamma K_Z+\frac{m(p-1)}{\gamma^2}
        \right)
        |Y_t^j|^{p-2}\langle Y_t^j,\hat Z_t^j\rangle
        -
        pK_Y|\hat Z_t^j|^{p-2}\langle \hat Z_t^j,Y_t^j\rangle
    \right]\mathrm d t
    \notag\\
    &\quad
    +
    \left[
        \frac m\gamma |Y_t^j|^{p-2}|\hat Z_t^j|^2
        +
        \frac{m(p-2)}{\gamma}
        |Y_t^j|^{p-4}\langle Y_t^j,\hat Z_t^j\rangle^2
    \right]\mathrm d t
    \notag\\
    &\quad
    +
    \mathcal T_{\mathrm{noise}}^j(t)\,\mathrm d t
    +
    \mathrm d M_{p,t}^j
    \Bigg\},
    
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm d M_{p,t}^j
    :=
    p|\hat Z_t^j|^{p-2}
    \left\langle \hat Z_t^j,\mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}}\right\rangle
    +
    \frac m\gamma |Y_t^j|^{p-2}
    \left\langle Y_t^j,\mathrm d M_t^{j,\mathrm{center}}\right\rangle .
\end{equation}
We denote $ M_{p,t}:=\frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J M_{p,t}^j$ as the local martingale part of \(L_p(t)\). The noise trace satisfies
\begin{align}
    \mathcal T_{\mathrm{noise}}^j(t)
    &=
    \frac12
    \operatorname{Tr}
    \left(
        \nabla^2(|\hat Z_t^j|^p)\,
        \mathrm d\langle M^{j,\mathrm{center}}\rangle_t
    \right)
    \notag\\
    &=
        \frac{p\sigma^2}{2m^2}\left(1-\frac1J\right)^2 |\hat Z_t^j|^{p-4}
        \left[
            (p-2)\left|S(X_t^j-\mathcal M_\alpha)^\top\hat Z_t^j\right|^2
            +|\hat Z_t^j|^2\norm{S(X_t^j-\mathcal M_\alpha)}_F^2
        \right] \notag \\
        &\quad
        +\frac{p\sigma^2}{2m^2J^2}\sum_{k\ne j}|\hat Z_t^j|^{p-4}
        \left[
            (p-2)\left|S(X_t^k-\mathcal M_\alpha)^\top\hat Z_t^j\right|^2
            +|\hat Z_t^j|^2\norm{S(X_t^k-\mathcal M_\alpha)}_F^2
        \right]\\
        & \leqslant
    \frac{p\sigma^2\chi_S}{2m^2}
    |\hat Z_t^j|^{p-2}
    \left(
        |Y_t^j+\Delta_\alpha(t)|^2
        +
        \frac1J\sum_{k=1}^J |Y_t^k+\Delta_\alpha(t)|^2
    \right).
    
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

Then there are invertible matrices P (m x m) and Q (n x n) over R such that P A Q = D is diagonal in the sense that its only nonzero entries are d_1, ..., d_r in positions (1,1), ..., (r,r), with each d_i dividing d_{i+1}. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:18:19.413157+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e6f9e9d7ec2498c7cb28bfb52e107a4ef3ff20917a8c2f635ef00dcfe2ad1c75","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Conjecture conj:barcode_kernel_intro of arXiv:2507.22011, 'Random Lozenge Waterfall:\\Dimensional Collapse of Gibbs Measures'] Around any macroscopic point $(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})$ in the waterfall region $\mathcal{W}$, the
	random configuration of square lozenges
	on a horizontal slice
	converges to a
	determinantal \textbf{barcode process} on $\mathbb{Z}$ with the symmetric correlation kernel
	$\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s,t)$.\footnote{In particular, 
	we conjecture that the limit (equation eq:K_barcode_intro of the paper) exists for all integers $s\ge t$.}
	The barcode process depends only on the parameters $q$ and $\kappa$,
	but not on the geometry of the hexagon or the macroscopic location $(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})$
	inside $\mathcal{W}$, as long as the waterfall phase is present, i.e., $\mathsf{N}<\mathsf{T}$.
	
	The limiting kernel is $2\times 2$ block Toeplitz, that is,
	\begin{equation*}
		\begin{pmatrix}
			\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s,t)& \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s,t+1)\\
			\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s+1,t) & \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(s+1,t+1)
		\end{pmatrix}
		=
			\begin{pmatrix}
				\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{00}(s-t) & \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{01}(s-t)\\
				\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{10}(s-t) & \mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}_{11}(s-t)
			\end{pmatrix},
			\qquad s,t\in 2\mathbb{Z},
	\end{equation*}
	and satisfies
	$\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(0,0)=1-\mathcal{K}^{\mathrm{barcode}}(1,1)$ 
	(the plot of this function
	in $q$ and $\kappa$ is given in (fig:density_rho_even_3d of the paper)).
	Consequently, the barcode process has global density $1/2$
	for every choice of $q$ and $\kappa$, and it is invariant
	under even but not odd shifts. (Stated as a conjecture by the paper; open unless the paper says otherwise.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:18:13.294863+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e728a09a852f93852d34e3f95dbbcc26f263235526c6e2a1e3cac7d63bce212c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:resampling_target of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] Let $\Gamma$ be a ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}${} in $D$.  Let $W\subseteq D$ open and $r > 0$. Suppose that we are given the following random variables.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item $M^*<\infty$.
\item  A set $\{(\ell_i^1,\ell^2_i)\}_{i=1,\ldots,M^*}$ of pairs of arcs in $\Gamma$ with $\ell_i^1,\ell^2_i \subseteq W$ and such that none of them overlap with each other.
\item A set of $M^*$ points $\underline{y}$ such that
\begin{itemize}
 \item $y_i\in  \ell_i^1\cap \ell^2_i$ and $B(y_i,4r)\subset W$ for $i=1,\ldots,M^*$,
 \item the endpoints of $\ell^1_i, \ell^2_i$ lie outside $B(y_i,4r)$,
 \item $B(y_i,4r)\cap B(y_j,4r)=\varnothing$ and $(\ell_i^1 \cup \ell_i^2) \cap B(y_j,4r) = \varnothing$ for all $i\neq j$.
\end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}
We denote these target pivotals by $\mathfrak F_{W,r} = \{(\ell^1_i,\ell^2_i,y_i)\}_{i=1,\ldots,M^*}$.

If $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}$ is a resampling of $\Gamma$, then we say that $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}$ is $\mathfrak F_{W,r}$-successful if the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
 \item The loops and strands of $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}$ are identical when restricted to the set $D \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{M^*} B(y_i,4r)$.
 \item Let $\tau_i^j$ (resp.\ $\overline{\tau}_i^j$) be the first (resp.\ last) time that $\ell_i^j$ is in $\overline{B}(y_i,4 r)$, for $i=1,\ldots,M^*$, $j=1,2$. Then in $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}$ the connections between the four strands $\ell_i^1|_{[0,\tau_i^1]}$, $\ell_i^1|_{[\overline{\tau}_i^1,1]}$, $\ell_i^2|_{[0,\tau_i^2]}$, $\ell_i^2|_{[\overline{\tau}_i^2,1]}$ (assuming that they are parameterized on $[0,1]$) are flipped, i.e.\ the strand $\ell^{{\mathrm{res}},1}_i$ (resp.\ $\ell^{{\mathrm{res}},2}_i$) in $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}$ starting with $\ell_i^1|_{[0,\tau_i^1]}$ (resp.\ finishing with $\ell_i^1|_{[\overline{\tau}_i^1,1]}$) is linked to $\ell_i^2|_{[0,\tau_i^2]}$ or $\ell_i^2|_{[\overline{\tau}_i^2,1]}$. Moreover, it holds again that $\ell^{{\mathrm{res}},1}_i \cap \ell^{{\mathrm{res}},2}_i \cap B(y_i,r) \neq \varnothing$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform measure on {-1, 1}^n","rho in [-1, 1]"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:12:41.902710+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_e737cfe2b9e22a83f83792125510b47705abd24c9fe60ef07368b63549ab5473","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. For rho in [-1, 1], T_rho is the noise operator: T_rho f(x) = E[f(Y)] where the Y_i are independent with P(Y_i = x_i) = (1 + rho)/2, so T_rho chi_S = rho^|S| chi_S. For a rho-correlated pair (X uniform, Y the noisy copy), Stab_rho[f] = E[f(X) f(Y)] = <f, T_rho f> = sum_S rho^|S| f^(S)^2 = sum_k rho^k W_k. So the level weights are W_m = S^(m)(0)/m! for the polynomial S(rho) = Stab_rho[f], with S(1) = ||f||^2, S(0) = (E f)^2 and S(-1) = E[f(X) f(-X)]. On [0, 1], r -> Stab_r[f] is nondecreasing and convex; it is strictly increasing iff f is not constant, and strictly convex iff some level k >= 2 carries weight. For f with values +-1 and Y obtained by flipping each bit independently with probability delta, P(f(X) != f(Y)) = (1 - Stab_{1 - 2 delta}[f])/2 = (1/2) sum_S (1 - (1 - 2 delta)^|S|) f^(S)^2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Auxiliary oracle and unprotected answers independent of every protected truth bit AND witness location","Circuit-description and query counts as specified in proof","Leakage extension: at most 2^a fixed reference auxiliary oracles, not merely polynomial-length individual answers"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:53:38.862927+00:00","domain":"computational complexity; conditional sampling; relative entropy; autoregressive scoring","id":"claim_e74459875ae07accc7ad90654b77b750f76fd67f9d09c17ac5023aeed2979731","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Status: proof (unaudited); owner-work claim T410-w739-C006 version 2; independent review pending. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:16:53.595219+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e77108d69273ab028a1744f0813b99f2291b438ccad572ffcfaf6dc41b2d0df7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:diffusion+jumpHKE of arXiv:2412.05030, 'Characterization of Subordinate Symmetric Markov Processes'] (Diffusion+jump type heat kernel estimates [CKW2020])

{"assumptions":["H real separable Hilbert, W isonormal Gaussian on H","the L^2 space is with respect to the sigma-algebra GENERATED BY W","f_n symmetric, and then unique"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e77fa0481be857539e984e1e66a556b4287a9c335209411aaef62032c500226b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a real separable Hilbert space and let W = { W(h) : h in H } be an ISONORMAL Gaussian process, that is a centred Gaussian family with E[ W(h) W(g) ] = <h, g>_H. Then the H_n are mutually ORTHOGONAL and L^2( Omega, sigma(W), P ) is their orthogonal direct sum. Equivalently, every square-integrable functional F of the Gaussian process has a unique expansion F = E[F] + sum_{n >= 1} I_n(f_n) with f_n a symmetric element of the n-fold symmetric tensor power of H, where I_n is the multiple Wiener-Ito integral, and the Ito isometry gives E[F^2] = E[F]^2 + sum_{n >= 1} n! ||f_n||^2. For H = L^2([0,T]) and W Brownian motion, I_n(f_n) is the n-fold iterated Ito integral of f_n and the expansion is the classical chaos expansion. In the window the explored set has size V^{2/3} = 2^{2d/3}, which is a vanishing fraction of V, but the DEPLETION seen by a single vertex is not uniform: the explored vertices cluster geometrically, so the walk's drift correction is a functional of the geometry, not of the total explored mass as in G(n,p). This is exactly why the hypercube is harder than the Hamming graph (where the geometry is 'mean-field enough' and the scaling limit was obtained by Federico-van der Hofstad-den Hollander-Hulshof for the Hamming cube). A reduction: the scaling limit follows if the exploration's drift satisfies E[step | past] = theta 2^{-d/3} - (explored mass)/V + o(2^{-d/3}) uniformly over the window, i.e. if the local depletion is asymptotically equal to the global depletion; this is a 'non-backtracking randomness' statement about the geometry of critical hypercube clusters (that they are spread out like independent samples), which is the mean-field cluster geometry conjecture and is open. Obstruction: Local versus global depletion in the exploration walk; needs spread-out geometry of critical hypercube clusters.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:10.197113+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e7a383e6e8a4882c83dceb16fa43d908c014c42efb8a516fc5d67ed46e77a32d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 30 of arXiv:2605.03851, 'The Relay Random Tree:\\A stochastic geometry approach of multihop relay in an urban visib'] \textbf{Distribution of the Stoppage Point.}

For $a\in \R$, let us note the $h_a(\mathrm{R})$ highest point in $\mathrm{R}$ above $a$:
\[h_{\mathrm{R}}(a):= \sup \{b: (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}\}.\]
In the last definition we can for instance adapt the convention that the supremum of an empty set is minus infinity.

Let $\landsc$ be a given random landscape.\\
Then, for $(x, y) \in \Half$ the stoppage point $X_{stop}(x, y)$ of $(x, y)$ in $\landsc$ has its CDF given by the following reformulation of events:
\[\{X_{stop}(x, y) \geq t\} =  \mathrm{below}([x, t],h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)})\cap \{t\leq\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}\} .\]

When $\landsc$ is a Poisson Building Process of intensity $\lambda$ and height distribution $\mathcal{L}$, Lemma \ref{dessous_diago} yields the following:
\[\p (X_{stop}(x, y) \geq t) = \exp \left(\int_{x}^{t} -\lambda \mathcal{L}(]h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(a), \infty[) \rm{d}a \right)\mathds{1}_{t \leq \max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}} .\]
In other words, $X_{stop}(x, y)$ has its law equal to
\[g\times\Leb_{|[x,\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}]}+ \ \exp \left(-\lambda\bigintsss_{\hspace{-10pt}x}^{\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}} \hspace{-90pt} \mathcal{L}(]h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(a), \infty[) \rm{d}a \right)\delta_{\max\{a : \exists (a, b)\in \mathrm{R}+(x, y)\}},\]
where 
\[g: u\mapsto \lambda \mathcal{L}([h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(u), +\infty[)\exp\left(-\lambda \int_{x}^{u}\mathcal{L}(h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(a), +\infty[ \rm{d}a\right).\]

Moreover, conditioned on the stoppage point, the stoppage height is distributed according to $\mathcal{L}$ conditioned on being greater that $h_{\mathrm{R}+(x, y)}(X_{stop}(x, y))$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

On the annulus U = {1 < |z| < 3} the function f(z) = 1/z is holomorphic with no singularity in U at all, yet the integral over the circle |z| = 2 equals 2πi, not 0: the circle winds once around 0, a point outside U. 'No singularities inside the contour' is not the hypothesis; 'winding number zero about every point off the domain' is. (2) Winding numbers multiply the residues. For the curve γ(t) = e^{2it}, 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π (the unit circle traversed twice), the integral of 1/z is 4πi = 2πi times n(γ,0) Res, with n(γ,0) = 2. A figure-eight curve can even give cancellation, with winding numbers +1 and -1 about two poles. (3) The singularities must be isolated and f single-valued. f(z) = 1/sin(1/z) has poles at z = 1/(kπ) accumulating at 0, so 0 is not an isolated singularity, no residue is defined there, and the circle |z| = 1/2 encloses infinitely many poles: the residue theorem does not apply as stated (one must exhaust or use a different region). Similarly log z and sqrt(z) are not single-valued holomorphic functions on any punctured disk about 0, so they carry no residue at 0; a branch cut and a keyhole contour are required. Two further habits worth checking: a residue of 0 does not mean the singularity is removable (1/z^2 has residue 0), and when the contour is closed 'in the upper half-plane' the estimate showing the added arc's contribution tends to 0 (Jordan's lemma or an explicit bound) is part of the proof, not a formality.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378680+00:00","domain":"computability theory","id":"claim_e7c278a5c929afee616c48ad2dda5bb811314d807cba3f15b58d3461e5e114d4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A (deterministic, one-tape) Turing machine consists of: a finite set of states Q with a designated start state and designated halting states (for decision problems, an accept state and a reject state); a finite tape alphabet Gamma containing a blank symbol and an input alphabet Sigma not containing the blank; and a transition function delta mapping (non-halting state, tape symbol) pairs to (state, tape symbol, direction) triples with direction left or right. The machine operates on an infinite tape of cells each holding one symbol of Gamma, with a single head; initially the tape holds the input string from Sigma* followed by blanks, and the head is at the leftmost input cell. A configuration records the state, tape contents, and head position; each step applies delta to the current state and scanned symbol, rewriting the cell, changing state, and moving the head one cell. The machine halts upon entering a halting state; it may also run forever. It computes a partial function from strings to strings (output read off the tape at halting); it decides a language L if it halts on every input, accepting exactly the strings in L, and it recognizes (accepts) L if it accepts exactly the strings in L, possibly failing to halt off L. The Church-Turing thesis asserts that Turing machines capture exactly the effectively computable functions; the model is robust under adding tapes, two-way infinite tape, larger alphabets, or nondeterminism (for computability).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a real-valued sequence, or for the approximate version a sequence with a controlled, typically o(n) or summable, subadditivity defect","the subadditive inequality a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n holding for all, or eventually all, pairs m, n","boundedness of a_n/n from below, or explicit acceptance that the limit may be -infinity, for the limit to be meaningful in context","for statistical-mechanics applications: correct identification of the quantity, such as a log partition function, as subadditive under the relevant combination operation, such as concatenation or union of volumes"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.997292+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e80a55c79ea7ae42ed54422481e1478f6dc6886bfc54622384ee814fe9cfdb74","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). If a real sequence (a_n)_{n>=1} is subadditive, meaning a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n for all m,n>=1, then lim_{n->infinity} a_n/n exists, possibly equal to -infinity, and equals inf_n a_n/n. This elementary but powerful lemma converts a one-directional combinatorial inequality into existence of a limit, and is the deterministic backbone behind results such as convergence of the free energy per site in statistical mechanics or the growth rate of a combinatorial quantity, for instance existence of the connective constant for self-avoiding walks, or existence of free energy limits in the Ising or Potts models under volume-doubling or concatenation subadditivity. An approximate or almost-subadditive version, a_{m+n} <= a_m + a_n + e(m,n) with a controlled error term, such as e(m,n)=o(m+n) or a summable correction, still yields convergence of a_n/n to an infimum-type limit under mild additional conditions, a form often needed when exact subadditivity fails because of boundary effects. It does not give any rate of convergence, only existence of the limit, and it does not apply to sequences that are only superadditive or that fail monotonicity entirely without the appropriate sign flip; Kingman's theorem is the random, ergodic-theoretic generalization for stationary sequences and is not itself implied by Fekete's lemma. Typical failure: Verifying subadditivity only for a convenient special subsequence, such as powers of 2 or specific volume shapes like cubes, and then applying Fekete's lemma as though the inequality had been established for all m, n; the lemma genuinely requires the inequality for all pairs, or at least a cofinal family closed under addition, and skipping intermediate cases silently assumes exactly the regularity, such as shape-independence of the volume limit in statistical mechanics, that itself needs a separate van Hove or Fisher-type argument. Canonical reference: Fekete, 1923, Mathematische Zeitschrift; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM, Chapter 1.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.498624+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_e81aae0473c7fafb255ac8990b980331175a03e8cb21895d97485ccf7955480b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"On a bounded domain, sup over the domain of |f| equals sup over the boundary. On an unbounded domain this is false without a growth restriction, and the Phragmén–Lindelöf principle is exactly the repair: the conclusion |f| ≤ M inside holds only under a subcritical growth bound, and the critical rate is attained by explicit functions. Load-bearing hypothesis and its failures: (1) Strip of width π, S = {|Im z| < π/2}. The function f(z) = exp(exp(z)) is entire, satisfies |f| = exp(e^x cos y), so |f| = 1 on both boundary lines Im z = ±π/2, yet |f(x)| = exp(e^x) → ∞ along the real axis. Its growth is exp(exp(|Re z|)), i.e. exactly the critical rate α = 1, so the hypothesis 'α < 1' cannot be relaxed to 'α ≤ 1'. (2) Sector of opening π/2, S = {|arg z| < π/4}. The function f(z) = exp(z^2) has |f| = 1 on both boundary rays (there z^2 is purely imaginary) and |f(x)| = exp(x^2) → ∞ on the axis of the sector; its growth exp(|z|^2) matches the critical exponent β = α = 2, so again the strict inequality β < α is needed. (3) Three-lines theorem without boundedness on the closed strip: f(z) = exp(-i exp(iπ z)) is entire, |f(x + iy)| = exp(e^{-πy} sin(πx)), so |f| = 1 on both lines Re z = 0 and Re z = 1, while on the middle line Re z = 1/2 it equals exp(e^{-πy}), which is unbounded as y → -∞. Hence M(0) = M(1) = 1 but M(1/2) = ∞: log-convexity of M fails without the boundedness hypothesis. {"assumptions":["a centered Gaussian process, almost surely bounded on the index set, for Borell-TIS","for Slepian/Sudakov-Fernique: two Gaussian processes on the same index set with pointwise increment-variance domination E[(X_s-X_t)^2]<=E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2]","for the classical Slepian tail comparison specifically: equal marginal variances (then increment domination is equivalent to E[X_sX_t]>=E[Y_sY_t]); no correlation-sign condition replaces them","measurability and separability of the process so the supremum is well defined"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e8207cb5ab491259a97da1f7e7a1894939cc36b16bef511c7e7ace855947706c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a centered, almost surely bounded Gaussian process (X_t)_{t in T}, let M = sup_t X_t and sigma^2 = sup_t Var(X_t). The Borell-TIS inequality states P(|M - E[M]| >= u) <= 2 exp(-u^2/(2 sigma^2)) for all u >= 0, giving Gaussian concentration of the supremum around its mean at the scale of the process's maximal pointwise variance, regardless of the cardinality or geometry of the index set. Separately, Slepian's inequality compares two centered Gaussian processes on the same index set with equal marginal variances: if E[(X_s-X_t)^2] <= E[(Y_s-Y_t)^2] for all s,t, then E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], and with the equal marginal variances the same condition, equivalently E[X_s X_t] >= E[Y_s Y_t] for all s,t, also gives the tail comparison P(sup X > u) <= P(sup Y > u) for every u; no condition on the sign of the correlations is needed, and none can replace the equal variances. The Sudakov-Fernique inequality removes the equal-variance requirement, needing only the pointwise increment domination, but concludes only the expectation comparison E[sup X] <= E[sup Y], not the stronger distributional comparison. Together these tools reduce bounding E[sup] of a complicated Gaussian field to bounding it for a simpler, dominating comparison field. Borell-TIS does not give the value of E[M] itself, which requires a separate chaining or Dudley-integral bound, and Sudakov-Fernique is strictly weaker in conclusion than the classical Slepian inequality even when both sets of hypotheses happen to hold. Typical failure: Invoking the classical Slepian inequality's tail or distributional comparison after only verifying the weaker Sudakov-Fernique hypotheses, namely increment domination without equal variances; Sudakov-Fernique licenses comparing E[sup X] to E[sup Y] only, and treating the two comparison theorems as interchangeable overstates what has actually been proven. Canonical reference: Borell, 1975, Inventiones Mathematicae; Tsirelson, Ibragimov and Sudakov, 1976, in Proceedings of the School-Seminar on Random Processes; Slepian, 1962, Bell System Technical Journal; Fernique, 1975, Ecole d'Ete de Probabilites de Saint-Flour, Springer Lecture Notes in Mathematics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving on a probability space; for the one-sided version T need not be invertible","A is measurable with log^+ ||A|| integrable","the splitting version additionally needs T invertible, A(x) invertible a.e., and log^+ ||A^{-1}|| integrable","all statements hold for mu-a.e. x; exponents depend on mu"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents, smooth dynamics","id":"claim_e82eac33ac8c92bb29c9b15bfd94cbfbd85cf0c046e3d5255a98565d37d2934a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \to M_d(\mathbb{R})$ a measurable cocycle with $\log^+ \|A\| \in L^1(\mu)$; write $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x)\cdots A(x)$.

ONE-SIDED (FILTRATION) VERSION - no invertibility of $T$ or of $A$ needed. For $\mu$-a.e. $x$: (a) the limit $\Lambda(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \big(A^n(x)^{\mathsf T} A^n(x)\big)^{1/2n}$ exists (a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix); (b) there are an integer $1 \le k(x) \le d$, exponents $\infty > \lambda_1(x) > \lambda_2(x) > \dots > \lambda_{k(x)}(x) \ge -\infty$ (only the smallest may be $-\infty$; this happens at every $x$ whose orbit meets the set where $A$ is singular, hence almost everywhere when $T$ is ergodic and $A$ is singular with positive probability, and can also happen for a.e.-invertible $A$ when $\log^+\|A^{-1}\|$ is not integrable), and a filtration of linear subspaces $\mathbb{R}^d = V_1(x) \supsetneq V_2(x) \supsetneq \dots \supsetneq V_{k(x)}(x) \supsetneq V_{k(x)+1}(x) = \{0\}$, measurable in $x$, such that $A(x) V_i(x) \subset V_i(Tx)$ and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x) \quad\text{for every } v \in V_i(x) \setminus V_{i+1}(x);$$
(c) $k$, the $\lambda_i$ and the multiplicities $m_i = \dim V_i - \dim V_{i+1}$ are $T$-invariant functions of $x$ (constants when $T$ is ergodic); (d) $\lim \frac1n \log |\det A^n(x)| = \sum_i m_i \lambda_i(x)$, and more generally $\lim \frac1n \log \|\Lambda^p A^n(x)\|$ (norm on the $p$-th exterior power) equals the sum of the $p$ largest exponents counted with multiplicity; (e) the $\lambda_i$ with multiplicities are exactly the limits $\lim \frac1n \log \sigma_j(A^n(x))$ of the singular values, i.e. the logarithms of the eigenvalues of $\Lambda(x)$.

TWO-SIDED (SPLITTING) VERSION. If moreover $T$ is invertible, $A(x) \in GL_d(\mathbb{R})$ a.e. and $\log^+ \|A^{-1}\| \in L^1(\mu)$, then for a.e. $x$ all exponents are finite and there is a measurable $A$-equivariant splitting $\mathbb{R}^d = E_1(x) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{k(x)}(x)$, $A(x)E_i(x) = E_i(Tx)$, $\dim E_i = m_i$, with $\lim_{n \to \pm\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x)$ for all $v \in E_i(x) \setminus \{0\}$ (the SAME exponent forwards and backwards), $V_i(x) = \bigoplus_{j \ge i} E_j(x)$, and the angles between the Oseledets subspaces decay subexponentially along orbits: $\lim_{n\to\pm\infty} \frac1n \log \sin\angle\big(E_i(T^n x), \bigoplus_{j\ne i} E_j(T^n x)\big) = 0$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without $\log^+\|A\| \in L^1$ the limits need not exist: for $d = 1$ the theorem IS Birkhoff's theorem for $\log|a|$, which fails when $\log^+|a| \notin L^1$. (2) Without $\log^+\|A^{-1}\| \in L^1$ (or with $T$ non-invertible) there is in general NO equivariant splitting, only the forward filtration: the subspaces of vectors with exponent exactly $\lambda_i$, $i \ge 2$, are not canonically defined and the 'slow' directions are not invariant under $A$. (3) The exponents depend on the measure $\mu$: different ergodic measures for the same $T$ and $A$ generally have different exponents, and a point outside the full-measure set need not have exponents at all. (4) Convergence is not uniform in $x$, and the Oseledets subspaces are only measurable, in general not continuous, in $x$. (5) The theorem is about $\|A^n(x)v\|$ along ONE orbit; it says nothing about eigenvalues of $A^n(x)$ or about $\|A^n\|$ averaged over $x$.","status":"unverified"}

# Opposite-head balanced two-cycles: exact family and full linear stability

Claim T328-W698-016, v1. Target 1. PROOF, UNAUDITED.
This is a family classification, not a classification of all balanced cycles or a global GD theorem. No novelty claim is made.

## Exact family

Let b,kappa>0. There is a unique T in (1/2,1) with

    cosh(T)^2 = 2 cosh(T/4)^2.

Put a=b(tanh T+tanh(T/4))/2, H=b(tanh T-tanh(T/4))/2,
d=b*kappa*sech(T)^2, V=sqrt(H/(4d)), w=sqrt(T/kappa),
g=(1+exp(-VH))^(-1), eta=2V/(gH).
For logistic loss log(1+exp(-v*h(kq))) and h(s)=a+b*tanh(kappa*s),
simultaneous Euclidean GD has the exact two-cycle

    (V,w,-w) -> (-V,w/2,-w/2) -> (V,w,-w).

Both states have margin -VH and loss log(1+exp(VH))>log 2.
Since 0<a<b this is a legitimate separable two-token link. Repeating the same signed link permits any number of examples and either raw label, but this theorem makes no claim about distinct links.

Indeed, h(-w^2)=-H, h(-w^2/4)=H, and h'(-w^2/4)=2d.
The head increments are -2V and 2V. Writing delta=eta*v*g*h',
the factor multipliers are delta_0=1/2 and delta_1=-1; on k=-q the
k multipliers are 1-delta, namely 1/2 and 2. All cycle identities follow.

## Full spectrum

Set tau=(1-g)VH, R=2T(tanh T+tanh(T/4)),
D0=1/2+2T*tanh T, D1=2-T*tanh(T/4).
On balanced coordinates (v,k), the two Jacobians are

    Jj = [[1-2tau, B], [B/2, Dj-R*tau]],
    B=-w(1+tau)/V,  B^2/2=2R(1+tau)^2.

The full two-step Jacobian has spectrum {0, eigenvalues(J1*J0)}.
The zero multiplier is the normal coordinate k+q. The larger balanced
multiplier is >25/12 throughout the family, so these cycles are never attracting.
Here and below a multiplier is an eigenvalue of the two-step derivative,
not a one-step derivative between the two different points.

Let S=D0+D1, P=D0*D1 and define

    Q(tau) = q0 + q1*tau + q2*tau^2,
    q0 = 2R(2R-S-2),
    q1 = 20R^2-8R-4P+4,
    q2 = 4(P-1)+10RS+24R^2-4R.

There is a unique positive root tau_c of Q. The other balanced multiplier
lambda_minus is positive and is <1, =1, or >1 exactly when tau is <tau_c,
=tau_c, or >tau_c, respectively. Thus the full linear spectrum consists of
one contracting zero multiplier, an always expanding positive multiplier,
and a positive multiplier with this exact threshold. At equality no nonlinear
classification along the unit eigendirection is asserted. Both strict regimes
are realized as b/sqrt(kappa) varies. The cycle always has an unstable direction.

## Root and elementary bounds

The function cosh T/cosh(T/4) has positive logarithmic derivative
tanh T-(1/4)tanh(T/4) for T>0. At T=1/2 its value is <sqrt 2:
cosh(1/2)<=8/7, since (2n)!>=2^n bounds the cosh series geometrically.
At T=1 its value is >sqrt 2, because cosh 1>37/24 and
cosh(1/4)<=32/31, and (1147/768)^2>2.
The intermediate value theorem and strict monotonicity prove uniqueness.

For the cosh series at 1, the terms beginning at 1/24 have consecutive
ratios at most 1/30. Consequently

    cosh 1 <= 3/2 + (1/24)/(1-1/30) = 179/116 < 31/20 < 8/5.

Also 7/3<e<3 (the lower bound follows from 1+1+1/2; the upper follows
from 1/n!<=1/2^(n-1) for n>=2, strictly for n>=3). Hence
tanh(1/2)>2/5 and tanh 1<4/5.

Write A=tanh T, B0=tanh(T/4). The root equation gives

    A^2=(1+B0^2)/2,
    R = 2T*sech(T)^2/(A-B0) = 2T(A+B0).

Since A-B0 is the integral of sech(u)^2 from T/4 to T,

    (8/3)*sech(T)^2 < R < 8/3.

In particular R>3200/2883>11/10, and also R>25/24. Further,

    9/10 < D0 < 21/10,    1 < D1 < 2.

For y=VH>0, tau=y/(1+exp y) satisfies 0<tau<1/3: the Taylor lower bound
exp y>1+y+y^2/2 implies 1+exp y>3y since (y-2)^2/2>=0.
Thus alpha=1-2tau>1/3. Both diagonal terms of the balanced Jacobians
are positive, since

    D0-R*tau > 9/10-8/9 = 1/90,
    D1-R*tau > 2-T*tanh(T/4)-8/9 > 1/9.

Put C=B^2/2=2R(1+tau)^2>25/12. The monodromy trace is

    tr(J1 J0)=alpha^2+2C+(D0-R*tau)(D1-R*tau)>25/6.

Its two off-diagonal entries are B*(alpha+D0-R*tau) and
(B/2)*(alpha+D1-R*tau), both negative. Its eigenvalues are distinct and
real, since their discriminant is the squared diagonal difference plus
four times a strictly positive off-diagonal product. The larger eigenvalue
is therefore greater than half the trace, hence >25/12.

Moreover

    det Jj = (1-2tau)*Dj - R*(2+5tau) < Dj-2R < 0.

For j=0 use Dj<21/10<2R, and for j=1 use Dj<2<2R. Thus
det(J1 J0)>0 and, its trace being positive, both balanced multipliers are
positive. Direct expansion gives

    det(J1 J0-I) = Q(tau).

Since lambda_plus>1, the sign of Q is exactly the sign of lambda_minus-1.
Finally q0<0: using R=2T(A+B0),

    2R-S-2 = 2T*A+5T*B0-9/2
             < 8/5+5/4-9/2 < 0.

Also q1>13/5, since P<21/5 and the function 20R^2-8R is increasing for
R>11/10, with value 77/5 at 11/10. The coefficient q2>0 follows from
P>0, S>0 and 24R^2-4R>4. These signs give the unique positive root and
all the asserted eigenvalue comparisons.

## Both strict regimes occur

For completeness we verify tau_c<1/4 without floating point. The same
geometric tail bound gives, at x=9/10,

    cosh x <= 1+x^2/2 + (x^4/24)/(1-x^2/30).

The square of this rational upper bound is strictly less than
2*(1+(x/4)^2/2)^2. Thus T>9/10. The exponential Taylor bounds
exp(9/5)>17/3 and exp(9/20)>3/2 imply A>7/10 and B0>1/5, so
R>81/50>8/5. These finite rational comparisons are reproduced in
scripts/verify_opposite_cycle_exact.py.

At tau=1/4, expansion yields

    8Q(1/4)=84R^2-11RS-50R-6P+6.

Using S<41/10, P<21/5, R>8/5, and monotonicity of
84R^2-(951/10)R on R>=8/5, the right side exceeds

    84*(8/5)^2-(951/10)*(8/5)-6*(21/5)+6 = 1092/25 > 0.

Hence 0<tau_c<1/4. The quantity y=VH is a positive constant times
b/sqrt(kappa), so it ranges over all positive numbers. Since tau(y)->0
as y->0 or y->infinity, while tau(1)=1/(1+e)>1/4, both strict regimes
occur. This is a full linear stability classification for this family,
including the unit-multiplier threshold, not a proof about other cycles.

## Differentiation and ambient-coordinate check

At a balanced point (v,k,-k), let s=-k^2, h=h(s), d=h'(s), e2=h''(s),
g=(1+exp(vh))^(-1), delta=eta*v*g*d. The balanced Jacobian is

    J11 = 1-eta*g*(1-g)*h^2,
    J12 = -2*eta*k*g*d*(1-(1-g)*v*h),
    J21 = J12/2,
    J22 = 1-delta+2*k^2*eta*v*(g*e2-g*(1-g)*v*d^2).

Substitution gives the displayed J0,J1. In full coordinates U=k+q obeys
U_+=(1+delta)U. Along U=0 its derivative has no dependence on the
balanced perturbations, since the term U*d(delta) vanishes. Its two-step
multiplier is (1+1/2)*(1-1)=0. The derivative is block triangular with
balanced block J1 J0, so this accounts for its complete three-dimensional
spectrum even without assuming an imbalance invariant for GD.

The independent ambient numerical check differentiates the loss as
Lvv=g(1-g)h^2, Lvs=g(1-g)vhd-gd,
Lss=g(1-g)v^2d^2-gv*e2, Ls=-gvd, and uses

    Hessian L = [[Lvv, q Lvs, k Lvs],
                 [q Lvs, q^2 Lss, kq Lss+Ls],
                 [k Lvs, kq Lss+Ls, k^2 Lss]].

This numerical comparison is evidence only. The proof above uses exact
real identities and explicit rational inequalities, with every series tail
bounded geometrically or used as a nonnegative Taylor remainder.

## Scope and unresolved obstruction

The normal multiplier alone would falsely suggest attraction: the balanced
block always has an expanding eigenvalue. This family therefore supplies
no positive-volume attracting third fate. The remaining route is to classify
asymmetric opposite-head cycles (unequal head magnitudes), factor-sign-flip
cycles, longer periods, or nonperiodic bounded orbits. Nothing here proves
almost-everywhere convergence for factored GD or excludes those alternatives.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.176978+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e87893e03c3956901ebb73d020004cb8882eac031dff045929b18cde73468c35","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 73 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $\epsilon \in (0,1)$ and any function $p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ with $p(q_0)=0$ (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.5withzero}), there exists sufficiently large $L$
 (depending on $p,\epsilon$) and $\tilde p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ satisfying $1/L \le \tilde{p}(q_0) \le \epsilon$ and $\|\tilde{p}\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L$ (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.1}) 
 such that $\|p' - \tilde p'\|_1 \le \epsilon$. 
If $p$ is furthermore concave (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.3}), then the same conclusion holds with $\tilde p$ also concave (i.e., satisfying condition~\ref{it:3.1concave}). 
\begin{proof}
Since $p\in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ is absolutely continuous, we have $p' \in L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$. Since $p(q_0) = 0$ and $p(1) = 1$, we have $\|p'\|_1 = 1$. 

Throughout this proof, we use the term ``step function'' to refer to a function on $[q_0,1]$ that is piecewise constant with finitely many discontinuities. Since step functions are dense in $L^1([q_0,1];[0,+\infty))$, there exists a step function $g_1 : [q_0,1] \to [0,+\infty)$ such that
	\[\|p' - g_1\|_1 \le \epsilon / 6\,.\]
For sufficiently large $L$, there exists a smooth function $g_2 : [q_0,1] \to [0,L]$ with $\|g_2\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L/10$, such that $\|g_1 - g_2\|_1 \le \epsilon / 6$, which implies
	\[\|p' - g_2\|_1 \le \epsilon / 3\,.\]
Since $\|p'\|_1 = 1$, we have $\|g_2\|_1 \le 1 + \epsilon/3$. 
We then define
	\[\tilde p(t) = 1 
		- \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg)
		\int_t^1 g_2(s)\,ds\,,\]
and we note that $\tilde{p}$ is smooth and nondecreasing with
$\|\tilde{p}\|_{C^2([q_0,1])} \le L$. For $\epsilon < 1$, we can bound
	\[
    \|p' - \tilde p'\|_1
    = \bigg\|p' - \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg) g_2\bigg\|_1
    \le \|p' - g_2\|_1 + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \|g_2\|_1
    \le \frac{\epsilon}{3} + \bigg(1+\frac{\epsilon}{3}\bigg) \frac{\epsilon}{2}
    \le \epsilon\,.
\]
Since $p(1) = \tilde p(1) = 1$, it follows that
\[
    \tilde p(q_0) \le p(q_0) + \|p' - \tilde p'\|_1
    =\|p' - \tilde p'\|_1
     \le \epsilon\,.
\]
For sufficiently large $L$, we also have
\[
    \tilde p(q_0) = 1 - \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg) \|g_2\|_1 
    \ge 1 - \bigg(1-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\bigg)
    	\bigg(1+\frac{\epsilon}{3}\bigg)
	\ge \frac{\epsilon}{6} 
    \ge \frac{1}{L}\,.
\]
Thus $\tilde p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1}, as desired.

{"assumptions":["(Omega_1, mu) and (Omega_2, nu) are sigma-finite measure spaces","L^2(mu) and L^2(nu) are separable","k is in L^2(nu ⊗ mu) in part (a); T is Hilbert-Schmidt in part (b)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.572679+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, integral operators","id":"claim_e88f4cb77b3cc3163a131050495e2a27716c9e4fb987bc783cad197ba892ce26","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega_1, mu) and (Omega_2, nu) be sigma-finite measure spaces such that L^2(mu) and L^2(nu) are separable. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.480013+00:00","domain":"commutative algebra and algebraic number theory","id":"claim_e89bd28c5484e7e479a76fd3746c437dac0762bede0ee46e5d42cae90e3d1519","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"An integral domain R (not a field) is a Dedekind domain if it is Noetherian, integrally closed in its field of fractions, and every nonzero prime ideal is maximal (Krull dimension 1). Equivalent characterisations: every nonzero proper ideal factors uniquely as a product of prime ideals; every nonzero ideal is invertible (the fractional ideals form a group under multiplication); the localisation at every nonzero prime is a discrete valuation ring and R is Noetherian; R is Noetherian, integrally closed, of dimension 1. Examples: every principal ideal domain (Z, k[x]); the ring of integers O_K of any algebraic number field K; the integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite separable extension of its fraction field (which is how O_K is proved Dedekind); the coordinate ring of a smooth affine curve over a field. Non-examples: Z[sqrt(-3)] (not integrally closed; its normalisation Z[(1 + sqrt(-3))/2] is Dedekind), k[x, y] (dimension 2). Facts: a Dedekind domain is a unique factorisation domain if and only if it is a principal ideal domain, if and only if its ideal class group (fractional ideals modulo principal ones) is trivial; for O_K the class group is finite (Minkowski) and its order is the class number; every ideal in a Dedekind domain is generated by at most two elements, and every fractional ideal is projective of rank 1; a nonzero prime p of Z factors in O_K as p O_K = P_1^{e_1} ... Dedekind domains are exactly the one-dimensional regular Noetherian domains, so 'Dedekind' is 'smooth curve' in arithmetic.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.319832+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e89ff28c01a4f11fd7a249da36523ae526b230dec0177d0895e280ea1524aa16","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma le:aux-W-l-1 of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] \mbox{}\\
  Let the graph $G$ be finite and $l\in\{0,\ldots,r\}$. 
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item 
    Given $(W^{(l)}_e)_{e\in E_l}$, the random vector $\beta^{(l)\neq}$ has the
  conditional distribution $\nu_{\Lambda_l}^{W^{(l)\neq}}$. 
  \item 
    Assuming $l\ge 1$, take an arbitrary edge $\bar e=e_{j,l-1}\in E_{l-1}$ with
      $e\in E$ and $1\le j\le 2^{l-1}$; see Figure (fig:splitting-an-edge of the paper).
      Call $v=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j-1)}\in \Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_{l-1}\subseteq\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_0$
      its midpoint.
      It splits $\bar e$ into the two edges $e'=e_{2j-1,l}$ and $e''=e_{2j,l}$ in $E_l$. 
      Then, one has 
      \begin{align}
        
   W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e}=\frac{W_{e'}^{(l)}W_{e''}^{(l)}}{2\beta_v^{(l)\neq}}.
 \end{align}
\item 
  Assume $l\ge 2$, which implies that $\Lambda_{l-1}\setminus\Lambda_0\neq\emptyset$. 
  Take an arbitrary vertex
      $\bar v=v_{e,2^{-(l-1)}j}\in\Lambda_{l-1}\setminus\Lambda_0$ with $e\in E$ and
      $1\le j\le 2^{l-1}-1$. In particular, $\bar v$ belongs also to
      $\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_0$; see Figure (fig:splitting-an-edge of the paper).
      Call $e^1=e_{2j,l}\in E_l$ and $e^2=e_{2j+1,l}\in E_l$ the
      two edges adjacent to $\bar v$ in $G_l$. Call
      $v^1=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j-1)},v^2=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j+1)}\in\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_{l-1}\subseteq\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_0$
      the two neighboring vertices
      of $\bar v$ in $G_l$. Then, one has 
      \begin{align}
        
        2\beta_{\bar v}^{(l-1)\neq}=2\beta_{\bar v}^{(l)\neq}-\frac{(W_{e^1}^{(l)})^2}{\beta_{v^1}^{(l)\neq}}
      -\frac{(W_{e^2}^{(l)})^2}{\beta_{v^2}^{(l)\neq}}.
    \end{align}
  \item
     Assume $l\ge 1$ again. 
    Given $(W^{(l)}_e)_{e\in E_l}$, the random variables $\beta^{(l)\neq}_v$,
    $v=v_{e,2^{-l}(2j-1)}\in\Lambda_l\setminus\Lambda_{l-1}$, are conditionally independent with

    we use the notation $e'=e_{2j-1,l}$ and $e''=e_{2j,l}$ from item (item1 of the paper).
  \item 
    If the family of weights $(W_e)_{e\in E}$ is independent or even i.i.d.,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.687439+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e8a7a64b273f13396ae992a4626c7a30516ec88118f7b0c7a034782b1575de3e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 23 (Weak reparametrisation and reduced uniqueness) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space, and let $\xi:[0,A]\to E$ and $\widetilde\xi:[0,B]\to E$ be continuous bounded-variation paths with $\xi\sim_{\mathrm{rep}}\widetilde\xi$, witnessed by continuous nondecreasing surjections $\sigma:[0,1]\to[0,A]$ and $\widetilde\sigma:[0,1]\to[0,B]$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)}]
\item If $0\leq u\leq w\leq1$, $s=\sigma(u)$, $t=\sigma(w)$, $\widetilde s=\widetilde\sigma(u)$, and $\widetilde t=\widetilde\sigma(w)$, then
\[
\xi|_{[s,t]}\sim_{\mathrm{rep}}
\widetilde\xi|_{[\widetilde s,\widetilde t]}.
\]
The two subpaths have equal signatures and are constant simultaneously.
\item The equivalent reducedness conditions in \cref{prop:reducedness} are invariant under $\sim_{\mathrm{rep}}$.
\item If neither path has a nontrivial constant subinterval, then there is an increasing homeomorphism $h:[0,A]\to[0,B]$ such that
\[
\xi=\widetilde\xi\circ h.
\]
\end{enumerate}

	\]
for all $q_0 \le s\le t\le1$, and with $\nu_N(\{0\})=0$. By passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $\nu_N$ converges in the L\'evy--Prohorov metric to a limiting measure $\nu$. Since $(p^N)'$ converges to $p'$ almost everywhere, we immediately conclude that 
	\[\nu((s,t])
	=-\Big[ p'(t)-p'(s)\Big]
	\]
for almost all $s,t$. Now recall that $p'$ denotes the derivative of $p$ from the right, so in particular $p'$ is right-continuous: this implies that the above equality holds for all $s,t\in[0,1]$.         \[\P\bigg(
    \Big|F^{\riii}(k,\cB) - \E\tilde{F}^{\riii}(k)\Big|
    \ge \frac{\epsilon'}{10}

for any fixed partition $\cB \in \scB(\lambda,\mu)$.

\medskip
{\bf (1)} For $m\ge 2$ (resp.\ $m\ge 3$) we say that $\mu_{X;A}$ has exceptional $+1$ (resp.\ $-1$) jumps or that $\mu_{X;A}$ has jump type $1$ (resp.\ $-1$) if there exists $b\in A\cap\llbracket 1,p^s-1\rrbracket$ such that the function $\mu_{X;b}$ is non-constant and for each such $b$, $\mu_{X;b}$ attains its maximum (resp.\ minimum) at precisely one element of the source.

\smallskip
{\bf (3)} We say that $\mu_{X;A}$ has regular $\pm 1$ jumps if for each $b\in A$ the function $\mu_{X;b}$ is non-constant, attains its maximum at two or more elements of the source, and attains its minimum at two or more elements of the source.

\smallskip
{\bf (4)} For $m=2$ (resp.\ $m\ge 3$), we fix an $s$-tuple $(\epsilon_0,\ldots,\epsilon_{s-1})\in\{0,1\}^s$ (resp. $(\epsilon_0,\ldots,\epsilon_{s-1})\in\{-1,0,1\}^s$). \smallskip
{\bf (5)} We call the $2s$-tuple 
$$(\l_{0,0},|\mathbb J_{X;0}|,\l_{1,0},|\mathbb J_{X;1}|,\ldots,\l_{s-1,0},|\mathbb J_{X;s-1}|)\in(\mathbb N\cup\{0\})^{2s} $$
 as the multiplicity type of $\mu_X$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348748+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e91b1cd8927b86ad5e2a7ab443169724c0332be7cebe97a13d24ef45bdb005e0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 164 ($\bar{\bx}$ is Lipschitz) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Take $\bar{\bx}\equiv \bar{\bx}(q_d)$
 as in \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.x}, so it is measurable with respect to
 $\cG(q_d)$. Then
		\[
		\|\E\bar{\bx}\|^2
		\le \frac{Nq_0}{q_d} \le N\,.\]
and the centered random vector $\bar{\bx}  -\E\bar{\bx}$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $L^{O(1)}$.

\begin{proof} 
Recall $\chi(p)=\E R(p)$ with $R(p)$ as in \eqref{e:p.corr.overlap}, and $q_d=\chi(p_d)$. Note that
	\[
	\frac{\|\E\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N}
	= \frac{\|\E\cA(\bG)\|^2}{Nq_d}
	= \frac{\chi(0)}{q_d} 
	\le \frac{\chi(p_0)}{q_d} = \frac{q_0}{q_d}\le1\,,
	\]
which proves the first claim. Next note that we can write
	\[
	\sqrt{q_d}\bar{\bx}
	\stackrel{\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.x}}{=}
	\E\bigg( \cA
	\Big(\sqrt{p_d}\bar{\bG} +\sqrt{1-p_d}\bG'\Big)
	\,\bigg|\,\bar{\bG}\bigg)\,,
	\]
where $\bar{\bG} = \bG(q_d)/\sqrt{p_d}$ and $\bG'$ are independent $M\times N$ matrices, each with i.i.d.\ standard gaussian entries. Since $\cA$ is $L$-Lipschitz, and $p_d/q_d \le L^{O(1)}$ by \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound}, it follows that $\bar{\bx}$ is $L^{O(1)}$-Lipschitz with respect to $\bar{\bG}$. The claim then follows using Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:23:58.615594+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e9428f28481bae9e9505ada1331bf2b01b4592f1c8cddf307f724efe56e4c403","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 130 (Pointwise commutator estimates involving $\angLie$ ; \cite{abbrescia2022emergence}*{Prop.\,14.5}) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] Let $1 \leq N \leq \Ntop$ be an integer, and let $\varphi$ be a scalar function. 
	For any $\Singletan \in \Tanset$ (see definition \eqref{E:COMMUTATIONVECTORFIELDS}),
	iterated commutators can be bounded pointwise as follows
	on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$:
	\begin{subequations}
		\begin{align} 
			\left|
			[\Singletan, \tander^N] \varphi
			\right|
			& \lesssim 
			\auxbootsmall \left|\tander^{[1,N]} \varphi \right| 
			+ 
			\underbrace{\sum_{\substack {N_1+N_2 \leq N+1 \\ N_1,\,N_2\leq N}} 
				\left|\tander^{[2,N_1]}\controlvars \right| \left|\tander^{[1,N_2]} \varphi \right|}_{\mbox{Absent if $N=1$}},
			\\
			\begin{split}
				\left|[\muX, \tander^N]\varphi \right|,
				\,
				\left|
				[\Singletan, \comder^{N;1}] \varphi
				\right|
				& \lesssim
				\left|\tander^{[1,N]} \varphi \right| 
				+ 
				\underbrace{\sum_{\substack {N_1+N_2 \leq N+1 \\ N_1,\,N_2\leq N}} 
					\left|\tander^{[2,N_1]} \badcontrolvars \right| \left|\tander^{[1,N_2]} \varphi \right|}_{\mbox{Absent if $N=1$}}
				 
				\\
				& \ \
				+ 
				\underbrace{\sum_{\substack {N_1+N_2 \leq N \\ N_1 \leq N-1}} 
					\left|\tander^{[1,N_1]} \muX \wavearray \right| \left|\tander^{[1,N_2]} \varphi \right|}_{\mbox{Absent if $N=1$}}.
			\end{split}
		\end{align}
	\end{subequations}
	
	In particular, 
	for any $\Singletan \in \{\Lunit,\Yvf{2},\Yvf{3}\}$,
	we have the following pointwise estimates
	on $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{[\leftubar,\ubarboot)}{[\moreinterestingu_1,\moreinterestingu_2]}$:
	\begin{subequations}
		\begin{align} 
			\left|[\Singletan, \tander^N] \varphi \right| 
			& 
			\lesssim 
			\auxbootsmall \left| \tander^{[1,N]}\varphi \right|,
			&
			\mbox{if } 1 \leq N \leq \Ntop - 11,
			\\
			\left|[\muX, \tander^N]\varphi \right|,
			\,
			\left|
			[\Singletan, \comder^{N;1}] \varphi
			\right|
			&

			& 
			\mbox{if } 1 \leq N \leq \Ntop - 12.

	Moreover, the following pointwise estimates hold:
	\begin{subequations}

			\left|
			[\Singletan, \comder^{N;2}] \varphi
			\right|,
			\,
			\left|
			[\muX, \comder^{N;1}] \varphi 
			\right|
			& 
			\lesssim 
			\left| \comdersmall^{[1,N];1} \varphi \right|,
			&
			\mbox{if } 1 \leq N \leq 5,
			
			\\
			\left|
			[\Singletan, \comder^{N;3}] \varphi
			\right|,
			\,
			\left|

	Finally, if $\upxi$ is an $\ell_{t,u}$-tangent one-form or an $\ell_{t,u}$-tangent type $\binom{0}{2}$-tensorfield

\right|_{\gtorus}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.773278+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e9689f07be8757b3b3405abf734ed997e836e49b13d95f11df9468796fc25828","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (The Cauchy stability of finite-energy  Einstein areal flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Consider one of the three Einstein--matter models in \autoref{theo-main-results} with $\Tbb^2$ symmetry on~$\Tbb^3$.
In the Einstein--Navier--Stokes case, assume that the model is admissible and torus-adapted, and that its matter stress tensor~$T_\chi$ obeys the coercive stress condition in \autoref{def-Tchi-coercive}.
In the Einstein--Euler case, we use the conventions $T_\chi=T_{\rm E}$, $\vNumb_\chi=\vNumb_\Jbb$, and $\zeta=0$.
Prescribe\footnote{Equivalently, prescribe a signed areal time~$t_0$ and initial data $(\mathring\Phi,\mathring\Psi,\mathring\zeta)$ for the \JKL{} formulation of the areal flow, together with the conformal modulus of one symmetry orbit.}
 an initial data set $(\mathring g,\mathring k,\mathring\Jbb,\mathring\zeta)$, consisting of a Riemannian metric, second fundamental form, fluid momentum, and relaxation field (absent for the Einstein--Euler model) satisfying Einstein's constraint equations and invariant under two commuting Killing fields $Y,Z$ with closed orbits, and assume that the orbit area constant and equal to $|t_0|\neq 0$.

Consider a regular Cauchy development $(\Phi,\Psi,\zeta)$ on $\Tbb^3\times[t_0,t_1]$ of these initial data for the chosen Einstein--Euler or Einstein--Navier--Stokes model in the areal foliation, with an areal time interval $I = [t_0,t_1] \subset \RR\setminus\{0\}$.
\bei
\item Assume that the initial spatial volume, the initial energy norm~$\mathcal E(t_0)$, and the bounded-variation norm of $\mathring\Psi=(\mathring\ell,\log\mathring\Omega,\mathring\Kpar)$ on~$\Tbb^3$ are bounded by a constant~$\mathcal I_0$.

\item In the future-contracting regime, assume that the conformal length has a positive lower bound $\mathcal L_{\min}$ on $I$; in the future-expanding regime, this lower bound is $\mathcal L_{\min}=\mathcal L(t_0)>0$, which is part of the initial data controlled by~$\mathcal I_0$.

\item Assume either that the fluid velocity is orthogonal to the symmetry orbits or, more generally, that the parallel momentum per particle is uniformly bounded in the sense that~\eqref{intro-parall-perpart-bounded} holds at $t=t_0$ for some constant $C^\parallel>0$.
\eei
Then the following Cauchy stability properties hold.

\begin{enumerate}

\item The parallel momentum per particle remains uniformly bounded at all times by~$C^\parallel$ in the sense that~\eqref{intro-parall-perpart-bounded} holds on $[t_0,t_1]\times\Tbb^3$.

\item There exists a constant
\be
C=C\bigl(\mathcal I_0,t_0,t_1,\mathcal L_{\min}^{-1},C^\parallel\bigr)
\ee
such that the $L^2$ norms of~$\Phi$ and bounded-variation norms of~$\Psi$ on areal time slices (constant~$t$) and on timelike slices orthogonal to the areal foliation (constant~$x$ in the \JKL{} formulation) are controlled as
\bel{equajKD93}
\aligned
& \sup_{t\in I}\bigl(
\|\Phi\|_{L^2(\Tbb^3,\dVtrois)}
+ \|\Psi\|_{\BV(\Tbb^3)}
\bigr)
\\
& + \sup_{x\in\Sbb^1}\bigl(
\|\Phi\|_{L^2(\Interval\times\Tbb^2,\dVundeux)}
+ \|\Psi\|_{\BV(\Interval\times\Tbb^2)}
\bigr)
+\int_{I\times\Tbb^3}\!\!\mathfrak d_*\,\dVuntrois
\leq C.
\endaligned
\ee
Here, $\dVuntrois,\dVtrois,\dVundeux$ are volume forms of the (Lorentzian) metric~$g$ and of (Riemannian) induced metrics on spatial and temporal slices.

\item The last term in \eqref{equajKD93} represents the total non-negative production measure and vanishes for the Einstein--Euler system.  For the particle-production Einstein--Navier--Stokes system it is the produced particle number density $\mathfrak d_*=\zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}$, while for the dissipated-energy Einstein--Navier--Stokes system it is the dissipated mass-energy density $\mathfrak d_*=\zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}/(-n_\alpha\beta^\alpha)$.

\item Moreover, these conclusions allow vacuum, arbitrarily large mass-energy density, and arbitrary finite rapidity. For the two Einstein--Navier--Stokes systems, the constant $C$ is independent of the relaxation rate map~$\mathscr B$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["subadditivity of the doubly indexed array X_{m,n} under the relation X_{m,n}<=X_{m,k}+X_{k,n}","joint stationarity of the array under the shift (m,n) -> (m+1,n+1)","integrability, E[X_{0,1}^+]<infinity, together with a lower bound preventing a degenerate -infinity limit","for an almost-surely-constant limit: ergodicity, not merely measure-preservation, of the underlying shift"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.997492+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_e96ecd8a6581efaccba61539497e251c17654ec41003ba9f77fa5109ab6ea0af","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let (X_{m,n})_{0<=m<n} be a doubly indexed family of random variables satisfying subadditivity X_{m,n} <= X_{m,k} + X_{k,n} for m<k<n, stationarity, that the joint law of (X_{m+1,n+1})_{m<n} equals that of (X_{m,n})_{m<n} under a measure-preserving shift, and integrability, E[X_{0,1}^+] < infinity together with a lower bound such as E[X_{0,n}] >= -cn preventing a trivially degenerate -infinity limit. Then X_{0,n}/n converges almost surely and in L^1 to a random variable X, equal to lim_n E[X_{0,n}]/n = inf_n E[X_{0,n}]/n, and X is almost surely constant if the underlying shift is ergodic rather than merely measure-preserving. This is the random, non-i.i.d. generalization of Fekete's lemma, which is its deterministic special case, and of the classical ergodic theorem, which is its additive special case, and it is the fundamental tool establishing existence of limiting growth rates in first-passage percolation (the time constant), longest increasing subsequence problems, and last-passage percolation, with the closely related Furstenberg-Kesten theorem giving Lyapunov exponents for random matrix products via an analogous but distinct subadditive argument. It does not give the value of the limit X, only its existence as an abstract limit or infimum, and does not by itself give a rate of convergence or determine whether X is almost surely constant unless ergodicity, not merely stationarity, of the shift has been separately established. Typical failure: Invoking Kingman's theorem to conclude the limiting growth rate is deterministic without separately verifying ergodicity of the underlying probability-preserving transformation, checking only stationarity; stationarity alone gives convergence to a possibly random limit X that can be a genuine mixture over ergodic components, so asserting a single deterministic time constant or growth rate without checking ergodicity is a common gap, especially in models built from a mixture of environments. Canonical reference: Kingman, 1968, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B; Kingman, 1973, Annals of Probability; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the pool protocol: members fitted on training data, the test rows split 40/60 into calibration and evaluation with a fixed permutation, metric = mean per-sample relative L2","the small-calibration arms subsample the calibration rows only; evaluation rows are never touched"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:07:15.583115+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning / covariance estimation","id":"claim_e9a54df9848e9c966074eb757b8cd899d5745113e3c0dcbfb1a664e5434d1869","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Measured 2026-09-05 on the EMIT stacking pool (23 members, 285 outputs, the per-sample relative metric; PLACEHOLDER_CELLS). The error covariance of the members is rank-deficient in practice: $\\lambda_{\\max}/\\lambda_{\\min}$ of $10^{6}$ to $10^{17}$, three to five eigenvalues below $0.05\\,\\sigma^2$ (members that are near-linear combinations of one another). Inside the long-only minimum-variance stack, eight cleaners of that covariance were compared on the same cells, the same split and the same small-calibration draws: the raw sample covariance, the $\\eta$-regularised rotationally invariant estimator with floors $0, 0.05, 0.2, 1.0\\,\\sigma^2$, Ledoit-Wolf 2004 linear shrinkage, Ledoit-Wolf 2020 analytical nonlinear shrinkage and Lam's NERCOME. Result: raw, RIE without floor, LW2020 and NERCOME tie - PLACEHOLDER_TIE - at full calibration ($n = 932$) and in the $n = 60/120/240$ arms; the floor $0.05\\,\\sigma^2$ is marginally negative, floors $0.2$ and $1.0$ lose PLACEHOLDER_FLOORS, linear shrinkage loses PLACEHOLDER_LW2004, and the sum-to-one (unconstrained-sign) forms of the same cleaners lose PLACEHOLDER_S1. Mechanism (seed 101, medians over outputs): the constraint keeps 7-11 of 23 members; the condition number falls from $10^{6}$-$10^{17}$ on the full covariance to $4\\times10^{2}$-$3\\times10^{4}$ on the active principal submatrix; eigenvalues under the floor fall from 3-5 to 0-1; the active sets of raw, RIE and LW2020 overlap at Jaccard 0.86-0.90 (0.80-0.83 at $n = 60$). By the active-set lemma the weights depend on the covariance only through $S_{AA}$, which is well conditioned, and there every consistent cleaner is close to the identity; a floor or a linear shrinkage lifts the small eigenvalues of the full matrix before the constraint acts and distorts $w_A$. The reading of the whole program: random-matrix theory identifies what to clean (the error covariance, in the reported metric, with an intercept) and why the plug-in fails (the near-null directions of a collinear ensemble); the fix that survives the population is the long-only constraint, itself a data-determined covariance shrinkage, and the spectral cleaners are interchangeable inside it. The pre-registered contrary hypothesis - that the floor was a kernel-bandwidth artefact which LW2020's theory-fixed bandwidth would remove - was refuted on its first cell: consistent estimators correctly keep the tiny eigenvalues, because in the population they are tiny.","status":"unverified"}

for all $e\in\left\{ \pm\right\} $, and let $L^{2}\left(X,\sigma\left(X\right),\mu\right)$

$\mathbb{H}$-indefinite inner product $\left[,\right]$. Suppose
either 
\[
\mu_{+}\textrm{ is a classical probability, and }\mu_{-}=O,
\]

\[

\]

\[

\]

\[

respectively,

\]

respectively,
\[
\left[f,g\right]=0e_{+}+\left\langle f_{-},g_{-}\right\rangle _{2}e_{-}=\left(\int_{X}f_{-}g_{-}d\mu_{-}\right)e_{-}\in\mathbb{H}.

    \Big(\C_m^{\geqslant 0} \circ \D_m^{\geqslant 1}\Big).\C_m
    \cup \C_m^{\geqslant0} \Big].
\end{align*}
Its exponential generating function is hence
\[
  \hat\phi_G(z) = \left[ (1-p) \left( e^{z/m} - 1 \right) + 1 \right]^m.
\]
\begin{proof}
  It holds for all $i$ that
  \begin{align*}
    \hat\phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}}(z)
    
    &= e^{z/m} - e^{(1-p)z/m}\\
    &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty
        \frac{(z/m)^n - ((1-p)z/m)^n}{n!},\\
    \phi_{{\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}}(z)
    &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty 
        (z/m)^n - ((1-p)z/m)^n.
  \end{align*}
  Then we multiply by $\phi_{\C_i}(z) = \left(1-p\right)z\,m^{-1}$,
  \begin{align*}
    \phi_{\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}\right).\C_i}(z)
    &= \frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m} \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left[
      \left(\frac{z}{m}\right)^n - \left(\frac{\left(1-p\right)z}{m}\right)^n
      \right]\\
    &= (1-p)\sum_{n=1}^\infty
        (z/m)^{n}
      - \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      ((1-p)\,z/m)^{n},\\
    \hat\phi_{\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}\right).\C_i}(z)
    &= (1-p)\sum_{n=1}^\infty
        \frac{(z/m)^{n}}{n!}
      - \sum_{n=1}^\infty
        \frac{((1-p)z/m)^{n}}{n!}\\
    &= (1-p)\left(e^{z/m} - 1\right)
    - e^{(1-p)z/m} + 1.
  \end{align*}
  Finally add $\hat\phi_{\C_i^{\geqslant 0}}(z)
  = e^{(1-p)z/m}$ to achieve
  \begin{align*}
    \hat\phi_{
      {\left({\C_i^{\geqslant0}} \circ {\D_i^{\geqslant1}}\right).\C_i}
      \cup {\C_i}
    }(z)
    &= (1-p) \left( e^{z/m} - 1 \right) + 1,\\
    \hat\phi_G(z)
    &= \left[(1-p) \left( e^{z/m} - 1 \right) + 1\right]^m. \qedhere
  \end{align*}
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:21:10.899765+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ea0642ce49366d6d114e9360fb78404fba23608c7df6fc02c893da81d12c9df1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 28 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Given a configuration $\boldsymbol{\ell} \in \W_\N$ in a discrete ensemble of Section~\ref{Section_general_model}, the \emph{empirical measure} is the $H$-tuple of nonnegative atomic measures $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\N} = (\mu_{\N,h})_{h = 1}^{H}$ given by
\[
\forall h \in [H] \qquad \mu_{\N,h} = \frac{1}{\N} \sum_{i = 1}^{N_h} \delta_{\N^{-1}\ell_i^h}.
\]
This tuple $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\N}$ is equivalently specified by the measure $\mu_{\N} = \sum_{h = 1}^{H} \mu_{\N,h} = \frac{1}{\N} \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \delta_{\N^{-1}\ell_i}$. The empirical resolvent is the tuple $\boldsymbol{G}(z) = (G_h(z))_{h = 1}^{H}$ defined for any $h \in [H]$ and $z \in\amsmathbb{C} \setminus [\hat{a}_h,\hat{b}_h]$ by
\begin{equation}
 G_h(z) = \sum_{i = 1}^{N_h} \frac{1}{z - \frac{\ell_i^h}{\N}} = \N \int_{\hat{a}_h}^{\hat{b}_h} \frac{\dd \mu_{\N,h}(x)}{z - x} = \N \Gm_{\mu_{\N,h}}(z).
\end{equation}
It is a holomorphic function of $z$ in this domain, such that for any $h \in [H]$, we have $G_h(z) \sim \frac{N_h}{z}$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$.

We sometimes recenter the empirical measure by subtracting the equilibrium measure $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and introduce $\Delta \boldsymbol{G}(z) = \boldsymbol{G}(z) - \N \Gm_{\boldsymbol{\mu}}(z)$. In other words, for any $h \in [H]$ and $z \in \amsmathbb{C} \setminus \amsmathbb{A}_h^{\mathfrak{m}}]$ we have
\[
\Delta G_h(z) = G_h(z) - \N\Gm_{\mu_h}(z).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are normed spaces over the same field R or C","T: X -> Y is linear"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571085+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator theory","id":"claim_ea377968f9c0845c7f4fd6c6c2aa4f7c83561cc34ce0b88f7e0503bd67c3c35c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be normed spaces over R or C. A linear map T: X -> Y is compact if the image T(B_X) of the closed unit ball B_X = {x : ||x|| <= 1} is relatively compact in Y, i.e. its closure in Y is compact. Equivalent forms: (i) for every bounded sequence (x_n) in X the sequence (T x_n) has a subsequence that converges in Y; (ii) when Y is a Banach space, T(B_X) is totally bounded. Every compact operator is bounded, and every bounded operator of finite rank is compact. The set of compact operators X -> Y is written K(X,Y), and K(X) = K(X,X). The identity operator of X is compact if and only if X is finite-dimensional (Riesz's lemma). Terminology warning: older texts say 'completely continuous' for compact; in current usage 'completely continuous' means 'maps weakly convergent sequences to norm convergent sequences', which is implied by compactness but is weaker in general (it is equivalent to compactness when X is reflexive).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.521083+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ea3b28480bb46496d7d97bd1152f16281b0a0e958d9ab539625d242ded353d48","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:PTASEP-kernel of arXiv:2608.02772, 'Non-Abelian Hirota-Miwa Equations for the KPZ Universality Class'] We have
\[

\{Y_{n_i}(t) > a_i\}\Bigr)
= \det(I - K_{t, \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{n}})_{\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})},

\[

$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:45:32.093666+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eae6ccbf63efc8eb091be350e312350763bc3ea312937a763b95e1bc41c83357","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def Mixing of arXiv:2411.14350, 'Randomized Geodesic Flow on Hyperbolic Groups'] Let $G$ be a group acting on a probability space $(X,\mu)$ and let $r\geq 2$ be an integer. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item [(1)] We say that the action of $G$ on $(X,\mu)$ is {\bf mixing of order $r\geq 2 $}, if for all $f_1,...,f_r \in L^{\infty}(X,\mu)$, and for all $g_1,g_2,\dots, g_r \in G$ we have 
$$
\bigg| \int_{X}\prod_{i=1}^r ( f_i\circ g_i){\rm{d}} \mu- \prod_{i=1}^r  \int_{X}f_i{\rm{d}} \mu\bigg| \to 0  \qquad\mbox{as $\min_{\ell\neq k} \, d(g_\ell,g_k)\to \infty$}.
$$

\item [(2)] We fix an $G$-invariant sub-algebra $\mathcal A$ of $L^{\infty}(X,\mu)$, and a family $N = (N_s)_{s\in \mathbb{N}}$ of semi-norms on $\mathcal A$. Then we say that the action of the group $G$ on  $(X,\mu)$ is {\bf exponentially mixing of order $r$} with respect to $d$ and $(\mathcal A,N)$, if there exist $\delta_r > 0$ and an integer $s_r\in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $s > s_r$, $f_1,...,f_r \in  \mathcal A$ and $g_1,\dots,g_r\in G$, 
$$
 \bigg| \int_{X}\prod_{i=1}^r ( f_i\circ g_i){\rm{d}} \mu- \prod_{i=1}^r  \int_{X}f_i{\rm{d}} \mu\bigg|  \leq C {\rm e} ^{-\delta_r d_r(g_1,..,g_r)} \prod_{i=1}^r N_s(f_i) 
$$
for some finite constant $C=C(s,r)$. In this case, $\delta_r>0$ is called {\bf the rate of mixing}. 
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:57:28.735462+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eb1a4e3a7e43ae50d30296220ad5d188d2da624a42c741f4df03f966d1c8b274","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 of arXiv:2609.01268, 'Resultant multiplicity via projective degrees\\ and applications to tensor eigenvalues'] Assume that $I\neq (0)$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.652876+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eb1a55346ce127bdb7a56979e5b75aa5a67209493c2a21e694c7b7614fe8e168","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Mainthm thm:density of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $d\ge1$ and $r>0$.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item \emph{(Positivity, uniformly in $\lambda$.)} For every $\mu\in(0,\infty]$ there is
  $\bar\eta=\bar\eta(\mu,r,d)>0$ such that
  \[
    \eta_c(\lambda,\mu)\ \ge\ \bar\eta(\mu,r,d)\qquad\text{for every admissible }\lambda\in(0,\infty] ,
  \]
  that is, for every $\lambda\in(0,\infty]$ when $\mu<\infty$ and for $\lambda=\infty$ when
  $\mu=\infty$. Equivalently, the infection started from a single particle dies out almost surely
  at every intensity below $\bar\eta$, whatever the infection rate.
\item \emph{(Finiteness at $\lambda=\infty$.)} For every $\mu\in(0,\infty]$ and every $d\ge1$,
  $\eta_c(\infty,\mu)<\infty$.
\item \emph{(The Boolean bound, $d\ge2$.)} For $d\ge2$ and every $\mu\in(0,\infty]$,
  \[
    \eta_c(\infty,\mu)\ \le\ \eta_c(\infty,\infty)\ \le\ \eta_c^{\mathrm{B}} ,
  \]
  so the critical density at infinite infection rate is bounded above by the critical intensity of
  the static Boolean model, uniformly in the recovery rate.
\end{enumerate}
In particular $\eta_c(\infty,\mu)\in(0,\infty)$ for every $d\ge1$ and every $\mu\in(0,\infty]$.
That is, the instantaneous infection dies out almost surely for $\eta<\eta_c(\infty,\mu)$ and
survives with positive probability for $\eta>\eta_c(\infty,\mu)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Jointly trained scalar head and factored attention p=kq have open positive-three-dimensional-measure inferior-selection basins for arbitrary n>=2 distinct two-token examples and every fixed eta>0. In the stated sign regions all parameters escape, factors are O(sqrt(log |v|)), loss tends to zero, and actual (v,k,q)-normalized margins are Gamma_-<Gamma_+. The complete finite stationary set is a saddle curve v=0,kq=p_bar, with one zero tangent and opposite-sign normal Hessian eigenvalues.

# Target 1: joint head, key and query training retains open inferior basins

Version 1. Proof unaudited. Owner own work; global novelty unestablished.

## Statement

Let n>=2, b_i,kappa_i>0 and 0<a_i<b_i. Set
h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s),
L(v,k,q)=mean_i log(1+exp(-v h_i(kq))).
Train all three scalar parameters by simultaneous Euclidean GD, at any fixed eta>0.
Write r_min=min_i atanh(-a_i/b_i)/kappa_i<0.
The following nonempty open subsets of R^3 are forward invariant:

 B_-={v<0,k>0,q<0,kq<r_min},
 B_+={v>0,k>0,q>0}.

The simultaneous sign reversal (k,q)->(-k,-q) supplies two more invariant regions.
On B_-: v->-infinity, k->+infinity, q->-infinity, kq->-infinity,
L->0, and (v,k,q)/sqrt(v^2+k^2+q^2)->(-1,0,0).
On B_+ the three coordinates tend to +infinity and the normalized limit is
(1,0,0). The normalized minimum signed margins, defined here as
min_i v h_i(kq)/sqrt(v^2+k^2+q^2), tend respectively to
Gamma_-=min_i(b_i-a_i) and Gamma_+=min_i(b_i+a_i).
The largest attainable limiting normalized margin is Gamma_+; Gamma_+>Gamma_-.
Consequently the inferior basin has positive three-dimensional Lebesgue measure.
These are invariant-region results, not a classification of all initializations.

The two-token cross-attention and genuine first-token self-attention embeddings
in proofs/004 and 006 remain exact after replacing their attention parameter p
by kq. Thus the claim includes distinct examples and both labels.

## Exact updates and invariance

For s=kq put g_i=1/(1+exp(v h_i(s))),
F=mean g_i h_i(s), G=mean g_i h_i'(s)>0. The exact simultaneous updates are

 v_+=v+eta F, k_+=k+eta vqG, q_+=q+eta vkG.

In B_-, F<0, vq>0 and vk<0. Each sign is therefore preserved and the
product becomes more negative. In B_+ all increments are positive, since
s>0 and h_i(s)>a_i>0. No restriction on eta is needed.

Analyze either branch using positive variables u,w,r. On B_- take
u=-v,w=k,r=-q, x=wr=-s, t_i(x)=b_i tanh(kappa_i x)-a_i.
On B_+ take u=v,w=k,r=q,x=wr=s,t_i(x)=b_i tanh(kappa_i x)+a_i.
Both obey exactly

 Delta u=eta mean g_i t_i, w_+=w+delta r, r_+=r+delta w,
 delta=eta u mean g_i t_i', g_i=(1+exp(u t_i))^-1.

Here x,u,w,r increase, and t_i(x)>=c:=min_i t_i(x_0)>0.
Let H=max_i(a_i+b_i), M=max_i b_i kappa_i, kappa_0=min_i kappa_i.
All t_i<=H and t_i'<=4M exp(-2 kappa_0 x).

## Escape

If u remained bounded, u t_i<=u H would keep every g_i bounded below,
contradicting Delta u>=eta c mean g_i. Hence u->infinity.
If x remained bounded, min_i t_i' would have a positive lower bound d>0.
The exact product update is

 Delta x=delta(w^2+r^2)+delta^2 x.

Using w^2+r^2>=2x_0>0 and
delta/Delta u=u(mean g_i t_i')/(mean g_i t_i)>=u d/H,
we obtain Delta x>=2x_0 d u Delta u/H. The sum of u Delta u diverges
(already u>=u_0>0 and sum Delta u=infinity), contradicting bounded x.
Thus x->infinity, and the loss tends to zero.

## Factor growth is negligible relative to the head

This step is essential: it compares the margin in the actual three parameters,
not the collapsed (v,p) norm. Let D=w-r. The exact relation is
D_+=(1-delta)D. Since g_i<=exp(-c u),
0<delta<=eta M u exp(-c u)->0. Hence eventually delta<=1, and |D| is
bounded by a finite constant D_* (a finite earlier excursion is harmless).
Therefore w^2+r^2=2x+D^2<=2x+D_*^2.
Eventually delta<=1, so

 Delta x<=delta(3x+D_*^2),
 delta<=4 eta M u exp(-c u) exp(-2 kappa_0 x).

The function (3x+D_*^2)exp(-2 kappa_0 x) is bounded for x>=x_0>0.
Consequently Delta x->0, and eventually Delta x<=1. Also

 delta/Delta u<=4M u exp(-2 kappa_0 x)/c.

The mean value theorem now gives

 Delta exp(kappa_0 x)
 <=kappa_0 exp(kappa_0) exp(kappa_0 x) Delta x
 <=C (3x+D_*^2)exp(-kappa_0 x) u Delta u
 <=C' u Delta u.

Summing, using 2u Delta u<=Delta(u^2), yields
exp(kappa_0 x)<=C''(1+u^2). Thus x=O(log u), and
w^2+r^2=O(log u). In particular w/u,r/u->0. Since x->infinity and
|w-r| is bounded, both w,r tend to infinity. This proves every stated
coordinate and normalized limit.

## Margin optimality and positive measure

Endpoint limits give Gamma_+ and Gamma_-. For any parameters, let
N=sqrt(v^2+k^2+q^2). If v>=0, choose an index minimizing a_i+b_i:
min_i v h_i/N<=Gamma_+. If v<0, choose an index minimizing b_i-a_i:
min_i v h_i/N<=Gamma_-. These inequalities remain valid when that
chosen signed prediction is negative. B_+ attains the larger endpoint
asymptotically. Gamma_+>=Gamma_-+2 min_i a_i>Gamma_-.
B_- is nonempty and open; for example take v=-1,k=R,q=-R with
R^2>-r_min. A sufficiently small ball around that point lies in B_-.

## Finite stationary set (flow stability, separate from the GD basin claim)

The only finite stationary points are v=0, kq=p_bar, where
mean_i h_i(p_bar)=0. Indeed v!=0 would force k=q=0 from the factor
gradients, but F(v,0)=mean_i a_i/(1+exp(v a_i))>0.
At v=0 the remaining condition is exactly the displayed mean root.
It is negative, so k,q are nonzero. Put A=mean_i h_i(p_bar)^2/4>=0,
B=mean_i h_i'(p_bar)/2>0. The loss Hessian is

 [[A,-Bq,-Bk],[-Bq,0,0],[-Bk,0,0]].

It has one zero tangent eigenvalue and eigenvalues
(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2(k^2+q^2)))/2 of opposite sign. Thus each point
on this critical curve is a saddle with one attracting and one repelling
normal direction for gradient flow. This does not assert a global
stable-manifold classification or small-step GD stability uniformly along
the noncompact curve.

## Prior work and limits

Tarzanagh et al., arXiv:2308.16898, PDF pp.3-4 defines KQ-ERM with
the explicit phrase 'for a fixed head'; Theorem 2 treats the factored
regularization path and nuclear-norm bias. Sheen et al., arXiv:2403.08699,
source sections/preliminariesAr.tex line 17 likewise fixes the linear
prediction head; its main diagonal/general theorems concern gradient flow
and exponential loss. Neither checked scope is this joint-head logistic
arbitrary-step invariant-region statement. This is a bounded comparison,
not a claim that no such result exists elsewhere. Factor-balance identities
and nuclear-norm bias are prior work, not claimed as discoveries here.
The result does not cover matrices, multiple heads, or the full R^3 basin partition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["q is a prime power and U is uniform on F_q^m","the coefficient vectors form an indexed family, repeats allowed","k >= 1 in the k-wise statement"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T12:14:23.635863+00:00","domain":"finite fields, linear algebra and independence","id":"claim_eba6dd79d22bf9641a03278d6cf52f8d375d65d722da060c6fff3fab3105bd34","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let q be a prime power, U uniform on F_q^m, and a_1, ..., a_r in F_q^m. For an index set I, the forms (a_i . U)_{i in I} are uniform on F_q^|I| (equivalently, mutually independent with each a_i . U uniform on F_q) if and only if the indexed family (a_i)_{i in I} is linearly independent, a repeated vector counting as a dependence. Consequently, for every integer k >= 1, the forms are k-wise independent with each form uniform on F_q if and only if every indexed subfamily of at most k coefficient vectors is linearly independent.
