{"assumptions":["(K1) subadditivity of the array","(K2) the joint law of the array is invariant under the index shift","(K3) E[X_{0,1}] finite and E[X_{0,n}] >= -cn","ergodicity is needed only for the conclusion that the limit is a constant"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542246+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory","id":"claim_ebec7808fe9525a999343d3c0f7cd49f6b8e5b5e3f851984870ca1aa89e16652","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"A SUBADDITIVE PROCESS is a family {X_{m,n} : 0 <= m < n} of integrable random variables satisfying: (K1) X_{0,n} <= X_{0,m} + X_{m,n} for every 0 < m < n; (K2) the joint distributions of the shifted family {X_{m+1,n+1}} are the same as those of {X_{m,n}} - full joint stationarity of the array under the index shift; (K3) E[X_{0,1}] is finite and E[X_{0,n}] >= -c n for every n, for some constant c. Then gamma = lim_n E[X_{0,n}]/n = inf_n E[X_{0,n}]/n exists and is finite, X = lim_n X_{0,n}/n exists almost surely and in L^1 with E[X] = gamma, and if the underlying shift is ERGODIC then X = gamma almost surely. (K3) is what stops the limit from being minus infinity; without the lower linear bound the almost sure limit can be -infinity. (K2) is a strong hypothesis and is exactly what Liggett's version weakens. For i.i.d. first-passage percolation on Z^d the array X_{m,n} = T(m e_1, n e_1) satisfies (K2) directly, because the whole environment is i.i.d. and the shift by e_1 is measure preserving and ergodic; that is why Kingman's original form already delivers the time constant along a coordinate axis. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.852796+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec046ef5bfbae7d7c5f49984291891d74af12d504cff7374a41c044c4d9ece2f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 17 (Eigenvector master equation — Wishart case) of arXiv:2511.12623, 'The eigenvector bead process'] Fix integers $N, T \ge 1$, and let $\{\lambda_i^{(N)}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ 
denote the (ordered, positive) eigenvalues of the Wishart matrix 
\(
W^{(N)} := X_{N}^{\!\top} X_{N} \in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}.
\)
Let $\{\mathbf{u}_i^{(N)}\}_{i=1}^{N}$ be the associated orthonormal eigenvectors. 
Consider the rank–one extension
\[
X_{N+1} = \big( X_N \;\; g \big),
\qquad g \in \mathbb{R}^{T},
\]
that is, $X_{N+1}$ is obtained by appending the column vector $g$ to $X_N$.
Let $W^{(N+1)} = X_{N+1}^{\!\top} X_{N+1}$, with eigenvalues 
$\{\lambda_i^{(N+1)}\}_{i=1}^{N+1}$ and eigenvectors $\{\mathbf{u}_i^{(N+1)}\}$.
We define
\(
g_i^{(N)} \;=\; \langle v_i^{(N)},\, g \rangle,
\)
where $v_i^{(N)}$ denotes the eigenvector associated with the eigenvalue 
$\lambda_i^{(N)}$ of the matrix $X_N X_N^{\!\top}$.

\smallskip
\noindent
Then the overlap coefficients
\(
\Omega^{(N)}_{ij} := 
\big\langle \mathbf{u}_i^{(N+1)},\, \mathbf{u}_j^{(N)} \big\rangle
\)
satisfy the relation
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\Omega^{(N)}_{k j}}{\Omega^{(N)}_{k i}} 
&= 
\frac{g_j^{(N)}}{g_i^{(N)}}
\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_j^{(N)}}{\lambda_i^{(N)}}}
\frac{\Delta_{k,i}^{(N)}}{\Delta_{k,j}^{(N)}},
\qquad 1 \le i,j \le N, \qquad
\frac{\Omega^{(N)}_{k,\,N+1}}{\Omega^{(N)}_{k i}} 
&= 
\frac{\Delta_{k,i}^{(N)}}{g_i^{(N)}}
\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda_i^{(N)}}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where
\(
\Delta_{k,i}^{(N)} := \lambda_k^{(N+1)} - \lambda_i^{(N)}.
\)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:06.155594+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec0f6d093f41e4be9467d6e9fa5464dee78c1ad78af1b3785ec7ea17a4cf83a9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 17 of arXiv:2608.22534, 'Entropy power inequalities in compact groups'] Let $G$ be a connected compact abelian group, let $\mu$ be its 
Haar probability measure and $Y$ be a random variable on $G$ with density $f_Y \in L^2(G)$. Let $S$ be a set of positive Haar measure and 
write $g_S = \frac{1}{\mu(S)}\mathbb{I}_S$ for the density of the 
random variable $U_S$ having the uniform distribution on $S$ and 
being independent of $Y$. Then,
\begin{equation} 
    \int_{G}(f_Y\ast g_S(x) - 1)^2\, dx \leq \eta_S\int_{G}(f_Y(x)-1)^2\, dx,
\end{equation}
where,
$$\eta_S = \left(\frac{\sin(\pi \mu(S))}{\pi \mu(S)}\right)^2.$$
Equivalently, 
\begin{equation} 
\chi^2(Y+U_S\,\|\,U_{G}) = \chi^2(Y+U_S\,\|\,U_{G} +  U_S)
\le
\eta_S\,\chi^2(Y\,\|\,U_{G}),
\end{equation}
where
$U_{G}$ is uniformly distributed on $G$ and independent of $U_S$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.671750+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ec285511def467c9a0f5b4cc56a7440330929154434848666fd8fb693871fd96","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 13 (Polynomial continuity on bounded sets) of arXiv:2608.04824, 'Strong Convergence for a General Class of Random Matrix Models'] Let \(Q=\sum_w\alpha_ww\) be a noncommutative \(*\)-polynomial in
\(d\) variables.  For \(M\geq1\), set
\[
 \operatorname{Lip}_M(Q)
 =\sum_{|w|\geq1}|\alpha_w|\,|w|M^{|w|-1}.
\]
If two tuples \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_d)\) and \(B=(B_1,\ldots,B_d)\) satisfy
\[
 \max_\kappa\bigl(\|A_\kappa\|,\|B_\kappa\|\bigr)\leq M,
 \qquad
 \delta=\max_\kappa\|A_\kappa-B_\kappa\|,
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 \|Q(A,A^*)-Q(B,B^*)\|\leq\operatorname{Lip}_M(Q)\delta.
\end{equation}
The same right-hand side bounds the difference of the normalized traces when

More generally, if \(Q=\sum_w C_w\otimes w\) has coefficients in a fixed
matrix algebra, the conclusions hold with

 \operatorname{Lip}_M(Q)
 =\sum_{|w|\geq1}\|C_w\|\,|w|M^{|w|-1}
\]
and with the tensor-product operator norm and normalized trace.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Bernoulli percolation on a locally finite TRANSITIVE infinite graph","the exponential-decay statement is asserted for finite-range models","the mean-field bound is quoted in the form stated in the paper's abstract"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543363+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ece8d7f1c3d22584194ee5dead73ab7ab9a536555aea7cc7a03d5465c516a331","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For Bernoulli percolation on an arbitrary locally finite transitive infinite graph, the phase transition is SHARP: (a) for every p < p_c the susceptibility is finite, chi(p) = E_p |C(0)| < infinity, and for FINITE-RANGE models the probability of an open path from the origin to distance n decays exponentially in n; (b) for every p > p_c the mean-field lower bound P_p(0 <-> infinity) >= (p - p_c)/p holds. {"assumptions":["a finite, irreducible, reversible Markov chain arising from a weighted graph with conductances c_e","the two states a, b are distinct vertices of the graph","the graph is connected, so hitting and commute times, and R_eff, are all finite","consistent normalization of the total conductance c_G matching the specific convention used for R_eff"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993395+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ecfa965d432e2bd30d8bada02d7468db0f78ae6ff3009f102b45977594aa17a9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For an irreducible, reversible Markov chain arising from a weighted graph with conductances c_e and total conductance c_G equal to the sum of conductances over all edges, the commute time C(a,b) = E_a[tau_b] + E_b[tau_a] between two vertices a, b satisfies the exact identity C(a,b) = 2 c_G R_eff(a,b), where R_eff(a,b) is the effective resistance in the associated electrical network. The identity is derived by checking that h(x) = P_x(hit a before b) is harmonic away from {a,b} and coincides with the network's voltage function, then relating expected hitting times to the network's energy dissipation. It converts questions about hitting, commute, and cover times of a reversible random walk into purely electrical or combinatorial resistance computations, enabling resistance-based bounds via series-parallel laws, Rayleigh monotonicity, or the Nash-Williams inequality on infinite graphs, on quantities such as cover time and mixing time. It does not directly give the individual one-way hitting time E_a[tau_b] alone, only the symmetrized commute time; and it is specific to reversible chains, since non-reversible walks lack the electrical-network correspondence and require substantially different techniques. Typical failure: Using the commute-time identity to bound a one-directional hitting time E_a[tau_b] alone by simply halving C(a,b), which is valid only under a separate symmetry argument between a and b; in general E_a[tau_b] and E_b[tau_a] can differ substantially even though their sum equals 2 c_G R_eff(a,b), so treating the identity as giving each one-way time individually, without additional justification, is a common overreach. Canonical reference: Chandra, Raghavan, Ruzzo, Smolensky and Tiwari, 1996, Random Structures and Algorithms; Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, 2016, Cambridge University Press, Chapter 2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.020696+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ed0ffd4b12f7995d8d423830dc3a8aaf9d1a97b601ac94daf24df36ec3d473ff","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 40 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(Z\) be a connected complete normal klt complex space of dimension

 d\mathfrak m=(4\pi)^{-(m+1)}e^{-f_Z}\,dV_{g_Z}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.666852+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ed3996b98d5415426cfd1f66d7ecdd8bdf7d751880578f07c083a451db55d37c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn Censored two-source exploration of arXiv:2609.00110, 'Phase Transition and Fluctuation Results for First-Passage Percolation on Spread-Out Cycle'] Initially,
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_1(0)=\{0\},
 \quad
 \widehat \mathsf{T}_1(0)=0,
 \quad
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_2(0)=\{U_n\},
 \quad
 \widehat \mathsf{T}_2(U_n)=0,
\end{align*}
and every other vertex is unlabelled.

Suppose that $q$ is an exploration time immediately after a vertex addition. For $i\in\{1,2\}$, define the active oriented boundary of label $i$ by
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\partial_i(q)
 :=
 \big\{(a,b):
 a\in\widehat\mathcal{A}_i(q),\
 b\notin\widehat\mathcal{A}_1(q)\cup\widehat\mathcal{A}_2(q),\
 \{a,b\}\in\mathcal{E}_n^{(\ell)}
 \big\}.
\end{align*}
If an unlabelled vertex remains, the next vertex-addition time is
\begin{align*}
 q^+
 :=
 \min_{i\in\{1,2\}}
 \min_{(a,b)\in\widehat\partial_i(q)}
 \big\{\widehat\mathsf{T}_i(a)+\go_{a,b}\big\}.
\end{align*}
On $\Omega_*$, this minimum has a unique minimizing triple $(i,a,b)$.
At time $q^+$, assign label $i$ to $b$ and set
\begin{align*}
 \widehat\mathsf{T}_i(b):=q^+,
 \qquad
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_i(q^+)
 :=\widehat\mathcal{A}_i(q)\cup\{b\},
 \qquad
 \widehat\mathcal{A}_{3-i}(q^+)
 :=\widehat\mathcal{A}_{3-i}(q).
\end{align*}
The labelled sets remain unchanged between successive vertex-addition times.

An edge is called a \emph{bridge} once its endpoints carry different labels. From that time onward, the bridge is censored: its weight is not tested against any further threshold, and the edge is never used for a subsequent vertex addition. The exploration is run without stopping at the first collision. After all vertices are labelled, the process is held fixed.

In rescaled time, define for $s\geqslant0$
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal{C}_i(s):=\widehat\mathcal{A}_i(s/\mathfrak{a}_\ell ),
 \qquad
 N_i(s):=|\mathcal{C}_i(s)|,
 \quad i=1,2,
\end{align*}
and let the bridge set and its cardinality be
\begin{align*}
	\mathcal{B}_s:=\big\{\{u,v\}\in\mathcal{E}_n^{(\ell)}:u\in\mathcal{C}_1(s),\ v\in\mathcal{C}_2(s)\big\},
 \qquad
 B_s:=|\mathcal{B}_s|.
\end{align*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:47:41.430489+00:00","domain":"first-order PDE","id":"claim_ed54d7f2f7b7a7d96dbbc8a67228d4b6ca38b4b45884e2cb0b37af76ddb0e0a2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a first-order quasilinear PDE a(x,y,u) partial u/partial x + b(x,y,u) partial u/partial y = c(x,y,u) for unknown u(x,y), the method of characteristics reduces the PDE to a family of ODEs. Parametrize characteristic curves (x(s),y(s)) together with z(s)=u(x(s),y(s)) along them by dx/ds=a(x,y,z), dy/ds=b(x,y,z), dz/ds=c(x,y,z). Along a solution of this system, u is automatically consistent with the PDE, since the chain rule gives dz/ds = (partial u/partial x)(dx/ds) + (partial u/partial y)(dy/ds) = a(partial u/partial x)+b(partial u/partial y), which equals c(x,y,z) exactly when the PDE holds. Solving the PDE with data prescribed on a noncharacteristic initial curve reduces to solving the characteristic ODEs from each point of that curve and assembling the resulting family into the solution surface, then, where the map from characteristic parameters to (x,y) is invertible, reading off u(x,y). The same idea extends to fully nonlinear first-order PDE F(x,u,Du)=0 via characteristic ODEs derived from F, which also propagate Du along the curves.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.022269+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ed572525f4f507948cfbb3986ce8e039c22f865556d7c1cb10be69898c62e346","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Informal) of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] Let $D$ be the Riemannian distance on the Stiefel manifold $\mathrm{St}(n,k)$~\footnote{For $1 \le k \le n$, the Stiefel manifold is
$\mathrm{St}(n,k)=\{ X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k} : X^\top X = I_k \}$.} and let $W_D$ be Wasserstein distance with cost $D$. Let $P^T(X)$ denotes the probability distribution induced by running the $k$-column walk for $T$ steps starting with $X \in \mathrm{St}(n,k)$. Then, for every $X,Y\in\mathrm{St}(n,k)$, the Wasserstein distance $W_D\left(P^T(X),P^T(Y)\right)$ is at most $\epsilon$ as long as 
\[
T = \Omega\big(n(k+\log n) \cdot \log (D(X,Y)/\epsilon) \big)~.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.747035+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ed581388fad192fa6e9c8864deb4a8c8567e01328d7f749d001c0ddead79debf","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 25 (Supercritical shape) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] If $p = \omega(1 / m)$ then $p \, (1-p)^m \,
  (T_{m,p} - m \log{m})$
  converges in law to an exponential distribution with rate $1$.
  \begin{proof}
    Recall from Lemma \ref{thm:coupling} that we can
    decompose $p \, (1-p)^m \, (T_{m,p} - m \log{m})$ as
    the sum of independent random variables
    $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m, 0} - m\log{m})$
    and $p\,(1-p)^m \, (T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$.
    The second random variable~has an exponential limit
    by Theorem~\ref{thm:supercritical}.

    The classical problem has mean
    $\E T_{m, 0} = m\log{m} + O(m)$ and
    variance $\Var(T_{m,0}) = O(m^2)$. Therefore,
    the first random variable's mean is 
    \[
      \E \left[ p\,(1-p)^m\left(T_{m,0} - m\log{m}\right) \right] = p \, (1-p)^m \, O(m) =
      O\left((p\,m) \, e^{-pm}\right) = o(1),
    \]
    and its variance is
    \[
      \Var\left( p\,(1-p)^m\,\left(T_{m, 0} - m\log{m}\right) \right) =
      p^2 \, (1-p)^{2m} \, O(m^2) =
      O\left((p\,m)^2 \, e^{-2pm}\right) = o(1).
    \]
    This implies $p\,(1-p)^m \, (T_{m,0} - m \log{m}) 
    \stackrel{P}{\to} 0$.
    Extend the convergence result using Slutsky's theorem.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.495356+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ed791b3a38e469c3cd0927559d5d4496e1d34909ecb000469b88dc55188b7a0f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm random coordinate change of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Suppose the driving function $\theta_t$ evolves according to the stochastic differential equation
\begin{equation}
d\theta_t = \sqrt{\kappa}\, dB_t + b\left(\theta_t; \Psi_t(\theta_1), \ldots, \Psi_t(\theta_n)\right)\, dt,
\end{equation}
where $B_t$ is standard Brownian motion, and $\Psi_t := \widetilde{h}_t \circ \tau \circ h_t^{-1}$ is the conformal coordinate change defined as in Theorem~(Loewner coordinate change in angular coordinate of the paper).

Define the transformed driving function
\[
\widetilde{\theta}_t := \Psi_t(\theta_t),
\]
and introduce the reparameterized time
\[
s(t) := \int_0^t |\Psi_u'(\theta_u)|^2 \, du.
\]

Then the process $\widetilde{\theta}_s := \Psi_{t(s)}(\theta_{t(s)})$ satisfies the following SDE:
\begin{equation}

d\widetilde{\theta}_s = \sqrt{\kappa}\, dB_s + \frac{b\left(\theta_s; \Psi_{t(s)}(\theta_1), \ldots, \Psi_{t(s)}(\theta_n)\right)}{\Psi_{t(s)}'(\theta_s)}\, ds + \frac{\kappa - 6}{2} \cdot \frac{\Psi_{t(s)}''(\theta_s)}{[\Psi_{t(s)}'(\theta_s)]^2} \, ds.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_i independent and mean zero","each X_i sub-exponential with finite psi_1 norm K_i","no boundedness and no identical distribution required","c is an absolute constant"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627795+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eda4180819f0b7157752389f126936b1be16f6ab1c12b592bae8cb80e5ad04c2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_N be independent, mean-zero, SUB-EXPONENTIAL random variables, and write K_i for the Orlicz norm ||X_i||_{psi_1} = inf{ s > 0 : E exp(|X_i|/s) <= 2 }. Then there is an absolute constant c > 0 such that for every t >= 0, P( | sum_{i=1}^N X_i | >= t ) <= 2 exp( - c min( t^2 / sum_{i=1}^N K_i^2 , t / max_i K_i ) ). The bound has TWO regimes and that is intrinsic, not an artefact: for small t the tail is Gaussian with variance proxy sum K_i^2, and for large t it is exponential with rate 1/max_i K_i. No almost sure bound on the summands is assumed, which is what distinguishes this from the classical bounded-summand Bernstein inequality; the price is that the sub-Gaussian regime ends at t of order sum K_i^2 / max K_i rather than continuing forever. Squares of sub-Gaussian variables are sub-exponential, which is why this is the inequality behind chi-square tail bounds and the Hanson-Wright inequality. The constant c is absolute and no attempt should be made to read a specific numerical value out of this statement. [standard; e.g. Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, Theorem 2.8.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.660216+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_edb1719bbf891ca09a000a2aeddc3b01b83a954c684d37ff15859bbb70863c52","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 24 of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] Let $\mathbf X \in G\Omega_p(V)$. For each $N\in\mathbb N$ and each $1\le i\le d$, let
\(
A_i^N:\Omega\to\mathfrak h_N
\)
be a Hermitian random matrix defined on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. Assume that the following hold.

First, for every $k\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\sup_{N\in\mathbb N}\sup_{1\le i\le d}\sup_{1\le m,l\le N}
\mathbb E\big[|A_i^N(m,l)|^k\big]\le c_A(k)<\infty,
\]
and moreover
\[
\mathbb E[A_i^N(m,l)]=0,
\qquad
\mathbb E[|A_i^N(m,l)|^2]=1.
\]

Second, there exists $K>0$ such that, for every $r\in\mathbb N$,
\[
\sup_{N\in\mathbb N}\sup_{0\le s<t\le T}
\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{1}{N^{r/2}}\|A_i^N(m,l)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^r\right]
\le K^r\Gamma\!\left(\frac{r}{2p}+1\right).
\]

Finally, assume that the sigma-algebras
\[
\bigvee_{i=1}^d \sigma(A_i^N(m,l)),
\qquad 1\le m\le l\le N,
\]
are independent, and that
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[A_i^N(m,l)A_j^N(m,l)\right]=0,
\qquad i\ne j.
\]

Define
\[
M^N\in\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb R^d,\mathfrak h_N),
\qquad
M^N(\eta)=\sum_{i=1}^d A_i^N\,\eta^{(i)}.
\]
Let $Z^N(\mathbf X)\in\mathcal D^p([0,T],U(N;\mathbb C))$ denote the solution of
\begin{equation} 
dZ^N(s,t)=\frac{i}{\sqrt N}M^N(d\mathbf X_t)\,Z^N(s,t),
\qquad
Z^N(s,s)=I_N.
\end{equation}

Then, for every $0\le s\le t\le T$ and for $\xi_N \in \mathcal{P}(\mathfrak{h}^d_N)$ denoting the law of the hermitian matrices $A^N_i$, the limit
\[
K(s,t)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\,
\mathbb E_{\xi_N}\!\left[\operatorname{Tr}(Z^N(s,t))\right]
\]
exists and is given by
\begin{equation}
K(s,t)=\sum_{|L|=0}^\infty i^{|L|}\varphi(L)\,S^{(L)}(\mathbf X)_{s,t}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, \(K\) solves the two-parameter RDE
\begin{equation}
K(s,t)=1-\int_s^t\int_s^r f(K(s,u),K(u,r))\,d\mathbf X_u\,d\mathbf X_r,
\end{equation}
where
\[
f:\mathbb R^2\to \mathrm{Hom}(V\boxtimes V, \mathbb{R}),
\qquad
f(z_1,z_2)[\eta,\xi]=z_1z_2\langle \eta,\xi\rangle_V.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A_n and A are self-adjoint on a common Hilbert space H","the mode of convergence (strong or norm resolvent) is as in the definition of resolvent convergence","in (a) the function f is continuous and vanishes at infinity","in (b) the function f is continuous and bounded on R","f(A) means the bounded functional calculus supplied by the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.091074+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, functional calculus","id":"claim_edb40d994798192517bbbdee299a16a72daef10511a135ab38712d7a8be01de0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A_n and A be self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space H, with no assumption relating their domains. (a) If A_n -> A in the NORM resolvent sense, then f(A_n) -> f(A) in operator norm for every continuous f : R -> C vanishing at infinity. (b) If A_n -> A in the STRONG resolvent sense, then f(A_n) -> f(A) strongly for every BOUNDED CONTINUOUS f : R -> C, where f(A) is given by the functional calculus of the spectral theorem. In particular exp(i t A_n) -> exp(i t A) strongly for every real t, and for a fixed vector the convergence is uniform for t in compact sets. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) 'bounded continuous' cannot be relaxed to 'bounded Borel'. On H = C take A_n = multiplication by 1/n and A = 0 (convergence in every sense) and f the indicator of (0, infinity): then f(A_n) = 1 for every n while f(A) = 0. Convergence of spectral projections therefore needs a separate hypothesis - typically that the endpoints of the interval carry no spectral mass for A - and even then it is only strong convergence. (ii) In (b) one gets strong, never norm, convergence, because strong resolvent convergence does not imply norm resolvent convergence: on l^2 let P_n be the orthogonal projection onto the coordinates with index at least n and set A_n = P_n, A = 0; then A_n -> 0 strongly and in the strong resolvent sense, while the resolvent difference has constant operator norm. (iii) Unbounded f is outside the theorem and the natural statement is false: strong resolvent convergence does not give A_n psi -> A psi, even for psi in every domain (rank-one examples with growing coefficients show this). (iv) Nothing is assumed about domains - that is exactly why the hypothesis is phrased through resolvents rather than as pointwise convergence of the operators.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T03:42:25.818122+00:00","domain":"probability, Brownian motion, ergodic theory","id":"claim_edd3ee191057c39ca763758870773c942f09e028e8ea0142c98e648c2215a077","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Burdzy and Scheutzow, Forward Brownian motion (arXiv:1302.6958), Problem 7.5 (p. 26) asks: for any process {X_t, t >= 0} whose law is equivalent to Brownian motion, can one find a random piece to put in front of X so that the new process is a Brownian motion? Our result (id P0032, 2026-09-08): YES - and under absolute continuity rather than equivalence, which is weaker than the problem assumes. The mechanism is a filling-scheme lemma: for theta an invertible ergodic measure-preserving transformation of a standard Borel space (E, P) and Q = f P, there is an almost surely finite integer N >= 0 with law(theta^N Z) = Q for Z distributed as P. Apply it with E = C_0(R) under two-sided Wiener measure and (theta w)(t) = w(t+1) - w(1), lifting the one-sided density of X's law to two-sided paths; the lemma returns a finite N for which {Z(N+t) - Z(N)} has X's law while {Z(t) - Z(0)} is a Brownian motion whose first N units are exactly the prefix. Verification as the source words it: the filling construction was implemented on a finite ergodic system (Z/n with the +1 shift) for n = 5, 7, 12, 60 with random densities - total accepted mass 1.000000000000 every time, the law of theta^N Z matching f P to about 1e-16, E[N] finite - and the negative control is the informative one, since with a non-ergodic theta exactly half the mass is ever accepted and half survives forever. The L^1 ergodic-theorem step in the infinite-dimensional setting was not verified, only read; it is standard but checked by eye only. NOVELTY IS THE WEAK POINT and the campaign's own proof file volunteers it: the lemma is a filling construction related to classical work of Chacon-Ornstein, Rost and Thorisson - sound mathematics, very likely a known consequence. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:31:20.863608+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ee65f7ce8f796ef704dd111b50a83716c68b98a02bd912c123476de1e13a2c89","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 3 of arXiv:2506.10856, 'The space of multifurcating ranked tree shapes: enumeration, lattice structure, and Markov'] The space $\mathcal{T}_{N,K}$ is in bijection with the set of vectors $\{t, l\}$, each of length $K$ that satisfy the following constraints:  
\begin{enumerate}[label={S\arabic*.}]
    \item $t_1=0$ and $1\leq t_i\leq i-1$: the parent of the root is labeled 0 and the parent of node $i$ must have smaller rank (label) than $i$. 
    \item $\sum_{i=1}^K l_i=N$: the total number of leaves is $N$.

{"assumptions":["One FCFS server","Poisson arrival rate lambda>0","Independent exponential service rate mu>lambda","Deterministic nonnegative setup tau and grace g","Setup is never cancelled; setup arrivals queue"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T08:07:30.221932+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ee901e9ab6079a52e8000f515d63eeed51c6cfe36449a529fc20f5c928a510cc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"PROOF OF THE STATED SCOPED RESULT; independent audit pending. Consider one FCFS server with Poisson arrival rate lambda>0 and independent exponential service rate mu>lambda. After becoming empty it remains on for deterministic grace g in [0,infinity], then switches off. A cold arrival triggers deterministic setup tau>=0, which is never cancelled; arrivals during setup wait. Put p=exp(-lambda g), x=lambda tau, rho=lambda/mu and y=p/(1+xp), with p=0 at g=infinity. The stationary mean queueing wait is lambda/[mu(mu-lambda)] + tau(1+x/2)y. If busy, on-idle, off and setup powers are B,I,O,U, average power is rho B+(1-rho)I+(1-rho)[O+xU-(1+x)I]y. Hence varying the grace period traces an affine waiting-power curve. The formula includes arrivals during setup and the subsequent busy period. It addresses k=1 and does not claim the many-server frontier or optimality among other policies.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:08.851897+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ee995522ed1e15c70f74b190d4e70387624f9742de07d15197ca3b2f7a63597a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 5 (Hard edge, \(q=1\)) of arXiv:2511.12623, 'The eigenvector bead process'] Fix \(K\in\mathbb{N}\) and an integer \(\alpha > K\).
Let \(T - N = \alpha\).
For each \(s\in\{0,\dots,K\}\), let \(\{\lambda^{(s)}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N+s}\) denote the spectrum of the matrix \(X_{N+s}^\top X_{N+s}\),
and define the point process
\[
\Theta_{N}^{(s)} \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{N+s} \delta_{\,4N\,\lambda_{j}^{(s)}}.
\]
Then the process \(\big(\Theta_{N}^{(s)}\big)_{s=0}^{K}\) forms a Markov chain in \(s\) and converges in distribution to the Markov chain driven by the operator \(\mathcal{T}\).
The limiting point process of eigenvalues
\(
\Theta^{(s)} \;=\; \lim_{N\to\infty} \Theta_{N}^{(s)}
\)
is the \emph{Bessel point process} of parameter~\(\alpha\), describing the universal statistics at the hard edge of the spectrum. \cite{forrester1993hard,tracy1994bessel,forrester2010log} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:44.527446+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_eec33edf4ae78009e0b5b174b9c69aad0c4d069c0fef2aa28876ddd785928871","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 8 of arXiv:2604.01748, 'Largest-loop-first loop-erased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^{4}$'] \begin{itemize}
   \item[(D1)] Let $b_{n} = n (\log n)^{-2}$ and $M = (\log n)^{2}.$ We divide the time interval $[0,n]$ into $M$ subintervals of equal length ($= b_{n}$) as follows. Let 
$$I^{1} (j) = \big[ n - j b_{n}, n - (j-1) b_{n} \big] =: [t^{1}_{j}, t^{1}_{j-1}] \ \ \ \text{ for \ \  $j =1, 2, \cdots , M$.} $$
 Note that $ 0 = t^{1}_{M} < t^{1}_{M-1} < \cdots < t^{1}_{1} < t^{1}_{0} = n. $

Similarly, we divide the time interval $[n,2n]$ in the same way as follows. Let 
$$I^{2} (j) = \big[ n + (j-1) b_{n}, n + j b_{n} \big] =: [t^{2}_{j-1}, t^{2}_{j}] \ \ \ \text{ for \ \  $j =1, 2, \cdots , M$.}$$
 Note that $ n= t^{2}_{0} < t^{2}_{1} < \cdots < t^{2}_{M-1} < t^{2}_{M} = 2n.  $

$$ L^{1} (j) = \text{len} \, \Big( \text{LE}^{\ast} \big( S [t^{1}_{j}, t^{1}_{j-1}  ] \big) \Big) \ \ \ \text{and } \ \ \ L^{2} (j) = \text{len} \, \Big( \text{LE}^{\ast} \big( S [t^{2}_{j-1}, t^{2}_{j}  ] \big) \Big). $$

As in (20) of \cite{DS-SW-4d}, we let 
$$ L^{\ast} = \max \big\{ j + k \ : \ I^{1} (j) \leftrightarrow I^{2} (k) \big\} $$
denote the size of the longest intersection. Here, for two intervals $I, J \subset [0, \infty)$, we write 
$$ I \leftrightarrow J \ \ \text{ if } \ \ \{ S(i) \ : \ i \in I \} \cap \{ S(j) \ : \ j \in J \} \neq \emptyset.$$
Clearly, $ 2 \le L^{\ast} \le 2M $. 

\item[(D3)] Set 
$$ L_{n}' = \text{len} \, \Big( \text{LE}^{\ast} \big( S[n,2n] \big) \Big). $$
Note that $L_{n}$ and $L_{n}'$ have the same distribution.

\item[(D4)] A time $k \in [0,n]$ is called a cut time (up to $n$) if $S[0,k] \cap S[k+1,n] = \emptyset$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.018469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ef0e055983c45f9e84e4f03798dc1e5f1c33166be79eb5ba51218262b537df3c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 19 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(n\ge2\).  Every tangent space at \(\xi\) is a metric soliton
flow with a distinguished probability measure.  Its time-\((-1)\) model
has the following properties.
\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Metric-flow conclusions.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(H\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em,
series=limitingpackage]
\item The regular locus \(\mathcal R\) is connected and dense,
\(d|_{\mathcal R}\) is its intrinsic length distance, and \(Z\) is a
complete locally compact length space equal to the metric completion of
\(\mathcal R\).
\item There is a smooth function \(f\) on \(\mathcal R\) for which
\begin{equation}
 \Rc_g+\nabla^2f=\frac12g\qquad\text{on }\mathcal R;
\end{equation}
the distinguished probability measure satisfies
\begin{equation}
 d\mathfrak m=(4\pi)^{-n}e^{-f}\,dV_g\quad\text{on }\mathcal R,
 \qquad \mathfrak m(Z\setminus\mathcal R)=0,
 \qquad \mathfrak m(Z)=1,
\end{equation}
and \(\mathfrak m\) has finite second moment.
\item The tangent space is an exact self-similar metric soliton flow.
On regular convergence charts, in time-compatible gauges, the rescaled
metrics and distinguished densities converge smoothly to \(g\) and the
positive density in \eqref{sp:eq:measure}.
\item For every compact \(K\subset Z\) and every \(p\in(2,4)\), the
zero extension of \(r_{\rm Rm}\) is one-Lipschitz and
\begin{equation}
 \Vol_g\bigl(\{r_{\rm Rm}<\varepsilon\}\cap K\cap\mathcal R\bigr)
 \le C_{K,p}\varepsilon^p,
 \qquad 0<\varepsilon<1;
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{K\"ahler conclusions.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(H\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em,
resume=limitingpackage]
\item The regular soliton \((\mathcal R,g,J)\) is K\"ahler, \(J\) is
parallel and time invariant, and the rescaled complex structures converge
smoothly to \(J\) on regular convergence charts.
\item If \(n=2\), then \(Z\) is a K\"ahler orbifold and
\(\Sing Z\) consists of isolated orbifold points.
\end{enumerate}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Complex-analytic conclusions.}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(H\arabic*)},leftmargin=3em,
resume=limitingpackage]
\item The space \(Z\) is a normal klt complex space.  Its analytic and
metric topologies agree, and its analytic and metric regular loci
coincide.  The regular K\"ahler form extends locally across \(\Sing Z\)
as a positive current with bounded potential.  Every point has a local
closed analytic embedding \(V\hookrightarrow\Omega_V\subset\C^L\) such
that, on \(V\cap\mathcal R\),
\begin{equation}
 \omega_g\ge c_V\omega_{\C^L}|_V.
\end{equation}
\item The function \(f\) extends uniquely to a locally Lipschitz function
on \(Z\).  The flow of \(\nabla f\) is complete, preserves
\(\mathcal R\), and extends to a one-parameter group of biholomorphisms
of \(Z\).
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X strictly stationary","phi the uniform mixing coefficient as defined in the survey"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.449097+00:00","domain":"probability, mixing conditions","id":"claim_ef18e259110a08c2a66fb270a7e1c1dc2a1d971060b11e339498f0c02a909fe1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Bradley, Basic properties of strong mixing conditions: a survey and some open questions (arXiv:math/0511078), Question 7 (Section 4.2, p. 19) asks: given an arbitrary nonincreasing sequence (b_1, b_2, ...) in [0,1], is there a strictly stationary sequence X with phi(n) = b_n for all n >= 1? Our result (id D0035, 2026-09-08): NO, refuted in one line from a result Bradley himself quotes - if phi(n) < 1/2 for some n >= 1 then X is phi-mixing, i.e. phi(n) tends to 0. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:59:58.430110+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ef1a0d92385511f20c92ada76cd9dcdfaba73515e539fad46827078b69a68363","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:extended.filtered.gaussian of arXiv:2604.22453, 'Adapted Wasserstein Barycenters of Gaussian Processes'] Let
\[
\mathscr L_K(T,d):=\{\mathbf L = (\mathbf{L}_{t,s})_{s,t = 1}^T \in (\mathbb{R}^{d\times Kd})^{T \times T}: \mathbf L_{t,s}=0\textup{ whenever }s>t\},
\]
where each $\mathbf{L}_{t,s}$ has $K$ column blocks $\mathbf{L}_{t,s}^{k} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$. For $a \in \mathbb{R}^{Td}$ and $\mathbf{L} \in \mathscr{L}_K(T, d)$, define the filtered process
\[
\mathbb{G}_K^{a,\mathbf L}:=\left(\mathbb{R}^{TKd},\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^{TKd}),\mathcal{N}_{TKd}(0,I),\mathbb{F}^{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}},X=a+\mathbf {L}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right),
\]
where $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}=(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t)_{t=1}^T$, $\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_t=(\epsilon_t^1,\ldots,\epsilon_t^K)$, is the canonical process and $\mathbb{F}^{\boldsymbol\epsilon}$ is the filtration generated by $\boldsymbol\epsilon$. Explicitly, for each $t$ we have
\begin{equation} 
X_t = a_t + \sum_{s = 1}^t \mathbf{L}_{t,s} \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_s = a_t + \sum_{s = 1}^t \sum_{k = 1}^K \mathbf{L}_{t,s}^{k} \epsilon_s^k. 
\end{equation}
We call $\mathbb{G}_K^{a,\mathbf L}$ an ensemble filtered Gaussian process and denote the corresponding space by $\mathcal{FG}_K(T,d)$, and its $\mathcal{AW}_2$-completion by $\mathrm{FG}_K(T,d)$. Letting $K=1$ recovers the standard filtered Gaussian process.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Deterministic initial coordinates with h_j e0,j squared=j^-gamma","Bt mutually independent fresh Gaussian inputs with covariance diag(j^-alpha)","Finite expected risk at deterministic t; finite-variance independent centered label noise","Updates lie in the span of observed inputs; data-dependent coefficients allowed","Independent review pending; optional optimal-step corollary depends on unaudited C02/C03."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:59:03.292447+00:00","domain":"stochastic optimization","id":"claim_ef32f8b8a5c7f1a6674c7630d45b5382c9f5f570bddb934911b55c4caa2768ce","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"PROOF (UNAUDITED), w741-T422-C06 v1. Not independently checked.
# T422 Target 2: a finite-sample-span upper confidence bound

Status: proof (unaudited), C06 v1. The constants below are explicit but the
bound is not asserted to have the sharp epsilon exponent of a typical noise
scale. The fixed-time theorem does not depend on C02 or C03; its final optional
optimal-step corollary inherits their unaudited status.

## Statement

Use the fresh Gaussian online least-squares model: H=diag(h_j),
h_j=j^(-alpha), alpha>1, deterministic initial errors satisfying
h_j e_0,j^2=j^(-gamma), gamma>1. Gaussian L2 predictions are used if the
coefficient vector is not in ordinary l2, as explained in model_conventions.md.
Labels have independent centered noise of finite variance sigma2>=0.
Each of t>=1 deterministic steps uses B>=1 independent fresh samples,
B an integer. A fixed positive step suffices. More generally, the proof
only requires that every update be a finite linear combination of that
step's input vectors, that the Bt inputs remain mutually independent with
law N(0,H), and that expected risk at t is finite.

For ell=1,2 define

    V(e)=sum_j h_j e_j^2,
    W_(ell+1)(e)=sum_j h_j^(ell+1)e_j^2,
    v_t=E V(e_t), Z_r=zeta(r),
    R_ell(e)=1+Z_(ell alpha)(V(e)+sigma2)/W_(ell+1)(e).

These are the single-example instantaneous noise scales: ell=1 is unweighted,
ell=2 is Hessian-weighted. Fix confidence parameter theta in (0,1), and put

    K=Bt, d=K+1,
    A_d=sum_(j=1)^d e_0,j^2/h_j=sum_(j=1)^d j^(2alpha-gamma)>0,
    L_den=h_d^(ell+2) A_d theta^2/(16d)>0.

Then

    P(W_(ell+1)(e_t)>=L_den)>=1-theta/2.                  (S1)

Consequently, with probability at least 1-theta, e_t!=0 and

    1+Z_(ell alpha) <= R_ell(e_t)
      <=1+[16d Z_(ell alpha)/(h_d^(ell+2)A_d theta^2)]
                   [2v_t/theta+sigma2].                  (S2)

The probability of e_t=0 is zero. If t is a finite first EXPECTED-risk
hit v_t<=epsilon Z_gamma, substitute that upper bound for v_t in (S2).
The hitting index is deterministic here; a realized-risk stopping time
requires an additional argument.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.098159+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ef9119e3836453638b603be47316c63ff5bce085976292045e49b4fde40c0310","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:supernode of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] After a weak chronological order has been fixed, a \emph{supernode} is

equality block contains at least two occurrences, or if its fused tensor
contains a nonsingleton packet, the time-indexed $-2N^{-1}W_i$ Jacobi
child, or a special root.  In particular, every surviving same-time
nonsingleton is hard, whether or not its occurrences are
column-connected.  Otherwise the block consists of exactly one occurrence
and is a passive singleton supernode carrying one of the four star

{"assumptions":["entries of Z i.i.d., mean zero, variance one (finite second moment suffices for the almost-sure convergence in the Bai-Silverstein form)","the spectral distribution of Sigma converges weakly to H; p/n -> c in (0, infinity)","Sigma and Z independent (Sigma may be random)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T07:53:48.737960+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_ef9d87ff35f4c090aed907a91632374e92ff38ec27c2bf7bbb3585b46a41183e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X = Z\\Sigma^{1/2}$ be $n \\times p$ with $Z$ having i.i.d. entries of mean $0$ and variance $1$, $\\Sigma$ positive semidefinite, and let $S = \\frac{1}{n}X^T X$. Then almost surely the empirical spectral distribution of $S$ converges weakly to a nonrandom probability measure $F = F^{c, H}$, characterised as follows: with $\\underline F = (1 - c)\\delta_0 + cF$ (the limiting spectral distribution of the $n \\times n$ companion $\\frac{1}{n}XX^T$) and $\\underline m(z) = \\int \\frac{d\\underline F(t)}{t - z} = -\\frac{1 - c}{z} + c\\,m_F(z)$, for every $z \\in \\mathbb{C}^+$ the value $\\underline m(z)$ is the unique solution in $\\mathbb{C}^+$ of $$z = -\\frac{1}{\\underline m} + c\\int \\frac{\\tau\\, dH(\\tau)}{1 + \\tau\\,\\underline m}.$$ Equivalently, $m_F$ solves $m_F(z) = \\int \\frac{dH(\\tau)}{\\tau\\,(1 - c - c z\\, m_F(z)) - z}$. {"assumptions":["independent coordinates with finite ranges","f real valued"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:50:16.134016+00:00","domain":"Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition on finite product spaces","id":"claim_efbdb008ccb6e350f19afa4b831a7f5eb8be29254ef907e1f0e1aedf7377ba81","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. Let A_q be a random set, independent of X, containing each coordinate independently with probability q in [0, 1], and M(q) = E over A_q of E Var(f | X_{A_q^c}). Then M(q) = sum over nonempty S of [1 - (1 - q)^|S|] w_S = Var(f) - J(1 - q), with J the Bernoulli reveal profile, and M(q) = (1/2) E[(f(X) - f(X^(A_q)))^2], where X^(A) redraws X_A independently from its own law. For every r >= 1, (-1)^(r+1) M^(r)(q) = sum_{k=r}^n (k)_r (1 - q)^(k - r) W_k >= 0 with (k)_r = k(k - 1)...(k - r + 1); so M is increasing and concave, M'(0) = sum_k k W_k = sum_i E Var(f | X_{-i}), and the derivatives at any q determine the spectrum. For a pure order-d function, J(p) = p^d Var(f) and M(q) = [1 - (1 - q)^d] Var(f).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:01:22.619863+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_efe18efd23b33db04725be1aa644693c5c20d0ef2dd75cbe7d84c4866c540a24","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Th th_2d_structure of arXiv:2606.23648, '\textsc{Optimal Stopping for a Diffusion with Unobserved Bernoulli Drift}'] In the setting of Theorem~(th_fixed_x_solution of the paper), the two-dimensional continuation region $\mathcal{C}$ has the sectional representation
    (equation C_sectional_representation of the paper), where each nonempty section \(\mathcal C_x\) is a bounded interval \((a(x),b(x))\). On this region the value function is given by
    \[
        U(x,y)=Q(x)G(y)+R(x)-cyG(y),
        \qquad a(x)<y<b(x),
    \]
    in the notation of (equation def_q_R_coefficients of the paper), (equation def_G of the paper),
    while \(U(x,y)=k(x+y)\) outside \(\mathcal C\).

    \noindent \textbf{(i)} \quad 
    The continuation region expands diagonally: if \((x,y)\in\mathcal C\) and
    \(h\ge0\), then
    \(
        (x+h,y-h)\in\mathcal C.
    \)
    Consequently, \(\mathcal I\) of (equation def_I_active of the paper) is a right-interval, \(d(x)=x+a(x)\) is non-increasing on \(\mathcal I\), and diagonal contact is sticky: if
    \(a(\bar x)=-\bar x\) for some \(\bar x\in\mathcal I\), then
    \(
        a(x)=-x,\, x\in\mathcal I,\, x\ge\bar x.
    \)
    
    \noindent If, in addition, (ass_3 of the paper) holds, then the continuation region expands vertically:
    \[
        (x,y)\in\mathcal C,\ h\ge0
        \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
        (x+h,y)\in\mathcal C.
    \]
    In particular,
    \[
        a(x+h)\le a(x),
        \qquad
        b(x+h)\ge b(x),
        \qquad x\in\mathcal I,\ h\ge0.
    \]

    \noindent \textbf{(ii)} \quad 
    The free boundaries satisfy the integral equations (equation interior_boundary_system_2d of the paper), (equation active_boundary_system_2d of the paper) below. If the relevant side branches of \(y\mapsto\Phi(x,y)\) have no flat portions, then the boundary functions are continuous on intervals where the boundary regime is fixed. At regular points, where the corresponding values of \(H\)  of (equation def_H_2d of the paper) do not vanish, the boundaries are of class \(C^1\) and satisfy the differential equations of Proposition~(prop_boundary_regular_odes of the paper).

    \noindent \textbf{(iii)} \quad 
    The value function is non-decreasing in both $x$ and $y$ variables. Moreover, it satisfies smooth fit in the displacement variable $y$ at the upper boundary and at every interior lower boundary. At regular boundary points it also satisfies horizontal smooth fit.

    \noindent \textbf{(iv)} \quad 
    Finally, if \(k'(0+)\le c\), then the lower boundary never touches the diagonal:
    \[
        a(x)>-x,\qquad x\in\mathcal I.
    \]
    If \(k'(0+)>c\) and \(k(r)=o(e^{2r})\) as \(r\to\infty\), then the lower
    boundary eventually coincides with the diagonal:
    \[
        a(x)=-x
        \quad\text{for all sufficiently large }x\in\mathcal I.
    \]
    In the non-contact case, under the same subcritical growth condition and assuming that
    \(
    \rho
    \coloneqq
    \sup\{r\ge0:k'_+(r)\le c\}
    \)
    is finite, one has
    \(
        x+a(x)\to\rho
    \)
    as $x\to\infty.$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:24:20.646987+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f01efc4c1dae1d5ba2c3d43b8a0c4eb7d59495e3d46b36542a90b2f8eb385184","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma LemGroundStateVisitation of arXiv:2608.11178, 'A submartingale for the probability of avoiding the origin in one-point interaction ground'] Fix \(d\in\{2,3\}\), \(T,\gamma>0\), and \(x\in\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}\). X_t
=
x

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.763741+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f03b3d2f17cb0c0e4939269befce52ca52c06989d6166c07e7deb999b918fd50","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 8 (Integration regimes) of arXiv:2512.04646, '\textbf{Canonical Rough Path over Tempered Fractional Brownian Motion: Existence, Construc'] Let $B_{H,\lambda}$ be a tfBm and $X$ a suitable integrand path.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item For $H > 1/2$, the rough path integral
    $\int X\,d\mathbf{B}_{H,\lambda}$ coincides with the Young
    integral $\int X\,dB_{H,\lambda}$ and equals the limit of
    left Riemann sums.
  \item For $H \in (1/4,1/2]$, the Young integral does not exist in
    general, but the rough path integral
    $\int X\,d\mathbf{B}_{H,\lambda}$ is well-defined via the
    Sewing Lemma \cite[Lemma~4.2]{FrizHairer2014}.
  \item For adapted square-integrable integrands and $H > 1/4$,
    the rough path integral agrees with the stochastic integral of
    \cite{MeerschaertSabzikar2014}.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542735+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f03dd267f4dbe993abe345addd53bd73d98a6535068e27ed077b61bcdaa98a66","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"In BOND percolation on a graph G with parameter p in [0,1], each edge is declared open with probability p and closed otherwise, independently; P_p denotes the resulting product measure on {0,1}^{E(G)}. The open cluster C(x) of a vertex x is the set of vertices reachable from x through open edges. Write theta(p) = P_p( |C(0)| = infinity ) for a fixed origin. Coupling all parameters on a common family of independent uniform variables - edge e open at level p exactly when U_e <= p - shows theta is nondecreasing, so the CRITICAL PROBABILITY p_c(G) = sup{ p : theta(p) = 0 } = inf{ p : theta(p) > 0 } is well defined. SITE percolation is defined analogously with vertices; the two have different critical values on the same graph, and p_c^{bond} <= p_c^{site} on any graph. On Z^d with d >= 2 one has 0 < p_c < 1, with the explicit elementary bounds 1/(2d-1) <= p_c^{bond}(Z^d) < 1. The value is known exactly only in special cases, most famously p_c^{bond}(Z^2) = 1/2. Whether theta(p_c) = 0 in every dimension is a celebrated open problem: it is known for d = 2 (Harris and Kesten) and, by lace-expansion methods, in high dimensions - Hara and Slade for large d, later reduced to d >= 11 by Fitzner and van der Hofstad - and it was still open for the intermediate dimensions 3 <= d <= 10 at the time this node was written. [standard; e.g. Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Chapters 1 and 8]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U bounded open subset of R^n, T > 0","coefficients a^{ij}, b^i, c continuous and bounded on U_T, a^{ij} symmetric","uniform parabolicity a^{ij} xi_i xi_j >= theta |xi|^2, theta > 0","u in C^2_1(U_T) cap C(closure of U_T)","(i) c identically 0; (ii) c >= 0; (iii) c bounded, any sign"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.105343+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_f03e386fb9557b285d496bfc6d87098fa7e50ca3e1ef3cd59aee58e564394ae8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $U\\subset\\mathbb R^n$ be bounded and open, $T>0$, and let $\\partial_t+L$, $Lu=-a^{ij}u_{x_ix_j}+b^iu_{x_i}+cu$, be uniformly parabolic with coefficients continuous and bounded on $U_T$. Then there is a DETERMINISTIC, convex, COMPACT set B_nu in R^d with NON-EMPTY INTERIOR, symmetric about the axes, such that for every eps > 0, P( (1-eps) B_nu is contained in B(t)/t which is contained in (1+eps) B_nu for all large t ) = 1. The set B_nu is the unit ball of the time constant. Condition (i) is NOT merely convenient: if it fails then for every C > 0 the sum over x of P(m(x) > C|x|) diverges, where m(x) is the minimum weight over the edges at x, and Borel-Cantelli forces T(0,x)/|x| > C for infinitely many x almost surely, so the shape statement itself fails. Condition (ii) is what keeps the shape bounded: if F(0) >= p_c the time constant vanishes (Kesten) and B_nu is all of R^d; zero-weight edges percolate when F(0) > p_c, but at F(0) = p_c they do not in d = 2 or in high dimensions, so it is the vanishing time constant, not percolation of zero-weight edges, that unbounds the shape. What is NOT known, and is repeatedly imported elsewhere as an unproven hypothesis: whether the boundary of B_nu is STRICTLY CONVEX, whether it is DIFFERENTIABLE, and whether it has uniformly positive CURVATURE. Those are open for every non-degenerate weight distribution in every dimension, which is why the Newman-Piza exponent bounds and the directed-geodesic results carry non-constructive curvature or differentiability hypotheses. B_nu is not computed explicitly for any non-trivial F. [Cox and Durrett (1981), verified against Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Section 2.2]","status":"unverified"}

    \begin{enumerate}

        We call $\langle \Pi_{\lambda\in \Lambda}\mathcal{B}_\lambda\rangle$ the \emph{direct product bornology} on $\Pi_{\lambda\in \Lambda} S_\lambda$.
        \item Let $P$ be a set and $f$ a map from $P$ to the bornological space $S$.
        Then the family $f^*\mathcal{B}_S:=\{f^{-1}(B)\subset P\mid B\in \mathcal{B}_S\}$ forms a bornological base on $P$.
        We call $\langle f^*\mathcal{B}_S \rangle $ the \emph{inverse image bornology} of $\mathcal{B}_S$ by the map $f$. 
        In particular, if $P$ is a subset of $S$ and the map $f$ is the inclusion map, the bornology $f^*\mathcal{B}_S =\langle f^*\mathcal{B}_S \rangle $ is called the \emph{subbornology} of $\mathcal{B}_S$.
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

We assign the height $v$ to the boundary of the domain. Thereby, each gasket in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ can be uniquely attached a height corresponding to the sum of labels of loops $s_\ell$ in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ strictly surrounding this gasket, including the boundary of the domain. Equivalently we can attach a height to each loop in CLE$_4^{\rm nest}$ by considering the sum of labels of loops surrounding and including this loop and the boundary. In particular, for each $z \in D \cap \mathbb{Q}^2$, the boundary of the connected component of

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.378087+00:00","domain":"set theory","id":"claim_f0d630daf2b020660e71ada6912cbc65cadaabb956acfe1ff58ddf76f6278e47","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The axiom of choice (AC) states: for every family {A_i : i in I} of nonempty sets, indexed by any set I, there exists a choice function c defined on I with c(i) in A_i for every i. Equivalently: every Cartesian product of nonempty sets is nonempty; every surjection has a right inverse; every set of nonempty pairwise disjoint sets has a transversal selecting one element from each. Over the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms ZF, the axiom of choice is equivalent to Zorn's lemma and to the well-ordering theorem, and also to Tychonoff's theorem for arbitrary compact spaces. AC is independent of ZF: Godel (1938) showed ZF plus AC is consistent if ZF is (constructible universe), and Cohen (1963) showed ZF plus the negation of AC is consistent if ZF is (forcing). Countable and finite choices do not follow from ZF alone in general, but AC is provable in ZF for finite index sets I by induction.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:15:16.652975+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f109537594b0900804d470c77d7ea62e778c46fc9f5f9d964e6ab5f7804411a6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] Set
\(
  U_1
  :=
  |\Phi_1|_{\sigma_0}^2
  =
  \frac{|\phi_1|^2}{\rho^2}.
\)
Then
\begin{equation}
  \dot H_0=0,
  \qquad
  \ddot H_0
  =
  -4(\Delta_0-2)^{-1}U_1.
  
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every $k\ge 0$,
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
  \widehat\sigma_t
  ={}&
  \sigma_0
  +2t\operatorname{Re}\Phi_1
  \\
  &+
  \frac{t^2}{2}
  \left[
    2\operatorname{Re}\Phi_2
    +
    \left(
      2U_1-4(\Delta_0-2)^{-1}U_1
    \right)\sigma_0
  \right]
  +O_{C^k}(t^3).
  \end{aligned}
  
\end{equation}
Here $O_{C^k}(t^3)$ means that, after subtracting the displayed
terms up to order two, the remainder $R_t$ satisfies
\(
  \|R_t\|_{C^k(X_0,\sigma_0)}\le C_k |t|^3
\)
for $|t|$ sufficiently small. Equivalently, all covariant derivatives
of $R_t$ up to order $k$, computed with respect to $\sigma_0$, are
uniformly $O(t^3)$.
Equivalently, in the coordinate $z$,
\begin{equation}
  \begin{aligned}
  \widehat\sigma_t
  ={}&
  \rho\,dz\,d\bar z
  +
  t\left(
    \phi_1\,dz^2+\overline{\phi_1}\,d\bar z^2
  \right)
  +
  \frac{t^2}{2}
  \Bigg[
    \phi_2\,dz^2+\overline{\phi_2}\,d\bar z^2
  \\
  &+
    \left\{
      \frac{2|\phi_1|^2}{\rho^2}
      -
      4(\Delta_0-2)^{-1}
      \left(
        \frac{|\phi_1|^2}{\rho^2}
      \right)
    \right\}
    \rho\,dz\,d\bar z
  \Bigg]
  +O_{C^k}(t^3).
  \end{aligned}
  
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

	\begin{enumerate}[\rm (1)]

	\item $\omega \mapsto \int_{S_n} X^n_s \, \nu_n(\od s)$ is $\cF/\cB(\cX)$-measurable and Bochner $\bP$-integrable.
	
	\item $\int_{S_n} \lt\|X^n_s\rt\| \nu_n(\od s) < \infty$ a.s. and $\bE\|X^n_s\| < \infty$ for $\nu_n$-a.e. $s \in S_n$.
	\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:52:57.674714+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f1b8f83343792a4f9b6990d619b4dfba6e5168dd8bb6f1e2602b63a42d5dd632","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 7 of arXiv:2609.02686, 'The Bonnet-Myers theorem on Finsler manifolds with integral weighted Ricci curvature bound'] Let $(M, F, m)$ be an $n$-dimensional $(n \geq 2)$ forward complete Finsler metric measure manifold with $\Lambda_F<\infty$. Assume that $\mathbf{S}\geq -\vartheta$ for some $\vartheta \geq 0$.
Given constants $p \in (\frac{n}{2}, n]$, $\alpha\in [\frac{1}{2},1)$ and a fixed point $x_{0}\in M$. Then,  for $0 \leq r < R_{0}$ and an arbitrarily fixed point $x\in M$ satisfying that $d_{F}(x_{0}, x) \leq \Lambda_{F}^{-1}\left( R_{0}-r\right)$, there exist positive constants $D_{1}=D_{1}(n, p, \vartheta , R_{0})$ and $D_{2}=D_{2}(n,p,\Lambda_{F},\vartheta,\alpha,R_{0})$, such that, when $\overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{0}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, \vartheta}<D_{1}^{-\frac{2p-1}{p}}$, we have
\beq
&& \left(\frac{m\left(B_{\Lambda_{F}^{-1}r}^{+}(x)\right)}{m\left(B_{R_{0}}^{+}(x_{0})\right)}\right)^{\frac{1}{2 p-1}} \geq  \Big[\frac{1}{4} \left(1-D_{1} \overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{0}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, \vartheta}^{\frac{p}{2p-1}}\right)
e^{-\frac{\vartheta R_{0}}{2 p-1}}\Lambda_{F}^{-\left(2 \vartheta R_{0}b(p,\alpha)+\frac{5n}{2p-1}\right)}   \nonumber \\
&& \times \left(\frac{r}{R_{0}}\right)^{\vartheta R_{0} b(p,\alpha)+\frac{4n-2p}{2p-1}}  -  \frac{D_{2}\overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{0}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, \vartheta}^{\frac{p}{2p-1}}}{1-D_{1} \overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{0}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, \vartheta}^{\frac{p}{2p-1}}} \Big] \left(\frac{r}{R_{0}}\right)^{\frac{2p-n}{2p-1}}, 
\eeq
where

{"assumptions":["Abel: sum a_n converges","Tauber: f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below and n a_n -> 0 (Littlewood: a_n = O(1/n) suffices, with a harder proof)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476957+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_f1cba3555b43f0874b98c5a0afc289242890ff7c78565e100e36b9d11679d3e9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Abel's theorem (the Abelian direction): if the series sum a_n converges to s, then the power series f(x) = sum a_n x^n converges for |x| < 1 and f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below. The converse is false in general: f(x) = sum (-1)^n x^n = 1/(1 + x) tends to 1/2 while sum (-1)^n diverges. Tauber's theorem (the Tauberian direction): if f(x) = sum a_n x^n converges for |x| < 1, f(x) -> s as x -> 1 from below, and n a_n -> 0, then sum a_n converges to s. Littlewood strengthened the condition to a_n = O(1/n) (Littlewood's Tauberian theorem, 1911), and Hardy and Littlewood showed that a one-sided bound n a_n >= -C also suffices. 'Abelian' theorems pass from a summability method's convergence to a weaker one; 'Tauberian' theorems go back under an extra growth condition on the terms.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the operator is trace class, or the kernel is continuous and positive semidefinite (Mercer) on a compact space with a finite Borel measure of full support","the kernel is a continuous representative, so that its diagonal values are defined","an L^2 kernel alone determines only a Hilbert-Schmidt operator, whose diagonal is undefined"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573486+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, integral operators, operator ideals","id":"claim_f1fc0fc20e90cd54d10bec9762389999f830637cbe5b30da36ffa8f104d5b56e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For an integral operator T_k on L^2 with kernel k, the formula tr T_k = integral of k(x,x) dx is not a definition and not automatic. (1) An L^2 kernel is an equivalence class modulo null sets, and on a nonatomic space the diagonal is a null set, so k(x,x) has no meaning at all without choosing a distinguished representative; different representatives give different 'diagonal integrals'. (2) Continuity of the kernel is not enough for trace class. Carleman's example: there are continuous 2pi-periodic functions g whose Fourier coefficients are not absolutely summable. The convolution operator (T f)(x) = (1/(2 pi)) times the integral over the circle of g(x - y) f(y) dy has the continuous kernel k(x,y) = g(x - y)/(2 pi), is normal with eigenvalues the Fourier coefficients of g and eigenfunctions the exponentials, so its singular values are the moduli of those coefficients; hence T is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class, while the naive diagonal integral is the finite number g(0). (3) What does hold: if T is trace class on L^2([a,b]) and has a continuous kernel on [a,b] x [a,b], then tr T = integral of k(x,x) dx; and by Mercer's theorem, if k is continuous, symmetric and positive semidefinite on a compact interval (more generally on a compact metric space with a finite Borel measure of full support), then the associated operator is trace class, the eigenfunction series converges absolutely and uniformly, and tr T = integral of k(x,x) dx = sum of the eigenvalues. So the safe routes are positivity plus continuity (Mercer), or an independent proof of trace class plus continuity; 'the kernel is nice' by itself is not a proof.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:11:02.375742+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f228afb5fec46a77ed7a68dc1f47d716ae8d82f9cf50f0d93b7eb9f226275609","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] We have $S_1\sim\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}(n-\sqrt{n})^{1/2}$
    \begin{proof}
        We may compute $S_1$ explicitly. We have, via a combinatorial identity,
        \[S_1=\frac{n-2m-3}{2^{n-2m-4}}\binom{n-2m-4}{\frac{n}{2}-m-2}\]
        By a special case of Stirling's estimate, we have
        \[\binom{n}{n/2}\sim 2^n(\pi n/2)^{-1/2}\] 
        This gives
        \[S_1\sim \frac{(n-2m-3)(2^{n-2m-4})}{(2^{n-2m-4})\sqrt{\pi(\frac{n}{2}-m-2)}}=\frac{(n-2m-3)}{\sqrt{\pi(\frac{n}{2}-m-2)}}\]
        \[=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(\frac{n-2m-3}{\sqrt{n-2m-4}}\right)\]
        \[=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(\frac{n-\left\lceil\sqrt{n-1}\right\rceil-2}{\sqrt{n-\left\lceil\sqrt{n-1}\right\rceil-3}}\right)\]
        \[\sim\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}(n-\sqrt{n})^{1/2}\]
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a well-defined nonnegative counting or indicator-sum random variable X = sum_i X_i","a computable or boundable first moment E[X]","a computable or boundable second moment E[X^2], in particular control of the pairwise correlations E[X_i X_j]","the correlation sum not growing asymptotically faster than (E[X])^2"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.982598+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f22c0577c492845332c3c1bfdcfe54194e3ac9704f0f1fdb3d81ba1f6e0e27d5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a nonnegative random variable X, typically a count of some combinatorial structure written as X = sum_i X_i for indicator random variables X_i, the Paley-Zygmund inequality gives P(X > 0) >= (E[X])^2 / E[X^2]. Expanding E[X^2] = E[X] + sum_{i != j} E[X_i X_j], the method succeeds in proving P(X>0) is bounded away from 0 exactly when the pair-correlation sum sum_{i != j} E[X_i X_j] is of the same order as (E[X])^2, that is, when correlations between the indicators do not overwhelm the square of the mean. This is the standard route to existence results, such as an infinite cluster, a long crossing, or a large clique, once a first-moment computation has already established that E[X] is large or diverging, complementing the first-moment method, which by Markov's inequality only ever gives upper bounds on P(X>0). The method does not give any rate of convergence beyond the crude Paley-Zygmund ratio, gives no lower bound at all if the correlation structure is not controlled, and can produce a vacuous (near-0) bound whenever the variance is dominated by rare, strongly correlated configurations even though the mean itself is large. Typical failure: Computing a large or diverging first moment E[X] and declaring existence of the structure without bounding E[X^2]; if the indicators X_i are strongly positively correlated (a common situation for overlapping structures), the pair-correlation term can dominate (E[X])^2, making the Paley-Zygmund bound vacuous even as E[X] -> infinity, which is exactly the situation where a large first moment gives a false sense of near-certain existence. Canonical reference: Paley and Zygmund, 1932, Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society; Alon and Spencer, The Probabilistic Method, fourth edition, Wiley.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:14:57.697915+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f28cced144ddd8d12a6fff5a14ac4b95f1bf1902889b9a579971a1efe1c90cdb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma area Lemma of arXiv:2605.29095, 'Asymptotics of the number of components of random polynomial lemniscates'] [Area Theorem] [Ahlfors], [crane-polynomialpreimage] 
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Let \( f \) be a univalent (injective holomorphic) function on a domain \( D \subseteq \mathbb{C} \), and let \( K \subset D \) be a measurable set. Then the area of the image \( f(K) \) is given by:
\[
\text{Area}\big(f(K)\big) = \int_K |f'(z)|^2 \, dA(z),
\]
where \( dA(z) = dx \, dy \) denotes the Euclidean area element in \( \mathbb{C} \).
\item Let \( p \) be a polynomial of degree \( n \) over \( \mathbb{C} \), and let \( K \) be any measurable subset of the complex plane. Let \( n(z, p, K) \) be the number of preimages of \( z \) under \( p \) that lie in \( K \) counted with multiplicity. Then,
\begin{align}
    \int_{\mathbb{C}} n(z, p, K)\, dA(z) = \int_K |p'(z)|^2\, dA(z).
\end{align}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:54:12.629651+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2985b380df672ca006dd72171da5601738e771bd695b2c1682f7e5387b705ab","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma L:basis-for-comparison of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $y_1 \le y_2 \in \mathbb{Z}, t \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $[x,1]_{\textsf{L}}\le [y_1,t]_{\textsf{L}}$ and $[x,1]_{\textsf{L}}\le [y_2,t]_{\textsf{L}}$, and take $f:\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. on the event where a geodesic in $E^f$ from $[0,0]_{\textsf{L}}$ to $[y_1, t]_{\textsf{L}}$ intersects $\{[r, 1]_{\textsf{L}} : r \ge x\}$. Similarly,

E[x, 1; y_2, t]_{\textsf{L}} - E[x, 1; y_1, t]_{\textsf{L}} \ge E^f[0,0; y_2, t]_{\textsf{L}} - E^f[0,0; y_1, t]_{\textsf{L}},

{"assumptions":["rows i.i.d. with finite fourth moments","M/n -> c > 0, m/n -> r in (0,1)","the two parts of the split are disjoint (independence of V_1 and S_2 is what carries the argument)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:40:20.563112+00:00","domain":"covariance estimation","id":"claim_f2a2a51ee2fc2c34c5acc49ed5282836e853f6346ca1c35a46bb72807e699342","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X$ be $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^M$ with covariance $\\Sigma$. Split the rows into two independent parts of sizes $m$ and $n - m$ with sample covariances $S_1 = V_1\\Lambda_1 V_1^T$ and $S_2$. The nonparametric eigenvalue-regularised covariance estimator is $\\hat\\Sigma = V_1 \\operatorname{diag}(V_1^T S_2 V_1)\\, V_1^T$, averaged over $K$ random splits. Then: (i) $\\mathbb{E}[V_1^T S_2 V_1 \\mid V_1] = V_1^T \\Sigma V_1$, so each diagonal entry $v_i^T S_2 v_i$ is an unbiased estimate of the population variance in the direction $v_i$ - the Ledoit-Peche oracle $d_i^* = v_i^T\\Sigma v_i$ evaluated on independent data; (ii) as $M, n \\to \\infty$ with $M/n \\to c > 0$ and $m/n \\to r \\in (0,1)$, $\\hat\\Sigma$ is asymptotically optimal in Frobenius loss among estimators of the form $V_1 D V_1^T$ with $D$ diagonal (Lam 2016, Theorem 1); (iii) $\\hat\\Sigma$ is positive semidefinite and carries no bandwidth, floor or shrinkage constant beyond the split fraction (Lam recommends choosing $m$ by minimising $\\|\\hat\\Sigma_m - S\\|_F$ over a grid; $m = n/2$ is the usual default). A population direction of genuinely small variance keeps a small estimate (its held-out variance is small too); a direction whose small sample variance was a finite-sample cancellation receives the variance it actually has out of sample.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E and C symmetric p x p; the estimator class is restricted to the eigenvectors of E"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:50:37.943255+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_f2c72c8f5c4a1fb5da7d3fb5c8cdf44405907d5be714dd864209131af7efd314","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $E$ be a symmetric $p \\times p$ matrix with eigen-decomposition $E = \\sum_k \\lambda_k u_k u_k^T$ (for instance a sample covariance) and let $C$ be any symmetric $p \\times p$ matrix (the population covariance). Among all estimators of the form $\\Xi = \\sum_k \\xi_k u_k u_k^T$ - the same eigenvectors as $E$, free eigenvalues - the Frobenius loss $\\|\\Xi - C\\|_F^2$ is minimized by the oracle choice $\\xi_k^{\\mathrm{or}} = u_k^T C u_k$, the projection of the population matrix onto the $k$-th sample eigenvector, with minimal loss $\\|C\\|_F^2 - \\sum_k (u_k^T C u_k)^2$. In particular the oracle eigenvalues are convex combinations of the population eigenvalues (they lie between the smallest and largest population eigenvalue) and their sum equals $\\operatorname{tr} C$: a rotationally invariant estimator that is optimal in Frobenius loss never moves the trace and always shrinks the spread of the sample spectrum toward the population spread.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:29:00.756992+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f2c8ae5ef5ac85c776bfa5f4ce43dd5aa65d1dc2314cc459488cebd658f030a8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 11 of arXiv:2512.03884, '2512.03884'] Let $\alpha$ be a quadratic irrational, let $ax^2+bx+c$ be its minimal polynomial with $a,b,c \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\mathrm{gcd}(a,b,c)=1$ and $a>0$, and let $Q(x,y)=ax^2+bxy+cy^2$ be the corresponding binary quadratic form. For any constant $\theta>1$ and any integer $M \ge 1$, we have
\[ \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{1}{m^{\theta} \| m \alpha \|^{\theta}} = c(\alpha, \theta) \log M +O(1) \]
with an implied constant depending only on $\alpha$ and $\theta$. The constant $c(\alpha, \theta)$ is given by
\[ c(\alpha, \theta) = \frac{D^{\theta/2}}{\log \varepsilon} \sum_{\substack{n \in \mathbb{Z} \\ n \neq 0}} \frac{R_Q(n)}{|n|^{\theta}}, \]
where $D=b^2-4ac>0$ is the discriminant, $R_Q(n)$ is the number of primary representations of $n$, and $\varepsilon=(t_0+u_0\sqrt{D})/2$ with the smallest positive solution $(t_0,u_0)$ of Pell's equation $t^2-Du^2=4$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X_n) a martingale with respect to (F_n)","for the optional stopping consequence: tau an almost surely finite stopping time and the martingale uniformly integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627236+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3381e7ccdd3a3ab4f50fa4aa3f0083f4b6eac81113da66a80d044e9f35491f6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_n)_{n >= 0} be a martingale for a filtration (F_n) and let F_infinity be the sigma-algebra generated by the union of the F_n. The following are equivalent: (i) the family {X_n} is uniformly integrable; (ii) X_n converges almost surely AND in L^1 to some X_infinity; (iii) there exists Y in L^1 with X_n = E[Y | F_n] almost surely for every n, that is the martingale is CLOSED. When these hold one may take Y = X_infinity, and X_infinity = E[Y | F_infinity]. Consequences: for a UI martingale, E[X_infinity] = E[X_0], and the optional stopping identity E[X_tau] = E[X_0] holds for EVERY almost surely finite stopping time tau, with no boundedness assumption on tau or on the martingale - this is a genuinely stronger conclusion than the standard three sufficient conditions (bounded tau, bounded martingale, or E[tau] finite with bounded increments). An L^1-bounded martingale need not be UI, and then only the almost sure half of (ii) survives. For p > 1, an L^p-bounded martingale is automatically UI by de la Vallee Poussin and converges in L^p as well; p = 1 is the exceptional case. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Theorems 13.3 and 14.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each f_n Riemann integrable on the compact interval [a,b]","uniform bound |f_n| <= M","pointwise convergence to f, AND f Riemann integrable - an independent hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752811+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_f36289c5312e1ca03cfca5ba87601f4ac8063f5554a56039a9f33e45b9a5702a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f_n : [a,b] -> R be Riemann integrable, uniformly bounded (|f_n| <= M for all n), and suppose f_n -> f pointwise on [a,b] where f is ALSO Riemann integrable. Then integral_a^b f_n -> integral_a^b f. The Riemann integrability of the limit must be ASSUMED and does not follow: enumerate the rationals of [0,1] as q_1, q_2, ... and let f_n be the indicator of {q_1, ..., q_n}. Each f_n is Riemann integrable with integral 0, the family is bounded by 1, and f_n increases pointwise to the indicator of the rationals, which is not Riemann integrable. This is the essential defect that the Lebesgue integral repairs: the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem needs only measurability of the limit, which is automatic for a pointwise limit of measurable functions. Historically Arzela proved this in 1885 by a direct and rather delicate covering argument, before the Lebesgue theory existed. [Arzela (1885); see e.g. Luxemburg, 'Arzela's dominated convergence theorem for the Riemann integral', Amer. Math. Monthly 78 (1971)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:26:40.361341+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f37bff03ece2c067d6056469a0ba4bb794ee80373ec4455c04f963ec5c1de767","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 49 (Trunk paths and vertices) of arXiv:2511.09517, 'From Cannings model to Brownian motion conditioned on local time profile'] Under $\q^m_n$, we have 
\[
X_j = m, \quad \text{for all } \bar{h} \le j \le \bar{h} + \lfloor c_0 n \rfloor.
\]
In other words, for each $j$ between $\bar{h}$ and $\bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n\rfloor$, there are exactly $m$ vertices in $\cX_j$. These vertices belong to $m$ distinct ancestral lineages that remain separate at height $\bar{h}$. 
Let $\mathsf{T}_1,\ldots,\mathsf{T}_m$ be the $m$ coalescent subtrees at height $\bar{h}$.  
For $\bar{h}\le j \le \bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n \rfloor$ and $1\le i\le m$, denote by 
\(z^j_i \in V(\mathsf{T}_i)\)
the unique vertex of $\mathsf{T}_i$ at height $j$. 
The sequence
\[
Z_i := \big(z^{\bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n \rfloor}_i, z^{\bar{h}+\lfloor c_0 n \rfloor-1}_i, \ldots, z^{\bar{h}}_i\big)
\]
is called the trunk path of $\mathsf{T}_i$, and its elements are referred to as the trunk vertices of $\mathsf{T}_i$.  
The remaining $q_n(j)-m$ non-trunk vertices at height $j$ are denoted by $y^j_1, \ldots, y^j_{q_n(j)-m}$, where the subscripts are assigned arbitrary.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.667215+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_f3d0f4a43e1234f642677f9825b3630dc54cd55f6fb84c3189154d5d54f82428","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn eq:Ae-def of arXiv:2609.00110, 'Phase Transition and Fluctuation Results for First-Passage Percolation on Spread-Out Cycle'] Let $e=\{u,v\}$ be a bridge, where $u$ has label $1$ and $v$ has label $2$. 
Its original activation time and the lower bound recorded at activation are
\begin{align*}
 \gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}
 &:=
 \max\{\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u),\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\},\\
 L_e^{\mathrm{act}}
 &:=
 \big(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}-\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}-\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align*}
The corresponding residual in the cumulative-hazard scale is
\begin{align*}
 R_e
 := H(\go_e)-H(L_e^{\mathrm{act}}) 
 = \go_e^\theta-(L_e^{\mathrm{act}})^\theta.
\end{align*}

For $q\geqslant\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}$, define the collision threshold
\begin{align*}
 L_e(q)
 :=
 \big(q-\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(q-\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align*}
In particular, $L_e(\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}})=L_e^{\mathrm{act}}$.

For $s\geqslant\mathfrak{a}_\ell\gt_e^{\mathrm{act}}$, define the rescaled bridge age by
\begin{align}
 A_e(s)
 :=
 \big(s-\mathfrak{a}_\ell\widehat\mathsf{T}_1(u)\big)
 +
 \big(s-\mathfrak{a}_\ell\widehat\mathsf{T}_2(v)\big).
\end{align}
Then $ L_e(s/\mathfrak{a}_\ell)=\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell}$.

The cumulative bridge hazard at rescaled time $s$ is
\begin{align}
 \gL_s
 &:= \sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_s}
 \left[ H\left(\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell}\right) - H(L_e^{\mathrm{act}}) \right]
 =\sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_s}\left[\left(\frac{A_e(s)}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell }\right)^\theta
 -(L_e^{\mathrm{act}})^\theta\right]
 \notag\\
 &=\int_0^s \frac{2\theta}{\mathfrak{a}_\ell ^\theta}
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal{B}_q} A_e(q)^{\theta-1}\,\mathrm d q.
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149599+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_f3f681977eb9ae940809b4e58a616eac3c6360d8024519e4cff1f440e2681399","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: an interior ball touching the boundary at the point x0 in question (and, for the strong maximum principle, the fact that such a ball can always be produced inside the open set where the solution is strictly below its maximum). Without it the conclusion 'the inward derivative at a boundary minimum is strictly positive' is false. Counterexample at a convex corner: in the plane let Omega be the sector {0 < theta < beta, 0 < r < 1} with 0 < beta < pi and u(r, theta) = r^{pi/beta} sin(pi theta/beta). Then u is harmonic in Omega, continuous on the closure, u > 0 inside and u = 0 on both straight edges, so 0 is a strict boundary minimum of u; but pi/beta > 1, so for every direction e pointing into Omega the difference quotient (u(te) - u(0))/t = O(t^{pi/beta - 1}) tends to 0: there is no Hopf gain at the vertex. No interior ball touches the vertex, exactly as the hypothesis requires. How far the hypothesis can be relaxed: the interior sphere condition may be replaced by an interior C^{1,Dini} (or interior paraboloid/cone-with-Dini) condition, but not by mere C^1 regularity of the boundary; there are C^1 domains where a positive harmonic function vanishing on the boundary has vanishing gradient at a boundary point - for instance the image of the upper half-plane near 0 under the conformal map z -> z log(1/z), whose boundary is C^1 but not Dini smooth at 0, and for which the inverse map has derivative tending to 0. Practical rule for an auditor: a proof that invokes Hopf's lemma (to get strict inequality, strict monotonicity, a sign of the normal derivative, simplicity of the first eigenvalue, or the strong maximum principle at the boundary) must say why the domain has the interior ball property at the relevant point; convex corners and cusps of the domain are where this silently breaks.","status":"unverified"}
